reading: As the sun's rays fall into water seen in a pot, when will I keenly know the form I have taken?
nuance: The one sun reflected in many pots is the Vedanta figure for the one self in many bodies. கொண்ட சொரூபம் may be the poet's own true form or the reflected one he has taken on; the verse asks to know which.

reading: When one wears the gold one puts on, does the gold carry the body? When will I see this in the thought that sees?
nuance: The rhetorical question seems to say that the body bears the ornament and not the reverse, so the body is the bearer and the ornament a weight; what the poet is to see in his thought is not stated, and the point may instead be that the gold is not changed by being worn.

reading: Like verdigris on copper, the three malas that have swallowed Siva and stand seething: when will I separate them off?
nuance: The three malas (anava, karma, maya) are named as மும்மலம். Verdigris is the metal's own corrosion, not a coating from outside, which fits the Siddhanta view that the malas are with the soul from the start.

reading: What stands in my soul as breath stands in the body: when will I, sinner, know it and hold my mind to it?
nuance: ஆவியும் காயமும்போல் gives the Lord's relation to the soul as the breath's to the body, inside and unseen; பாவி is the poet's name for himself.

reading: The joy that a mute who dreamed cannot tell: when will the day come for us to know it?
nuance: The mute's dream is a stock figure for an experience that cannot be reported; the poet asks for the experience, not the report.

reading: For those who never fail the feet of the undying Siva, when will it be that the body that does not go departs and goes?
nuance: போகா உடல் is the crux: a body that does not perish (the siddha's), or a body that will not let go. The line may ask when the devotee leaves the body for good, or when the imperishable body is itself left behind.

reading: Leaving fixed meditation, letting thought and knowing slip away, when will I stand mingled in the open space?
nuance: நிட்டை, the fixity of meditation, is itself to be left; the state asked for is past the practice, as in 151. வெட்டவெளி, the bare open space, is the Siddhars' name for the goal.

reading: The bare void that grew in the open space: when will I see it with resolve and become clear?
nuance: The void (பாழ்) is placed inside the open space (வெட்டவெளி) as something that arose there, and seeing it is to be done திட்டமுடன், deliberately; the void is a thing to be seen, not a lack.

tamil: எங்கும் பரவடிவாய் என் வடிவு நின் வடிவாய்க்
reading: Everywhere as the supreme form, my form as your form, when will I see you without night or day?
What I ate, and the pleasure I found joined with women: when will I see even these as you?
nuance: Food and sex are not renounced here but reread as the Lord; the verb is past tense (உண்டதுவும், கண்டதுவும்), so the pleasures may be past ones now to be understood, rather than a licence.

reading: What was heard as the hum, what stood within me, and what was said as Om: when will I reach and know them?
nuance: ஈம் is the inner hum (the nada heard in yoga), and ஓம் the uttered syllable; between them is what stands within. The verse asks whether the three are one thing.

tamil: சத்தம் பிறந்த இடம் தன் மயமாய் நின்ற இடம்
reading: The place where sound was born, the place where it stood as its own nature, the place where the mind was born: when will I discern and know them?
The one thing that strikes, standing as going and coming, as outside and inside: when will I meet it?
nuance: போக்கு வரவு is the out-and-in of the breath on a yogic reading, and the coming and going of births on a plain one. தாக்கும், strikes, suits the breath that beats in the body; the verse names neither.

tamil: நான் எனவும் நீ எனவும் நாம் இரண்டு மற்றொன்றும்
reading: 'I' and 'you', 'we two', and the other one: when will it come right in my thought that all of these are you?
nuance: நாம் இரண்டு மற்றொன்றும், we two and a further one, makes three, which tradition matches to the Siddhanta triad; the verse resolves them into the one 'you', an advaitic move inside a work that elsewhere (153) keeps them apart.

reading: Knowing awareness by awareness, so that awareness does not stand parted within awareness: when will I hold it?
nuance: அறிவு occurs five times. The verse asks for knowing in which knower and known are not two, the state 158 approached from the side of forgetting speech.

tamil: நீடும் புவனம் எல்லாம் நிறைந்துசிந் தூரம் அதாய்
reading: The holy dance that fills all the extended worlds and is red as vermilion: when will I know it?
nuance: சிந்தூரம் gives the dance a colour, red, the colour of the dancing Lord and of the dawn light in 171; the dance is cosmic here, not in the hall.

reading: The dance called thithi and the sounds of the holy anklets: when will I hear them with devotion and bow?
nuance: தித்தி is a dance syllable (the drum-sound to which the dance is set). The dance of 196 is now heard rather than known, and the response is bhakti.

reading: In the supreme space one reaches, like the space in the eye, when will I lie down and attain?
nuance: நயனத்திடை வெளி is the clear space within the eye, or the space between the eyes; tradition takes the second as the brow centre where the gaze is held. சயனித்து, lying down, is the yogi's rest in that space.

reading: In the thousand-pillared hall in the midst of the waterfall mountain, when will I see the holy play and have sight of it?
nuance: Plainly a shrine: a thousand-pillared hall on a hill with a waterfall, where the Lord's sports (திருவிளையாடல்) are seen. In cipher the thousand pillars are the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown and the waterfall the nectar that flows there. Both readings stand.

tamil: மீனை மிக உண்டு நக்கி விக்கி நின்ற கொக்கதுபோல்
reading: Like a heron that ate too much fish and stands licking and hiccupping, when will I eat honey to surfeit and stand sated?
nuance: A comic self-portrait: the poet asks to be glutted on the honey of bliss as the heron is on fish. தெவிட்டி, cloyed, is a strong word for the fullness asked.

title: மெய்ஞ்ஞானப் புலம்பல்
theme: The lament turns inward to the dismantling of the self: before the body is thrown away, to learn the impossible art of milking the stone cow; to be as one dead, without breath, speech, memory or forgetting; to lose my will, the world's hold and even self-command and rest on grace; to forget myself, the place, karma and even the Lord and be alone; to bar the head-door and sleep within. Similes of pervasion (oil in sesame, juice in cane, the swan parting milk from water, the lotus in the sky) frame the void and the supreme space in which maya is to die, and the chapter ends in bliss that staggers like toddy, and in the eye of wisdom that sees all as him and still takes refuge.
structure_note: No fixed order; the couplets alternate similes (206 to 208, 212, 213, 218, 221) with direct askings. 214 to 217 form a run on losing will and forgetting; 222 is a unit from the second edition, placed between 221 and 223. Every couplet ends on the refrain எக்காலம்.
source_issues: Unit 222 (id siddhar:meynjanap-pulambal:0155-192) is from a second edition: unnumbered in the main edition, without the refrain's question mark, interleaved between 221 and 223.
218 first line: இன்பமுறும் gives the anril joy on parting, against the lore that it dies on parting; the text looks faulty. தூல் in the second line is read as நூல்.
223 prints ஞானவிழியா ல்அறிந்து with a space inside the word.

tamil: கல் ஆவின் பால்கறப்பக் கற்பது இனி எக்காலம்?
reading: Before this evil body is thrown away, when will I learn to milk the stone cow's milk?
nuance: Milk from a stone cow is a stock figure of the impossible, yet here it is a skill (கற்பது) to be learned in this life. Tradition reads it as drawing the yogic nectar from the hard body or from the skull; plainly it is doing the impossible before death. பொல்லாத காயம் is the poet's standing contempt for the body.

reading: Sadasiva who shines within the bare open space: when will I seek him so that he comes near and shows me kindness?
nuance: சதாசிவம் is the Siddhanta name for the Lord at the level where he is reached by souls; he is placed in the வெட்டவெளி of 187 and 188. கிருபை செய்வது has the Lord as its agent.

reading: Setting my mind unmoving in the great awareness, when will I stand rooted every day in the one awareness?
nuance: பேரறிவு and ஓரறிவு, the great awareness and the one awareness, are the same thing named from two sides: its size and its singleness.

reading: The way that stood within my soul, as if non-dual, to give release: when will I know it?
nuance: அத்துவிதம் போலும் is hedged: போலும் is 'like', so the way is only advaita-like, or an assertive particle, so it is advaita indeed. The poet names the doctrine without quite claiming it.

reading: Not perishing while I remain in the bond I stand in, when will I spread into the form in which you stand?
nuance: The bond (பாசம்) is the poet's present place, and the Lord's form (கோலம்) the place to be reached; the fear is of dying still in the bond.

reading: As with sesame, sugarcane, the fine flower and the body, standing inside and outside, when will I reach and know it?
nuance: Four containers of something hidden in them: oil, juice, scent, and the self in the body. The Lord is said to stand both within these and outside them; 159 used the sesame alone.

reading: As the swan parts the water off and drinks the nectar, when will I part myself off and sweetly see you?
nuance: The swan that separates milk from water is the stock figure of discrimination. என்னை வகுத்து, dividing myself, is the seeker's own sorting of what in him is water and what is nectar.

reading: Like a lotus that flowered on water in the sky and rose open, when will I hold my mind steady and have sight of you?
nuance: அந்தரத்தில் நீர்பூத்து, water flowering in space, is a strange image for an ordinary lotus; tradition takes the lotus in the inner sky as the lotus at the crown, opened by meditation. Plainly it is any lotus rising clear of the water.

reading: Without birth and death, without speech and breath, without forgetting and remembering, when will I be as one dead?
nuance: மாண்டிருப்பது, to be dead, is asked for as a state while alive: the three pairs removed are the marks of ordinary life. The stopped breath (மூச்சும் அற்று) is the yogic sign of the state.

reading: Shutting the enduring supreme space inside the space of the mind, when will I raise awareness within me as one thought?
nuance: The large is enclosed in the small: the supreme space (பரவெளி) is held within the mind-space (மனவெளி), and from it a single thought is to rise. This single thought is the exception to the thoughtlessness asked elsewhere (166, 219).

tamil: ஆசை கொண்ட மாதர் அடைகனவு நீக்கி உன்மேல்
reading: Putting away the dream of desire I have for women, when will I take up the sound of you and subside?
nuance: Desire for women is a dream (கனவு) to be ended; what replaces it is sound (ஓசை), the Lord heard rather than seen, as in 191 and 197.

reading: As I wandered carrying my own life, when will I carry your life and subside here?
nuance: To live by the Lord's life instead of one's own: the exchange is of the animating principle, not of conduct. இங்கு, here, keeps the goal in this world.

reading: This firm body, like a branch planted in mud: when will I see it as a puppet whirling in the wind?
nuance: சூத்திரம் is the string, hence the puppet worked by it; காற்று is the wind and also the breath, so the body is a puppet worked by the breath on a yogic reading. The planted branch looks rooted but is cut wood.

tamil: தன்வசமும் கெட்டு அருளைச் சார்ந்து இருப்பது எக்காலம்?
reading: My will lost, the hold that was here lost, and self-command lost, when will I rest upon grace?
nuance: Three வசம்: என் வசம் (my control), இங்கிருந்த வசம் (the hold that was here, the world's or the body's), தன்வசம் (one's own self-possession). The third is the hardest to place; it may mean the self's command of itself, so that even surrender is not to be one's own act.

reading: Forgetting myself, forgetting the state of the place, forgetting karma, when will I gain the goal?
nuance: தலத்து நிலை is the state of the place, the world one stands in, or in cipher the bodily centres (தலம்). கதி is the good end, release.

tamil: என்னை என்னிலே மறந்தே இருந்த பதியும் மறந்து
தன்னையும் தானே மறந்து தனித்து இருப்பது எக்காலம்?
reading: Forgetting me within myself, forgetting even the Lord who was there, forgetting myself by myself, when will I be alone?
nuance: Even the Lord (பதி) is to be forgotten, which puts the state past worship and past 161's plea that he never leave. தனித்து இருப்பது is the solitary state, the kaivalya of yoga.

reading: Forgetting myself by myself, barring the head-door, when will I sleep within, thinking of you?
nuance: தலைவாசல் is plainly the front door, which one bolts before sleep; in cipher it is the door at the head, the crown or the gates of the senses, barred so that the breath and mind do not go out. The sleep is the inward rest of 158, not slumber.

tamil: துணை பிரிந்தபோது அருள் தூல்தொடர்ந்து கொள்வது எக்காலம்?
reading: Like the anril bird, which has its joy only in not being parted from its mate, when my companion is parted from me, when will I take hold of the thread of grace and follow it?
nuance: The anril is the bird of lore that dies when parted from its mate, so இன்பமுறும் (finds joy) in the first line is surprising and the text may be faulty. துணை, the companion, may be the body, a human partner or the guru. தூல் is read as நூல், thread.

reading: With no dance at all and not the least movement to be seen, when will I seek the sky-thing that has no seeking?
nuance: தேட்டம் is both searching and the thing sought or desired; the verse asks to seek, in stillness, what is beyond seeking and desire, and keeps the paradox.

reading: If by former deeds my knowledge fails to ripen and then hides away, when will I seek the Mother and drink nectar?
nuance: The syntax is loose: the conditional about unripe knowledge seems to be the obstacle, and the Mother's nectar the cure. அன்னை is Shakti, and the nectar is the yogic amrita or simply the mother's milk the child seeks.

reading: By the bliss that gives delight as toddy does to the drinker, when will I be pushed about, stand dancing and be brought to a halt?
nuance: Drunkenness is used without disapproval as the figure for bliss; தடைப்படுவது, being stopped, is the end of the stagger, when the drunk can go no further.

reading: The egoism that says 'I' and the tattvas destroyed and gone, when will the very speech of 'I' come to rest?
nuance: A unit from the second edition. ஆணவம் is the primal mala of Siddhanta, here named with its characteristic word 'I'. தங்கிநிற்பது can mean to stay or to be stilled; the sense wants the 'I'-talk to cease, but the verb can be read the other way.

tamil: தான் அவனாய் நின்று சரண் அடைவது எக்காலம்?
reading: Knowing with the eye of wisdom that all I see is 'I am he', standing as he, when will I take refuge?
nuance: நான் அவனாய் is the 'I am he' of Vedanta, yet the line ends in சரண் அடைதல், taking refuge, which needs two. The poet holds identity and surrender in one breath.

reading: Within the endless Supreme, seeing bliss, when will I sit settled?
Gazing intently into the space that has come near, there in the sky, when will maya die out and leave nothing?
nuance: The gazing (உற்றுப் பார்த்து) is the practice and maya's death the result; மற்றமற, without remainder, insists nothing of it is left.

title: மெய்ஞ்ஞானப் புலம்பல்
theme: The close of the lament: a vision of the Lord's face with its lotus, eyes of compassion and earrings; the passage beyond the thirty-six tattvas into the bare space where the dark mind dies; the ship of love launched on the sea of knowledge; the three questions, who am I, who are you, who is the Supreme, whose answer ends tapas; the Lord who stands for each as each conceives him; the light seen straight at the forehead; and a closing apology, I do not know even myself, with a plea for the company of the good and a last praise of the five-handed god's feet.
structure_note: Eleven couplets, the last short chapter of the work. 226 to 232 are the final askings; 233 is the poet's apology to the ancients, 234 (a unit from the second edition) asks for good company, 235 sums up the three removals (maya, karma, body), and 236 ends with Ganesha, as Sivavakkiyar's work begins. The refrain எக்காலம் holds to the end.
source_issues: Unit 234 (id siddhar:meynjanap-pulambal:0155-201) is from a second edition: unnumbered in the main edition, without the refrain's question mark, interleaved between 233 and 235.

reading: The opened-petalled lotus, the two eyes of compassion and the studded earrings: when will they appear to me?
nuance: A face, not a doctrine: the lotus may be the face itself or the seat, and the earrings are the Lord's or the guru's; the verse asks for a sight, which the rest of the work seldom does.

tamil: மை இருளில் நின்ற மனம் மாள்வது இனி எக்காலம்?
reading: Leaving behind the five sixes and the six, in the bare open space, when will the mind that stood in pitch darkness die?
nuance: ஐயாறும் ஆறும் is thirty and six, the thirty-six tattvas, as tradition counts them. The mind is itself among the tattvas, so it dies when they are left; மை இருள், the kohl-black darkness, is the primal mala in Siddhanta reading.

reading: Launching the ship of love on the sea of knowledge that grace shows, when will I sink in the sea of compassion it kindles?
nuance: The sea is doubled: knowledge is the sea sailed and compassion the sea drowned in. The ship is love, so love is the means and sinking the end; the poet wants to go under, not to cross.

tamil: நான் யாரோ நீ யாரோ நன்றாம் பரமான
reading: Who am I, who are you, who is the good Supreme himself: when will I realise this and bring tapas to its end?
nuance: Three 'who's, the self, the addressed Lord and the Supreme beyond both, which may mirror the Siddhanta three or the Vedanta distinction of the Lord from Brahman. Tapas ends with the answer, so the answer is the whole point of tapas.

reading: However each person saw you and in whatever way they thought of you, you stood for each of them in that very way: when will I know this?
nuance: The Lord takes the form each conceiver gives him; the verse grounds the diversity of sects in one Lord without ranking them.

reading: The bliss that gives light when one looks and looks: when will I see it straight at the forehead and be fixed there?
nuance: நெற்றிக்கு நேர் is plainly 'level with the forehead', before the eyes; tradition takes it as the brow centre, the place in the body where the inner light is seen. The repeated looking (உற்றுற்றுப் பார்க்க) is the practice of 225.

reading: As the sun hides the shining stars, when will I see your sight, free of any stain?
nuance: The stars are not put out but outshone; the Lord's appearing hides all else by its light, and களங்கமற may qualify the sight or the seer.

tamil: என்னையே நான் அறியேன் இந்த வண்ணம் சொன்ன தெல்லாம்
reading: I do not know even myself; all that I have said in this way, when will I lay before the ancients in homage, so that they accept it?
nuance: The poet's apology for the whole lament: the one who has asked two hundred times for knowledge admits he does not know himself. முன்னையோர், those who went before, are the earlier siddhas or the learned.

reading: As one removes the poisonous snake and takes the good gem, when will I take as companions the good who have ended the quarrel of words?
nuance: A unit from the second edition. The gem is the one said to be in the cobra's hood, taken only when the snake is dealt with. சொற்சரவை echoes நச்சரவை and may be a pun, word-snake, as well as word-quarrel; the good are those who have put disputation away.

reading: Removing maya, laying waste the deeds to come, making the body separate, when will I see you?
nuance: வருவினை is the karma still to come, not the stored or the ripening kind; the three removals (maya, karma, body) answer to the three malas, with the body standing for the primal one.

reading: Praising the paired feet of the five-handed one, setting them in my heart, when will I gain firmness?
nuance: ஐஞ்சு கரத்தான், the five-handed, is Ganesha (four hands and the trunk). The work ends where Tamil works usually begin, with the elephant-faced god, and with the plainest devotion after so much that passes beyond it.

title: திருவேகம்பமாலை
theme: The first half of Pattinathar's Thiruvekambamalai, twenty-five venbas each closing on the address கச்சியேகம்பனே. The poet turns on everything a householder holds, wife, children, kin, town, wealth, the body itself, and shows each as impermanent, as maya, or as the pit of the woman's body into which he fell; against them stand the Lord's feet, the five letters, the devotees, and the rare inward renouncer. Half the stanzas are confession or petition, half are rebukes of the ungiving and the lustful, and the Lord is asked why he made such people at all.
structure_note: No order is imposed; the stanzas alternate between self-reproach (242, 245, 247, 248, 250, 259), satire of others (252, 254, 255, 257, 260, 261) and short arguments (237, 240, 251, 253, 256). 245 and 264 (next chapter) share the whole closing line எல்லாப் பிழையும் பொறுத்தருள்வாய்; 249 and 277 run the same catalogue of town, kin, name, women, children, wealth. 255 and 261 use the same form, a list of what the wicked do not do, ending இருந்தென்ன, போயென்ன.
source_issues: 248 line 3 ககமென்று is corrupt; the sense requires அகமென்று.
257 line 2 கம்பன்னராய்க் cannot be construed with confidence.
The ids are the work's own numbering (thiruvekambamalai:1 to 25); the unit printed as 279 in the next chapter is unnumbered (u1) and is a different metre.

reading: Greater by crores than the man who does dharma is the man who has left his house; greater by a hundred crores than him is the man whose renunciation is in the heart; and of the one who forgot all, stayed in knowledge, and died free of both kinds of impression, the poet cannot tell the greatness.
nuance: The ladder has four rungs and the top one is inward and invisible: உள்ளத்துறவு, renunciation in the heart, outranks leaving the house, and the knower who has died free of இருவாதனை, the impressions of good and bad deeds, outranks even that. மறந்தான் அறக்காற்று is read as 'forgot completely'; the object forgotten is not named, and tradition supplies the world or the self.

reading: The wife and children who hug and embrace, when Time the carpenter cuts the body down like a tree, beat their breasts and wail; but once they have reached the edge of the cremation ground, will they step one step beyond it?
nuance: காலத்தச்சன், Time as carpenter, fells the body as a tree; the embrace of the first line and the single step of the last measure how far love goes. The question expects the answer no.

reading: The wife who, while the husband who holds her hand is asleep, lifts his hand, sets it down on the far side without stirring him, goes to the next compound, spends her sleep with another and comes back to sleep beside him: how, the poet asks, can he trust her?
nuance: The stanza is a scene, not an argument, and the poet's distrust of women elsewhere in the work (247, 250, 259, 260) rests on it. ஒப்புடன் (fittingly, or with a partner) and துயில் நீத்து (giving up sleep) leave the adultery implied rather than stated; tradition connects the stanza with the biography of Pattinathar's renunciation.

reading: A string puppet fitted with a good cord: if the cord fails, will it dance and tire itself? In the same way I move only by you, and if I were parted from you, is there anything I could do by myself?
nuance: The puppet confesses no agency apart from the Lord, which 290 in the Thiruthillai makes a doctrine: one in the hall makes all eat, sleep and dance on the rope of the two deeds. Here it is also a plea, since the poet is asking not to be parted.

reading: Apart from the company of the good, love of your worship and knowledge, is there any other standing? House, wealth, wife, kin, sons, livelihood and the fine body: all of it is an outer bewilderment.
nuance: வெளிமயக்கு, the bewilderment outside, sets what is within (company, love, knowledge) against what is outside; the same word returns at 265 for the painted women, and 253 ends on விழிமயக்கு, the eye's bewilderment.

reading: Wicked, not on the path, not a conqueror of the five senses, unlearned, one who does not go to the true devotees, does not speak the truth, has no love for your holy feet: why, the poet asks, was such a one as he born on earth?
nuance: Seven negatives in -ஆதவன் ending in a question about his own birth; the list is the poet's standard of a good life stated in the negative, with the devotees (மெய்யடியவர்) placed beside learning and truth.

reading: Nothing was brought at birth and nothing is carried away at death; what shall the poet say of the slaves who, not knowing that the wealth they mark as theirs in between was given by Siva and is to be given on, die holding it?
nuance: The argument makes wealth a loan between two empty-handed moments: since Siva gave it, giving it on is the only right use. குலாமர் (slaves) is the poet's word for those bound to possessions, as in Sivavakkiyar's use of the same word for those bound to outward authority.

reading: The thought of food is the one thought; when that is settled, the thought just named is a thought that never ends; the thought of fine-plumed women is the thought that returns many times: what thought, the poet asks the Lord, have you set in this sinful heart?
nuance: விசாரம் is repeated eight times and its sense shifts between care, worry and inquiry. The second line, சொன்ன விசாரம் தொலையா விசாரம், is the crux: 'the thought mentioned' may be the thought of food that goes on after eating, or may point forward to the thought of women; a few editors read the whole as a lament that the mind's cares are only food and women. The last line asks what the Lord intends by this, and may also mean 'what thought of yourself have you set in it?'

tamil: சொல்லாப் பிழையுந், துதியாப் பிழையுந், தொழாப் பிழையும்
reading: The fault of not learning, of not reflecting, of not standing melted and weeping, of not meditating, of not saying your five letters, of not praising, of not worshipping: forgive every fault, the poet asks.
nuance: All seven faults are omissions in the inner and outer worship of the Lord; 264 in the next chapter repeats the closing line for faults of commission in speech, thought, deed and hearing.

reading: Leaving the deceitful friends and the women who are the undying mala, running outside, going with the mother who is true grace, then joining the father, and then forgetting the mother: that, he said, is nishtai.
nuance: An allegory of the path in family terms. Tradition takes the mother as grace or Shakti and the father as Siva, so that grace leads the soul to Siva and is then itself left behind; தாயை மறந்து, forgetting the mother, is the step that distinguishes the stanza. மாயா மலம் எனும் மாதர், women who are the mala that does not die, applies the Siddhanta term to women rather than to anava. என்றான், 'he said', attributes the teaching to another, perhaps the guru, and the stanza does not say who.

reading: Having gone into infatuation with women whose eyes are striped spears, the poet laments and does not say the five letters; and for whom is this lone body prey: the fox, the vulture and kite, the fierce dog, or the fire?
nuance: The body that lust cherished is auctioned among scavengers and the pyre; the question இரை எதற்கோ, prey for which, is left open as the only certainty. எழுத்தஞ்சும் சொலேன் makes the failure to recite the five letters the specific loss.

reading: The maya that comes before the poet's eyes showing itself as ear, nose and eye and calling itself a woman: this evil mind, which does not take it for the messenger Death sent but seeks it as its own home, how shall he describe?
nuance: The woman is dissolved into named parts and then into maya, and then into Yama's envoy: desire for her is the summons to death. ககமென்று in line 3 is corrupt and is read as அகமென்று, 'as home' or 'as self'; the sense of the stanza does not change with either.

reading: The town is not lasting, kin are not lasting, the name one has won is not lasting, nor women, nor children, nor glory, nor wealth, nor anyone in the country; your feet are what lasts.
nuance: சதம் (from Sanskrit sat, the real or permanent) is denied seven times and affirmed once. 277 runs the same list again with இருந்தென்ன, 'what if there is', so that the second stanza asks the use of what the first calls impermanent.

reading: Raging karma took the form of a woman, gathered and rounded into the breasts men speak of and into flesh, and by its cruelty pushed the poet into the great pit from which filth and blood tear and pour; he has not seen the bank by which to climb out.
nuance: The woman is not a person but வினை, deed, given a body; the பெருங்குழி is the vulva named by what flows from it, and ஏறும் கரை, the bank to climb, returns as the petition of 270. The stanza is as hostile to the female body as anything in the corpus and should be read as the poet's own state, not as doctrine.

reading: As men of means are known by their acts, warriors on the battlefield and the clear-minded by their faces, so those who have grace are to be recognised by their austerity, their nature, their grace and love, and even by their obscure words.
nuance: இருளுறு சொல், words wrapped in darkness, is the mark the stanza ends on: the speech of the graced is dark to others, a near description of the Siddhars' own cipher. The Kural's மறைமொழி (28) makes the same point for the great.

reading: Swelling their bellies like a cotton bale, they feed their own bellows with the six tastes, but will not take the trouble to feed those who have renounced; why, the poet asks, has the Lord kept such people on this wide earth?
nuance: துருத்தி, the bellows, is the belly as a leather bag, an image 263 applies to the whole body. The complaint is the renouncer's: he lives on what householders give, and the stanza is less about greed than about the failure of that obligation.

reading: As the sun that drives off the wicked dark is itself darkness to the owl's bird-eye, so what is plain in the hearts of the knowing is, for those who cannot know, only bewilderment; all is a bewilderment of the eye.
nuance: The owl is blind in light, so the light is not at fault; knowledge is present and the unknowing cannot see it. The last line, எல்லாம் விழிமயக்கே, can be the poet's summary (the whole world is an optical confusion) or the owl's view of the sun; both readings stand.

reading: They go to disputes and fights, come back and argue lawsuits, lend a hand to evil, daily find some gift to give to a woman and lose themselves in her, until their fate runs out: for what, the poet asks, were they born?
nuance: விதி மாளுமட்டும், until the allotted fate ends, sets a term on the life described, and the question ஏதுக்கு பிறந்தார் treats birth as something that should have a purpose.

reading: They lie without ceasing, revile the good, abuse the mother who bore them, commit a thousand treacheries, do not study the sastras, do no kindness to others and give nothing to those who come to them: what does it matter whether such people live or die?
nuance: இருந்தென்ன போயென்ன, what if they stay, what if they go, is the refrain of this stanza, 261 and (as இருந்தென்? இறந்தென்?) 277: the wicked and the useless are already as good as dead.

reading: Though water is white, it takes on without fail the nature of whatever ground it lies in and so comes to have many differing qualities; in the same way, says the stanza, I stand in souls unripe and ripe, my father the Lord.
nuance: The speaker of the last line is unclear. Read with எந்தைபிரான் as a vocative, the poet says he too stands in varying states as water does; read as the Lord's own word (இப்படியே நிற்பன்), the Lord stands in every soul coloured by its ripeness (பக்குவம்), the Siddhanta term for a soul's readiness for grace. The second reading is tradition's and fits the ripeness vocabulary better.

reading: A dog, when born, hunts well and gives pleasure; but why, the poet asks, did the Lord create men who, born from a mother's womb, are like a tree without fruit, a dried-up tank and a cow that gives no milk, men who do not give?
nuance: கம்பன்னராய்க் in line 2 is obscure; it may be a corrupt form or a jibe at Kamban as a byword for the self-important. The three similes are of things valued only for what they yield, and the dog, which at least hunts, is placed above the ungiving man.

reading: Do not let my love be like tamarind dissolved in a river; cherish it and hold it in your holy mind, you who burned the three cities, whose foot subdued Death, who hold the mountain as bow and the bull as banner.
nuance: ஆற்றில் கரைத்த புளி, tamarind dissolved in a river, is a stock figure for what is wasted without trace; the plea is that love offered to the Lord be kept, as the deeds named in the second half were kept.

reading: A deceitful demon came in the form of a woman, caught the poet, frightened him with her eyes, bewildered him with her breasts, pushed him into the sore-pit at her hips and stole the substance of his understanding; not thinking, he forgot the Lord.
nuance: போதப்பொருள் பறித்தல், stealing the substance of awareness, is the specific loss the stanza charges, and மறந்தேன், I forgot you, is its result. The woman as பிசாசு follows 248's maya and Death's messenger.

reading: They say sweet words to fill the tongue, 'if I am parted from you I shall die', and eat together; and when a man's hand runs dry they say 'go, come back' and hit him on the back of the head: is it the written fate of those who give to such women?
nuance: கை வறளின், when the hand dries, is the end of money; the blow to the back of the head is the dismissal. தலைவிதி, the fate written on the head, puns on the head that is struck.

reading: They do not learn Siva's story, do not speak the truth to the good even in a dream, do not give food to the hungry, do not stand by what the guru said, do not think of dharma, and have no thought at all of the Lord's name: tell me, what if they live, what if they die?
nuance: The list pairs with 255; here the omissions are of devotion and dharma, with the guru's word and the Lord's name as the last two. கனவிலும், even in a dream, is the Kural's measure of a settled nature (819, 1054).

title: திருவேகம்பமாலை
theme: The second half of the Thiruvekambamalai (verses 26 to 42) and the unnumbered Thiruvekamba viruttam. The body is a leaking bag and a pot of rice; women are painted bewilderment and a pit of filth; the poet confesses killing, flesh-eating and forgetfulness and asks forgiveness, or asks only to finish his worship before he is killed. Beside the confessions run the rebukes: of flesh-eaters, of those who revile guru, linga and jangama yet want release, of the learned who blame Siva after the fact, of the ungiving and the lustful. The two closing units turn outward: the Lord bears blows from devotees because he has no parents, and the poet asks how many mothers, fathers and births he has had and how many remain.
structure_note: The order is not argued. 264 repeats the closing line of 245; 277 repeats the list of 249; 275 asks of the wicked what 257 asked of the ungiving, ஏன் படைத்தாய். 270 answers 250 with a petition. The last unit (279) is a viruttam of eight lines, not a venba, and closes on கச்சியேகம்ப நாதனே rather than the refrain.
source_issues: 263 line 2 is spaced பீற்றற் து ருத்தியைச் for பீற்றற் துருத்தியைச்.
267 line 3 காதங்கரணங்களும் is loose for கரணங்களும்; the metre may have required the extra syllable.
279 (thiruvekambamalai:u1) is unnumbered in the source and headed திருவேகம்பவிருத்தம்; it is a viruttam appended to the venba sequence and not part of the forty-two.

reading: Those who do not know the taste of heaven's nectar reckon the taste of a hard fruit to be nectar; so for those who have not a little of the clear knowledge that is honey-nectar, is not the taste of the base nectar good enough?
nuance: அமுதம் is said four times and graded: heavenly, the fruit's, the honey of knowledge, and the base (ஈனம்) nectar of worldly pleasure. The last line is irony; the stanza explains rather than condemns why the ignorant are content.

tamil: பீற்றற் து ருத்தியைச் சோறிடுந் தோற்பையைப் பேசரிய
காற்றிற் பொதிந்த நிலையற்ற பாண்டத்தைக் காதல் செய்தே
reading: The oozing body, the obscene shed, the torn bellows stuffed with flesh, the leather bag into which rice is put, the unspeakable, unstable pot filled with wind: the poet loved it, carried it about and wandered.
nuance: Five names for the body, each a container: a shed, a bellows, a bag, a pot. காற்றிற் பொதிந்த, packed with wind, names the breath as what the pot holds and what makes it unstable. The second and third agavals expand the catalogue to dozens of names.

reading: The fault that comes by speech, the flaw that comes by thought, the evil deed done, the sins of the glance, the harm of listening to what is not the book of merit: all these and every other fault, forgive.
nuance: Faults by speech, thought, deed, sight and hearing: the stanza is the counterpart of 245, which asked forgiveness for what was not done. புண்ணியநூல் அல்லாத கேள்வி counts hearing the wrong book as a sin.

reading: Women who grind turmeric without lumps into oil and polish their faces, who put on ornaments and the forehead dot and shine up their brass-leaf earrings, and in broad daylight cast an outward bewilderment: remove my desire for them, the poet asks.
nuance: The beauty is manufactured in detail, down to the cheap brass ear-leaf (பித்தளையோலை), and the phrase வெளிமயக்கு from 241 is applied to it; the petition is not that they be punished but that his இட்டம், his liking, be taken away.

reading: Born on earth with disease lodged in him, forgetting the great bliss, infatuated with small pleasure, flitting and reeling among base women, seeking gold and giving it to those women: did the Lord command the poet to die so?
nuance: பேரின்பம் and சிற்றின்பம், the great bliss and the small pleasure, are the Saiva pair; the stanza's charge is that the second has made him forget the first. The question இறந்திடவோ பணித்தாய் puts the responsibility back on the Lord, as 244 did.

reading: Without the elements, without the senses, without the five that they grasp, without difference and quality, without great desire, without before and after, without the inner instruments: in that vision of bliss the poet will stay, his faults cast off.
nuance: The negatives strip the tattvas in order: elements, organs, their objects, qualities, desire, time and the கரணங்கள் (mind, intellect, will, ego). காதங்கரணங்கள் is loose for கரணங்கள். What remains is called a காட்சி, a seeing, so the end is not emptiness but bliss seen.

reading: Good one, grant me one request: before you kill and throw away this wicked man without knowledge, let the usual worship, the japa, the recitation, the many good observances of the temple and the hymns all be finished, and then kill.
nuance: மனு is a petition. The stanza is wry: the poet accepts the killing and bargains only for time to complete the rites, and by listing the rites as what must be finished first he treats them as a debt owed rather than a means. கொல்லுகண்டாய் is an imperative to the Lord.

reading: For the sake of the inert pot of a body they seek prey, kill many lives, bite into carcass, sit proud, waste away, and wander eating what they have killed; when Death takes them by the hand and bites them on the left, what will they do?
nuance: சடக்கடம் is the body as a lifeless vessel; விடக்கு is flesh as carcass. மிகமெலிந்து (greatly thinned) and படங்கடித்து are hard to construe, and இடக்கடிக்கும் (Death bites on the left, or bites back) is read by sense as Yama returning the bite the eater gave. The argument is retributive: the biter is bitten.

reading: The stinking body, the bundle of rice for foxes, the pot the poet fills daily with rice and curry: grant, he asks, that it not fall into the pit from which women's filth and blood flow, but climb out.
nuance: The petition answers 250, where the poet said he could not see the bank to climb; here he asks for the climbing (ஏறும்படி). The body and the woman are both described by what flows into and out of them, rice into one, filth from the other.

reading: Like thieves who drug a palace, enter and rob it, and then go and petition the kings of the quarters, they revile Siva, revile guru, linga and jangama greatly, and still desire release: what shall the poet say of these great ascetics?
nuance: குரு லிங்க சங்கமம் is the Veerasaiva triad of guru, linga and the wandering devotee (jangama), named here as the three things not to revile. எக்குப் பெருந்தவர் is sarcastic. The simile makes reviling the Lord and asking him for release the same act as robbing a king and appealing to kings.

reading: Those who will not gladly give plenty of food to the guests who come, yet live in prosperity, and the sinners who do not daily think of praising the name of the one who shares his body with the woman of unsucked breasts: what, asks the poet, is their being on earth?
nuance: அருந்தா முலைப் பங்கர், the one who shares (the body) with her whose breasts have never been sucked, names the Lord by Uma as the virgin mother. The stanza sets feeding guests and saying the name side by side as the two duties of a householder.

reading: Having learned and known everything, they still do not realise that the Able One knows what is within us; their minds confused, they quarrel in words, grieve according to the fate that closes round them, and afterwards say 'all is Siva's doing'.
nuance: The last line can be the learned men's belated excuse, which the stanza mocks, or the poet's own conclusion, which the learned reach too late; the Tamil allows both. Read the first way the stanza is about blaming fate after one's own folly; read the second, it agrees with 290 and 294 that nothing is done apart from the Lord. எல்லாம் அறிந்து படித்தே is the recurring Siddhar target of book-learning.

reading: They think of gold and seek it hard, they think of the flower-like woman and melt for her; the wretches on this earth who do not think of you and do not worship you, why, the poet asks, have you kept them here for me to see?
nuance: நினைந்து three times: the stanza is about what thought is spent on. உலுத்தர் is a strong word, misers or wretches. என்னை இருந்து கண்டாய் may mean 'why have you made me see them' or 'what have you seen in them'; the first fits the series of ஏன் questions.

reading: Harsh-tongued idlers, the base, gluttons, lechers, utter fools who do cruel sin, who grow in this world like tall palmyras without knowing the way of the good: why, the poet asks, did the Lord make such troublesome people?
nuance: நெடும்பனை போல, like a tall palmyra, is growth without use, as the palm gives nothing to those at its foot; the question ஏன் வகுத்தாய் repeats 257's ஏன் படைத்தாய். இடும்பர், people who are இடும்பை, trouble, is the poet's coinage.

reading: The poet killed many lives, then killed and killed again and ate, and did harm besides; saying 'let that end', he stood in the Lord's presence, trusting that for that reason the Lord would bear the fault.
nuance: The confession is specific (killing and eating) and the ground of hope is only standing before the Lord (நின்சன்னிதிக்கே நின்றேன்); no penance is offered. Set beside 269, the poet counts himself among the flesh-eaters he threatened with Death's bite.

reading: What if there is a town, what if there are good people, people of name who help, the mother who bore one, the tender wife, glory, distinction, beauty, in this country: what of it, Lord?
nuance: The list of 249 returns with இருந்தென்ன, 'what if it is there', so that the question is no longer whether these last but whether they are of any use. வல்லாய் (able one) is the Lord as the only one who can answer.

reading: To be struck with a bow, kicked with a sandal, pelted with a stone by one in anger, beaten with a cane: is it not because the Dancer of Tillai, whose groves hum with bees, has no mother and father?
nuance: The four blows are the devotees' legends: Arjuna's bow, Kannappar's sandal, Sakkiyar's stones and the cane of the Pandya's overseer on the Lord who carried earth at Madurai. The joke is that the Lord submits as an orphan does, with no parents to object; underneath it is the doctrine that he is unborn (அன்னைபிதா இல்லாதவன்) and that love from his devotees is received in whatever form it takes.

reading: How many mothers and how many fathers, how many wives and how many children, how many births before: the fool did not know; and how many births are still to come? What is he to do, Lord of Ekambam at Kachi?
nuance: எத்தனை எத்தனை eleven times; the relations the earlier stanzas called impermanent are here multiplied across births so that no single mother or wife is one's own. The count forward (இன்னம் எத்தனை) is the only question with weight.

title: திருத்தில்லை
theme: Pattinathar's Thiruthillai, twenty venbas to the Lord of the hall at Chidambaram. The living are corpses who weep over the dead; kings burn to a fistful of ash; the wealth and theatres of rulers vanish when the Lord's mind turns. Against this the poet asks for a different wealth, the one that comes with not killing, not lying, not being angry and not being refused by the asker, names the Lord as the one who makes all eat, sleep, embrace and dance on the rope of deeds, and finds in remembering the feet and chanting the five letters the medicine against dying and the way out of birth. The Lord's own entourage of bull, serpent and ghouls, his begging in a skull and his dance seen only after aeons of tapas close the picture.
structure_note: 283, 284 and 285 share the refrain செல்வந் தருவாய், சிதம்பர தேசிகனே and are lists of abstentions in -ஆமல். 290 and 293 are catalogues of what the Lord makes happen (-விப்பான், -பான்). 289 alone is addressed to the goddess Sivakama Sundari; 288, 295 and 296 to the poet's own mind or heart. The rest address the Lord of the hall under different names (சங்கரன், அம்பலவாணர், சிதம்பர தேசிகன், ஆனந்தத் தாண்டவன்).
source_issues: 296 line 4 has a stray character, நீ£செபித்தாற், for நீ செபித்தாற்; and செவியாமல் in the same line cannot be construed as it stands (read as சலியாமல்).
287 line 1 காலையுபாதி and line 3 மாலையுபாதி are printed as single words; the stanza's ஆலமுகந்தரு ளம்பலவா is spaced across the word boundary.
297 lines 2 to 4 have no clear subject for the torments described; the text may have lost a word (see the verse's nuance).

reading: Having left the many desires that cling to women with broad shoulders like bamboo, to gold and to land, and died, the corpse that goes: the corpses that will die later gather round it in a crowd, roll on the ground and cry. What, asks the poet, is he to do?
nuance: போம்பிணம் and சாம்பிணம், the corpse that goes and the corpses that will die, make the mourners already corpses; the dead man's one act was to leave his desires, which the mourners have not.

reading: The land gives rice and the rubbish heap gives cloth; when the poet sees the devotees his hands rise and his evil deeds descend; and whenever he sees the dance of the ash-smeared Lord of the little hall, his eyes well, his heart melts, and so does his inner self.
nuance: The first line is the renouncer's economy: food from any country, clothing from what is thrown away. The stanza is the one place in the chapter where the poet speaks of what he has rather than what he lacks, and the dance is its object.

reading: Instead of melting like butter in fire and doing austerity standing in the shade of the Lord of the golden hall, the poet took garlands fitted to the hair of cruel women, did them menial service, and poured pearls from a sieve to water worthless grass: such was his fate.
nuance: விழலுக்கு முத்து இறைத்தல், irrigating vizhal grass with pearls, is a stock figure for waste; here the pearls are his years of service. விதிவசம் puts the waste down to fate, as 260 did, which the chapter's later stanzas on the Lord as sole agent complicate.

reading: Without running off, without toiling for waste, without joining those who speak with partiality, without leaving the company of the good, without harbouring hot anger in the heart, without slipping from what is good, without seeking and putting off to today and tomorrow: give me wealth, teacher of Chidambaram.
nuance: The wealth asked for in 283 to 285 is tradition's riddle: either literal wealth that costs none of these faults, or the abstentions themselves as the only wealth. The last clause, இன்றைக்கு நாளைக்கென்று தேடாமல், not hunting day to day, tells against the literal reading.

reading: Without saying 'there is nothing' to those who ask, without even looking; without sins drawing near through speaking of faults; without the mind fainting and straying; without leaving service undone; without joining those who have not won love: give me wealth, teacher of Chidambaram.
nuance: The first abstention is the sharpest: refusing an asker without so much as looking at him (பாராமல்). The poet, himself a mendicant, asks for wealth on condition that it never be concealed from askers.

reading: Without killing, without eating what was killed, without learning deceit and seizing, without consorting with tricksters, without lying even in a dream, without listening to idle words, without going into the maya of women: give me wealth, teacher of Chidambaram.
nuance: Killing and eating the killed head the list, as they do in the poet's confession at 276. கனவினும் பொய் சொல்லாமல் uses the Kural's test of a settled nature.

reading: Crowned kings and all the rest are in the end burnt to a fistful of ash and become earth; even having seen this, people think of nothing but this grasping life, and no one knows that to be saved we must reach the feet of the Lord of the golden hall.
nuance: கண்டு பின்னும், having seen and still: the reproach is not ignorance of death but the failure to let what is seen change anything. பிடிசார்ந்த வாழ்வு, the life one holds in a fist, answers பிடிசாம்பர், the fistful of ash.

reading: The morning's condition is excrement and urine; besides that, at high noon the heavy condition is hunger and thirst, and the accumulated deeds; the evening's condition is sleep and lust. Remove these, Lord of the hall who wears the poison, and take me as yours.
nuance: உபாதி, the limiting adjunct of Siddhanta, is applied to the body's daily needs by the three times of day. சஞ்சிதம், the store of past karma, sits oddly between hunger and sleep; it may be a fourth condition or may qualify noon's hunger as the fruit of past deeds. ஆலமுகந்தருள் is read as 'who took the poison' (ஆலம் உகந்து).

reading: If you go near the Lord of the hall of famed Tillai, the bull charges and the serpent bites; if you follow behind him, ghosts, his troops and the big-headed bhutas follow you. Where will you go, mind? To the place where the dwellers of the corpse-forest go.
nuance: The Lord is approached through his terrifying retinue, and the last line is a wry answer: the mind's only destination is the cremation ground, which is where the Lord himself dwells and dances. பிணக்காடவர் may be the Lord as dweller of the corpse-forest or the dead who are taken there; the two readings converge.

reading: He takes a skull, wraps a hide about him, strolls slowly from house to house collecting alms like a man without a destiny, and with a maddening grace stands here in the hall: what, the poet asks Sivakama Sundari, is the reckoning in seeking out this mendicant?
nuance: Siva as Bhikshatana, the begging ascetic, is described to his consort with the irony of a complaint: what can be gained from a god who begs? ஆடுமருள், dancing or maddening grace, and கணக்கு, account, carry the sense; the stanza may also be the poet's self-mockery for seeking such a god. It is the only stanza addressed to the goddess.

reading: The one who makes us eat and makes us sleep, who sets one thing against another and makes us embrace, who shows the deeds we have done, and who makes us dance along the bond-rope of the two deeds: there is such a one in the hall of Tillai.
nuance: Eight causatives in -விப்பான் make the Lord the agent of everything from eating to quarrelling; the puppet of 240 is here the doctrine of a single mover. The rope is இருவினைப் பாசக் கயிறு, the two deeds as the bond, so the Lord works through karma rather than apart from it.

reading: If one bows at the feet of the Lord of the hall who is easy for his devotees, one may win the boon of a wealth that does not die; we are those who see the family of the grace of the eternal, stainless one whom the tall one who measured the seven worlds and Brahma could not see, and he is our clan deity.
nuance: மடியாமற் செல்வம், wealth that does not die, is the wealth 283 to 285 asked for. குலதெய்வம், the family god, and அருட்குடி, the household of grace, turn the clan vocabulary the Siddhars attack into the devotees' own kinship.

reading: Divine Lord of Chidambaram, if your mind turns away, where is the dream-like life of kings built on lies, where the earth, where the wealth called real, where the platforms of the provincial lords, where the theatre halls they set up with their hands? All of it is a bewilderment of the eye.
nuance: The condition is the Lord's will (உன் சித்தம் திரும்பிவிட்டால்), so the stanza makes royal splendour depend moment by moment on him. நாடகசாலை, the theatre, is the Kural's image for wealth's crowd (332). கண்மயக்கு closes as விழிமயக்கு closed 253.

reading: The one who clothes and the one who feeds milk-rice, the one who saves a man and the one who ruins him, the one who asks 'what is this?', the one who gives so that the goal is reached, the one who begs saying 'give', and the one who stands and prevents the giving: are you not all of these, dancer of bliss of Tillai?
nuance: The Lord is both the beggar and the one who stops the gift, both saviour and destroyer; the stanza refuses to leave him on one side of any transaction. It extends 290 from the bodily life to giving and refusing, the chapter's own concern.

reading: Though one talks grandly, climbs on stilts, chants 'thaththaara' and dances the pavuri, though one speaks of one's elder brother's or younger brother's ambition, does anything come of it? Apart from the word of the Maker who fills Tillai there are no deeds.
nuance: சோங்கு is taken as stilts and பவுரி as a whirling dance; தம்முன் தம்பி அத்தாசை is obscure, perhaps the ambitions of brothers for one another. The point of the catalogue is display without result; கன்மங்கள், deeds, exist only as the Maker's (கத்தா) word, which makes 290 explicit.

reading: One must win the boon of not being born; and having been born, there is a medicine for not dying, see how it is: heart, do not forget the lotus feet of the Lord of the dharma-rich hall of Tillai; see, that is the good medicine for you.
nuance: இறவாதிருக்க மருந்து, a medicine against dying, is the Siddhars' promise, usually kept by breath or kalpa herbs; Pattinathar names remembrance of the feet as the drug. Whether the deathlessness is bodily or the end of rebirth is not said.

reading: Do not despair, heart: if you chant without flagging, by the five letters, the Sankara who dwells in Tillai, the mine of knowledge who fills the earth, the destroyer of the cities, the lamp that does not go out, the dancer in the golden hall, the release that is not being born again will be attained.
nuance: செவியாமல் in line 4 is read as சலியாமல், without wearying, since the sense needs a manner of chanting; பிறவா முத்தி, release as not being born, defines the goal negatively. The stanza follows 295's medicine with the method.

reading: Those who trust the Lord of the hall, who is the meaning of the four Vedas, yet stay without once going to serve him: they are made to lift black stones onto their heads, their hands are nailed into fetters, they are set again on one leg, and his servants come and bind them.
nuance: The syntax is strained: நம்பியவர் and சேவிக்கொணாதிருப்பார் may be one group (those who trust but do not serve) or two, and the torments of lines 3 and 4 read as Yama's punishments for failing to serve, with the agents left unnamed. கிட்டியும் may be a crushing device. The reading is the sense most editors give it.

reading: Those who do not praise the Lord of the hall who dances adorned with the river and the thumbai flower have a sign on this earth: no food, no comfort, no kin, no cloth, and even if they beg, no alms, so that they stay pining.
nuance: Poverty is read as the visible mark (அடையாளம்) of not praising the Lord, a karmic claim the chapter does not make elsewhere; 281, where the renouncer eats from any land and clothes himself from the rubbish heap, is its counterweight.

reading: To see the Father, the overlord of the thirty-three crore gods, the eternal one, the lover of the mother Sivakama Sundari, our dancer, the lord who dances in the golden hall, how many crores of ages have these eyes been doing tapas!
nuance: The eyes, not the poet, are the ascetics: seeing the dance is the fruit of aeons. The stanza closes the work on the sight that 281 said melts him.

title: முதலாவது கோயிற்றிருவகவல்
theme: Pattinathar's first Koyil Thiruvagaval, one long unit addressed to the poet's own mind. Framed by the refrain 'think, mind, think of Siva of the golden hall', it argues from the reversibility of everything (what is born dies, what is eaten becomes excrement, what is loved becomes hated) and from the mind's own history across births, in which it has killed and been killed, eaten and been eaten, sat in heaven and lain in hell, to the body it has taken for stronger than stone, which is a hut of grass with openings for rheum, wax, mucus, spit, wind and urine and ends as burnt bone. Knowing this, the mind is to think of the Siva-bliss that stands beyond 'I' and 'mine', the two deeds, the malas, coming and going, night and day and this world and the next.
structure_note: Three movements inside the refrain: the pairs of reversal (பிறந்தன இறக்கும் ... உவப்பன வெறுப்பாம்), the mind's own career through births (கொன்றனை, தின்றனை, பெற்றனை, ஓம்பினை, each returned on it), and the anatomy of the body's openings, followed by the string of அற negatives that define the Lord and the closing call. The refrain stands at the head and the foot.

reading: Think, mind, of Siva of the golden hall and do not cherish the false life of the world or the body that staggers on the wheel of a demon's chariot: whatever is born dies and the dead are born, the large grows small and the small large, the known is forgotten and the forgotten known, what is eaten turns to excrement and what is adorned to dirt; through birth after birth you have killed all and all have killed you, eaten and been eaten, borne and been borne, rejoiced in wealth and wept in poverty, sat in heaven and lain in hell, and never once saw it as one; and this cage of the two deeds, a grass hut of a shelter with one opening for rheum, one for wax, one for mucus, one for spit and phlegm, one way for wind and excrement and one for urine and pus, stinking from within and ending as burnt bone, you took for firmer than stone. Knowing the bodily life from within, think of the god with konrai and matted hair, the unending Siva-bliss joined to you as a shadow that never leaves, free of 'I' and 'mine', of the two deeds and the malas, of coming and going, delusion and darkness, night and day, this world and the next, the First who rose as light in Tillai, the king of the hall, the dancer of bliss; melting like lac in fire, think of him, mind.
nuance: The argument is not that the world is unreal but that it is reversible: every pair runs both ways (பிறந்தன இறக்கும், இறந்தன பிறக்கும்), so nothing holds a state. The mind's career across births is told in a chiasmus, கொன்றனை அனைத்தும், அனைத்தும் நினைக் கொன்றன, which makes every act suffered as well as done; ஒன்றென்று எழியாது உற்றனை, that it never grasped all this as one, is the fault named. The body is counted by its openings, as in the Naladiyar and Tirumular's nine gates, and the stone the mind took it for returns in the Tirumanthiram as what the mind itself should become. அலகைத் தேரின் அலமரு காலின் is read as the staggering wheel of a demon's chariot; the simile is loose and some take அலகை as a kite or a mirage. நிழலெனக் கடவா நீர்மை, the nature that does not depart like a shadow, is the one positive description of the Lord's relation to the soul; everything else is said in அற, 'without'.

title: இரண்டாவது கோயிற்றிருவகவல்
theme: Pattinathar's second Koyil Thiruvagaval, one unit. The poet, whose love and thought run after women and who has not won the fortune of wearing the Lord's feet, names his own body in some forty figures: a wilderness raided by the five thieves, a chest of urine and excrement, a casket of the two deeds, a village where wind, bile and phlegm lodge, a stinking pot, a top spinning on the rope of desire, a ship of unending disease, a cage of death, a bellows for rice, a kite in the wind, a log the god of fate cuts, a shirt the four-faced tailor sews, a feast for the pyre, a leaf shrivelled in the fire of lust, a lump that walks as a bridegroom and lies as a corpse, and then a run of the stock images of impermanence, frost before the sun, a rainbow, a cloud's shadow, a bubble, writing on water, a dream, and worse than all these a stain of maya. It ends 'enough, enough, Lord', and asks to be taken and ruled by the dance of bliss while Uma cries 'live'.
structure_note: A confession (lines 1 to 6), the body catalogue in short two-foot phrases (ஆசைக் கயிற்றிலாடும் பம்பரம் and the rest), and a closing petition. The catalogue moves from containers and places (பேழை, பெட்டகம், சீறூர், பாண்டம்) to things driven or cut (பம்பரம், மரக்கலம், கட்டை, சட்டை) to the brief things (பனிக்கூட்டம், இந்திரசாபம், குமிழி, நீர்மேல் எழுத்து, கனவு). The third agaval reuses many of the same phrases.
source_issues: Line 12 நான்முழத் தொன்பது பீற்றத் துண்டம் and line 18 தூற்றம் பத்தம் cannot be construed with confidence; the second may be corrupt (தூற்றும் பத்தம், a scattering sheaf, or தூறும் பத்தம்).
Line 29 பிணமாய்க் கிடக்கும் பிண்டம், பிணமேல் runs the next phrase onto the line; the division is the source's.

reading: The poet, whose love and thought go only to the quarrelsome, sinful women whose eyes run to their ears and who play with the sore at their hips, and who has not been granted the fortune of wearing the Lord's two lotus feet, describes his own body as a wilderness where the five thieves raid, a chest of urine and excrement, a casket of the two deeds, a hamlet where wind, bile and phlegm lodge, a bloody frame of filthy skin, a stinking pot, a torn rag of four cubits and nine, a garden of bitter gourd, a mound in the great cremation ground, a top spinning on the rope of desire, a ship of ceaseless disease, a changing illusion, a cage of death, a bellows for rice, a kite flying in the wind, a log that fate's Dharma cuts, a shirt the four-faced tailor stitches, a feast thrown to the pyre, a dry leaf shrivelling in the fire of lust, a tuber worms dig, a forked branch up which the shoot of sin climbs, a lump that walks as a bridegroom and ends lying as a corpse, a burden the town will not let lie, a heap of pulai flowers against the wind, frost before the morning sun, a rainbow moving in the sky, the passing shadow of a thundering cloud, a bubble on water, writing on water, a sight seen in sleep's dream, and, worse than all of these, a stain of maya; and says enough, enough, Lord, enough: show the dance of bliss while the daughter of the mountain cries 'live', take me and rule me, for that is the beauty of your grace.
nuance: The names fall into kinds: the body as a container of waste, as a thing moved by what is not itself (the top on the rope of desire, the kite in the wind, the puppet of 240), as a thing already prepared for death (the log Dharma cuts, the shirt Brahma sews, the feast for the fire), and as the stock brief things, which the poet caps by saying the body is worse than a bubble or a dream because it is a மாயக் களங்கம், a stain made of maya. சதுர்முகப் பாணன், the four-faced tailor, is Brahma stitching the body; விதிவழித் தருமன் is Yama as Dharma. நான்முழத் தொன்பது பீற்றத் துண்டம் is obscure: a torn cloth four cubits long with nine (holes), or nine torn pieces of four cubits. ஊரிற் கிடக்க ஒட்டா உபாதி uses the Siddhanta word உபாதி loosely for the corpse the town hurries out. The petition at the end is brief, and the grace asked for is to be ruled (ஆண்டுகொண்டருள்), not to be released.

title: மூன்றாவது கோயிற்றிருவகவல்
theme: Pattinathar's third Koyil Thiruvagaval, one unit built on the word அடைக்கலம், refuge, said eighteen times. The poet takes refuge in the Siva who held the ocean's poison in his throat, subdued Death with his foot and holds Brahma's skull in his left hand; then he lays out what he brings to that refuge, a dream life, a dirty mind, a thought born of anava mala and nesting in it like a worm in fat, and the whole roll of faults from deceit and envy to murder and fear, the three gunas and the five senses; and then the body that holds them, a hut the bird of life flies from, bound with bone and nerve and thatched with fat, a pot of mala, a pit of rice and sorrow, a cage of murderous weapons, a smith's bellows for the fire of anger, a cage of the five bird-senses, a top on the rope of desire, a windmill spinning for coins, a cart-wheel rolled over the void, a ship driven by the wind of lust into the sea of birth, a body that trembles when the Arbiter comes. When he lays it down as a corpse and sets out, he asks refuge at the lotus feet, and closes with the bull-rider, the unblinking-eyed, the one easy to devotees, the sea of mercy who dances in the hall of Tillai.
structure_note: Three parts: the Lord's deeds with the refrain (lines 1 to 8), the roll of the mind's faults (padirum, paavamum ... idumbaiyum piniyum), and the body catalogue in -ஐ accusatives that all depend on the single verb at line 42, பிணமெனப் படுத்தி யான் புறப்படும் பொழுது, when I lay it down as a corpse and set out; then the closing refrain. The body catalogue shares phrases with the second agaval (ஆசைக் கயிற்றிலாடு பம்பரம், சோற்றுத் துருத்தி, இருவினை).
source_issues: Line 25 பலவுடற் புட்டிலைத் and line 29 கோள்சரக் கொழுகும் are hard to construe and may be corrupt (see the verse's nuance).
Line 13 ஆணவ மலத்துதித் தளைந்ததி னுளைத்திடும் is spaced across word boundaries (மலத்து உதித்து அளைந்து அதினுள் ஐத்திடும், or similar); the division is the source's.
Line 36 மயங்குங் திகிரியைக் has a sandhi fault (மயங்குந் திகிரியை expected).

reading: The poet takes refuge in the Siva who held in his throat the fierce poison churned from the milk ocean, who subdued the cruel-sceptred Death with a lifted foot, who tore off a head of Brahma, maker and owner of the whole world, and holds it in his left hand, the rich lord of the golden hall; and lays before him the dream-like life that spends itself along the mind's road, the dirty mind that knows no great meaning, the thought born of anava mala and writhing in it like a worm in fat, deceit, sin, blameworthy thinking, error, envy, miserly false oaths, guile, lies, great anger, strife, murder, baseness, enmity, fear, rashness and trembling, the folly of the three gunas and the bewilderment of the five senses, trouble and disease, all packed into the body: a hut from which the bird that is life flies off, bound at the middle with bone and nerve and thatched with fat flesh, leaking, a hut of red blood and small worms, a pot of mala-body, a bag of many bodies, an endless pit of rice and sorrow, a cage where many murderous weapons lie, a rubbish heap of weary deeds, a torn sack leaking the goods of the planets, a smith's bellows that kindles the fire of anger, a cage where the birds of the five senses roost, a hollow tree where cares breed, a top spinning on the rope of desire, a windmill whirling for coins and money, a wheel confused by the deeds of its children, a cart-wheel rolled across the great void, a cruel ship that enters the sea of birth with a cargo of sin, is tossed by the wind of lust and makes the shore by the way of ruin, a grass boat moving in the shackle of the two deeds, a body that shudders when the Arbiter comes calling: when he lays this down as a corpse and sets out, he asks refuge at the lotus of the Lord's feet; refuge with the god of the white bull that charges like a thunderbolt in the open, the unblinking-eyed king, the one easy to devotees, the sea of mercy who dances in the hall of Tillai of the Vedic Brahmins and whom gods and sages praise; refuge, king of the hall, with you.
nuance: The grammar carries the meaning: some thirty accusatives, the faults and the body's names alike, hang on one verb, 'when I lay it down as a corpse and set out', so that what is handed over at the refuge is everything the poet is, not a purified self. ஆணவ மலத்து உதித்து, born of anava mala, is the Siddhanta origin of the mind's own thought, and the worm in fat (நிணவைப் புழு) its figure. உயிரெனும் குருவி விட்டோடும் குரம்பை, the hut the bird of life flies from, is the Kural's image at 338 reversed, the body named from the bird's leaving. பலவுடற் புட்டில், a bag of many bodies, is loose: perhaps the body of many parts, or the body that has worn many bodies. கோள்சரக்கு, the goods of the planets, may be the planets' influence or a corrupt phrase for கோழைச் சரக்கு, phlegm. மறையவர் தில்லை, Tillai of the Brahmins, places the dance among the three thousand Dikshitars without comment, unusual in a Siddhar text that elsewhere attacks the twice-born.

title: நான்காவது கச்சித் திருவகவல்
theme: Pattinathar's fourth agaval, the Kachchi Thiruvagaval, one unit addressed to the men who, having won a human birth among the seven, do not bow at the feet of Uma's lord but delight in women. The poet takes the stock praise of the female body limb by limb, soles like cotton, shins like leaping fish, thighs like plantain stems, belly like a banyan leaf, breasts like lotus buds, hands like kanthal, neck like areca, mouth like the murukku flower, teeth like pearls, nose like the kumizh, eyes like lilies, ears like vallai stalks, hair like a dark cloud, and sets against each the sweat, bone, excrement, mucus, wax and lice it covers; then names the vulva as the gate of hell the praisers desire, the field where embryos grow, the way of the menstrual flow, the sore covered with a cloth, the great road by which every man and woman is born, and tells them not to call it sweet but to worship the twin feet of the one Lord of Kachi, who pities a devotee even for a leaf, and to stop praising the women of pleasure.
structure_note: An exordium naming the audience (மானிடர்க் கெல்லாம் யானெடுத் துரைப்பேன்; விழிவெளி மாக்கள் தெளிவுறக் கேண்மின்), the catalogue of limbs from the sole upward to the hair, each in the pattern 'the X that does Y, they call Z', a second catalogue of some twenty names for the female organ in -வழி and -வாயில், and a closing call to the Lord's feet. The ascent from feet to hair reverses the head-to-foot (கேசாதிபாதம்) order of courtly praise.
source_issues: Line 19 சிலந்தி போலக் கிளைத்துமுன் னெழுந்து is obscure as a figure for the breasts; the word may be corrupt.
Line 32 உள்ளுங் குறும்பி யழுகுங் காதை (the ear where wax rots) is the only limb given without a stated function; the construction is otherwise uniform.
The unit is headed நான்காவது கச்சித் திருவகவல் and counted with the three Koyil Thiruvagavals though addressed to Kachi (Kanchipuram), not Tillai.

reading: To all the men who, born human among the seven births that Brahma, son of Vishnu, arranged, do not bow at the flower feet of the mountain daughter's lord and reach the Siva-state but delight in women and celebrate love, the poet speaks, and bids the blind-eyed listen: the soles that toil over thorns and stones they call cotton; the shins that are white bone they praise as leaping varal fish; the thighs of flesh and bone they call plantain stems; the waist that carries the long body they call a drum; the belly rolling with excrement, urine, slime and wrinkles they call a banyan leaf; the breasts that spread like a spider's web, swell, ooze, are scratched by nails, dry, shrink and hang for people to laugh at they call lotus buds, 'I say this to the blind of lust'; the hands that stretch, fold, take goods, feed and knead they call kanthal flowers; the neck of sweat and grime they call the areca palm; the hot and foul mouth they call the murukku flower; the teeth that chew rice and curry they call pearls; the sharp nose that drips water and mucus they call the kumizh fruit; the eyes that run with water and rheum they call water-lilies; the ears where wax rots they praise as vallai stalks; the hair on the skull, where lice and nits breed if oil is not combed in, they call a dark cloud; and saying such things in praise they go to the gate of hell they desire, the pit of lust where skin and flesh ooze pus, the field where embryos grow, the way the menstrual flow passes, the holed gate, the great road down which the eight-span body comes, the hidden place where earthly lust is spent, the gate where the dog of lust sits desiring, the sluggish road where those without the grace of the moon-crested one linger, the sore they cover with a cloth saying 'this is a wound', the rich sore that sounds with running water, the way the deluded enter and the sick never leave, the pit the proud lechers fall into, the great road by which woman and man are born, the water gate beside the gate where excrement falls: do not say this is sweet; bow instead at the twin feet of the one Lord of Kachi, who pities his devotees even for an offered leaf and grants the release of the Siva-state, lord of release, ageless First, who saw all the worlds in all the eggs, and give up praising the women of pleasure.
nuance: The method is to quote the convention and then name the referent: each limb is given first as function or matter (bone, sweat, mucus) and then as the poets' figure, so that the figure is convicted by what it covers. The second catalogue is unusually literal, and தூமைக் கடவழி, the way of the menstrual flow, uses the Siddhars' word for the womb's impurity; பெண்ணும் ஆணும் பிறக்கும் பெருவழி concedes that the same gate is the way of every birth, including the hearer's. The attack is on the eye and the convention, not on women as persons, though the text does not make that distinction itself. சிலந்தி போலக் கிளைத்து, spreading like a spider or its web, for the breasts' first growth is obscure; இடைகழி வாயில் is the vestibule gate. பச்சிலை இடினும், even for a green leaf offered, is the standard measure of the Lord's easy grace.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: Pattinathar's shrine songs for Thiruvenkadu, Thiruchengodu and Thiruvotriyur: pleas to a Lord whose will cannot be read. The poet asks for a day when 'you and I' stand as one beyond the tattvas and nada, confesses that his days have passed in eating, wearing, saying and seeing the same things, does not know whether Siva will push him back into the womb or give the feet, and asks only that at death someone put ash on him and teach him the five letters. The devotees who walk the shrine's street can do what the poet cannot: their feet on his head tear the leaf of fate.
structure_note: 304 to 307 are the Thiruvenkadu verses (the fourth marked வேறு, a different metre), 308 is a single verse on Thiruchengodu, and 309 and 310 open the Thiruvotriyur set. The refrain இறைவனே ஏகநாயகனே closes 304 and 305. Each verse ends on the shrine's name, so the shrine stands in for the Lord addressed.
source_issues: Unit 308 (own id siddhar:thiruppadal-thirattu:u1) is unnumbered in the source and sits between the Thiruvenkadu set and the Thiruvotriyur set; it names Sengodu (Thiruchengodu), not either shrine.
Unit 307 (own id 0270-u1) is marked வேறு, a change of metre, and is unnumbered in the Thiruvenkadu run.

reading: Is there a day when you and I stand as one in the space beyond the elements, the inner instruments, the senses and their five fields, the three gunas and nada itself? Ocean of the bliss of the mind's dissolving, beyond debate and the differences of sects: I know nothing at all; whatever is, is your doing, Lord, sole master.
nuance: The first two lines climb the tattvas in order, from the five elements through the inner instruments and the senses to the gunas and nada, and place the meeting in the வெளி beyond them all. மனோலயம், the mind's dissolving, is a yogic term for the state in which the mind ceases, and the verse makes the Lord that bliss rather than its giver. The closing surrender, யாது நின் செயலே, returns at 308 and 350.

reading: Whoever may stay and whoever may thrive and whoever may be kin to us, is there any direction for me but you, as your holy mind knows? You who, taking pity on one poet's fine Tamil, became his errand-boy and went about all night to turn Paravai's mind, Lord, sole master.
nuance: The second half recalls the story told of Sundarar: Siva went by night as a messenger to Paravai to reconcile her to him. உடலை மாற்ற reads literally as 'to change her body'; the legend makes it changing her stance or mind. The point is the Lord's willingness to be a servant for a devotee's Tamil, which the poet uses to claim him as his only refuge.

reading: Eating what was eaten, wearing what was worn, saying again and again what was said, seeing what was seen and hearing what was heard: so all my days have gone by. Lord of Venkadu of the festival street, where the swan sits on the opened lotus, father who dances in the hall as the gods praise, grant that this change.
nuance: The verse has no sin to confess; its complaint is repetition, a life that only repeats itself and so has not begun. மாறருளே is read as 'grant grace that this be changed'; it could also be the vocative 'you who grant grace', which leaves the verse a bare confession.

reading: Pure one, stainless form, whom the dark one of the churning and the one who abides on the flower seek daily and do not see: you who removed the fetters the king put on the hands of Sendan of Nangur, where carp leap in the field channels, show yourself before me, you who dwell in Venkadu.
nuance: மத்தளை இருண்டான் is obscure; I take it as Vishnu (dark, of the churning) paired with Brahma on the lotus, the usual two who fail to find Siva. The Sendan of Nangur freed from a king's handcuffs is a local legend I cannot verify; the verse uses it as precedent: the Lord who showed himself to free one devotee is asked to appear to this one.

reading: What the mind of the fire-bodied one who sits beside the shade of the aathi tree at Sengodu may be, I cannot tell: will it push me once more into the dyeing-pit of a mother's womb, or give the holy feet that Kannan could not see? Siva's doing cannot be known.
nuance: கருப்ப சாயக் குழி, the dye-pit of the womb, makes rebirth a vat one is thrown back into. The verse sets the two outcomes, another birth and the feet, as equally possible and the Lord's choice alone; Kannan who could not see the feet is Vishnu digging as the boar, the standard measure of their unreachability.

reading: When phlegm follows on phlegm, the eyes close, awareness fails and the body itself turns false, one thing I will ask: you who own Thiruvotriyur of the fields, put holy ash on me, make my hands worship, and teach me to recite the five letters.
