nuance: The request is for the deathbed rites of a Saiva, ash, folded hands and the mantra, asked for as a grace the dying man cannot perform for himself. மெய்யும் பொய்யாகி plays on மெய் as body and as truth: the body becomes false at the moment it stops.

reading: Those who are to be burned do not know it; the Lord who once burned the three cities is the Lord of southern Otriyur with its firm great walls. See, mind: to roll about so that the golden feet of those who walk its streets touch our head is what tears the leaf of fate.
nuance: சுடப்படுவார் அறியார் can be the people of the three cities, who did not know they were being burned, or all mortals, who do not know they will be burned on the pyre; the pun on சுடுதல் carries both. The fate-leaf torn by the devotees' feet, not the Lord's, puts the devotees' street above the shrine's sanctum.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: Three shrine verses, two for Idaimarudur and one for Kazhukkundram, that strip renunciation of its outward marks: forest, air-eating, rags and the begging bowl are nothing without inner love, and the true lover reaches the bliss of knowledge even living with women at home. When wealth goes, mother, wife, child and kin all turn enemy, so the Lord's feet alone are freedom; and wherever this lone body falls, forest or porch, those feet are the life's companion.
structure_note: 311 and 312 belong to the Idaimarudur set (the work's own 2.1 and 2.2); 313 is an unnumbered Kazhukkundram verse placed after them. 313 is built as a string of alternatives (காடோ செடியோ ...) answered by one line, a pattern Pattinathar uses again at 328.
source_issues: Unit 313 (own id siddhar:thiruppadal-thirattu:u2, திருக்கழுக்குன்றம்) is unnumbered in the source and is grouped by the tool with the two Idaimarudur verses.

reading: What if one takes to the forest, eats the wind, wears rags and carries the bowl? Those without inner love gain nothing. The true lovers of the Lord of Idaimarudur, even staying in the house beside their women, reach the bliss of the home of true knowledge, which is the land of the high gods.
nuance: The verse is the poet's own warning against the life he leads in the பொது verses (329 onward): rags, bowl and porch are only outward. வீடு is played on: the lovers stay in the house (வீடே இருப்பினும்) and reach the house of knowledge (ஞான வீடு), release. The line does not say the householder's way is better, only that love decides.

reading: Mother is an enemy, the wife one took a great enemy, one's own child an enemy, kin enemies, this whole world an enemy, when, on looking, rare wealth has gone. So, heart that steeps in this love, the golden feet of the Lord of Marudur are freedom.
nuance: The condition is in line 3: all these turn enemy when wealth leaves, so the verse is about kin as bought by wealth, not about kin as such. சுதந்திரம், freedom or independence, is the word chosen for the feet, against a family that has become a dependency. The marked question (நீங்கில்!) reads as a condition despite the punctuation.

reading: Forest or bush, the seashore, a heavy-laden land, a city or the heart of a city, a fine house or an outer porch: wherever this lone body falls, Lord of lofty Kazhukkundram, your feet are the companion of my life.
nuance: The list of places runs from wild to domestic, so the poet does not know and does not choose where he will die; the contrast is between the body that falls somewhere and the உயிர் whose companion is fixed. The outer porch (புறத்திண்ணை) is where the பொது verses say he sleeps.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: The six Kalahasti verses hold the body and its life up against the Lord. A life runs from the womb through silk, pearls and play to a corpse mourned by corpses-to-be; gold is useful to its owner but the owner is no use to gold, and so the worshipper is no use to the Lord; the poet cannot match the heroic devotions of the Nayanars and asks how else he can become a servant; and the Lord has arranged his eating, sleeping, lust and deathbed terror, so when will he see him? The last two verses turn on the body of the women he circles: a pit, an oozing wound, a hidden door of lust, from which the petty pleasure must be given up.
structure_note: All six verses end on Kalathi (Kalahasti) and its Lord. 314 and 315 are reflections, 316 and 317 are questions (how shall I become a servant, when shall I see you), and 318 and 319 are pleas to be taken and raised, built on the same image of the woman's body.

reading: Having entered the ten and been born and grown, wrapped in silk, decked in pearls and coral, having run and played and come to the end, one lies there a corpse; what is the reckoning of the corpses-to-be who wail beside it? See, Kalathi of Kailasa city.
nuance: பத்தும் புகுந்து is taken by tradition as the ten months in the womb; it could also be the ten airs or the ten senses entering the body. சாம்பிணங்கள், 'the corpses that will die', makes the mourners already corpses, so the wailing is one corpse over another.

reading: Gold is of use to those who possess it; what use is the possessor to the gold? In the same way, from you I have every use I could want; what use is there to you in me, who bow to you? Lord of Kalathi.
nuance: The analogy is exact and cuts against the worshipper: the Lord is the gold and the devotee the owner who gains everything and gives nothing. The verse neither asks for anything nor claims merit; it only states the one-sidedness of the relation, which is its humility.

reading: I am not one who can cut up my child with a sword and serve it; I am not one who can give up youth on the word of a woman's oath; I am not one who can serve and, on the sixth day, set my eye into the eye. How then shall I go now and become a servant to the father of Thirukalathi?
nuance: The three feats are those of the Nayanars as tradition tells them: Siruthondar who cooked his son for the Lord's guest, Thiruneelakanda who kept a vow of celibacy from youth at his wife's oath, and Kannappar at this very shrine, who on the sixth day of his service plucked out his eye for the bleeding image. The poet does not scorn these; he says he cannot do them, and leaves the question of another way open.

reading: You have arranged that I eat rice three times a day and sleep, that in infatuation I join women whose young breasts are like bronze, and that when the life departs my eyes are troubled, Lord. When will I be able to see you? Lord of Thirukalathi.
nuance: வைத்தாய், 'you set it so', gives the whole ordinary life, including lust and the terror of dying, to the Lord's arrangement; the complaint is that he arranged everything but the seeing. Read with 304 and 350, the surrender of agency is the poet's constant stance, here turned into a reproach.

reading: Wandering night and day for prey and growing weary here, circling the pit of misery at women's waists, the oozing hollow where fluid seeps, I am a lone one who goes round and round; take me and rule me, Kalathi who sits in grace under the stone banyan on the bank of the golden Mugali.
nuance: இரைக்கே, for prey or for food, makes the man an animal foraging; the woman's body is a pit (குழி) and a seeping hollow (புரை). கல்லால நிழல், the shade of the stone banyan, is the seat of Siva as Dakshinamurti, the silent teacher, set against the poet's restless circling.

reading: The reeking stream like a horse's water, the hole in the skin where pus seeps daily, the pit of filth, the doorway of lust, the hidden wound, the cleft of flesh within the inner chamber: grant me the state of rising, having left the petty pleasure that lies there, Lord of Thirukalathi.
nuance: The whole verse is one description of the woman's sex, in the register of disgust the Naladiyar uses for the body. சிற்றின்பம், the small pleasure, is the standard counter to பேரின்பம், the great bliss of 353; ஏறும் பதம், the rising state, is the ascent out of it. The verse asks the Lord to grant the leaving, not for strength to leave.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: The Kailasa verses are a series of 'when?' questions that draw the renouncer's life the poet wants: having left home, begging when hunger comes, toothless and white-mouthed, with no attachment and no word or meaning left, sleeping in bliss; free of thought, liking, act, remembering and not-remembering; standing in the Lord's presence with hair bristling and tears running down the chest; not flattering the rich; carried like a kitten by its mother; drinking the honey of the five letters in the company of the good. The closing Madurai verse asks whether any of this is possible without grace.
structure_note: 320 opens with a plea to end birth; 321 to 325 each end என்றோ or என்றிருப்பேன் (when will it be?), to the Lord of Kailasa; 326 and 327 shift from asking to stating what the poet is and will not do; 328, addressed to Sokkanatha of Madurai, is a string of விடப்படுமோ questions on the same pattern as 313.
source_issues: Unit 328 (own id siddhar:thiruppadal-thirattu:4.9) carries the shrine label மதுரை and addresses Sokkanatha, but is numbered as the ninth verse of the திருக்கைலாயம் set.

reading: King of the silver mountain where the forests lean, I have trusted your anklet-feet; end the birth in which flesh wastes away. Siva-sprout who, for the man of Kavur, leaned your good holy body, so that the deer leaned, the axe in your red hand leaned and the honey of the konrai you wear ran down.
nuance: The verse is built on சாய (to lean, to bend) in every line. காவூரனுக்காய் ... திருமேனி சாய்த்த refers to some occasion on which Siva bent his body for a devotee of Kavur, a story I cannot place; the plain sense is that the Lord who once stooped for one devotee is asked to end this one's birth.

reading: Having left the house, standing and begging there when hunger comes, my teeth gone and my mouth white, with no hold on anything, having lost both word and meaning, in the sleep of blissful ease: when will I be so, night and day, Lord of Kailasa?
nuance: The renunciation wished for is not dignified: toothless, white-mouthed, begging. சொல்லும் பொருளும் இழந்து, losing word and meaning, is both the wreck of speech in old age and the yogic end of language; சுகானந்தத் தூக்கம், the sleep of bliss, is named again at 322 as ஆனந்த நித்திரை.

reading: Free of thought, free of liking, free of action, free of what was thought and free of not-thinking, without thought, alone with myself, in the drowse in which the sleep of bliss settles: when will I stay so, Father, Lord of Kailasa?
nuance: The verse removes thought and then removes its absence too (நினைந்ததும் அற்று நினையாமையும் அற்று), so the state is not blankness but something past the pair. அனந்தல், drowsiness, is a plain word for a state the Tirumanthiram calls samadhi; the poet keeps the homely image of sleep.

reading: Having received with full hands and eaten standing there, wearing an unstitched black cloth, coming always to your presence, bowing with my whole body, the hair bristling within me, crying out 'Aiya': when will that be, Lord of Kailasa?
nuance: கரித்துணியைத் தையாது உடுத்து, wearing a dark cloth without stitching it, is the one outward mark the poet allows himself, set beside the bodily signs of devotion, bristling hair and the cry. The body that bows (மெய்யார நிற்பணிந்து) is the same body 319 reviled.

reading: The ash-smeared body's hair bristling, the heart breaking and breaking and softening to mud, melting and melting, in unchanging meditation on your glorious feet, taking on bliss, tears swelling into a river down the chest: when will I get this, Lord of Kailasa?
nuance: The sequence is the standard Saiva physiology of devotion, ash, bristling, melting, tears, but the poet asks for it as a gift (கிடைப்பது என்றோ), not as something he can produce. நெக்குநெக்கு and கசிந்து கசிந்து double the verbs of melting that the Tirumanthiram makes the one condition of reaching the Lord.

reading: Not going after the rich to speak of my hardship and show my teeth day after day in anxiety, but entering the bound of supreme bliss in a solitude that is a place for me, free of trouble: when will I stay so, Father, Lord of Kailasa?
nuance: பல்லினைக் காட்டி, showing the teeth, is the forced grin of the suppliant. The verse distinguishes the begging of 321 and 323, which is from anyone when hungry, from courting the rich, which it refuses; the alternative is ஏகாந்தம், solitude, as the place of bliss.

reading: I am not the monkey's young, which holds on by itself; a dog, though I know the custom, what can I do with a mind that keeps on thinking? Drive the evil from me and, like the cat that carries its kitten when they part, you are the one who belongs to my father, Lord of Kailasa.
nuance: The pair of images is the later Vaishnava and Saiva figure for two kinds of grace: the monkey's cub clings to its mother by its own effort, the kitten is carried by the cat. The poet says he is not the clinging cub, so must be carried. மந்திக் குருளை அத்தேன் இல்லை is read as 'I am not that (cub)'; the text is loose, and எந்தைக்கு உரியவன் (the one who belongs to my father) is obscure, perhaps 'you who are mine as a father'.

reading: I will not be born and die again and go the way of the deluding senses to grieve; I will not enter hell; I have stayed where those who praise you are, and I will not leave the company of the good; by your grace I will drink the rare honey that is the five letters, Lord of Kailasa.
nuance: After six verses of 'when?', the poet speaks in the future indicative: not born, not in hell, not leaving the company. The ground given is twofold, the company of the good already joined and the grace still to come, and the five letters are drunk as honey rather than recited.

reading: Can this worldly life be given up? Having given it up, can the mind grow firm? Without your grace, can the daily wandering be crossed? Must I go to the gates of the petty and suffer with tears welling? Sokkanatha, Sundara Pandya.
nuance: The questions of the first three lines are answered by the third's condition: none of it is possible without grace. The fourth line, standing at the door of the petty, is the fate the poet fears for one who leaves the world without grace, the same begging from the rich that 325 refuses. Sundara Pandya is Siva as the Pandya king of Madurai.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: The first run of Pattinathar's பொது (unplaced) verses, addressed mostly to his own heart: an inventory of the beggar's riches, a loincloth, a porch, leaves, water and the Lord's name, against the wealth, wives, children and kin that go only as far as the mouth, the street and the burning ground. The eyeless needle that will not come on the last road is the chapter's emblem. The Lord is not in stone and copper but in the word, the sky and the devotees; the body is the enjoyment of deeds and goes when they end; the detached cannot be told from worldly people; and the run ends with Siva come as a street beggar to seek the poet, and with a bliss beyond yoga's eight limbs that has swallowed him.
structure_note: The verses fall into loose groups: the beggar's inventory and the heart's folly (329 to 333), where the Lord dwells and what the body is (334, 335), the eyeless needle (336 to 339), what goes how far (340, 341), the body and the beggar's contentment (342 to 347), two verses of உபதேசம் to the heart (348, 349), and a close in the first person on the Lord's doing, the beggar-guru and the bliss beyond yoga (350 to 353). Verses 338 and 339 share the refrain காதற்ற ஊசியும் வாராது காணும் கடைவழிக்கே.
source_issues: The பொது run (own ids 0270-5.1 onward) is printed without word spacing in the source, so word division is the marker's; 342 in particular has broken syntax across lines and may be corrupt.
343 includes women for hire among the beggar's provisions; the line reads as printed and is not emended, but it sits oddly with the rest of the inventory verses.

reading: There is a loincloth to wear, an outer porch to sleep on, fallen leaves to eat here, water to drink, and for company the holy name of the Lord who rides the bull; in this world, what if the northern horn stands high or the southern horn leans, for the crescent in the sky?
nuance: The last line is proverbial: which horn of the moon is higher changes nothing for the moon, so the world's ups and downs change nothing for one who has these five things. அடைகாய் இலை may be the leaf used to wrap betel, or fallen leaves; either way the food is what no one owns.

reading: Release is ours: Thiruvalangadu. The bowl the Pure One gave us is a vessel that never runs dry; we have a thriving, wealthy land that gives whatever we ask, good heart. Is there anyone here to be called our equal?
nuance: வீடு is both house and release, so the first line gives the beggar a home and salvation in one word, and the shrine where tradition places his end. The wealth claimed is the begging bowl and the land that fills it; ஈடு, an equal, mocks the rich by their own measure.

reading: You did not set your sight on the Lord and seek him; you did not seek, dance and grow clear about the Master's feet; saying 'the world's maya has come and covered us' and 'Kama's weapons have raged', will you let yourself be gripped, heart? There are no madmen like you.
nuance: The heart's excuses, maya and Kama, are quoted back to it as the things it chose to be caught by, so the verse denies that they are forces one merely suffers. பித்தர், madman, is Siva's own epithet elsewhere; here it is only abuse.

reading: One hand doing the rite, one eye wandering, one mind calculating, one false and deceitful tongue speaking, one flesh-smelling body leaning on something, one ear wanting to hear something else: how will you accept the puja I perform, remover of deeds?
nuance: ஒன்று repeats for each organ to show them each doing a different thing: the puja is performed by a body whose parts are not together. The poet does not say puja is worthless, only that his is divided, and leaves the acceptance to the Lord.

reading: There are eyes to see and a mind to look, a melting heart and a tune to sing, ears to hear, and fresh leaves to count out and offer; and while the Lord stands before you, you go to the earth. Alas, ruin on you, you humans!
nuance: The verse answers 332 from the other side: there the organs were present and divided, here they are present and unused. மண்ணுண்டு போகுது, going to eat earth, is dying unused; ஈசன் இருக்கையிலே, with the Lord right there, is the shrine or the inner presence, the verse does not say which.

reading: In the word and at the end of the word, in the Vedic hearing, in the night and in the stainless sky, in the house of those who have inquired and finished, and among the devotees: these are the places where the Lord stays. Will our brow-eyed one dwell in stone and in copper?
nuance: The question is rhetorical and the answer the verse expects is no, but the list before it is not a denial of place: the Lord is in speech, scripture, sky, the jnani's house and the devotees, so the attack is on the material image, not on worship. அல்லில், in the night, may be darkness as the unmanifest or a corrupt word.

reading: See, a body is only the enjoyment of deeds; see, once the deeds are spent it will not stay the time of a millet grain. It joins those who think of Siva's feet and leaves those who do not. If you stand on this path, mind, is there anyone like you, my own kin?
nuance: The third line is ambiguous: the subject of மேவும் and நீங்கி may be Siva's foot, which comes to those who remember it, or the body-and-deeds of the first two lines. The first reading fits the exhortation that follows; both make remembrance the hinge. The mind is called உற்றவர், one's own, in contrast to 312 where every kin is an enemy.

reading: Tearing the silk, taking out the thick needle with care, rolling it up tight and giving it into the hands of my wife with her swarming hair; was it so that all the desire of this heavy maya-woman, who held me bound, should leave and part from me that Siva turned back like this?
nuance: The verse belongs to the story of Pattinathar's renunciation, in which a needle sent to him in a box carried the message that not even an eyeless needle goes with one at death; the details of silk and rolling cannot be recovered from the verse alone. கனமாயக்காரி, the heavy sorceress, is the wife as maya; சிவன் மீண்டது, Siva turning back or returning, is the poet's name for what happened to him.

reading: Deceitful breasts, union with deer-like women, the wealth that surrounds: what could they do for the fight that has come upon me? Was it so that, by merit I had done, I might clear myself from the mind of the faultless king, that he put the eyeless needle into my hand?
nuance: போதுற்ற பூசல், the battle that has arrived, is death or the crisis of renunciation. தீதற்ற மன்னவன் சிந்தையினின்று தெளிவதற்கோ is obscure: to grow clear within the mind of the faultless Lord, or to escape the king's notice, as in the legend of the poet's trial. The one who gave the needle is read as the Lord acting through the sender.

reading: Heart that always takes refuge in the flower feet of Annamalai of the strong shoulders that stood in contest: in this world the riches you sought as wealth and the treasure you buried, see, not even an eyeless needle will come on the final road.
nuance: The eyeless needle is the least thing that could be carried and the one the legend made the poet's emblem; the refrain line is shared with 339. The buried treasure is the hoarder's form of wealth, kept for a journey on which it cannot be taken.

reading: Did you not hear the word of the one who taught the inner meaning of the Veda, to give up the woman and the hunger for land? When, through merit done, it grows bright like the sun and the moon, see, not even an eyeless needle comes on the final road.
nuance: Who the teacher of the Veda's inner meaning is, the guru or the Lord, is not said. The third line is loose: the subject of வெளிச்சமதாம் (becomes light) may be the inner meaning made clear by merit, or the poet himself at the moment of death. The refrain fixes the sense: nothing goes with one.

reading: Wife, children, livelihood and wealth reach only as far as one's own mouth; the kin of one's own kind only as far as the cremation ground. What is the companion for the road? Even a millet grain or a sesame seed of austerity done before is what rules; the other world is truly attained.
nuance: The verse measures each possession by how far it goes: wealth to the mouth, kin to the burning ground, tapas beyond. தனை ஆள, 'to rule', is read as the tapas that governs what follows; the syntax is compressed and it could also be 'to make it one's own'. பரலோகம் சித்திக்கும் is the plain promise of a next world that the Siddhars elsewhere mock.

reading: Property and livelihood go only as far as the house; the women with arrow-eyes streaming tears only as far as the street; the children who sob with both hands on their heads only as far as the burning ground. What follows, clinging, is the pair of deeds, merit and sin.
nuance: A variation on 340 with the stations made concrete: house, street, cremation ground. பற்றித் தொடரும், what follows holding on, inverts the word for attachment: what one clung to stays behind, what clings to one is karma.

reading: Pus, blood, rich fluid and slime pressed together and rising and flowing, when there is not even a cloth to cover it, day and night; the womb that flies and ants enter: for the humans who die day and night there is no medicine to keep them from dying.
nuance: The syntax is broken across the lines and the verse may be corrupt: the yoni in line 3 is where flies and ants enter, which can be the womb one is born from or the dead body's orifices. The close is a direct denial of the medical Siddhars' claim: there is no remedy against death.

reading: For the cold frost there is a tight rag; when hunger comes each day there is rice in every house for you to eat; when the thought rises there are good women for hire in the streets of this world. Why, heart, have you grown weary, always wounding yourself?
nuance: The third line is the surprise: the beggar's inventory of 329 and 344 here includes women for hire. It can be read straight, as a Siddhar's refusal of the ascetic's sexual anxiety, or as the heart's own argument quoted against it, since the heart is reproached for wounding itself. The verse does not resolve it, and I leave both.

reading: There are rivers and groves, fine streets and the hall itself; there is water, a rag and a long loincloth, day after day; heart that wanders bewildered, there is going from house to house eating rice, sleeping, and then simply being still; there is joy in that too.
nuance: சும்மா இருக்க, to be simply still, is the Siddhars' and later Tamil mystics' name for the state without effort; here it comes after eating and sleeping as the last item on a list of ordinary things, so the highest state is made the plainest.

reading: To wear and to cover, when cold wind and sun press close, there is an old dhoti to keep them off; to lie down there are outer porches everywhere in the whole world; when hunger comes there is Siva to give. Heart, we have no lack.
nuance: The inventory is the same as 329 and 344, but the giver is named: Siva gives when hunger comes, so the begging bowl is held out to the Lord, not to householders. குறைவில்லை, no lack, is the beggar's word of plenty.

reading: 'There are cattle, calves and children': all such rejoicing, we have heard, ends in ruin; now listen, heart. We have a bowl and a rag, the five letters to recite within, and the devotees of the Lord with the earring as our companions too.
nuance: தோடுண்ட கண்டன் is read as the Lord who wears the earring, after தோடுடைய செவியன்; கண்டன் may also be 'the one of the throat' (that held the poison). The inventory adds two things the earlier ones lacked: the mantra inside and the devotees outside.

reading: Do those who have left the great states and the bewilderment of the city of maya have any fixed observance? Loving the Eternal, when they sweat they bathe, when hungry they eat, they close their eyes and sleep; looked at, those free of attachment are just like the people of the world.
nuance: மாத்தான அவத்தை is unclear: the great states (the avasthas of the soul, as in 353) or great hardship. நிஷ்டை is fixed practice or a vow; the verse says the detached have none, and that from outside they are indistinguishable from the worldly, which turns the usual complaint about sham ascetics inside out.

reading: Hold that there is one; hold that God exists; hold that all high wealth is nothing; look at the face of the hungry; hold that good virtue and friendship are good; without leaving the middle, be always as it has been set for us. Heart, this is the teaching for you.
nuance: The teaching is in the imperative இரு, 'be', repeated for each clause, so it is a way of standing rather than a doctrine. ஒன்றென்றிரு may be 'be one' or 'hold that it is one'; நமக்கிட்டபடி, as set for us, accepts what is apportioned, the Kural's ஊழ், without naming it.

reading: Hold the feet of the true guru as your aim and trust them; hold the wretched body as a puppet show; hold the crowd of kin as a heap of rags pressed together, and life as water from an overturned pot. Heart, this is the teaching for you.
nuance: The second உபதேசம் verse gives one positive item, the guru's feet, and three figures for what to let go: the body as a doll dance, kin as bundled rags, life as water running out. குடங்கவிழ் நீர் is the pot tipped over: once it has started to pour, nothing holds it.

reading: Nothing whatever is my doing; now, God, I have come to know that all is your doing. Since I took up this flesh I have done no evil deed; is it then the evil done before this birth that has come and blazed up like this?
nuance: The two halves sit uneasily: all is the Lord's doing, yet what has come upon him is explained by his own deeds in a former birth. The verse does not reconcile them; it holds the Saiva position that karma is the Lord's instrument without saying so.

reading: Taking a holy guise and walking the street, he came seeking me and said with kindness, 'give alms'; I bowed at the feet of that one. Was it to take me, who was minded to reach the shore of the sea that is the womb, and make me into a form of his own, that Siva came like this?
nuance: The beggar at the door who turns out to be Siva is the poet's initiation as tradition tells it. கருவாகும் ஏதக் கடற்கரை is obscure: the shore of the sea of birth, which the poet wished to reach, or a fault (ஏதம்) of the womb. உருவாக்கிக் கொள்ள, to make into his own form, is the guru making the disciple like himself.

reading: I have left the world; I do not desire; I will not go near the vain with their two deeds, nor listen to their words, which are ruin; I have touched the state in which truth does not decay; I have cast off joy and sorrow; and the Supreme that the ancient four Vedas say they do not reach has come to me here.
nuance: The verse is a series of first-person perfects, the poet's own account of arrival, unusual in a chapter of questions and exhortations. நான்மறைக்கும் எட்டேன் எனும் பரம், the Supreme that says even to the four Vedas 'I am not reached', comes of itself (வந்து எய்தியது), so the reaching is the Lord's.

reading: Having left and climbed past the eight-limbed yoga, the six supports and the five states, in the open space I saw one wonder: growing round and drinking the milk that wells from the red moon, rejoicing, a great bliss that cannot be cut has swallowed me.
nuance: The verse lists the yogic system (ashtanga, the six adharas, the five avasthas) only to pass beyond it; the open space (வெளி) is the same term as 304. செம்மதிப் பாலூறல், the milk welling from the red moon, is the Siddhars' cipher for the nectar held to drip from the moon-centre at the head, as tradition reads it; வட்டாகி, becoming round, may be the moon's fullness or the poet's. The bliss swallows the poet, not the poet the bliss.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: The middle run of Pattinathar's general (பொது) verses: the body is a stinking frame that fire, worms, earth, kites, jackals and dogs each call their own, that mother, wives and sons abandon at the pyre, and that lust for women, whose every part stinks, keeps the mind bound to. Against it the poet sets the beggar's wealth (a loincloth, a bowl, the outer verandah, the five letters, holy ash), the renunciant who lives like a ghost and a corpse and a child, and a worship that has no drawn chakra, no spoken mantra, no built lingam, taught by the guru.
structure_note: The verses are addressed by turns to the body (354, 364, 375), to the poet's own heart (361, 365, 368, 370, 373), to the Lord (356, 366, 377) and to the townsfolk (367). Lists are the chapter's form: what claims the corpse (354), what the beggar owns (357, 360), what stinks (359), what the renunciant resembles (363), what the ritualist does (372), what the body is not for (377), what inner worship lacks (378). Several verses close on the refrain உனைப்போல் இல்லை பித்தரும் / பித்தனும் (361, and 388 in the next chapter).
source_issues: 370 line 2 தொடைப்பு is doubtful; the expected third act of the three gods (destruction) is not clearly named.
376 line 3 பேயும் நடனமிடுங் கடமாம் is obscure; கடம் may be a corrupt word.
378 line 2 இனிமுடிந்து sits awkwardly between the water and the lingam and may belong to another line.

reading: Fire says 'it is mine', the worm says 'mine', this earth says 'mine', the kite says 'mine, to eat', the jackal says 'mine', the base dog says 'mine': this stinking body I reared with love, and what gain do I have from it?
nuance: The six claimants are the six ends of a corpse: cremation, decay, burial, and the scavengers of the burning ground. The verse's bite is in பிரியமுடன் வளர்த்தேன், that the poet fed with love what was never his but already spoken for.

reading: This town where the Lord's street is the king's seat, where the ornamented soldiers and the command of the thirty-six (four nines) reach, with its kitchen comfort for sudden hunger: countless ages we have let it go to waste, past counting.
nuance: The verse reads as cipher: இவ்வூர், this town, is taken by tradition as the body, with the Lord's street its central channel and நாலொன்பது, four nines, the thirty-six tattvas as the soldiers who serve it. A plain reading, a real town with a royal street, garrison and alms-kitchen wasted for ages, is possible but makes the number idle. The last line, that incalculable time has been lost, is the same on either reading.

reading: The mothers who bore me reviled me as a corpse and left; the wives who got my gold said 'go' and wailed and left; the sons I got went round behind me and broke the pot; so, Lord, apart from clinging to you there is no clinging at all.
nuance: குடம் உடைத்தல் is the funeral rite in which the son circles the pyre and breaks the water pot, the last act of kinship. The three lines run through the three bonds of a man's life and end each at the burning ground; the conclusion is not grief but a transfer of attachment to the one party who does not leave.

reading: Unstained teeth, a loincloth of rag, a heart patient and without guile, poor food, the outer verandah, sleeping on the ground and the bowl one begs with: the great Veda calls out, so the world may know, that this is wealth without lack.
nuance: கறையற்ற பல் may be teeth unstained by betel, a mark of the man who has given up the householder's pleasures, or simply clean. The claim that the Veda itself proclaims this is the poet's authority for inverting wealth; the list is of things anyone could have, so the wealth is in wanting nothing more.

reading: The light that stands as one in the eight directions and sixteen corners, everywhere, surging and sprouting and rising high: fools all bind it and roll it up and keep it under their arm, and do not keep it in thought; they are the wrongdoers who call broad day night.
nuance: கட்டிச் சுருட்டித் தங்கக் கக்கத்தில் வைப்பர் is the gesture of tying up palm-leaf books and carrying them under the arm, so the fools are the learned who hold the all-pervading light as a text and not in the heart. எட்டுத் திசையும் பதினாறு கோணமும் may be a plain figure for everywhere or a yantra's eight directions and sixteen petals; the sense does not turn on it.

reading: The mouth stinks of spittle, the knotted hair stinks, the kohl-painted eyes stink, the body stinks of excrement, the great pit of the mouth stinks like a burst corpse, the yoni stinks of pus, the mud of the senses stinks and spills: how did the mind cling to women like this?
nuance: A catalogue of disgust in the manner of the Naladiyar's body verses, aimed not at women as such but at the mind that chose them (மனம் பற்றியதே). The word நாறும் is repeated seven times; the verse argues by smell alone.

reading: I have the good five holy letters to say, and say them as told; I have holy ash to wear with pride; from the street rubbish heap I have a rag to wear as a loincloth; I have resolved to beg from any caste: there is nothing I lack.
nuance: எந்தச் சாதியிலும் இரக்க, to beg from any caste, is the renunciant's indifference to who gives the food, and so a quiet refusal of caste rules on eating. The verse answers 357: the same inventory, now in the first person.

reading: You have suffered, and still you have not come to know, 'this is what will befall me next'; you have not gone to the good; with petty understanding you were tormented; in the bewitchment of young women's arts you were made a fool, O heart; there is no madman like you.
nuance: மடமானார் கல்வி மயக்கம் is read here as the spell cast by women's accomplishments; it could also be the delusion of learning in general, with மடமானார் as a separate object of torment. பாடு in line 1 is what one undergoes, so படும் பாட்டை is the coming suffering, not a song.

reading: Free of craving, free of hard deeds, free of kin and of occupations, free of the hidden hand-holding of women, free of worry, praising with a full mouth the Lord who comes, the mind subdued and no spreading out: is that not, Supreme One, supreme bliss?
nuance: The verse defines bliss by subtraction, six அற்று (free of) in a row, before the one positive act of praise. பரப்பற்று, without spreading, is the mind not reaching outward; the whole is a description of the renunciant's state rather than an instruction.

reading: They wander like ghosts, lie like corpses, eat whatever alms are given like dogs, roam like jackals, regard good women as their mother, speak humbly to everyone as to kin, and stay like children: see, these are the ones clear in true knowledge.
nuance: The seven comparisons are to what the world despises (ghost, corpse, dog, jackal) and to what it protects (mother, kin, child); the jnani is placed outside honour on both sides. The verse is a portrait of the poet's own way of life, as 357 and 360 are.

reading: Prey for kites, feast for vultures, twist made by the vain one with the water pot, dwelling where worms come to stay, carcass without any good, bondage that even the mother who bore it will not touch once the instruments go slack: I have carried you, and what pleasure is there in you for me?
nuance: கமண்டல வீணன் is Brahma with his water pot, called a wastrel for making this body; முடக்கு, a bend or twist, is the crooked thing he made. கருவி, the instruments, are the senses and organs; when they fail the body becomes untouchable even to its mother. Addressed to the body, as 354 and 375 are.

reading: What use is weeping, what use is grieving, it does not help; what use is worshipping; what use is the harm of someone speaking to burn you; will good and evil come otherwise than as the lotus-born one wrote? Do not be shaken, my poor heart.
nuance: The verse puts worship (தொழுதல்) in the same list as weeping and grief, as things that cannot change what Brahma has written. This is a counsel of steadiness, not of fatalism as a doctrine: its point is சலியாதிரு, do not waver, and the fate argument is the reason given.

reading: Not following the rich and talking them up and showing my teeth every day in anguish, let me enter within the bounds of supreme bliss, rightly solitary, and stay free of trouble in the place that is mine, O rare substance in the banyan's shade.
nuance: ஆலநீழல் அரும்பொருள் is Dakshinamurti, the silent teacher under the banyan, the fitting addressee for a prayer to be left alone. பல்லினைக் காட்டி, baring the teeth, is the forced smile of the dependent; the verse refuses patronage, not wealth as such.

reading: Townsfolk, hear a teaching for you: smear over your whole body the ash that sent the Jains to the stake, lie on the outer verandah, leave the tangle of kin and let the world laugh; the Lord himself will give you his twin feet.
nuance: சமணைக் கழுவேற்று நீறு is the holy ash of Sambandar's Madurai contest, after which the Jains were impaled, so the ash is named by its victory. The teaching is the poet's own practice (357, 360) offered to the town, with ridicule (சக நகைக்க) counted as part of the method.

reading: What is it to put on ash, what is it to go and bathe, my heart, when you have not learned the way to be born differently; what did you see of the seven crore mantras loaded in the great Veda-book; lying in the river, you drift without knowing the ford.
nuance: மாற்றிப் பிறக்க வகை, the way to change one's birth, is the thing the rites and the Veda have not given; ஆற்றிற் கிடந்தும் துறை அறியாமல் makes the river both the bathing place and the river of birth. The verse does not reject ash and bathing, it says they are no use without the knowing.

reading: If one knows the fruit of the single seed that came and sprouted rightly in the drop that stood as Om, then the fourteen worlds, without leaving, leave; one fills the unfilled and becomes the filled form; and for those who were ego, the Eight-fold one comes near and stays.
nuance: The verse is cipher throughout. ஓங்காரமாய் நின்ற அந்து (bindu) and the seed sprouting in it is the manifestation of the world from Om and bindu, as tradition reads it, or the forming of the body from the drop in the womb; both are Siddhar readings and the poet may intend both. எட்டர் is taken as Siva of the eight forms (அட்டமூர்த்தி); ஆங்காரமானவர்க்கு, for those who were ahankara, is read as 'even for the egoists', though it may be those who have become the I-sound. The sense turns on these terms and the reading given is a tradition, not the verse's plain statement.

reading: Brahma's creating, Vishnu's protecting and the hurling (of destruction) by the lord of wide Kailasa will not come near us; take supreme bliss as your goal, hold all the rest as a dream in sleep and do not regard it, my heart; see, this is good medicine for you.
nuance: தொடைப்பு is hard; it may be the Kailasa lord's act of throwing down, i.e. destruction, completing the three gods' three acts, or a corruption. The claim is that one who takes bliss as the goal is outside the whole cycle of creation and dissolution; the dream figure makes the world unreal only relative to that.

reading: The dog has the stick and we have alms; to defeat Death we have the five-letter mantra in the mouth; for ghosts that come without regard we have ash; for the bewildered disease of birth we have the gracious look of the teacher's eye.
nuance: A verse of remedies, each உண்டு (there is) matched to a threat. The first line is self-mocking: what the beggar gets at the door is placed beside what the dog gets. The last, the guru's glance (அருள் நோக்கம்) curing the disease of rebirth, is the Saiva teaching of initiation by sight.

reading: Observances, vows, the Vedas, the Agamas, the way of right conduct, fire rites, water offerings, the twilight prayers, japa, mantra, the states of yoga, the names, sandal and holy ash put on with care, and the pujas these people do at every watch of the day: all of it is pretence.
nuance: சர்ப்பனை is read as சற்பனை, fabrication, so the whole list is false show. The list is wide enough to include யோக நிலை and the five names, which the poet elsewhere prizes (360, 371); the attack may fall on these people (இவர் செய்யும்) rather than on the practices. Whether the verse condemns the rites or their performers is open.

reading: However much sense I talked, you did not listen, good heart; why do you go astray like this and ruin yourself; like one who casts a strong hook for the fish in the sky where nothing is, you think of getting back what is gone: what sense is this?
nuance: வானத்தின் மீன், the fish in the sky, is a star (மீன் means both), so the hook thrown at it is desire for what cannot be reached. போனத்தை மீள நினைத்தல், wanting back what has passed, may be lost wealth, youth or past pleasures; the verse does not say.

reading: With the axe called the five letters I cut out at the root the stump of the five senses, the deceiving field of sense; I tilled and improved the ground, planted the knowledge called Sadasiva, pulled the weeds of the crowd, and raised the crop of Siva's enjoyment.
nuance: An extended farming figure: clearing, tilling, sowing, weeding, harvest. புஞ்சக் களை may be the weeds of the senses' crowd or the dry-land weeds; either way they are what grows back after the stump is cut. சிவபோகம், Siva-enjoyment, is the harvest, so the verse ends in bliss, not in bare renunciation.

reading: On the day you sink and mother, kin and wife cast you off and say 'who are you, who am I', at that very moment diseases come and settle in; and besides the disease you have taken on and a mat, what friend have you, O body?
nuance: நீயார் நானார், 'who are you, who am I', is the formula of disowning. The friends left at the end are a disease and a mat: the verse is addressed to the body and tells it that its own company deserts it before death, not only after.

reading: Look closely: in every hair-pore worms crowd and soak; when the body that has become a dung pit is burned, even the ghosts dance there, people say; did you not know this, and yet you thought of hunting wealth?
nuance: கடம் ஆம் is read as the body becoming a (burning) ground where ghosts dance; the line may instead say the body is a pot (கடம்). The argument is that seeking wealth for a body of this kind is the folly, not wealth itself.

reading: Not fit to wear as ornament, not for gold, not for seeing the earth, not for women, not for good sights, not for the feet of Siva who is beyond the far: with my thought ruined, the trouble this servant takes to rear a span of body is not small.
nuance: The body is weighed against every use, worldly and divine, and found fit for none, the last (சிவனடிக்கு அல்ல) being the surprise: even for the Lord's feet it is no instrument. சாண், a span, is the body's measure of contempt.

reading: A chakra not drawn, a mantra not spoken, a flower no one else can reach, holy water that does not run dry, a lingam not built once this is ended, a heart that does not think: puja that does not fail, within the thought itself: is that not what the guru taught?
nuance: Each item of outer worship (yantra, mantra, flower, water, lingam) is named by what it is not, so the puja is wholly inward; கருதாத நெஞ்சம், the heart that does not think, makes even the inner act an absence. இனிமுடிந்து is hard to place: 'henceforth, finished' or 'once this body ends'. The authority claimed is the guru's word, not the poet's own.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: The close of the general verses: birth is leaving the Lord's feet to enter the womb-egg, household life is maya's visible form that turns to an old tale, the body is a fortress of ego, anger and lust that no medicine or knowledge can mend and that is fit only for fire. The remedies are the company of devotees, love of Hara's worship, tears before the beginningless one, the guru who takes the poet as his subject, and the two bright feet held within against stone, plaster and copper.
structure_note: The heart (நெஞ்சே) is addressed in 381, 384, 386 and 388, the last closing on the refrain of 361, உனைப்போல் இல்லை பித்தனும். 385 and 387 are the chapter's two verdicts on the body, as useless and as disgusting, and 389 is a closing profession, the poet's own account of what he keeps and what he will not praise.
source_issues: 379 line 1 பிட்கின் is an unusual form, read as பிளக்கின் (when split).
387 line 3 is broken by the line division: பொய்யன்றுகா / னானாலும் should read பொய்யன்று காணானாலும்.

reading: Who weeps for the dung beetle's eggs that fall when the dung is split? Entering the womb-egg you went far from the Feet, and now you fools blubber like people struck by heavy loss; chant every day the name of Hara, which breaks every obstacle and gives release.
nuance: எருமுட்டை and கருமுட்டை are set against each other: no one mourns the beetle's eggs, but the human egg (the embryo) is a real loss, since it is the leaving of the Lord's feet. ஒரு முட்டும் வீட்டும் is read as 'breaks every obstacle (முட்டு)' with the pun on வீடு, release; the word play makes the exact sense open. The weeping fools may be mourners at a death or all who grieve.

reading: Kohl-eyed wife, sons, livelihood, house: Lord of the red fire, in this world of your maya's appearances in open form, what was real day after day, as the days went by, slowly went away as a plain lie, an old tale, a dream.
nuance: உருவெளித்தோற்றம், apparitions in the open, is a term for mirage-like seeing; the household is not denied but reclassified. The three words for its end, பொய், பழங்கதை, கனவு, mark a gradient from falsehood to memory to sleep.

reading: Having examined many arts and even gone to the pure great ascetics, you did not learn the truth; on this earth you fell and sank into the lust-disorder of bamboo-shouldered women and stare like a ghost: what madness is yours, my heart?
nuance: The heart had the two ordinary means, learning and the company of the holy, and both failed because the question of truth was never asked. பேயாய் விழிக்கின்றனை, staring like a ghost, is the dazed look of the possessed; the same word is used of the ascetic at 363, so possession can be by lust or by the Lord.

reading: Apart from the fellowship of devotees, love of Hara's worship and love, is there any gain on this earth? Kin, wife and livelihood, the household Brahma ordained, are like clay pots struck with a stick; yet people have not joined that company.
nuance: குயக்கலம் தடியால் அடியுண்டவாறு, pots beaten with a stick, is both the pot that breaks and the potter's own beating of his wares, so the household breaks as it was made to. இனம், the company, is the devotees named in line 1.

reading: Treasury of ego, granary of anger, palace that pride never leaves, hall built of lies, high rampart grown to the sky, mansion of lust: this body is a rag; bowing to you fittingly, how is wisdom to bear fruit?
nuance: The body is a fortified city, each building a vice. உனைப் பணிந்து is ambiguous: bowing to the Lord in such a body, or bowing to the body itself by serving it; the first makes the verse a complaint that worship in this frame cannot ripen, the second a reproach. கந்தல், rag, undercuts the fortress.

reading: Heart that has taken unending births and wandered, sighing and sighing: hear the medicine for the state that does not perish; think in the mind of the beginningless one, the one with axe and deer in his hands, who rides the great bull, let water pour from your eyes, sob and weep, asking only for good.
nuance: அவுடதம், medicine, is the Sanskrit word used for the remedy of rebirth; what it prescribes is thought and tears, not a formula. அனாதி here is an epithet of Siva as the one without beginning; the verse's cure is to hold the beginningless in the mind that has a beginning in every womb.

reading: Is there a medicine anywhere in the land for a dog's pregnancy? Can a ghost get hold of knowledge? Who would cook or who would eat a great strychnine fruit? Likewise this body: apart from being fuel for fire, tell me what it is for.
nuance: Three impossibilities, a cure for what is natural, learning for what cannot learn, and food from what is poison, make the body's uselessness a matter of kind rather than of degree. The verse is not that the body is bad, but that no use can be found for it.

reading: Poor heart, who with sidelong glances falling on the heavy breasts in the bodice stands in desire: stitch yourself to the feet of him who shares his side with Unnamulai, the fresh green creeper borne of Himavan; mind, there is never any fault in that.
nuance: The remedy for desire for a woman's breast is the goddess Unnamulai (she of the unsuckled breast) at Siva's side, so the verse answers lust with the one female figure it will allow. தைச்சுக்கிட, sew yourself in, is a strong image of attachment transferred rather than removed.

reading: I crossed over the glances of deer-eyed women and came; the living guru became my king and settled me in as his subject; there is no fault; whether I go or the gain remains, this good gain is no lie; and even so, staying on in this body is disgust.
nuance: குடியேற்றிக் கொண்டனன், settled me as a tenant, is the king's act of resettling subjects on his land, so the guru is a king who gives the poet a place. போனாலும் பேறிருந்தாலும் is hard: whether the poet dies or the attainment stays, or whether he goes away or remains. The last line keeps the body's disgust even after the guru's gift, so the verse holds both.

reading: You do not know yourself even a little; you will not fit to speak with those who have examined themselves, even when you reach them; you do not hold the state that is yours; you do not bow to the guru; you went to the harlots and got what you got; foolish heart, there is no madman like you.
nuance: Four refusals (self-knowledge, the company of the self-knowing, one's own state, the guru) and one act (going to the courtesans), with the refrain of 361. உனக்கான நிலை, the state that is yours, is the soul's own condition as against what it has taken up.

reading: The chiselled stone, the moulded plaster and the copper scrubbed with tamarind until it shines: I do not praise them as fine gold; that keeping the two shining feet within is the truth, I have made known, and shut them in and kept them; henceforth I want nothing else.
nuance: The three materials are the three kinds of image, stone, stucco and metal, and the tamarind-scrubbed copper is the processional image polished for the festival. The poet does not say the images are nothing, only that he will not praise them as gold; what he keeps is the feet, held inside and locked.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: The venbas Pattinathar is said to have sung while performing his mother's cremation: ten months of carrying, the breast, the cradle, the shoulder, the voice that called him honey and nectar, set against the firebrand he must now put to her head and the rice he must put in her mouth. The renunciant who has disowned every bond finds the one debt he cannot repay, and the series ends by naming the four fires, Tripura, Lanka, the fire she lit in his belly and the one he lights, and by declaring that the mother who sat in state yesterday and is ash today is, like everything, Siva.
structure_note: The editorial heading on 390 to 395 (தாயாருக்குத் தகனகிரியை செய்கையிற் பாடிய வெண்பா) is a modern editor's, as are the metre labels. 390 to 393 are four parallel venbas, each a list of what the mother did ending in the question of what the son now does (தீ மூட்டுவேன்); 394 and 395 are a pair on the mouth-rice and the firebrand; 396 is a single viruttam of four fires; 397 to 399 move from the burning to the question of where she went to the closing எல்லாம் சிவமயம்.
source_issues: The heading on 390 to 395 (தாயாருக்குத் தகனகிரியை செய்கையிற் பாடிய வெண்பா) and the metre labels on 396 to 399 are a modern editor's and not the poet's.
397 has the venba's third line run into the second after the dash (மாகக் குருவிபறவாமற்கோதாட்டியென்னைக்), so the line break is lost.
398 line 4 றன்னையயீன்றெடுத்ததாய் doubles the ய: read தன்னை ஈன்றெடுத்த தாய் (or என்றன்னை ஈன்றெடுத்த).
399 line 4 is spaced (எல்லாஞ் சிவமயமே யாம்) unlike the rest of the work, which is printed without word breaks; it may have been set apart by the editor.

reading: For ten months, every limb aching, she bore and gave birth, and the moment they said 'a boy' she lifted me with care in her two red hands and gave me her golden breast: in what birth shall I see her again?
nuance: The closing question, எப்பிறப்பிற் காண்பேன், is not answered; it can be grief (never again) or the renunciant's literal doubt whether any birth will bring her back. The verse itself only counts what she gave.

reading: She first lay in penance, then carried me three hundred days, worshipped Siva day and night, and bore me with her belly sagging as she carried: for that mother am I to kindle the burning flame?
nuance: முந்தித் தவங்கிடந்து is the penance undertaken for a child before conception, so the mother's giving begins before the pregnancy. The question தமக்கோ எரியத் தழல் மூட்டுவேன் is rhetorical in form but the son does light the fire; the verse is the cost, not a refusal.

reading: In the dish, in the cradle, on her chest, on her shoulder and on the bed she set me and loved me, folded me under her wing and guarded me and dandled me: for that mother am I to set fire to the firewood?
nuance: The five places are the stages of an infant's day, and சிறகிலிட்டு, under the wing, makes the mother a bird. The venba's second half repeats 391's turn to the pyre almost word for word; the four verses vary the list and keep the question.

reading: She bore me in pain and gave birth, held me so I would not hurt, gave the breast, raised me and lifted me without tiring, carried me in her arms day and night and kept me safe: for that mother am I to set fire to her body?
nuance: மெய்யிலே தீ மூட்டுவேன், fire to the body itself, is the barest of the four endings; the earlier verses said the flame or the firewood. The progression across 391 to 393 moves the fire closer to her.

reading: Am I to put rice into the mouth that, without taking pleasure in setting out portions and sharing them, called me 'honey, nectar, wealth, treasure, my deer': is that the rice I shall give?
nuance: அரிசி இடுதல் is the funeral rite of placing rice in the corpse's mouth (வாய்க்கரிசி); the verse turns on the irony that the mouth which fed him with names now receives a handful of raw grain. Line 2, வரிசையிட்டுப் பாத்து மகிழாமல், is hard: it may mean she did not stop to portion food out for others, giving all to him, or that she took no pleasure in being served herself.

reading: Is it rice that I scoop and put in, mother? Shall I set the firebrand on your head without flinching, on the mouth that softly laid face against face, kissed me and called 'my son'?
nuance: The pair of 394, now with the firebrand (கொள்ளி) added to the rice; கூசாமல், without shrinking, is the one word for the son's own state, and it is a question. The two rites, rice and fire, are the chief mourner's duties, and the eldest son's.

reading: The fire set of old on the three cities, the fire set afterwards on southern Lanka, the fire my mother set in the pit of my belly, and the fire I now set: let them all blaze, let them blaze.
nuance: Two fires are the gods' (Siva's at Tripura, Hanuman's at Lanka) and two are the family's. அன்னை இட்ட தீ அடிவயிற்றிலே, the fire the mother set in the belly, is read by tradition as the fire of grief she has left him by dying, or as the fire of hunger and birth itself that she gave by bearing him; both are Siddhar readings. மூள்க மூள்க, let it blaze, is the mourner's cry turned into consent, and the verse is sometimes read as the moment his renunciation becomes complete.

reading: It burns in the fire, it is burnt and turns to powder and ash, alas for me, sinner: the hand that cherished me and raised me, that dandled me so that the great bird would not fly away.
nuance: மாகக் குருவி பறவாமல், so that the sky-bird would not fly, is read as the mother guarding the infant's life (உயிர் as a bird that may leave the body), an image the Kural also uses; it may instead be a lullaby's bird. The verse watches a single part, the hand, go to ash.

reading: Has she burned, O skilful one of Sonagiri? Has she come to your feet? Has she forgotten me? The mother who bore me, who always looked to you and lay in longing for a boon.
nuance: சோணகிரி is Arunachala (Tiruvannamalai), so the mother is a devotee of that Lord, and the three questions run from the body (burned) to the soul (at your feet) to the bond (forgotten me). The last is the son's, not the ascetic's; the verse does not resolve it.

reading: She sat in state; she lay in the street; she was here yesterday and today has burned and become ash; without grieving 'come, all of you, to sprinkle the milk', all is Siva.
nuance: பாற்றெளித்தல் is the rite of sprinkling milk on the ashes the day after cremation, so the invitation refused is the last duty of mourning. எல்லாம் சிவமயம், everything is Siva, is the chapter's conclusion and the one line set apart in the text; it answers 398's questions by dissolving them, and it makes the mother's ash not less than Siva.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: Twelve venbas on shrines (Idaimarudur, Tiruvottriyur, Tiruvarur, Kanchi, Kalatti, Viruppaiyur, Tiruvaiyaru, Kutralam), each a single plea tied to the place: when will the night of eating and thirsting end, the dust of the devotees' feet is the medicine for the nine-mouthed wound, the pilgrims running from festival to festival seek fire while the lamp burns, how many mothers and names must there be, let no other womb take me, and say the Lord's name before Death, the blind eye and the townsfolk's fire arrive.
structure_note: The place names in the margin (இடைமருது, ஒற்றி, திருவாரூர், திருக்காஞ்சி, கச்சிக்காரோணம், திருக்காளத்தி, திருவிருப்பையூர், திருவையாறு, குற்றாலம்) are the shrines each venba names in its last foot, as the தலப்பாடல் form requires. 400 and 407 are the hunger verses, 402 and 405 the body verses, 406, 409 and 410 the rebirth verses (409 and 410 are a pair on the tired mother, the tired Brahma and the poet's tired feet), and 411 the close, which 412 to 430 in the next chapter continue at Kutralam.
source_issues: 402 line 4 has asterisks in the text (பெ*ரு*வாரடியிற்பொடி), an editor's mark of a doubtful reading; பெருவார் அடியிற் பொடி, the dust at the feet of the great, is assumed.
The place names printed beside the ids are editorial labels taken from each venba's last foot.
406 line 2 வேனென்றே / னித்த is broken by the line division: read வேண்டேன் என்றேன் நித்தம்.

reading: Chewing, swallowing, then seeking water to put out the thirst: when will the dawn come for me, my King, Marudha who burned the three cities of those who did not think on the good, now that I have come to your presence?
nuance: The round of eating and drinking stands for the whole of embodied life, and என்று விடியும், when will it dawn, makes that life a night. The verse asks the Lord of Idaimarudur for release from the body's needs, not for food.

reading: Black-throated, three-eyed, beautiful like the cosmic egg, a sugarcane standing by the sea at Ottri of rising fame, that is sweet so that the bodies of his servants melt.
nuance: The one verse of the chapter that asks nothing: a description of the Lord of Tiruvottriyur as sugarcane, the standard figure for sweetness, with the body's melting (உடல் உருக) as the devotee's response. அண்டத்தைப் போல அழகியது compares the Lord to the cosmic egg, as the whole.

reading: For the wound with nine mouths that drips with discharge and stinks, I have come to know the medicine: the dust at the feet of the great ones in the street of Tiruvottriyur of the god of gods who ate the poison.
nuance: The body is a single wound with nine openings, and the cure is not a drug but the dust of the devotees' feet, which the poet knows as a fact (அறிந்துகொண்டேன்). கடு அருந்தும் தேவாதிதேவன் is Siva who drank the halahala poison, so the Lord who took in poison presides over the cure.

reading: All the tanks are holy water, all the sand is white ash, all the groves are the Lord's attendant hosts: this on earth is Siva's world, say the true ascetics again and again, Tiruvottriyur.
nuance: A shrine praise in the ordinary manner, with the three things found at any place (water, sand, trees) renamed as the three things of Saiva worship (holy water, ash, the ganas). The authority is the true ascetics (மெய்த்தவத்தோர்), not the poet.

reading: While the Lord of Arur is right here, you wander from town to town saying 'it is the festival in that town'; see, you are mutes who never seek the sign within; while the lamp is burning, you go looking for fire.
nuance: ஆரூரர் இங்கிருக்க has a plain and a coded reading: the Lord of Tiruvarur is here in this shrine, so why run to other towns' festivals; or the Lord is here within the body (உளக்குறிப்பு, the inner sign, in line 3), so why go anywhere. The lamp and the fire make the second reading the stronger, since the lamp is what the seeker already carries. Both readings stand.

reading: For the womb-mouth that sits two fingers above the dung-mouth you let your eyes be troubled; you lie dead in Tiruvarur's chariot street, you, for a stream of running water.
nuance: The verse locates the object of lust by its distance from the anus and names it by what passes through it, in the manner of 359. நீரோடும் தாரைக்கா நீ, 'for a channel of running water', is the one phrase in doubt: the urine passage, or the stream of tears; the plain reading is the first. செத்துக் கிடக்கின்றாய், you lie dead, is the poet's verdict on the man alive in the festival street.

reading: How many towns, how many houses, how many mothers who bore me, how many names given to call me: 'enough, enough', I said, yet every day you will not relieve my weariness, Ekamba, Ekamba; is it your holy play?
nuance: The count is of births, each with its own town, house, mother and name; எத்தனை four times makes the number itself the complaint. திருவிளையாட்டு, the Lord's play, is the Saiva account of why the world is as it is; the poet turns it into a question whether his rebirths are a game.

reading: Teacher who gladly gives to every living thing from the elephant to the ant: hunger presses hard on me, sinner that I am, Lord; it grips and wrings my ruined belly, Karonar.
nuance: The appeal is from the universal feeder to the one belly left out, and the belly is called பாழ் வயிறு, waste, as if hunger itself were a fault of the body. Read beside 416, where the poet refuses to go to food, the verse is the cost of that refusal.

reading: You will not give up lying, you will not leave off flesh, you will not think of the Lord of Kalatti, you will not do what is right, you will not give up hot anger, you will not recite the five holy letters: mind, what greatness have you?
nuance: Six refusals, three of them the moral commonplaces (truth, no flesh, no anger, right conduct) and two Saiva (thinking of the Lord, the five letters). The verse treats these as one list; the Kural's ethics and the mantra are not ranked.

reading: My mother's body is worn out, my legs are worn out from the strong deed, and Brahma's hand too is worn out: Lord, Siva who dwells at Viruppaiyur, keep me from going yet again into some other mother's womb.
nuance: Three parties tire: the mother who bears, Brahma who writes the fate on the forehead, and the soul that walks the round. வல்வினையேன், I of hard deeds, gives the cause of the walking, so the plea admits the births are earned.

reading: So that the earth's heat may cool, the sky's smoke may clear, the rare mother may rest, the hand of Brahma who composes may rest and this servant's feet may rest, look on me, Lord, Lord of Tiruvaiyaru.
nuance: The pair of 409, with the same three tired parties, and two more that are hard: மண்ணும் தணல் ஆற, வானும் புகை ஆற, the earth cooling and the sky's smoke clearing, may be the pyre's heat and smoke, so that the poet asks for a death that is the last, or the elements wearied by remaking him. கண் பார், look on me, asks only for the Lord's glance.

reading: Before Death comes, before the eyes film over, before the milk you drink runs out at the corners of the mouth, before the kin fall on you and weep, before the townsfolk burn you: speak the name of the Lord of Kutralam.
nuance: Five முன்னே, before, running from the far (Death's approach) to the near (the mouth that can no longer hold milk) and then past death to the mourners and the pyre. The thing to do in time is the smallest possible act, saying a name.

title: திருப்பாடல் திரட்டு (தலப் பாடல்கள்)
theme: The Kutralam verses that close the Thiruppadal Thirattu: the beggar's creed in its plainest form (worship, stay where you like, take alms, sleep at the temple gate, go to no one's house even when starving), the heart told again and again not to trust this birth after seeing the corpse hiccup, the pampered body burned on logs, the vultures tear the nine-mouthed bag and the loincloth stripped off kings; the three conches of birth, marriage and death; and three closing claims, that the freed mind stays in silence whatever the body does, that examining pollution itself reveals the one, and that the guru's one word made everything, earth, gods, man and woman, melt.
structure_note: The editorial labels split the chapter by metre: ordinary venbas (412 to 419), venbas with a galloping last line (பின்முடுகு, 420 to 430), a viruttam (431) and two stanzas of another metre (432, 433). The பின்முடுகு venbas 420 to 423 share one form, a question to the heart about rebirth followed by கண்டு, 'having seen', and a scene from the burning ground. 429, 426 and 433 are the chapter's doctrinal verses and stand apart from the exhortations.
source_issues: The metre labels (பொதுவெண்பா, பின்முடுகு வெண்பா, விருத்தம், இதுவுமதுவேறு) are a modern editor's headings.
417 has the venba's third line run into the second after the dash (பட்டதுபட் டெந்நேரமுஞ்சிவனையேத்துங்கள்போற்றுங்கள்), so the line break is lost.
418 line 3 கடம்பும் is doubtful in sense; read as the kadamba garland.
431 line 1 is spaced (நாப்பிளக்கப் பொய்யுரைத்து) unlike the rest of the work; 432 and 433 return to unspaced text.
432 is obscure throughout and may be corrupt; the reading given is a guess at a body-city cipher.

reading: While the little hall and Siva are close at hand, we went seeking an empty hall; every day the foolish, ignorant heart seeks the place it was born from, and the eye seeks the place it was milked.
nuance: சிற்றம்பலம் is the hall of the dance at Chidambaram and, as the Siddhars use it, the small space within where Siva dances; வெற்றம்பலம், the empty hall, is the world outside, or a pun on வெற்று, vain. பிறந்த இடம் and கறந்த இடம் are the womb and the breast, so the heart's lust and the eye's are named by their infant origins.

reading: Peacock-woman with the garland of opening buds, those who sought you have now gone; be calm; if you go seeking and think of me, I will kick you in the waist; and if I think of you, kick me.
nuance: A verse to a woman, possibly the poet's wife or a courtesan, with the renunciation made mutual and physical: the same kick for either party's lapse. தேறியிரு, be consoled, is the one kind word, and it concerns the other men who have left her.

reading: I do not crave alms that will not come past the doorstep, Lord; the whole time I have spent dying of desire is enough, Supreme One; tell me the knowledge that is beyond pointing.
nuance: வாசற்படி கடந்து வாராத பிச்சை is read as alms that are not brought out to the door, which the beggar will not go in to fetch (as 416 says outright); it may instead be alms that never leave the giver's house at all. சுட்டிறந்த ஞானம் is taken as knowledge that goes beyond சுட்டு, demonstration or pointing, a term for what cannot be indicated as 'this'; a plain reading, knowledge in which desire is burnt and dead, is also possible, and the pun may be intended.

reading: To worship well the one who wears the poisonous serpent, to stay wherever one pleases, to take alms and eat them, and to come and sleep at the holy gate: this alone is happiness.
nuance: The whole of the beggar's day in four items, with தானே சுகம், this itself is happiness, as the claim; 417 repeats the formula with praise of Siva as its content. The temple gate (திருவாயில்) is the bed, so the shrine is used as a shelter and not only as a place of worship.

reading: If someone seeks out the place where I am and brings food for my hunger with eagerness, I will eat; even if they call me with much insistence I will not go, Hara; even if the body wastes away, from now on I will not go.
nuance: A vow stricter than begging: the poet will not enter a house even when invited, and eats only what is carried to him. ஏகம் இளைத்தாலும், even if the body wastes, accepts starvation as the price, which 407 shows being paid.

reading: Once you let go, sorrow leaves; the moment the breath leaves, the kin set about burning the body; whatever happens, happens, so at every hour praise and worship Siva alone; I have said it: that itself is happiness.
nuance: விட்டுவிடப் போகும் துயர் puts the whole of release in one act of letting go; the kin's haste to burn is the reason. பட்டது படு, let what happens happen, is indifference to outcome rather than fate as a doctrine.

reading: Even if breath and body perish, do not earn on this earth the name of sinner; grand display and the garland are not wanted, foolish heart; go about like the dead.
nuance: கடம்பு is read as the kadamba garland, standing for finery; it may be a corrupt word. செத்தாரைப் போலே திரி, wander like the dead, is the Siddhars' formula for the jnani alive in the world and is the verse's whole instruction; the garland and display are what the dead do not want.

reading: Unknown even to the open void, unseen by orders and by cash in hand, not clinging to those who said 'hold on with love': the sweetness he set in the heart of this sinner, saying 'this'.
nuance: The verse is a single inverted sentence whose subject, the sweetness (இனிப்பு) the Lord placed in the heart, comes last. வெட்டவெளி, the open expanse, is the Siddhars' word for the void that is the Lord's place, so a sweetness hidden even from that is beyond the highest state as well as beyond money and command; the phrase பற்றென்றார் பற்றாது is hard and the reading given is a guess. இற்றென, 'as this', may be the guru's pointing or the Lord's.

reading: Would anyone trust this birth, my heart, while the hoard lies there and the wife is at the door, having seen, as in a dream, the hiccup, the clenched teeth, the eyes rolled up, the cotton stuffed in, and the bag choke, die and empty itself?
nuance: The first of four venbas (420 to 423) on the same frame: a question to the heart about birth, then கண்டு, having seen, and a death scene. Here the scene is the deathbed itself, each symptom a word, with the cotton (பஞ்சு) stuffed in the nostrils of the corpse.

reading: You wanted to live still longer, and did not know the nature of the rider of the white bull, my mind; having seen the body that was pampered with cushions for its hands and feet and a mattress, then struck and beaten, laid on logs and burned.
nuance: குத்தி மொத்தப்பட்ட, pierced and pounded, may describe the sick body's treatment (massage, surgery) or the corpse being pressed onto the pyre; either way the pampered body ends on the logs. சீலம், the Lord's nature, is what the mind should have known instead of wanting more life.

reading: You set your love on the leather bag with nine mouths as if each day were yesterday, my heart, and wandered, having seen the cruel vultures hop and hop, strike off the shirt of skin, bite, tear, peck, cut and eat.
nuance: ஒருநாளைப் போலவே, as on one day, is loving the body as if it never changed. The last line is the metre's gallop put to work, seven verbs of the vultures' eating in one breath; சட்டை, the shirt, is the skin they tear off.

reading: Do you still consent to be born again, my heart, having seen the double loincloth of those who lived as 'these are kings' stripped off and rolled up and thrown on a log that had already burned?
nuance: Even kings go to the fire with one cloth, and that is taken away and thrown on a used log, so the last possession is less than the fuel. இசைவையோ, do you consent, treats rebirth as something the heart agrees to, not something that merely happens.

reading: The first conch feeds milk; the middle conch fastens the fine shackle of the thick-haired women; the last conch sounds 'he is gone': is this, or that, the whole of the good we lived on earth?
nuance: The conch is the infant's milk feeder, the instrument blown at the wedding and the one blown at the funeral, so one object marks the three events; the shackle (விலங்கு) is marriage. முதல், நடு, கடை சங்கம் also name the three Tamil academies, and the pun makes a life as short as the record of the sangams.

reading: The body gathered over so many days, is all of it not food for the earth? Holding the feet of the skilful one, slowly, in the place where night and day are no more, we shall settle in the dwelling above.
nuance: மண்டின்பது is read as மண் தின்பது, what the earth eats, so the body collected over a life is returned to the ground that fed it. கங்குல் பகல் அற்ற இடம், where night and day have ceased, is the Siddhars' description of the state beyond the sun and moon of the body, taken plainly as release; மேலைக் குடியிருப்பு is the upper dwelling, heaven or the head.

reading: Do not call things 'polluted' and talk of what is fit and unfit; you do not know where the pollution lives; if you examine the pollution itself and stay with it, oneness will show itself, and after that the mind will be free of all disease.
nuance: எச்சில் is saliva and the leavings of food, the ordinary thing that pollutes, and the Siddhars' test case for purity rules. The claim is that the rule's own object, examined, dissolves the rule into ஒருமை, oneness; what that oneness is (that all is equally polluted, or that pollution and purity are one) is not said. நிராமயம், without disease, is the Sanskrit term for the healthy or the Absolute, so the mind's cure and its freedom are one word.

reading: How many men have dug the pit, how many have touched the breast, how many have pulled at the lip; day after day they speak lies: leave the foolish women of this earth and be saved, be saved, be saved.
nuance: The three எத்தனை பேர் make the woman's body a shared thing, and the lies (பொய்) are what each man is told. உய்யடா repeated three times is the chapter's loudest line; the verse addresses men, and its target is the women who take many men, so it is about the courtesan rather than women as such, though it does not draw the line.

reading: Reckoning that staying is false and going is true, my heart, do not intend harm to anyone at all; while we hold the fat belly to be ours, the dogs, the jackals, the ghosts and the vultures hold it to be theirs.
nuance: The one verse of ethics toward others in the chapter, and it is grounded in impermanence: harming no one follows from the body not being one's own. The scavengers' claim repeats 354, now as a reason for conduct rather than a lament.

reading: Whatever work they do, whatever hardship they undergo, the minds of the freed stay in silence; skilfully, like the servant woman who comes playing and swinging both her arms as she walks, her mind is on the water pot on her head.
nuance: The figure of the water carrier is exact: the body is free to move and play because the attention is fixed elsewhere, and the pot does not fall. The verse frees the jnani's outer life from any required form, work or austerity, and so stands against the ascetic marks the poet himself lists elsewhere (357, 360); what is required is only where the mind is.

reading: In the evening she ground fragrant turmeric and bathed, took trouble and kept vigil, became pregnant, bore him, raised him, gave him a name; if the son she bore turns mad, what can she do after that?
nuance: பித்தன், the madman, is the God-mad renunciant the poet calls himself (361, 388), so the verse is his own mother's case stated as anyone's: the whole labour of motherhood undone by the son's renunciation, with no remedy. The turmeric bath and vigil are the woman's observances for conceiving, so the labour begins before the birth as at 391.

reading: Splitting your tongue with lies you seek the nine treasures, join women who know no good, split your lips with lies to them and beget children by the swarm, like termites; you do not know how to keep them and cannot abandon them; you have thrust your leg into the split of a wedged tree, like the monkey that shook loose the wedge: you are caught, caught to lie there and writhe.
nuance: The monkey that pulled out the wedge from a half-split log and was caught by the testicles is the opening fable of the Panchatantra; here it is the householder's own doing that traps him. புற்றீசல், the winged termites that swarm after rain and die the same night, is the figure for children bred without thought, and the verse's middle line, that one can neither keep them nor leave them, is the trap.

reading: The form, the self, youth, the daughter, the mother, the mother-in-law and those who took the ground: in a town, is it justice to celebrate blame? Is the newcomer a pauper, is the potter a dwarf, is the one standing in the middle an idler? The city has been plundered.
