source_issues: 633 ends மாண்டானே (he died) where the neighbouring units 634 and 635 end மாண்டேனே (I died); either the third person is deliberate or the vowel sign has dropped.
625 தலிராமல் is read as தளராமல்; the printed form is not a word.

reading: I expounded the sastras, which are mean words to men who have no skill in the word, and lost my own cleverness and was ruined.
nuance: Two readings of புன்சொல்: the sastras are poor words when given to men unable to take them, or the sastras themselves are poor words. சதுர் is skill or wit; the teacher lost what he set out to give.

reading: As my influence grew and grew, a new delusion came upon me; I stumbled and walked head downward and was ruined.
nuance: செல்வாக்கு is standing or influence rather than wealth as such; தலைகீழாய் நடந்து (walking upside down) is the picture of a life inverted by it.

reading: In the usual places of the world and in desire for land and gold, never slackening in habit, I lost the Lord and was ruined.
nuance: பதி is the Lord (Pati) and also a town or home; the refrain பதியிழந்து reads as losing the Lord and as losing one's place. தலிராமல் is read as தளராமல், not slackening.

reading: Saying 'all this rare earth, pegged with its boundary stakes, is our holding', I talked big and was ruined.
nuance: காணி is a land-holding; ஆணி the stake that marks it. The boast is of ownership of what is only staked out.

reading: Joining fools who had no conduct and talking pretence with them, I lost the Lord and was ruined.
nuance: பாசாங்கு is show or hypocrisy; the ruin is company and the speech it breeds, not any single deed.

reading: Joining the blind who had no guru's path, I lost my mind inside the path of the womb and was ruined.
nuance: குரு and குருடர் (the blind) play on each other. கருமார்க்கம் is the path of the womb (கரு), rebirth, or the path of action (கருமம், karma); both readings fit a verse that opposes the guru's way to it.

reading: Not thinking of the greatness of Hara who drank the poison, I took children and wives for real, lost the Lord and was ruined.
nuance: மெய் என்று, taking them as true or lasting, is the fault, not having them.

reading: Taking the great body that already smells of the corpse for real, through greed for money I lost the Lord and was ruined.
nuance: பிணவாசம் உற்ற, having the smell of a corpse, is said of the living body; the money-lust serves a body that is already dead.

reading: While the poets who saw me praised me heavily, the well-fed body puffed itself up and I was ruined.
nuance: உப்பரித்து, swelling, is of the body and the pride together; the praise is bought by feeding poets.

reading: Taking countless births I performed the worship of Siva and still did not escape; I lost the Lord and was ruined.
nuance: பிழையாமல் is 'without fault' or 'without escaping'; the first gives worship done faultlessly for countless lives that still lost the Lord, the second the same conclusion stated. Either way ritual worship repeated through births is what failed.

reading: The body that cannot bear even the touch of a small ant he handed over to be bound and burned, and he died.
nuance: The one verse in the third person; the man who shielded the body from an ant consents at the end to its tying and cremation. உறுக்க may also be 'to be reviled'.

reading: Without the sense to think that one's own body is one's own enemy, I took it for joy and died.
Skin, bone and flesh, and bones beside them grown on old rice: calling such bodies my kin, I swaggered and died.
nuance: மேல் எலும்பு, the other bones, are read as the bodies of relatives: kinship is one set of fed bones claiming another.

reading: With no dealings coming my way and no wealth coming in, I spoke wasted words, my mind churned, and I was ruined.
nuance: போக்குவரத்து is traffic or dealings and பொருள்வரத்து income; the verse may describe the poverty that followed ruin, or the anxiety of waiting for custom that never came. வாக்கழிவு, waste of speech, is idle or ruinous talk.

title: அருட்புலம்பல் - நெஞ்சொடுபுலம்பல்
theme: The first half of the plaint to the heart (நெஞ்சொடு புலம்பல்): Pattinathar tells his heart what it failed to do, praise the teacher who dances in the cremation ground, the Lord beyond the three voids, the true guru and the holy feet, and what it did instead, took gold, house, women, kin and the body as lasting, hoarded and buried wealth, and gave nothing to the hungry or the learned. Against each failure stands Yama, who takes the life while rings, retinue, kin and buried gold stay where they are.
structure_note: Four-line stanzas, nearly all closing on நெஞ்சமே (O heart) after a negative participle (போற்றாமல், ஈயாமல், not praising, not giving) and a verb of what the heart did. 641 addresses பாழ்மனமே instead; 648 and 661 end in the first person (ஆனேனே) and 657 and 659 drop the address. 647 alone is instruction rather than reproach: the poet tells the heart what to think.
source_issues: 639 line 4 துப்பாழாய் is not a known word; the line may be corrupt.
643 line 4 கைச்சட்டம் is obscure and may be a misprint.
647 line 1 துற்க்க (for துறக்க) has a doubled consonant sign.
648 and 661 end in the first person (ஆனேனே) and 657 and 659 lack the address நெஞ்சமே that the other stanzas carry; 659 ends in the plural இறைத்தோமே.

reading: Not praising the teacher who dances in the red cremation ground, having shown earth, gold and the darkness of maya for what they are, you were caught in the eye-nets of women who flash their eyes and talk, and wandered like a dog in the market, O heart.
nuance: மண், பொன் and the women of line 3 are the three cravings of Tamil moral talk (land, gold, women). தேசிகன் is the teacher; the dancer of the red ground is Siva, so the guru and the Lord are one figure.

reading: Lying on a flower couch and a gold-silk mattress, in peerless ornaments and with your gold never out of reach, before Yama takes the life from this mat you lie on, you did not praise and embrace the Threefold Void, O heart.
nuance: முப்பாழ், the three voids, is used as a name of the Lord (also 639, 658), as in the Arutpulambal's close (618). The silk mattress becomes இப்பாய், this mat, in the line where Yama arrives.

reading: The three voids void, the first void bare void, and beyond that void he dances; not praising him, trusting this life that is itself a void, and giving nothing to those who came begging, you let yourself be ringed by the deeds that came as your strength, O heart.
nuance: The first two lines pile பாழ் six times: the three voids, the first void, the void beyond, and this life as a void. துப்பாழாய் is obscure; துப்பு ஆழாய் (as your deep strength) or a corrupt துர்ப்பாழ் are both possible. ஏற்றவர் are those who come to receive, beggars.

reading: Given a birth in which to share rice and help those who wander here, you did not praise Siva's grace, and thought gold, house, lovely women and this life were still permanent, O heart.
nuance: சதம், permanent, is the recurring error-word of the plaint (644, 657). The verse makes human birth an opportunity for giving before it is one for worship.

reading: Not thinking that the wealth that came by the order of what you did in earlier lives was got only today, waste heart, you gave nothing to the destitute, did not consider Hara's worship, gave nothing to the learned, and forgot it all.
nuance: முற்றொடர்பு, the earlier connection, is past births; wealth is the fruit of former deeds and so not one's own achievement. The two classes owed a share, அற்றவர் and கற்றவர், are the destitute and the learned.

reading: Though you wear ruby, pearl and diamond and sit on a throne of pure gold, when Yama marks the body and takes it by the hand, we do not see the pure gold come along, O heart.
nuance: காணிப்பொன் and ஆணிப்பொன் are both fine gold; the gold that measured status stays on the throne.

reading: Though you wear a jewelled ring, fine ear-studs and a waist-cord, and become one of the lords honoured in each of the eight directions, when Yama plays ball with the life, we do not see your retinue come along, O heart.
nuance: கைச்சட்டம் is obscure: a hand ornament matching the ring and studs, or a band of followers. பற்கிட்ட (teeth clenched) describes Yama at play. The verse repeats 642 with rank in place of wealth.

reading: Unless the austerity you did before gathers in as all three, will gold, jewels and women come to you there? Not holding the true guru as your lasting good, you have become sightless like a blind man, O heart.
nuance: முப்பாலும் may be the three goods (virtue, wealth, pleasure) that past tapas yields, or a third of the account; the line says only that gold and women are the fruit of past merit, not of this life's striving. அந்தகன் is both a blind man and Yama.

reading: Not plucking pure flowers to worship and bow at the golden feet of the Supreme who wears the hooded serpent, you were proud, taking the bangles on the hand and the anklets on the foot for the truth, O heart.
nuance: The bangles and anklets are women's; the heart's truth was the ornamented body of the beloved, against which the verse sets the simplest ritual act, a flower at the feet.

reading: Not striving even once a day to praise the golden feet of Hara who gave the Lady half of himself, you sought wealth for contention and buried it in this earth: where did you think you were going, O heart?
nuance: வாதுக்குத் தேடி, seeking in order to argue or compete, is acquisition as rivalry; burying it in the ground is the hoarder's habit the verse turns into a question about destination.

reading: Heart, I tell you a thought: praising the grace of the five, cut off the five senses; put away deceit, and so that no second thought comes, meditate on the red feet.
nuance: அஞ்சருள் is read as the grace of the five, the five letters (அஞ்செழுத்து, 659) or the five-faced Lord; it is set against the five senses in the same line. The one stanza of the plaint that instructs rather than reproaches.

reading: Before this strange body and breath subside, I did not praise the true guru and gain austerity to live by, but trusted new-made gold, possessions and a great life, and became like a frog in a serpent's mouth.
nuance: The frog in the snake's mouth is still alive and still trusting; the image is of a man already taken who does not know it.

reading: Who are kin, who are parents, who are brothers, who are children? Whoever is there, will they help when you die? Melting like a young calf that has lost its cow, you joined yourself to petty pleasures, O heart.
nuance: கற்றா is the milch-cow (கன்று + ஆ); the calf's melting for its mother is the heart's dependence on kin, which the questions have just emptied.

reading: The house still there, the mother there, the needed wife there, honour there, food there, the children there, the cattle and calf there, the saved wealth there, and the cage itself there, you went: what a state, what a state that was.
nuance: கூடு, the cage or nest, is the body, left behind with everything else; the one who went is the life. The list has nine things that stay and one that goes.

reading: Sandal, kumkum, paste and perfumes wondrously smeared, finery and swagger, and the girls who wear fragrant flowers all still here, you did not consider in what manner you went, O heart.
nuance: Continues 650: the second list of what stays is the apparatus of pleasure and the women who shared it.

reading: Proud that you have fed the leaking bag of wind, this body of filth given over to harsh deeds, you did not look with pity and give rice to the hungry, but spread yourself abroad like a river in flood, O heart.
nuance: காற்றுத் துருத்தி is the bellows or wind-bag; ஊற்றைச் சடலம் the oozing body. அளாவினை, you spread and mixed, is the heart's dissipation set against the one directed act of feeding.

reading: Trusting this bubble life as a certainty, not giving even a nut's worth of rice to the hungry, you did not consider who would stand by you when Yama's messenger seizes and drags you in that struggle, O heart.
nuance: பாக்களவாம் அன்னம், rice the size of an areca-nut, is the least possible gift. ஆர்ப் படுவார் is read as 'who will be bound (with you)', that is, who will share it.

reading: Through the many wiles of a woman with a small brow, the breasts budding and swelling on her chest and their colour glistening, you were dazed and caught in the net, and never learned to share rice and eat, O heart.
nuance: சிலந்தி is a spider and also a kind of boil or swelling; here 'what sprouted on her chest and swelled' is read as the breasts. சின்னஞ்சிறு நுதலாள், she of the small brow, is a conventional beauty.

reading: Not praising with all your might the grace of the Siva-siddha who works this holed bag, this perishing worm-nest, you did not consider that the thing he shows is this: to open the house and summon the open space by light, O heart.
nuance: The third line is cipher: வீடு is the house (body) and release, வெளி the open space (the inner sky), ஒளி the light; tradition takes it as the yogic opening of the body's door so that the inner space is seen by light. The Lord is called சிவசித்தர், the siddha who moves the body as a puppet.

reading: Beyond carrying this flesh-packed body, this worm-nest, you did nothing, not praising the true guru; and seeing the forest-wide flood break its banks and go, you scattered into worry like fish spreading in it, O heart.
nuance: The fish spreading as the flood breaks is the mind dispersing with events; விசாரம் is anxiety, not inquiry.

reading: Taking as permanent the frame in which the life is shut up, and leaning on it in pride, when Yama breaks that frame and takes the life, the wealth you kept hidden will not come there.
nuance: உடக்கை is read as the body (உடல்) or its covering; சடக்கு the frame. The hidden wealth (அடக்கமாய் வைத்த பொருள்) picks up the buried gold of 646.

reading: Not praising the Threefold Void, the sweet honey, the clear nectar that never cloys, the seed of release, you let yourself be ringed by deeds that stand round you so that Yama grips you and binds you with his noose, O heart.
nuance: The void is given the sweetest names: honey, nectar, seed of release. முத்திக்கு வித்து makes the Lord the cause of release, and deeds (வினை) the ring that Yama's noose closes.

reading: Not praising the Lord who stands as the five letters, the eight letters, the fifty-one letters and the tender letter, caught in the net of deceitful full-breasted women, we chattered and searched and poured water on waste ground.
nuance: The counts are the mantra-letters of Saiva practice: five (நமசிவாய), eight, and the fifty-one letters of the alphabet; பிஞ்செழுத்து, the unripe or tender letter, is the Siddhars' name for the one subtle letter behind them, as in Sivavakkiyar. பாழுக்கு இறைத்தல், watering waste ground, is labour lost. பஞ்சரித்து is read as chattering.

reading: Not worshipping the holy feet of Sokkar who wears bone, arugu grass, konrai, thumbai and the crescent moon, you trusted the life with children, wives and kin and lovingly thought it would be there for all time, O heart.
nuance: சொக்கர் is Siva of Madurai; அக்கு is bone, worn as beads. எக்காலமும் உண்டு, 'exists for all time', is the heart's creed against which the plaint is written.

reading: Not greatly praising the grace of the guru who took me, not looking for the way to the house of Kailasa, I fell into the false maya of women with braided hair and became a kendai fish writhing on the hook.
nuance: கயிலாய வீடு, the house of Kailasa, is release named as a place; ஆண்ட குரு is the guru who ruled or claimed him. The hooked fish of this verse becomes the poisoned fish of 668.

title: அருட்புலம்பல் - நெஞ்சொடுபுலம்பல்
theme: The second half of the plaint to the heart: the heart failed to reach Kailasa, Sivaloka, the Lord of Tillai and Sokkar of Madurai, the Lord ciphered as a pattern of numbers and letters, and the higher light where bindu melts into nada, and is pictured in a run of images of ruin, a tree without a core, a corpse on the stake, a netted deer, a tangled thread, a dog at every eave, a fish that ate poison, an elephant in the jaws, a blind man who threw away his stick, a straw on the waves, wax in the furnace. Against the heart's ego stands a Lord who sold himself to a bard and ate a hunter's leavings.
structure_note: Four-line stanzas continuing the plaint; the address நெஞ்சமே is kept in 662, 664, 666, 667 and 673, while 663, 665, 668, 671 and 672 end in the first person (ஆனேனே, கெட்டேனே) and 669 and 670 in the plural or negative (பிழைத்தோமில்லையே, இருந்தேனில்லையே). 669 opens with a new address, ஊனமூடனே (flawed fool).
source_issues: 662 line 1 ஏணிப்பழுவாம் is obscure and may be corrupt.
665 line 3 (அடிக்கொண்டதில்லைவனத்தையனேநாயனையேன்) can be divided in more than one way; the stanza also lacks the closing address of its neighbours.
663, 665, 668, 671 and 672 end in the first person and 669 and 670 in the plural or negative, where the plaint elsewhere ends நெஞ்சமே.

reading: Without gaining Kailasa, worshipped by all who have cut the darkness that is the rung of the ladder, I, a slave, was dazzled by the things that come to be seen and became like a mango tree without a core, O heart.
nuance: ஏணிப்பழு, the ladder-rung, qualifying darkness, is obscure; perhaps the darkness is what the ladder of practice climbs through, or the word is corrupt. ஆணியற்ற மாமரம், a mango tree without its heartwood or peg, is a tree that stands but will not hold. Kailasa is release as a place, as in 661.

reading: Not reaching Kailasa, which holds all the worlds in strung light, melting, I this slave took on an alien form, melted within like a flood, and became a corpse set up on the stake.
nuance: The first two lines are compressed and may describe the Lord of Kailasa (who protects all the worlds with his light) rather than Kailasa itself. வேற்றுருவப்பட்டு, taking another form, is estrangement from one's own nature. The impaled corpse, கழுவில் இருந்த பிணம், is the harshest of the plaint's self-images.

reading: Before the life leaves its station in the body and goes, you did not reach him who ate the leavings of the hunter who drew the bow, but wandered like a deer caught in a net and were tangled like a thread that has lost its end, O heart.
nuance: The hunter is Kannappar, who offered Siva meat he had tasted; the Lord who ate his leavings (எச்சில்) is the Lord who accepts love over purity. தலைகெட்ட நூல், a thread with its head lost, cannot be wound.

reading: O Father of the Tillai grove whose feet I had taken: I, a dog, spoke sweet words of the waist and gait of lightning-like women with hair on their heads and whole bodies of wickedness, and became a beast that has lost its prey.
nuance: The second half of line 3 is read as அடிக்கொண்ட தில்லைவனத்து ஐயனே, நாய் அனையேன்; the printed string allows other divisions. முழுக்குரம்பை, the whole hut, is the body. விடக்கு is flesh or carrion: the beast that lost its meat is the lover left with nothing. Tillai is Chidambaram, the hall of the dance.

reading: Not praising the feet of Sokkar of famed Madurai, whom those who live on this earth praise, and not reaching Sivaloka, you wandered and roamed like a dog that puts its head into every house's eave, worthless heart.
nuance: சிவலோகம் is the Lord's world, the first of the graded releases. The dog at the eaves (தாவாரம்) answers the market dog of 637; பூவாணர் is read as those who live on the earth (பூ).

reading: Not praising the picture that stood matching ten and eight, two fives, thirteen, two and one, you fell into the triple snare that stood set, sowed seed there, and do not know how to let go, O heart.
nuance: The numbers are cipher. Tradition reads such counts as tattvas or letter-groups (eighteen, ten, thirteen, two, one as groups of the thirty-six tattvas, or of the mantra-letters), but the verse gives no key; ஓவியம், the picture, is the Lord as the pattern they compose. திரிகண்ணி, the three-stranded snare, is read as the three cravings or the three impurities. வித்திட்டாய், you sowed seed, is begetting or planting the seed of further birth.

reading: Not praising the lamp-light that stood supreme, five in form, and three fives and eight as one, and not catching it as fire catches cotton, I wandered like a fish that has eaten poison and was ruined.
nuance: அஞ்சு உரு is five in form, perhaps the five letters or the five faces; ஐமூன்றும் எட்டும் ஒன்றாய் (fifteen and eight as one) is cipher without a key here. பஞ்சில் இடு வன்னி, fire put to cotton, is instant catching: the light was there to be taken at once. The poisoned fish continues the hooked fish of 661.

reading: Flawed fool: without dying in this earth carrying the perishing worm-nest with pride, we did not go out and escape, as those five who ruled the country left it and went.
nuance: பஞ்சவர்கள் ஆண்டிருந்த தேசம் is either the Pandavas' kingdom, left for the forest and the last journey, or the body as the country the five senses ruled. On the second reading the escape is leaving the body's rule, which fits the worm-nest of line 1; on the first it is a renunciation like the Pandavas'. பிழைத்தோம் இல்லையே, we did not escape, is the one plural refrain.

reading: This salt-pot that leaks its ooze, this worm-nest that slips away stinking however it tries not to: how could I have desired the glorious city with this? I never withdrew to the land that does not cool.
nuance: வீறாம் புரம், the glorious city, is Siva's world; ஆறாத நாடு, the land that does not subside or cool, is obscure, perhaps the unfading land of release or, ironically, this restless world. நாறாமல் நாறி is stinking despite efforts not to.

reading: Not praising the supreme flame, the one First that even the rare ones sought and could not know, praised with tenderness, I trusted the dark great life, sank in lust, and became like an elephant caught in the jaws.
nuance: அரியவர் அரி தேடி can be read as 'the rare ones' or as Hari (Vishnu) who sought and did not know, the Puranic search for Siva's head and foot. அரிவாயிற் பட்ட கரி is the elephant in the lion's or crocodile's mouth (as in the Gajendra story); கரி can also be charcoal and அரிவாள் a sickle, but the elephant fits the plaint's animal images.

reading: Thinking on tantra and setting myself firmly to austerity, thinking on mantra, I grew confused and stumbled, and not seeing the higher light where bindu melts into nada, I became like a blind man who has thrown his stick into the air.
nuance: Tantra, tapas and mantra are the practices; what they are for is the light above bindu and nada, the two highest tattvas of Saiva cosmology and of the inner body. The blind man who throws away his stick has lost the one thing that guided him.

reading: Not praising him who was sold and became the famed slave of a bard, and who ate the leavings of the hunter with the bow in his hand, you were tossed by egoism like a straw on the waves and melted like wax in the furnace, O heart.
nuance: Two acts of the Lord's condescension to devotees: he sold himself into service for a bard (the Madurai sport for the bard Pattiran, or the story of Sundarar's bard), and he ate Kannappar's tasted offering (664). ஆணவம், egoism, is the first of the three impurities; the Lord who stooped is set against the heart that would not.

title: பூரணமாலை
theme: The opening fifth of Pattinathar's Puranamalai, a garland of two-line confessions each closing on the address பூரணமே, the Fullness. The first ten stanzas climb the body from the root triangle to the crown, naming the deity or thing the poet failed to look at in each place (the Maiden, Brahma, Mal, Rudra, Mahesvara, Sadasiva, nada-bindu, the crown-space, the nose-tip, the two channels), and the rest name the worldly trusts that took the looking's place: family, wealth, the body held as lasting, women, land and gold, pilgrimage to Kasi instead of the breath, and the uncounted parents of past births.
structure_note: Every stanza has the same shape: a thing not seen (பாராமல், காணாமல், போற்றாமல்) in the first line and the loss it caused (அறிவழிந்தேன், பொறியழிந்தேன், கலங்கினேன்) in the second, ending பூரணமே. The reading of each is what it names as unseen. 674 to 683 follow the yogic body upward; 684 and 696 bracket the second half with the same first line, that the Lord walked within the flesh unseen.
source_issues: The verses are printed without word division (each line is one unbroken string), so some readings depend on where the words are cut; 684 ஊனுக்குணீநின்று is ஊனுக்குள் நீ நின்று with the ள் lost in the sandhi, and 696 gives the undamaged form உடலுக்குள்நீநின்று.
676 ends அறிவழிந்தென்பூரணமே where every other stanza has அறிவழிந்தேன்; the ன் for ேன் is a copying slip.

reading: Not having praised the Maiden within the three-cornered chakra that rose at the root, the poet says he forgot his understanding.
nuance: மூலம் is the root centre and முக்கோண சக்கரம் its triangle, where tradition places the goddess as the coiled power; வாலை, the young goddess, is read by tradition as that power or the breath at the root, and the verse does not say which. The first stanza sets the addressee: பூரணம், the Fullness, is what all these failures were failures to see.

reading: Not having met and seen Brahma who stands risen in the lotus of the lower belly, the poet says he was ruined.
nuance: உந்தி usually means the navel, but since 676 gives the navel (நாவி) to Mal, tradition reads உந்தி here as the second centre (svadhishthana), whose presiding god is Brahma. The gods of the chakras are the creator, the preserver and the destroyer in ascending order, the Puranic trinity made into stages of the body.

reading: Not seeing tall Mal in the middle of the navel lotus, the poet says his life-breath was spoiled and his understanding lost.
nuance: நாவிக்கமலம் is the navel lotus (manipuraka), to which tradition assigns Vishnu. ஆவி கெட்டு, the breath or spirit spoiled, is the first of the chapter's losses to name the breath, which 694 will make the practice itself.

reading: Not seeing Rudra in the heart in truth, the poet says his purpose was lost and he was confused.
nuance: இருதயம், the heart centre (anahata), has Rudra as its god. உண்மையுடன் பாராமல் asks for a true seeing, not a doctrinal one; கருத்து, the lost thing, is the mind's purpose or intent.

reading: Not opening his eyes to see Mahesvara at the throat centre, the poet says he melted in hunger and his heart trembled.
nuance: விசுத்தி is the throat centre, named here by its Sanskrit name while the others are given by body-part; its god Mahesvara is the fourth in the ascending series. பசித்துருகி, melted in hunger, is a bodily hunger on the surface and, by the chapter's logic, hunger for what was not seen.

reading: Not seeing with understanding the stainless Sadasiva who has the eye in the brow, the poet says his senses were lost.
nuance: நெற்றி விழி, the eye in the brow, names the brow centre (ajna) and Siva's third eye at once; Sadasiva is its god, the fifth and highest of the series the chapter climbs. பொறி here, as in 680 and 689, is the senses or the faculties, lost by not seeing.

reading: Not seeing nada and bindu with care, the poet says his awareness was deluded and his senses lost.
nuance: After the five gods of the five centres the verse names no god but நாதம் and விந்து, sound and point, which the Tirumanthiram makes the first stage of manifestation above Sadasiva; tradition places them above the brow, below the crown. போதம், awareness, is the thing deluded.

reading: Not looking with firmness at the space at the crown, the poet says he lost his understanding in fear.
nuance: உச்சி வெளி, the space at the crown, is the top of the series begun at the root in 674; tradition calls it the thousand-petalled lotus or the void, and the verse calls it only space. அச்சமுடன், with fear, is the one emotion named in the ascent, set against உறுதியுடன், the firmness the looking needed.

reading: Not keeping his eyes open on the tip of the nose, the poet says his body was spoiled and his understanding lost.
nuance: முழித்திருந்து, staying with eyes open, makes the nose-tip gaze a waking watch and not a trance; the verse takes it as a thing to do, which Kakapusundar (2339) attacks as a false seat of the sushumna. ஆக்கை கெட்டு, the body spoiled, is the loss named for a bodily practice.

reading: Not able to know the nature of the ida and pingala channels, the poet says he hesitated with obstruction.
nuance: இடை and பிங்கலை are the left and right channels, sun and moon in the Siddhar cipher; இயல்பு, their nature, is their alternation, which the Tirumanthiram's வாரசரம் chapter teaches. தடை, obstruction, and தயங்கினேன், hesitated, describe a breath that would not move: the loss is in the practice itself.

reading: Not seeing you who stood and walked within the flesh, the poet says he lived as 'I' and lost his good.
nuance: நான் என்று இருந்து, staying as 'I', is the one cause the verse gives for not seeing the one who walked inside; the stanza turns the chapter from body-places to the self that failed to look. 696 repeats the first line with உடலுக்குள் for ஊனுக்குள்.

reading: Not trusting and desiring the true life and living it fully, the poet says he trusted the false life and lamented.
nuance: மெய்வாழ்வு and பொய்வாழ்வு, true life and false life, are left undefined; the stanzas that follow (686 to 689) list what the false life trusted in, so the pair reads as the inner life against the household one. புலம்பினேன், lamented, names the genre: the Puranamalai is itself a lament.

reading: Trusting that wife, children, father, mother and the kin that come with birth are real, the poet says his body was wasted.
nuance: உண்டு என்று நம்பி, trusting they exist, is the error named, not loving them: the kin are called unreal (not lasting) rather than bad. பிறவியுடன், with birth, marks them as what each birth brings and takes; 698 counts how many such parents there have been.

reading: Trusting that palanquins, litters and all possessions are real, the poet says his perception was lost.
nuance: தண்டிகை and பல்லாக்கு are the carried litter and palanquin, marks of rank; the poet whom tradition makes a rich merchant lists the furniture of his own former life. உணர்வு, perception, is what their trust cost.

reading: Bound in the belief that this body and life would always be permanent, the poet says he lost his footing.
nuance: சதம், permanent, is the word of the delusion, and பந்தம், bond, is the effect: belief in the body's lasting is itself the binding. பதம், the thing lost, is the state or standing one had.

reading: Fallen into the infatuation of women and the world, the poet says his awareness was deluded and his senses lost.
nuance: மாதர் பிரபஞ்சம் may be a pair, women and the world, or one phrase, the world of women; the second line is the same as 680's, so the delusion of desire and the failure to see nada and bindu have the same cost.

reading: Not looking to chariyai, kiriyai, yoga and jnana, the poet says his use was lost like a moon that has seen the sun.
nuance: The four Saiva paths are named as one thing neglected, not ranked; the chapter elsewhere prizes only the inner seeing, so the stanza is more orthodox than its neighbours. பரிதி கண்ட மதி, the moon that has seen the sun, is the moon paled at daybreak: the image is of a light that loses its use, not of a thing destroyed.

reading: Fallen into the infatuation of desire for land, women and gold, the poet says he was confused like a cow that has lost its eyes.
nuance: மண் பெண் பொன், land, woman, gold, is the fixed triad of desires in Tamil devotional verse, which Pattinathar uses elsewhere; the blind cow (கண்கெட்ட மாடு) wanders without direction, the picture of a desire that cannot see where it goes.

reading: Not seeing the sole First One and living alone with it, the poet says he was born here unjustly and stood wandering.
nuance: தனி முதல், the sole first, and தனித்திருந்து, staying alone, answer each other: the one is seen by one who is alone. அநியாயமாய்ப் பிறந்து, born unjustly or to no purpose, calls the birth itself the waste.

reading: Not examining and seeing the one who stood within the twelve cool kalas and danced, the poet says his understanding was lost.
nuance: ஈராறு தண்கலை, the twelve cool kalas, is cipher: the kalas are the digits of the moon and of the breath, and twelve is the sun's count in the Tirumanthiram (856), while தண், cool, is the moon's epithet; tradition takes it as the breath's measure, the twelve finger-breadths of the outgoing breath, in which the Lord dances. The dance (கூத்து) within the body is Tirumular's.

reading: Not watching the breath and praising you in gladness, the poet says he went as far as Kasi and wandered until his legs were weary.
nuance: வாசி, the breath as practice, is set against காசி, the pilgrimage city, in a rhyme that carries the argument: the one is within and free, the other far and tiring. காலலுத்தேன், my legs grew tired, is the physical cost, repeated at 696 for the hill shrines; the verse is the chapter's clearest statement that the practice replaces the pilgrimage.

reading: Not seeing with both eyes the one who mingled with the ninety-six instruments and played, the poet says he lost his standing.
nuance: கருவிகள் தொண்ணூற்றாறு, the ninety-six instruments, is the Tamil Saiva count of the tattvas and their adjuncts that make up the embodied person; the verse does not list them. இருவிழியால், with the two eyes, may be plain (the bodily eyes) or coded (the sun and moon, the two channels); ஈடு, the thing lost, is one's worth or standing.

reading: Not seeing you who stood and walked within the body, the poet says he wandered over every forest and hill until his legs were weary.
nuance: The first line repeats 684 with the body (உடல்) for the flesh (ஊன்); கடமலை தோறும், over every forest and hill, is the pilgrim's road to hill shrines, so the stanza pairs with 694's Kasi: the one walked inside while the poet walked outside.

reading: Saying that in every land and time we shall remain without dying, and not looking closely at you, the poet says he lost his form.
nuance: இறவாதிருப்பம், we shall not die, is the unspoken belief of ordinary life put into words; உருவழிந்தேன், lost my form, is the plain answer, the body gone. The stanza may also be read as a jibe at those who seek deathlessness in the wrong place, since 968 and 1033 claim it from the breath.

reading: The poet asks how many fathers and mothers he has been with, born and dying among them as a madman.
nuance: எத்தனை தாய் தந்தை, how many mothers and fathers, turns 686's kin into a count across births: each birth had its own parents, and the stanza asks for the total. பித்தன், madman, is the poet's name for the one who kept being born; 702 gives the number of births as eighty-four lakh.

title: பூரணமாலை
theme: The second fifth of the Puranamalai turns from what the poet failed to see to what the Fullness is: after a run of stanzas on the weariness of being born (mother, kin, Brahma and the fire are all tired of him, eighty-four lakh births), the refrain of failure gives way to a litany of the Lord's forms, as seed and shape, as guru, kundalini, Sakti, nada and bindu, as light and dark, as the three channels, as body and life, as every kin and all seven orders of beings, as male, female and neuter. Caste is one creation of his, the body a pot of filth, and the poet's whole claim is that he did not know the one who was all of this.
structure_note: 699 and 706 are the only petitions (புகலருள்வாய், வரமருள்வாய்); 699 to 702 share the word அலுத்தேன் (grew weary) and build to the count of births; from 716 the stanzas take a new shape, a chain of ஆய்/ஆகி participles listing the forms the Lord took, closed by அறியேன் (I do not know), which runs on through chapter 41.
source_issues: 711 breaks its first line in mid-word, போற்றாம / லகத்தினுடைய, so that the line division of the print falls inside போற்றாமல்; the text itself is sound.
716 and 717 have internal sandhi that the printing leaves joined (நாதவிந்தாய், இருளாயக்கினியாய் for இருளாய் அக்கினியாய்); not errors, but the words must be cut by the reader.

reading: The mother grew weary of bearing and the poet weary of being born; he asks the Fullness to give its golden feet and grant him refuge.
nuance: பெற்றலுத்தாள், she grew weary of bearing, is the mother of many births, not one; பொற்றுணைத்தாள், the golden pair of feet, is the refuge asked instead of another womb. The stanza is the first petition in the work after twenty-five confessions.

reading: Kin grew weary of weeping, the mourners of burning him, the mother of bearing him, and the poet of being born.
nuance: Four parties are tired: the weepers, the burners, the mother, the born. உறன்முறையார், those of the proper relation, are the kin whose office it is to cremate; the stanza makes a whole lifetime out of the two ceremonies that bracket it, and 701 extends the weariness to the gods.

reading: Brahma grew weary of creating, the poet of being born and dying, and the strong fire of consuming him.
nuance: The creator and the cremation fire (அக்கினி) are made as tired of the cycle as the one in it; the stanza's wit is that even the agents of birth and death want it to stop. உரமுடைய அக்கினி, the strong fire, has eaten him many times.

reading: Born through eighty-four lakh births and wounded by them, the poet says he lamented.
nuance: எண்பத்து நான்கு நூறாயிரம், eighty-four lakh, is the traditional count of the kinds of birth (as in Tirumanthiram 409), here taken as the count of the poet's own births. புண்பட்டு, wounded, is the only word for what the births did.

reading: While you were within me, not knowing myself and not knowing you, the poet says he lost the body.
nuance: Two not-knowings are set side by side, of oneself and of the Lord, and the Lord's being within (எனக்குள்ளே) makes them one failure. உடல் இழந்தேன், lost the body, is the ordinary death read as waste: the body was the place of the meeting that did not happen.

reading: The poet says he does not know how you, mingled as embryo and form and become the whole world, stood formless.
nuance: கருவாய் உருவாய், as seed and as shape, and then அருவாகி, becoming formless: the stanza holds the Lord as the embryo, its body, every world and no form at once, the first of the chapter's litanies of forms. The confession shifts from பாராமல் (not seeing) to அறிகிலேன் (not knowing).

reading: Not praising the holy feet in the red-gold lotus, the poet says he became a ghoul that dances when the drum is beaten.
nuance: செம்பொற்கமலம் may be a lotus of red gold, the Lord's feet themselves, or the crown lotus of the yogic body where the feet are placed; the verse does not fix it. பம்பை கொட்ட ஆடும் பசாசு, the ghoul that dances to the drum, is the possessed dancer of folk exorcism, a self that moves only as it is beaten.

reading: You being within me and I within you, the poet asks for the boon that ends the mind's distress.
nuance: The mutual indwelling (எனக்குள் நீ, உனக்குள் நான்) is stated as a fact and the boon asked on its strength; Sivavakkiyar (971) asks the same formula as a question. மனக்கவலை, the mind's distress, is the one thing the poet asks to have removed.

reading: Not seeing faultlessly the one who stood within the seven kinds of beings and played, the poet says he lost his use.
nuance: எழுவகைத் தோற்றம், the seven kinds of beings, is the Tamil count of the orders of life (gods, men, beasts, birds, crawling things, water creatures, plants), which 722 lists in full. விளையாடினது, played, is the Lord's sport in all of them.

reading: Not able to know the differences of caste for what they are, the poet says he stood deluded by habit.
nuance: சாதிபேதங்கள் தனை அறியமாட்டாமல் may mean not knowing what caste distinctions really are (empty, as 709 says) or not knowing them in the ordinary sense; 709 settles it toward the first. வாதனை is the Sanskrit vasana, the residual impression of past deeds, so the delusion comes from habit laid down in earlier births.

reading: Not knowing that you created lineage as one, the poet says he stood deluded inside the pot of filth.
nuance: குலம் ஒன்றாய் நீ படைத்த குறை is hard: குறை may be the point or the lack, so either 'the point that you made all lineage one' or 'the flaw in your making lineage one'; the first fits 708 and the Siddhars' general view. மலபாண்டம், the pot of filth, is the body, and the argument is Sivavakkiyar's: bodies of one stuff cannot differ by caste.

reading: The poet says he does not know the sign of the form you took, as atom within atom, in all the cosmos and the body.
nuance: அண்டபிண்டம் is the Siddhars' compound for the universe and the body as one; அணுவுக்கு அணுவாக, atom to the atom, makes the Fullness the smallest thing in both. குறிப்பு, the sign or intent, is what the verse says cannot be read.

reading: Not praising the true guru who sits above the thousand-petalled lotus, the poet says his understanding was lost through the anava of the inner self.
nuance: சகஸ்திரம், the thousand, is the crown lotus, and the guru placed above it is the Lord as guru rather than a human teacher, as tradition reads it. ஆணவம் is the first of the three impurities in Siddhanta, the soul's self-assertion; the verse makes it the one cause of not seeing.

reading: Not subduing the five senses and praising you, the poet says he wore away, melted and his heart trembled.
nuance: ஐந்து பொறியை அடக்கி, subduing the five senses, is set as the condition of praise, the Kural's tortoise (126) made the Siddhar's first step. The second line repeats 678's trembling.

reading: You made me dance this way as your holy dance; not knowing you, the poet says his body was wasted.
nuance: ஆட்டுவித்தாய், you made me dance, makes the poet's whole life the Lord's dance, with the poet as the puppet; the complaint is not that he was danced but that he did not know the dancer. திருக்கூத்து, the holy dance, is thus moved from the hall to a single life.

reading: Inside the stench of sinew, flesh, skin and bone, not able to know the limit, the poet says he was deluded.
nuance: The body is four tissues and a smell; வரம்பு, the limit or bound, is unexplained, and may be the body's own end, the measure of conduct, or the boundary between the body and the one inside it (684, 696). The stanza's pairing of the inventory with delusion is the Naladiyar's (46).

reading: Not seeing the good that was within the living creature, like a spider's thread, the poet says he lost his good.
nuance: சிலந்தியுடை நூல் போல், like the spider's thread, is a simile whose point is not stated: the thread is fine and easily missed, or it is spun from the spider's own body as the world is from the Lord, the Upanishadic image. நலம், the good, is both what was in the creature and what the poet lost, a pun the chapter uses often.

reading: The poet says he does not know how you, as guru, becoming the Supreme, as kundalini, Sakti, nada and bindu, became formless and formed.
nuance: குடிலை is the Agamic name of the primal power, the kundalini (kutila, the coiled); the chain குரு, பரம், குடிலை, சத்தி, நாதம், விந்து runs down the order of manifestation in Tirumular's cosmology (382, 384), with the guru placed first. Whether the guru here is the Lord or a man the verse does not say.

reading: The poet says he does not know the breadth of you who stood as light, as sun and moon, as the dark within, as fire, and became space.
nuance: The three lights (sun, moon, fire) and the dark are all the Lord, with உள்ளிருள், the inner darkness, named alongside the lights as his form; வெளி, space, is where the list ends, as the ascent of chapter 39 ended at உச்சி வெளி. கதிர் மதி is also cipher for the two channels, so the list may be read of the body too.

reading: The poet says he does not know the measure of you who stood as ida and pingala and as the suzhumunai that rose, as body and as life.
nuance: The three channels are named outright and the Lord is identified with them, not placed in them; எழுந்த சுழுமுனை, the whirl-channel that rose, is the middle channel the Siddhars prize, called risen because the breath rises in it. உளவு, the measure or secret, is what is unknown.

reading: The poet says he does not know the reckoning by which you stood as the root seed, sprouted and stayed in every body, and then destroy it as Kaalan.
nuance: மூலவித்து, the root seed, is the Lord as the origin of each body, which he then ends as Death (காலன்); creation and destruction are one agent, and கணக்கு, the reckoning, is the account by which he does both. The seed-and-sprout image recurs at 729 and 739.

reading: The poet says he did not know clearly that you were within the body, inside and outside at once.
nuance: உள்ளும் புறம்பும், inside and outside, undoes the chapter's own inside-outside argument: the Lord was not only within the body but outside it too, so the error was not of place but of clarity (தெள்ள).

reading: The poet says he does not know the state in which you stood as mother, father, kinsmen, relations and all the kin.
nuance: The kin that 686 called unreal are here the Lord's own forms; the two stanzas are not in conflict, since what was false was their lasting and what is true is who stood in them. தமர் and கிளைஞர் are the near and the wider kin.

reading: The poet says he does not know the intent with which you stood in the seven orders: beasts, birds, crawling things, the unmoving, the gods, the water-born and the human lines.
nuance: This is the full list behind 707's எழுவகை: விலங்கு, புள், ஊர்வன, அசரம் (the unmoving, plants), விண்ணவர், நீர்ச்சாதி, மனுக்குலம், seven in all. மனுக்குலங்கள், human lineages, is plural, so the human castes are one of the seven and not more.

reading: The poet says he does not know the manner in which you stood in glory, becoming male, female, neuter and other forms.
nuance: அலி, the neuter or hermaphrodite, is included among the Lord's forms without comment, and வேற்றுரு, other shape, leaves the list open. The verse says the Lord became these (ஆகி), where Tirumular (1872) says the inner light is none of them; the two can be reconciled by reading 'became' as 'appeared as', but the verse does not make the distinction.

title: பூரணமாலை
theme: The third fifth of the Puranamalai continues the litany of the Lord's forms begun in chapter 40 and closes it on the question of learning. The Fullness is the ages of a life, the false and the true, flower and scent, gold and its touch, the three worlds, body and the eye's light, seed and fruit, the five elements and every world, mind and dream and maya, Sakti and Siva who are two and end as one, sense and element and knowledge, the two breaths grown into one, the killer and the begetter, the thirty-two parts, the one soul in every body, and the inner faith behind the outer sects; and the last stanzas say that none of this is reached by learning, since those who say 'we have learned' do not see the feet and their births are not cut.
structure_note: 724 to 746 keep chapter 40's shape, a chain of ஆய்/ஆகி participles closed by அறியேன் (I do not know) with a changing noun for what is unknown (பயன், இயல், திறம், நிலை, அளவு, தரம், தலம், குணம்); 735 and 740, 741, 747 and 748 break the pattern to turn on others, the learned (கற்றறிவோம் என்பார்) and the poor (ஏழைகள்) who do not know what has been listed.
source_issues: 731 மாயைகையாய் is a doubtful form; மாயையாய் is expected and the reading follows it.
724 பாலையாய் and 737 செவ்வாய் are each uncertain words on which the stanza's sense turns; the readings are marked uncertain rather than emended.
743 names five inner faculties where the standard list has four; மகிழ் may be a corruption or an addition, and the reading keeps it as joy.

reading: The poet says he does not know the fruit of you who stood as the maiden stage, the ripe stage and the growing to old age, and as the stage before them.
nuance: வாலை, பக்குவம், கிழம் are the stages of a life, girlhood, ripeness, age, and on this reading the Lord is the ageing itself; but வாலை is also the Siddhars' young goddess, so a coded reading has the goddess ripening into the old one. பாலை is the puzzle: the infant stage (from பாலன்), the desert tract, or a corruption; the plain reading as the first age is taken here.

reading: The poet says he does not know the breadth of you who became the false, the earth and the famed ocean, and stood as the true.
nuance: பொய்யாய், as the false, is the striking term: the Lord is the illusion as well as the truth, the earth and the sea in between. The stanza undoes 685's pairing of true life against false life by making both his.

reading: The poet says he does not know the subtlety of you who became flower and scent, gold and its touch-grade, and the word on the tongue.
nuance: Three pairs of a thing and its inseparable quality: flower and fragrance, gold and மாற்று (its fineness as tested on the touchstone), tongue and speech; the Lord is each pair, so he is not a thing but the relation that cannot be split. நயம், the fine point or subtlety, is what is not known.

reading: The poet says he does not know the nature of you who became first and middle, the three entities and the three worlds, and stood as what is fitting.
nuance: முப்பொருள், the three entities, is the Siddhanta triad pati, pasu and pasam, as tradition reads it, though it could be any triad; மூன்று உலகு is the three worlds. முதலாய் நடுவாகி, first and middle, has no end, which may be the point (the Lord has none) or a dropped word. இதம் is the fitting or the pleasant.

reading: The poet says he does not know the power of you who became flesh, body and life, the light of the eye filling within, and the sweetness of honey.
nuance: உள் நிறைந்த கண்ணொளி, the eye's light filling within, is the one of the series that names a Fullness (நிறைந்த) inside the body; தேனாய் ருசியான, the taste of honey, makes the Lord the tasting as well as the thing tasted, as 726 made him the pairs.

reading: The poet says he does not know the power of you who became seed and tree, the fruit that ripened, the unripe fruit and the flower, and stood as the accomplished one.
nuance: The sequence is out of botanical order (seed, tree, ripe fruit, unripe fruit, flower), so the point is the whole cycle rather than its stages. சித்து, the accomplished or pure consciousness, closes the list, as in 739 சத்து (the real) does; the two stanzas are a pair.

reading: The poet says he does not know the power of you who, taking the five kinds, stood as the god in all the worlds, the eggs and the outer eggs.
nuance: ஐவகை is the five elements, from which worlds are made; அண்ட பகிரண்டம், the egg and the outside of the egg, is the cosmology of world-spheres and what lies beyond them, as in Tirumular. தெய்வம் என நின்ற, stood as god, is the one place the series calls the Lord a god rather than a thing.

reading: The poet says he does not know the state in which you became mind, dream and maya, stayed within and became thought.
nuance: Mind, dream and maya are the Lord's forms, so the deluding faculties are not opposed to him; மாயைகை is read as மாயையாய் with a shifted ending. 742 returns to the mind as remembering and forgetting.

reading: The poet says he does not know the power of you who were Sakti and Siva as two and at the end became one, and stood as a picture.
nuance: இரண்டாய் ... முடிவில் ஒன்றாகி, two and in the end one, is the Siddhanta account of Sakti and Siva, distinct in act and one in being; சித்திரம், a picture, may mean a wonder or that the two-in-one is drawn, as in the yantras. The verse states the doctrine as something it does not understand.

reading: The poet says he does not know the measure of you who became the senses, the sense-objects, the divisions of the differing elements, and knowledge.
nuance: பொறி, புலன், பூதம் are the sense organs, their objects and the elements, three of the tattva groups, with அறிவு, knowledge, as the fourth; the Lord is the instruments of knowing and the knowing. அளவு, the measure, is also the name of the means of knowledge, so the word may be pointed.

reading: As the sun and moon in the sky grew and then became one, the poet says he does not know the breathing of life within the fleshly body.
nuance: கதிர் மதி, sun and moon, are the two breaths in Siddhar cipher, and their growing and becoming one is their joining in the middle channel, as tradition reads; the plain reading, that the sky's two lights become one (at new moon, or in eclipse), gives the simile its surface. உயிர்ப்பு is the breathing itself, the one practice the whole litany names directly.

reading: Beyond speaking vain talk full of lies and baseness, the poet says, alas, he does not know how to speak of you.
nuance: பொய்யும் புலையும், lies and baseness (புலை is low or foul), is the poet's account of his own speech, and ஐயோ, alas, is the only exclamation in the work; the stanza is an apology placed in the middle of the praise it says it cannot make.

reading: The poet says he does not know the standing by which to say that the one who stood everywhere without end and played is the Supreme itself.
nuance: பரம் அதுவே என்ன, to say 'that is the Supreme', is the act the poet lacks the standing (பதம்) for; the stanza is about naming, after 735's confession about speech. விளையாடினது, played, is the sport of 707 and 695.

reading: You kill, you bring to birth, you stay in the union and take pleasure; the poet says he does not know the fitting act that is done within others.
nuance: கொல்வாய் பிறப்பாய், you kill, you are born (or you bring to birth), make the Lord the agent of both ends, as 719 did; கூடலிருந்தே சுகிப்பாய், you stay in the coupling and enjoy, puts him in the sexual act itself. செவ்வாய் is hard: the fitting way, or a vocative; பிறர்க்குள் செயல், the act within others, may be the Lord acting in every body or begetting in another.

reading: The poet says he does not know the place where you stood as the ocean, as all the lasting earth and all the cosmos and body, as the refuge.
nuance: அண்டபிண்டம் recurs from 710; தலம், the place, is the thing unknown, which is the point when the Lord is everywhere: there is no one place of a Fullness. சாருதி, the refuge or resort, is unusual and may be a formation from சார்.

reading: The poet says he does not know the rank of you who were seed and tree, space and light, and existed as the real.
nuance: The stanza pairs with 729 (seed, tree, ending in சித்து); here the end is சத்து, being or the real, so the two give the Lord as sat and cit, the Vedantic pair, in Tamil guise. தரம், rank or grade, is the unknown.

reading: The poet asks whether those who have looked at the tattvas and known themselves by their knowledge, but have not seen you by it, will be saved.
nuance: Self-knowledge gained from the tattvas (தன்னை அறிந்த அறிவு) is granted and then declared insufficient: knowing oneself through the categories is not seeing the Lord. உய்த்து ... பாராமல் makes seeing by that knowledge the missing step, not a different knowledge.

reading: Though you are one and stay as the life in every body, the poet says the poor never know it.
nuance: ஏழைகள், the poor, is pity rather than scorn: those who do not know are destitute, not wicked. ஒன்றாய் உயிராய் உடல் தோறும், one, as life, in every body, is the whole doctrine of chapters 40 and 41 in one line, and the stanza turns it from the poet's confession to a general statement.

reading: The poet says he does not know the wealth of you who created yesterday and tomorrow as remembering and forgetting and stood as change.
nuance: நேற்று என்றும் நாளை என்றும், yesterday and tomorrow, are made of memory and forgetting, so time is a work of the mind the Lord created; மாற்றம், change, is his form. Sivavakkiyar (971) uses the same pair, remembering and forgetting, for maya.

reading: The poet says he does not know the state in which you became mind, intellect, attention, joy and the ego-sense, and became the place of thought.
nuance: மனம், புத்தி, சித்தம், அகங்காரம் are the four inner instruments (antahkarana) of the tattva lists; மகிழ், joy, between them is not one of the four and may be a corruption of the fourth name or an added quality. The Lord is the faculties, not their object.

reading: The poet says he does not know the nature by which you, without difference of form, came as the high difference of sound and as the difference of gurus.
nuance: உருப்பேதம் இன்றி, without difference of form, against சத்தபேதம், difference of sound: the Lord who has one form becomes many as sounds (the letters, or the sects' teachings) and as the many gurus. Each reading of சத்தம் (sound, or the scriptures as heard) gives a different verse; குருபேதம் may be the differences among teachers or the Lord's coming as different teachers.

reading: You set out the differences of the outer sects, and then said that there is an inner sect besides, the poet says to the Fullness.
nuance: கட்சமயம், outer sects (கள் or கடை, the outside), and உட்சமயம், the inner one, are the verse's own terms; the Lord both made the sectarian divisions and declared a faith inside them, so the sects are neither false nor final. உரைத்தனையே, you said, is unusual: the Fullness is a speaker here.

reading: The poet says he does not know the power of the sleight of hand by which you set to work and created the thirty-two parts and stayed inside them.
nuance: முப்பத்திரண்டு உறுப்பு, thirty-two parts, is a count of the body's members that the verse does not itemise; the Tirumanthiram (146) has thirty-two rafters in the body's frame, read variously as ribs or teeth. செப்படு வித்தை, the juggler's trick (செப்பிடு வித்தை), makes the body a conjuring, and the maker is inside his own trick.

reading: The poet asks what it matters however much one has learned or whatever one has gained, and whether those who do not know you will be saved.
nuance: கற்றால் என், பெற்றால் என், what if learned, what if gained: learning and possessions are set together as things that do not save, so the chapter's attack on learning is an extension of chapter 39's on wealth. உய்வரோ, will they be saved, is a question with its answer in it.

reading: Those who say 'we shall learn and know' do not see your feet; the poet asks whether birth will be cut off for those who have not gained and known it.
nuance: கற்றறிவோம் என்பார், those who say 'we will know by learning', is the exact target: not learning but the claim that it brings knowing. பெற்றறியார், who have not gained and known, names the alternative, a knowing that is received, as the feet are; and பிறப்பறுமோ, will birth be cut, returns the work to the births of 699 to 702.

title: பூரணமாலை
theme: The fourth stretch of Pattinathar's garland to the Fullness (பூரணம்) turns from the question 'how did you become each thing' to the disputants and to the poet himself. Those who name you sky, cosmos, light, breath, silence, the Supreme, the sun or the five letters do not know themselves, your name, your way or the order of the letters; the poet confesses that lust, women, the body taken for a support, maya's stupor and puja mixed with worldly enjoyment cost him his understanding; and then he turns the complaint on the Fullness itself, which created and destroys, which divided night from day, sin from merit, heaven from hell, calm from anger, caste from caste, and which stands as bond, soul and Lord at once. The run closes on union: I am you and you are I, and when the two are one you do not cloy, like honey.
structure_note: Four groups: 749 to 754, the rival accounts of the Fullness and what their speakers do not know, with 753 as the poet's own admission that he cannot find the one thing under all of them; 755 to 764, confession in the first person, each verse ending in a verb of loss (பயனழிந்தேன், பிறந்திறந்தேன், கலங்கினேன், தட்டழிந்தேன், அறிவழிந்தேன்); 765 to 771, the Fullness as the maker of every division, each ending in அறியேன் or படைத்தனையே; 772 and 773, the plea and the union. The refrain பூரணமே closes every couplet and is the addressee, not the subject, of each.
source_issues: 757 line 1 prints வோற்றாமல் for போற்றாமல்; 753 line 2 prints அரிகிலேன் for அறிகிலேன் (alveolar for retroflex, a common 1887 spelling).
The work is printed without word spaces throughout 749 to 773, so some splits (மகத்துவமாய், பாந்தமென்றும்) rest on the reader.

reading: Those who call you sky, those who call you the cosmic egg, who speak knowledge with the mouth alone and say 'it is I': idle talkers, they do not know themselves.
nuance: வாய்ஞானம், mouth-knowledge, is the charge; தானென்பார் may be those who say 'I am it' (the Vedantin's claim) or those who speak only of themselves, and either way தனையறியார் answers it: the one who says 'I' has not known the 'I'. The verse opens a run (749 to 752) in which each line's என்பார் names a school.

reading: Those who say 'the beginning', those who say 'the end', those who say 'the light standing between the two': they do not know the work of nada.
nuance: நாதத்தொழில், the work of nada, is the coded term. Tradition takes nada as the first stir of sound from which the world unfolds, and in yoga as the inner sound heard when the breath is stilled; the verse may mean that the schools of beginning, end and middle light have not heard the sound, or have not understood how sound makes the world. The verse does not decide.

reading: Those who say 'breath', those who say 'the heart', those who say 'the release called silence', those who say 'speech': they do not know your name.
nuance: Four methods are named and set aside together: the breath (the Siddhars' own vaasi practice), the mind, silence taken as release, and speech (mantra and recitation). Silence is placed among the sayings, so even மோனம் is here something people 'say'. What they lack is உன்னுடைய பேர், your name, which the poem never supplies beyond the refrain.

reading: Those who say 'the Supreme', those who say 'the sun', those who say 'the boon that stands as the void expanse': they do not know your way.
nuance: பானு, the sun, can be the sun of the sky or, in the Siddhars' cipher, the right-hand breath; the plain list of schools (Vedanta's param, a sun cult, the teaching of the void) stands without the cipher. பாழ்வெளி, the void expanse, is a term the Siddhars use for the goal itself, and the verse counts even that as a saying that misses the way.

reading: However many people have taken you up and told you in their own words, I cannot discern the one thing that is common to all of them.
nuance: The verse closes the list of 749 to 752 with the poet's own admission: he does not claim a better account, only that the one thing under the many accounts (அத்தனை பேர்க்கு ஒன்றானது) escapes him. அரிகிலேன் is 'I do not know' (அறிகிலேன்), spelled with the alveolar.

reading: Those who say 'na and ma', those who say 'si in the middle', those who say 'va and ya': they do not know the order of the kinds.
nuance: The letters are those of நமசிவாய in sequence, with சி placed at the centre (நடுவே சிகாரம்). வகை, the kinds or arrangement, is what the reciters miss: the Tirumanthiram teaches orders of the five letters, and tradition reads 'knowing the order' as knowing what each letter stands for (Lord, soul, grace, bond, concealment). The verse keeps the mantra and faults the reciters, as Sivavakkiyar does.

reading: Sunk in the stupor of lust as though it were something great, unable to tell one thing from another, I threw away what life was for.
nuance: மகத்துவமாய் qualifies the poet's own state: lust held as a greatness, or the poet puffed up inside it. பகுத்தறிதல், discrimination, is the faculty named as lost, and the loss is of பயன், the fruit or use of the birth.

reading: Not gazing with love on the true substance, I was born and died again through infatuation with women.
nuance: பிறந்திறந்தேன் is a single compound verb, born-and-died, so the births are many and the cause is one. உண்மைப்பொருள், the true substance, is what the Fullness is called when it is an object of sight rather than of speech.

reading: Not praising you with a full mouth and rejoicing in you, I took a body and was thrown into confusion.
nuance: காயமெடுத்து, taking a body, is the cause of the confusion as well as its setting; the only remedy named is praise, the devotional act the poet's own Puranamalai performs. வோற்றாமல் is a spelling of போற்றாமல்.

reading: As a cloud hides the moon, so I, caught in bondage, do not see you.
nuance: The moon is not dimmed by the cloud; the figure puts the obstacle in the seer and leaves the Fullness unchanged. பந்தம், the bond, is the cloud, and the verse does not say what the bond is made of.

reading: Not praising the red lotus feet day after day, I stood without support and wandered here.
nuance: அந்தரமாய், in mid-air, is to stand on nothing; the feet are the support the poet failed to take, and அலைந்தேன் (I wandered) is the verb of 774, where the wandering is placed in a void.

reading: Taking this body, as unstable as a bubble on water, for my support, I was ruined.
nuance: தாரகம், the support or saviour, is the word for what carries one across; the error is not having a body but resting one's weight on it. The bubble on water is the common Tamil figure for the body's impermanence.

reading: Thinking of you with a melting heart and praising you, I still do not know how to drive out the long deceit.
nuance: நெடு வஞ்சகம், the long deceit, is not assigned an owner: the world's deceit, maya's, or the poet's own. The verse grants that the melting and the praise have happened and says they have not been enough, which separates it from the confessions around it.

reading: Not knowing in my heart that you stood filling everything like the oil in a sesame seed, I melted away.
nuance: Oil in sesame is the stock figure for a pervasion that cannot be seen from outside and is found only by pressing. உருகினேன் can be the melting of devotion or the wasting of grief; after அறியாது (not knowing) the second fits, and the melting is in vain because its object was already within.

reading: Fallen into the stupor of the world that is maya, I did not put an end to unceasing birth.
nuance: மாயாப்பிரபஞ்சம் makes the world and maya one compound, and ஓயாச்சனனம், birth that does not rest, is its product. The verse states the Saiva goal, ending birth, as the thing left undone.

reading: Through enjoyment, the puja and the pleasures of the world together, I grew greedy and lost my understanding.
nuance: Puja is set beside புவனபோகம், worldly enjoyment, under one word for enjoyment (போக்கியம்). This can mean puja performed for the sake of enjoyment, or that ritual worship was itself one more thing the poet enjoyed; on either reading worship is counted among what cost him his understanding, not among the remedies.

reading: You create and you destroy; and if you so much as look, you wipe out the letters Brahma wrote and make one shine as a deathless being.
nuance: பிரமாவெழுத்து is Brahma's writing on the skull, fate; தொடைத்து (wiping it off) sets the Fullness above fate. சிரஞ்சீவி, the long-lived or deathless, is read by the Siddhars as the body kept from death and by others as release from rebirth; the verse supports both, since what is wiped out is the written span of a life.

reading: Is it even fitting that I should know the device by which you stood as mantra, as sastra and as the four Vedas?
nuance: தந்திரம் is the device or art, and also the Tantra as a class of text beside mantra and sastra; the verse can list four kinds of scripture as forms of the Fullness, or ask after the trick by which the formless became text. தகுமோ, 'is it fitting', makes the ignorance a matter of standing rather than of effort.

reading: I do not know the connection by which you divided yourself into night, into day, and into the word called 'perpetual time'.
nuance: அனவரத காலம் is unending time, and it is named as a சொல், a word: the divisions of time are divisions in language. தொடர்பு, the connection, is what joins the undivided to its partitions, and the verse leaves it unknown.

reading: Though there are the two one goes to, hell and heaven, I do not understand what it is to say 'Hara, Hara'.
nuance: The verse grants the two destinations and sets against them the cry of the name, அரகரா, which belongs to neither. The point is left implicit: the name is what one says who is bound for neither place, and the poet cannot yet say it with understanding.

reading: By the division called sin and merit you create and destroy, and you planted longing here; the grace in that I do not understand.
nuance: ஆவல், longing, is set here by the Fullness itself, and the verse calls the arrangement அருள், grace, while confessing that it cannot see the grace in it. The Siddhanta position that the Lord gives the soul its deeds and their fruits as a help toward release is here stated from the side of the soul that does not feel helped.

reading: Calm and anger, the differences of caste, kinship and the intellect: all these you yourself created.
nuance: சாதி பேதங்கள், the differences of caste, are listed between anger and intellect as one more pair of the created world. பாந்தம் is read as பந்தம், the tie of kin or the bond; a reading as friendship (பாந்தவம்) also stands. The list makes caste real and made, not natural, which is both more and less than Sivavakkiyar's denial of it.

reading: As the bond you stood as the body, as the soul you stood as life, and in love you yourself stood as the substance.
nuance: The three categories of Saiva Siddhanta, pasam, pasu and pati, are mapped on to body, life and the Lord, and all three are said of the one Fullness in the second person. This folds the Siddhanta triad into a single being, which Siddhanta itself does not do; the word பொருள் for the third term, with நேசமுடன், keeps the Lord's place as the substance and the lover.

reading: Take pity on your devotees who have nothing, come into this world, and grant in grace that we bow low at your feet.
nuance: ஏதிலடியார் can be devotees without anything, or devotees who are strangers, without kin or standing; the plea is for the Fullness to come இகத்தில், into this world, which treats the pervading one as also absent. The couplet is the only direct petition in the chapter.

reading: I am you and you are I; when the two become one, you do not cloy, like the taste of honey.
nuance: தெவிட்டாய், 'you do not cloy', makes the union a taste that does not tire the tongue, so the bliss is continuing rather than momentary. The formula நானே நீ நீயே நான் is the Vedantic identity stated in the second person to a God; the verse keeps the two pronouns while claiming their oneness.

title: பூரணமாலை
theme: The last two couplets of the Puranamalai: the confession is summed up as having wandered in a void at the bottom instead of completing and seeing the void at the end, and the garland closes with its promise, that the Fullness will make knowledge flourish on earth for those who recite the Puranamalai with understanding.
structure_note: 774 belongs with the confessions of the preceding chapter and 775 is the work's phala-sruti; the tool's five-way split leaves them as a chapter of two verses.
source_issues: The tool's division of the Puranamalai into five chapters cuts 774 off from the confessions of 755 to 773 and leaves this chapter with two verses.

reading: Instead of standing at the end, bringing one void to its completion and looking, I wandered in a void at the bottom.
nuance: The verse uses சூனியம், the Siddhars' Buddhist-flavoured word for the void, twice, and the reading turns on which void is which. On the plain reading the void at the end (முடிவில்) is the emptiness in which the Fullness is seen, reached by completing the path, and the void at the bottom (அடியில்) is the empty world, or the nothing one wanders in without the path. Tradition also reads அடி and முடி as the foot and the crown of the body, the base centre and the summit of the yogic ascent, so that the poet confesses having circled at the base rather than finishing at the crown. Either way the verse admits two voids, a true and a false, and does not say what distinguishes them beyond their place.

reading: For those who recite this Puranamalai with understanding you will make knowledge flourish on this earth.
nuance: A phala-sruti, the conventional closing promise, but conditioned on புத்தியுடன், with understanding, which answers the garland's opening charge of mouth-knowledge (749): recitation alone is what the poem has been attacking, so the fruit is withheld from it. தாரணியில், on the earth, places the promised knowledge in this life.

title: நெஞ்சொடுமகிழ்தல்
theme: Pattinathar's Nenjodu Magizhdal, rejoicing with the heart: where the Puranamalai confessed what the poet failed to know, this work tells the heart, verse by verse, what it has reached. The heart has loved the subtle that stood hidden in the body, become one with the awareness that fills everything, passed beyond speech, pointing, sky, earth, light, name, town, sex and number, and joined the Supreme as salt joins water, a river the sea, a crystal the colour set against it, sweetness the milk, vapour the water, and as the sun withdraws from the pots it shone in. The union is described only by negation and by figures of merging; nothing is said about how it was reached.
structure_note: The verses fall into two kinds that alternate. The negations (776 to 784, 794, 797) run a chain of இறந்து, 'having passed beyond', over pairs (before and after, sky and earth, space and light, town and name) and end in a verb of union (ஒன்றினையே, ஏகரித்தாய், சேர்ந்தனையே). The figures of union (789 to 793, 796) each give one simile. 785 to 788 and 795 to 800 name states: not male, female or neuter; sleeping without sleeping; the open expanse without liking and disliking; the fourth state; remaining as one is. Every verse ends in a second-person perfect addressed to நெஞ்சமே, the heart, and the poet never says 'I'.
source_issues: 776 to 800 are printed without word spaces, while 801 to 807 (the next chapter) have spaces before the refrain and, in 805, between words; the two runs appear to come from differently prepared sources.
781 line 2, நீச்சிறந்து, is doubtful: நீச்சு (swimming) fits the chain of இறந்து but may be a variant or corrupt word.

reading: From that first day until today it has stood hidden in the body as the subtle; heart, you have come to love knowing that state.
nuance: அன்று முதல், from that day, is left undated: the day of birth, or the beginning of the world. The subtle (சூட்சியம்) is given no name, and the heart's achievement is only to have wanted to know it, which makes this verse the starting point of the sequence.

reading: In that which, as awareness here and as knowledge there, filled and became everything everywhere, heart, you were made one.
nuance: ஏகரித்தாய், you made one or became one, is the verb of union used again at 782. The pervading thing is described as உணர்வு and அறிவு, feeling-awareness and knowledge, not as a God; the work never names Siva.

reading: In the unmoving flood of great joy and bliss you stood firm, heart, having passed beyond form.
nuance: The flood (வெள்ளம்) does not move (அலையாத), which reverses the usual image of bliss as a torrent; the stability is the heart's and the flood's at once. உருவிறந்து, having gone past form, is the first of the chain of இறந்து that runs through the next verses.

reading: Without looking, without trembling, without drinking, without considering anything at all, heart, you became one with awareness.
nuance: Four negated verbs remove sight, agitation, consumption and inquiry, so that the union is with உணர்வு, bare awareness, from which the activities of knowing have been subtracted. The verse does not say that awareness is an object; the heart is one with it, not aware of it.

reading: Past theft and past killing, with things seen and the seeing itself gone, heart, you loved that which stands beyond measure.
nuance: The chain starts from the two gross sins, theft and killing, and passes at once to the end of object and perception (காண்பனவுங் காட்சியும்), so that the ladder from conduct to knowledge is a single line. A coded reading of களவு as the mind's thieving is possible but not needed.

reading: Past speech, past pointing, past after and past before, past the swimming, heart, you came to love that which stands.
nuance: சுட்டு is the demonstrative, the pointing by which a word indicates a thing, so the verse passes beyond both saying and indicating. நீச்சு, swimming, is read as the effort of crossing, the striving of practice, left behind once the far side is reached; it could also be a corrupt or variant form. 'After and before' are time, or the states before and after birth.

reading: Past sky, past earth, past space, past light and past thought, heart, you were made one with that which stands.
nuance: Space (வெளி) and light (ஒளி) are themselves the Siddhars' names for the goal, and the verse passes beyond them too; எண் is thought or number, and either way the countable is left. The pattern makes clear that nothing nameable is the end, including the words the Siddhars prefer.

reading: Wherever you looked, within and without, you took it as truth that it is the Supreme, strung through everything just as it is.
nuance: கோத்தபடி, as it is threaded, pictures the Supreme as the string through beads; உண்மையெனக் கொண்டனை, you took it as truth, is a conviction rather than a vision, the one verse in the work that describes the heart's attainment as a judgement.

reading: Past town and past name, past light and past space, past all distinction, heart, you joined that which stands.
nuance: ஊரும் பேரும், town and name, are the markers of a person's identity, and leaving them is the renunciant's act; here they are passed as the sky and light were. சீர், excellence or renown, is the last thing left. The verse repeats 782's light and space in reverse order, a mark of the kummi-like variation of one formula.

reading: Filled so that it is hard to call it male, female or neuter, and hard to see: that place, heart, you set your eye on.
nuance: The three grammatical genders are exhausted and the thing is beyond them; the verse does not say that it is a fourth, only that naming fails. காண அரிது, hard to see, is immediately followed by கண்ணுற்றாய், you saw it, so the difficulty is granted and overcome in one line.

reading: Putting away pride and fear, with knowledge, sleeping without sleeping, heart, you gained happiness.
nuance: தூங்காமல் தூங்கி, sleeping without sleeping, is read by tradition as the samadhi in which the body and senses rest as in sleep while awareness remains awake, the fourth state beyond deep sleep. The verse names ego and fear as the two things to remove first, and the sleep-that-is-not-sleep as what follows.

reading: The undivided all-fullness that stands as the First: heart, you reached the place where it is attained.
nuance: அகண்ட பரிபூரணம், the undivided plenum, is the Vedantic form of the Puranamalai's பூரணம். சாதியா நின்ற இடம் can be read as the place where it is attained (from சாதித்தல்) or as the place that stands without caste or kind (சாதி with the negative); the second would echo Pattinathar's listing of caste among the Fullness's creations (770), but the first is the simpler grammar.

reading: In the bare open expanse that has neither liking nor loathing, heart, you stayed, holding that simply to be there is happiness.
nuance: வெட்டவெளி, the bare expanse, is a Siddhar term for the ultimate as open space with nothing in it. The happiness is defined as இருப்பே, mere being there, with nothing done or gained, and the two attachments removed are the pair that drive action.

reading: Beyond and on this side of the great cosmos that no one reaches, heart, you gained a settled state like water and salt.
