nuance: Water and salt is the Siddhars' figure for a union with no seam and no added bulk; the verse applies it to the heart's relation to what lies on both sides of the universe. ஆரும் உறா, that no one reaches, is said of the cosmic egg itself, so the heart is placed beyond what is already beyond reach.

reading: With the one who is hard to perceive though he is present with you, heart, you mingled like river water and the sea.
nuance: உடனாகவே இருந்தும், though he is right there with you, states the paradox the Puranamalai confessed (762): the nearest thing is the hardest to perceive. The river and the sea figure a union in which the smaller is lost in the greater and nothing comes back.

reading: Driving out the long-standing ego and cutting off the vice that stood in you, heart, you clung to it like a crystal to the colour set against it.
nuance: நெடியகம் is read as நெடிய அகம், the long-standing 'I'; it could also be the tall house, the body. படிகம், crystal, is the standard figure for the soul that shows the hue of whatever it is joined to, so the clinging is a taking-on of the other's nature rather than a grasp. சழக்கு is fault or wrongdoing. The syntax of படிகத்துக்கும் போல் is compressed and the simile is supplied from the tradition.

reading: To the Supreme that shines everywhere and above all, heart, you held as the sweetness that wells in milk holds to the milk.
nuance: The taste cannot be separated from the milk, so the figure is for a union of quality and substance rather than of two things. Pattinathar uses taste for union again at 773 (honey) and 804 (toddy).

reading: As cool vapour parts from water and becomes water again, heart, you became one with the one who has no town and no name.
nuance: The figure grants a separation before the return: vapour was water, left it and becomes water again, so the soul came from and goes back to the One rather than joining a stranger. ஊரொடு பேரில்லான், the one with no town and no name, is what the heart itself became in 784, so the two are alike before they merge.

reading: Laying this birth waste so as to remain just as you are, heart, you reached the place that is hard to tell.
nuance: இருந்தபடியே இருக்க, to remain as one is, is the phrase for the natural or settled state in which nothing further is done; it recurs at 800. பாழ்படுத்தி, laying waste, is said of the birth, not the body: the life as a career is what is emptied.

reading: Leaving behind all the higher states one after another, examining, heart, you walked in the fourth state.
nuance: பதம் is a state or station. On one reading the fourth is turiya, beyond waking, dream and deep sleep, and the higher states left behind are those three; on another the fourth is sayujya, the union that follows the three graded releases (salokam, samipam, sarupam), which are then the 'higher states' given up. The verb நடந்தனை, you walked, makes the fourth a ground one moves on rather than a point reached.

reading: Knowing the place into which the sun that plays in pot after pot withdraws, heart, you came to love it.
nuance: The sun reflected in many pots of water is the stock figure for the one Self appearing as many; the verse adds அடங்கும் இடம், the place where the sun itself withdraws or is contained, so the heart's knowledge is of the source rather than of the reflections. ஊடாடி, playing through, treats the many appearances as the sun's own sport.

reading: In that which stands as the learned one, the hearer, the unseen one, the seer and the one near at hand, heart, you became one.
nuance: The list makes the one thing stand as every party to knowing: the one who learned, the one who heard, the one who is not seen, the one who sees, the one who is present. Learning and hearing are the Kural's two roads to knowledge, and here they are forms the One takes rather than means to it.

reading: Where the four inner instruments and the five senses they govern become one and stand composed, heart, you joined.
nuance: நாலுவகைக் கரணம் are the four inner instruments (mind, intellect, will and ego) of the tattva scheme; நல்கு புலனைந்து are the five senses they give rise to or direct. The nine are not destroyed but made one and steadied (சீலமுற்று), which keeps the body's apparatus inside the union.

reading: What is let go and what is touched, the place of the sky and the place of the earth: heart, you saw them as one nature that holds them all.
nuance: கட்டும் ஒரு தன்மை, one nature that binds, is the thread image of 783 again; the first pair, விட்டிடமும் தொட்டிடமும், the left and the touched, covers everything the heart has renounced and everything it still handles, so renunciation itself is placed inside the one nature.

reading: So as to remain, on every day whatever, just as you are, heart, you made that into a state beyond happiness.
nuance: சுகாதீதம், beyond sukha, places the final state past even the happiness named in 786 and 788, as the Tirumanthiram's அதீதம் lies past turiya; or it is the beyond that is itself happiness. The condition is the same as 794's, remaining as one is, and the verse closes the first run with it.

title: நெஞ்சொடுமகிழ்தல்
theme: The last seven verses to the heart: it has taken the lead in the mind's realm beyond speech, joined the awareness that fills every land and time, come to a life that is not living, drunk the toddy of bliss that does not cloy, and, with habit, fixed contemplation and even the kingdom of silence left behind, gained the place without difference. The work ends by crediting the whole attainment to the holy feet of the guru, which swept the heart's bondage away as the sun takes the dew.
structure_note: 801 to 805 continue the states and negations of the first run; 806 and 807 are two closing similes, mercury rejoining mercury and the sun on the dew, and 807 alone names the guru.
source_issues: 801 to 807 are printed with a space before the refrain நெஞ்சமே, and 805 with spaces between words, unlike 776 to 800; the run seems to come from a differently prepared source.
806 line 1, இரதம், is obscure (mercury, taste or chariot) and may be a variant spelling of இரசம்.

reading: In the mind's realm that stands past speech, heart, you took the lead in that which stands without a blow.
nuance: மனோகோசரம் is what lies within the mind's range, so the verse places the attainment beyond words but not beyond mind, where the common formula (வாக்கு மனாதீதம்) puts it beyond both; the compound may instead mean the mind's own realm as the field in which speech has ceased. தாக்கறவே, without a strike or impact, is agitation ended. தலைசெய்தாய் is to excel or to become the head, and the sense is approximate.

reading: Filling every land and excelling in every time, heart, you joined the place of the awareness that is awareness itself.
nuance: சித்தாய சித்து is chit that is chit, pure awareness as its own nature, in the Vedantic sense of sat-chit-ananda; சித்து is also the Siddhars' word for attainment and the siddha, and the phrase can be heard as 'the attained attainment'. The verse gives the heart the Supreme's two marks, pervading space and time.

reading: Neither sinking nor stretching, filled as that very nature, heart, you came to live a life that is not living.
nuance: தன்மயம், of its own nature or absorbed into it, makes the heart the substance rather than a thing in it. வாழாதே வாழ, to live without living, matches 786's sleeping without sleeping: the life of the person has stopped and a life goes on that is not his.

reading: Drinking within and without the toddy of bliss that never cloys, heart, you set your eye on that which stands.
nuance: கள், toddy, is the figure for an intoxication that does not stale (உவட்டாத); the Puranamalai's honey that does not cloy (773) is the same claim. உள்ளும் புறம்பும், within and without, is where the drinking happens, so the bliss is not inner only.

reading: With habit gone, fixed contemplation gone, even the great kingdom of silence gone, heart, you gained the place that stands without difference.
nuance: வாதனை is vasana, the residue of past action and habit; நிஷ்டை is nishta, the fixed absorption of practice; மா மௌன ராச்சியம், the great kingdom of silence, is the sage's silence itself. All three are passed, so the state of the silent sage, which the Siddhars usually make the goal, is here a stage left behind; what remains is defined only as பேதமற, without difference.

reading: As mercury that has been parted mingles again and becomes one, heart, leaving your pining behind you came to the fiery Lord's side.
nuance: இரதம் is read as இரசம், mercury, whose scattered globules run together and become one body again, an alchemist's figure for a union that restores what was one; it can also be 'taste' (as in 773 and 792) or 'chariot', which gives no clear sense. விரகம் is the pain of separation, or, as விரகு, cunning. அணல் is Siva as the fiery one; அணல்பால் may instead be 'the near side'. The simile's point, that the parted rejoins its own kind, holds on each reading.

reading: As the dew that lies around is swept away by the sun, heart, so you won the holy feet of the guru of the right way.
nuance: சோதியான், the one of light, is the sun; சூறை கொளுமாறு, taking as a whirlwind takes or as plunder is taken, describes the dew's vanishing. What the simile compares is unstated: the guru's feet are the sun and the heart's bonds the dew, or the heart itself was taken up as the dew is. நீதி குரு, the guru of righteousness or of the right way, is the only human agent the work names, and he appears in its last line.

title: உடற்கூற்றுவண்ணம்
theme: Pattinathar's Udarkootru Vannam tells the life of one body in four long units: the seed and blood that join in the womb and the child of five playing in the street dust; the youth of sixteen with his learning, his jewels and the women who take his capital, turning into the old man with a staff; the dying man fouled, speechless and signing with his hands as the four elements and the breath stop; and the corpse netted by Yama's messengers, washed, dressed, carried to the burning ground and burnt until not a handful of ash is left. Only the last word turns to the Lord: rule me, your servant, who trusts you now.
structure_note: The work is a single வண்ணம் in four stanzas, each a chain of participles that only closes in its last line (ஆகி விளையாடியே, ஆகியே, வரு நேரமே, ஆளுமே). The text is printed without word spaces, so the segmentation of several lines is the reader's. The stages are: conception to age five (808), sixteen to old age (809), decrepitude and death (810), funeral and prayer (811).
source_issues: 808: two lacunae marked [***] in the source, in the list of organs (செவிக[***]கைகளென்ற) and after மடந்[***]; the missing words are not recoverable from the text.
808: புகுந்து / ண்டு is broken across a line so that the word is split (புகுந்துண்டு).
809: செங்கையினி்லோர் carries a stray pulli (செங்கையினிலோர்); மங்கலசெங்கலசந்திகழ்கொங்கைம / ருவ splits a word across the line.
811: சிறுகுஞ்யும் is garbled, probably சிறுகுஞ்சியும் (small tufts of hair); தொங்கல்களபபணிந்து has a doubled consonant (களபம் அணிந்து).
The whole work is printed without word spaces, so segmentation is editorial throughout.

reading: A young woman and a man join; in the love that gives pleasure the senses blur and the seed flows and mixes with the welling blood; a drop half the size of a dew-drop enters the woman's belly and, like a lotus bud, becomes eyes, mouth, ears and hands and a form in which life grows; in the tenth month it leaves the womb and falls to earth, its day and star are noted, the women tend it, it kicks and drinks the nectar of the breast, grows from one sense to two, is kissed, crawls, lisps on the lap, is told 'come' and 'go', wears bells and a waist-cord, eats with the eaters, plays in the street dust with the boys, and reaches five years at play.
nuance: The conception is told physiologically (விந்து, சுரோணிதம்) and without disgust; the disgust is saved for 810 and 811. ஓரறிவு ஈரறிவு ஆகி வளர்ந்து uses the Tamil grading of living things by number of senses for the infant's growth. Two words are lost at the lacunae marked [***], one in the list of organs and one after மடந்[தை].

reading: At sixteen he has the teaching of a guru of lofty wisdom and the arts of Tamil to their shore, is praised as a waxing moon, dresses his hair with flowers that bees hum round, wears gold and gems and is bowed to by bards; women see him as Kama's form, crowd and throw their curved glances, and when they go like peacocks he runs after them, embraces, drinks the nectar of their lips and gives away the whole capital he had gathered; the hoarded wealth is lost to idleness, and calling this the pleasure and grief of Kama he parts from the youthful form; prosperity and youth change, the strong teeth fall, the two eyes darken, age ripens, grey hair and wrinkles come with wind, quarrel and anger, and a staff is in his red hand.
nuance: Learning and wealth are given to the youth only so that the women can strip them; the stanza does not call the women courtesans, but தேடிய மாமுதல் சேர வழங்கி (giving away all the capital he had sought) is the courtesan verses' plot. வாதவிரோதகுரோதம் can be read as the wind-disease of old age or as quarrelsomeness; தடி (staff) and நரைதிரை are the standard marks of age.

reading: A hunched back that comes and goes, a squatting walk like a monkey's, mind gone, ears numb, the mouth babbling without knowing, cough that will not let him sleep, throat and chest dried out, the cloth lost and shame gone, mocked by women and boys who ask whether the Kali age will respect such a one; faeces and urine come noisily and run down his legs and up; no clarity, speech stumbling, thought and heart shaken, firmness lost, grieving that there is no help; he sees that what Brahma wrote has come, that this is his end and his bond, that life in the world will not last, speaks of what he owes, and as his tongue falls asleep he speaks with his hands; gruel runs from the corner of his mouth, the four elements and the breath stop, and the heart falters: at that moment.
nuance: The stanza is the one place the dying man speaks: கண்டம் (the fatal hour) and தொந்தம் (the bond) are his own words, and கடன்முறை பேசும் (speaking of debts and duties) is the deathbed settling of accounts. பூதமு நாலு சுவாசமும் நின்று takes the body as four elements and the breath; the fifth, space, is not counted, perhaps because it does not depart. The chain ends mid-sentence (வரு நேரமே) and 811 begins the funeral.

reading: The teeth stand out like a crescent, the hair, matted locks and tufts grow long, the mind is dark and the form shows it; Yama's messengers come like a great mountain, cast their net and take the life; sons come bowed and weeping, the wife falls in his lap and wails that they fainted though they knew his time; neighbours say the old ones should see him, those standing by say put up the pandal and come beating the drum, asking that the corpse be burnt quickly; elders set many to work, some wash the corpse, they dress the stinking body in fine cloth, garlands and sandal and make a show of it, run crying 'lift it without breaking rank', the young sons bend and carry it, hurry to the burning ground, grieve that this is what human life is, cover it in firewood and set the fire; it burns, falls and breaks, the fat melts, the bones char and settle: a body that leaves not even a handful of ash. Rule me now, your servant who trusts you.
nuance: Only the final line (நம்பும் அடியேனை இனி ஆளுமே) addresses the Lord, so the whole four-stanza life is the ground of one prayer. மாழ்கினரே இவர் காலம் அறிந்து is hard: it may be the wife's cry that they swooned though they knew his time was near, or the neighbours' comment. ஓர் பிடி நீறும் இலாத உடம்பு (a body without even a handful of ash) is the price Pattinathar sets on the body, as Arunagirinathar does.

title: திருவிடைமருதூர் மும்மணிக்கோவை
theme: The first twenty-five units of Pattinathar's Mummanikkovai on Thiruvidaimaruthur: long agavals that praise Siva's half-woman form limb by limb, dissect the poet's own body and find no 'I' in it, farm the field of the heart until the five-letter fruit ripens, and set the lives of the householder, the self-tormenting ascetic and the devotee side by side, interleaved with short venbas and kalitthurais that tell the heart to say the name, hold the devotees' feet and give up women. Pattinathar's claim throughout is that birth is a prison and grace the only way out of it, and that grace answers a green leaf, a word or a thought as well as any austerity.
structure_note: A மும்மணிக்கோவை rotates three metres, ஆசிரியப்பா, வெண்பா and கட்டளைக்கலித்துறை, in that order (812, 813, 814; 815, 816, 817 and so on), and each unit begins with the last word of the one before (திருவடி / பொருள், வரும் / வருந்தேன், கதி / கதியாவது). The metre labels printed beside the ids accumulate the previous unit's metre and are not reliable for the unit they stand beside. 822, 834 (and 850, 852 in the Kazhumalam kovai) are akam fragments in a woman's voice, the kovai's love element.
source_issues: The metre labels printed beside the ids (நேரிசையாசிரியப்பா / நேரிசைவெண்பா and so on) carry the previous unit's metre over to the next and do not describe the unit they stand beside; 816, 819, 822, 825, 828, 831 and 834 are venbas, 817, 820, 823, 826, 829, 832 and 835 kalitthurais.
813 ends without a final punctuation mark and 815 lines ராரணந் தொடராப் and வேண்டு் carry stray or missing characters (ஆரணம், வேண்டும்).
821 line 22 காள கண்டமுங் கண்ணொரு மூன்றுந்' has a stray apostrophe; line 24 தோ ளிருநான்குஞ் is split mid-word (தோளிருநான்கும்).
818 and 833 carry editor's variant notes numbered [5] to [8] and [17] to [19] whose anchors are not marked in the text.
822 and 824 are headed with the previous unit's metre as well as their own; see the general note.

reading: The poet praises the Lord of Marudur limb by limb in two halves: one foot red as a divine lotus that kicked Death and that Vishnu as a boar could not dig to, the other a soft karpaka shoot that even anklets hurt; one waist in tiger skin belted with a snake, the other in red cloth with a jewelled girdle; one chest with snake, tortoise, boar tusk, rudraksha and white ash like a coral hill, the other with breasts that bore seven worlds; one hand with trident, axe and drum, the other with bangles, a ball and a parrot; one eye hot with sun and fire, the other cool as a lily pitying our confusion; one crown with nochi, datura, konrai, Ganga, skull, snake and moon on fire-red matted hair beyond Brahma's swan, the other blue hair in a garland of karpaka flowers; two forms in one body, the right eye and the left glance, the right hand caressing the left breast so that the hair rises: we praise the feet of this one God of Marudur who gives release even to devotees who offer a green leaf, so that, having died and been born and grown weary for long days, we may not enter the prison of the womb again but gain a life that does not return.
nuance: The whole description is organised by ஒருபால் (one side) to show the half-woman form, and the kovai's akam voice later treats Ganga and Uma as rivals (834). பத்தி அடியவர் பச்சிலை இடினும் முத்தி கொடுத்து, release for a green leaf, is the claim the work returns to (825, 830, 833, 853). சிறைக் கருப்பாசயம், the prison of the womb, is developed at 833.

reading: Wealth, lineage, fame, ability, grace and knowledge, all of it, come to those who say 'dark-throated one, ancient Lord of Marudur', even to those who say they want none of it.
nuance: ஒருவர் கருதா என்பார்க்கும் is compressed: it may mean these things come even to those who do not seek them, or that they come to those who hold no one else in mind. Either way the name alone is the condition.

reading: I will not grieve, dying and being born along the way of the deluding senses; I will not join that way and so do not enter birth; having scooped and eaten the great honey of famous Marudur, I stayed with no desire for anything else, and now I will not go and beg anything from anyone.
nuance: பெருந்தேன் முகந்து உண்டு, scooping and eating the great honey, is the poet's figure for the taste of the Lord that ends wanting; the venba before promised everything to those who say the name, and this verse answers that there is nothing left to want. இரவேன் ஒருவரை, I will not beg from anyone, is the Kural's language of இரவு turned to the mendicant poet's one refusal.

reading: After praising Marudur, its cloud-touching mansions, streets and women, and its Lord with the axe, the Lord the Vedas cannot follow, the full and ancient one, the cause-God Vishnu does not know, the single light, lord of the one and of yoga, the poet says he has one thing to tell: born in endless wombs in the endless world and spun like a whirling top, he knows the pain at birth, the pain the mother suffers and he suffers, and the pain at death, and who knows them but you; so he cannot bear birth again, and there is no way to wipe out birth except holding you; that way needs a mind that leans to neither wanting nor loathing, but his mind stands at the command of the five senses and takes another thing for itself, so how is he to think of you with it; who has ever swum the sea on a raft of stone; Lord, he must gain the crossing of the aeon, and the thought for crossing, and a heart that stands on the way for thinking, O one with the venom-fanged serpent, the dark throat and the eye in the forehead.
nuance: கற்புணை ஆகக் கடல்நீர் நீந்தினர் எற்பிறர் உளரோ, who else has swum the sea on a stone float, is the image for trying to cross birth with a sense-driven mind. கற்பங் கடத்தல் is read here as crossing the aeon, that is, outlasting the kalpa; it could also be crossing to the far shore in general. The three wants at the end (the crossing, the thought, the steady heart) are asked of the Lord, not of practice.

reading: Calling you our eye, our protection, the number we have learned and the root letter, O bright Lord of Marudur, if we do not praise you, is there any refuge beyond for thought to find?
nuance: கற்றிருக்கும் எண் and மூல எழுத்து treat the Lord as the thing counted and the root syllable of the mantra, so praising him is also reciting it. கதி (refuge, goal) is picked up as the first word of 817.

reading: There is no other goal; if you carry the bundle that is this body it will fall and go, and after it has gone some grieve and call it fate; who wants this; wisdom is to go and praise the anklet feet of the Lord of Marudur.
nuance: களேபரத்தின் பொதி, the bundle of the carcass, calls the body a load one carries until it drops. விதியாம் எனச் சிலர் நோவது treats the mourners' appeal to fate as the wrong response; the right one is to have praised the feet beforehand.

reading: The poet sets two lives side by side. One man says 'we have prospered', helps none below him, pities his own life and no other, covets whatever he sees for the sake of food and tells the cooks what flavours he wants, eats and fills the pit that cannot be filled, orders about elders who outdo him in excellence, lineage, conduct and learning as if they were boys, tells lies and meanness to his base fellows and drops truth, honour and nobility; trusting himself, he leaves the good wife the ancients gave him, who would die at his death, and keeps a kept woman who craves food; clinging like oil to sesame to women who sell pleasure by the measure of money, hearing of chaste women in other men's houses he looks for the way in and not the fault; to the needy who come showing their skills he smiles and speaks sweetly as if about to give and gives nothing, wastes their days and the strength of their feet, scorns kin, says there is no here and no hereafter, lives without fear, practises deceit, desires wealth that is lightning, and thinks himself someone. The other life is that of your servants in Marudur, where the Kaveri's fish fight and swans sit on lotus leaves: they hold your feet, drop fear, do not count children, wife, kin and fortune as substance, think of your grace, push away Indra's wealth and the eight siddhis whenever they come, wear a rag and a loincloth, eat standing from a broken pot when someone gives, sleep on bare ground, embrace the woman called unfailing fitness and look on all lives as their children. Set side by side, the two are a hoof-print puddle and the deluge sea: alike as things, unlike in power; so I will put on service to the servants of your servants, grow used to them over long days, live beside them in this stout body, and take their feet's command on my head; if I see what I have seen, is there anything else good; nothing else is mine.
nuance: The householder is condemned not for having a house but for greed, contempt, lies and faithlessness; the servants' poverty is described as chosen (இந்திரச் செல்வமும் எட்டுச் சித்தியும் வந்துழி வந்துழி மறுத்தனர், refusing Indra's wealth and the eight siddhis whenever they come). ஓவாத் தகவு எனும் அரிவையைத் தழீஇ makes their only wife an abstraction, fitness or grace. The end is the poet's resolve to serve the servants' servants, the stance of 833 and 843.

reading: I have parted from hell; I have learned the way not to be born; I have escaped the dense arrows of Kama and his fighting round bow, having come inside the circle of Marudur of the Ancient One.
nuance: மருதவட்டம், the circle or precinct of Marudur, is set against Kama's வட்ட வில், the round bow, so the place itself is the shield. The verse is one of the few in the work where the poet speaks of the escape as already made.

reading: Heart, see: when you see the devotees, bow; think unforgettingly of Hara's red-gold anklet feet; go and meet the great Marudur; if you do not, Yama's men will carry you off, push you, throw you into hell and trample you.
nuance: The three commands rise from the devotees to the feet to the place, and the threat is plain hell, with none of the yogic reading other Siddhars give Yama. The address to the heart (நெஞ்சே) recurs at 831 and 838.

reading: Are there firm gains without toil, or helplessness that does not come from failing to toil? So dig the stump of deceit root and all out of the field of the heart, clear it, lay out the bed called love, spread the manure called truth, plant the single seed of doubtless devotion, water it daily with the clear water of ardour, and fearing the five cattle that break in past every guard, go in and build the fence of peace; then the great sprout of knowledge rises, shows the tender shoot of compassion, the weeds of lust and anger are pulled, it grows straight, the hair bristles, tears bud, the fragrant flower opens and the rare fruit of the five letters appears, with poison throat, three eyes, eight shoulders, five bright faces, coral colour and white ash, sweeter than the six tastes, a joy to see, hear and think of; the ruby fruit of high Marudur ripens slowly into the hand, and our kind eat it and hold their heads high. Some do not come this way: they make the field of the mind a waste, let the forest of lust cover it where the hunters of the five senses rob, chase the mirage-chariot of pleasure that is never reached, the deer of untaught sense wanders, and when the seed of desire is dropped the great poison tree called 'I' shoots up, puts out branches of lies, spreads leaves of sin, buds cruelty, flowers harshness, hangs fruit of sorrow, ripens death and falls into the serpent's place: useless to themselves and others, they pass in the blink of an eye; such is their nature.
nuance: The allegory is worked out stage by stage on both sides, cultivation and neglect, and the two trees are the Lord (the five-letter fruit wearing his own iconography) and the ego (யான் எனப் பெயரிய நச்சு மாமரம், the poison tree named 'I'). The five cattle and the five hunters are the senses in both halves. நாகிடை வீழ்ந்து, falling among the serpent, probably means hell; a variant reading is not recorded.

reading: Shrinking at the sound of the waist-bells and folding its hood, the serpent goes softly as the Lord of Marudur goes begging alms, so that Kama's hand-arrow may enter the women of fine jewels: see.
nuance: Read as the Bhikshatana scene in which Siva begs in the forest and the sages' wives fall in love with him: ஐயம் புகுவது is going for alms, and the snake on his body quiets so as not to frighten the women. The syntax leaves open whose waist-bells sound and whether காண் addresses the heart or the reader. This is the kovai's first akam fragment.

reading: You see no goal; you do not learn the five letters so as to master them; you do not cherish temple service; you do not speak his praise out of longing; you do not wear rudraksha; you do not smear ash everywhere: idle ones, is it easy to reach the feet of the Lord of Marudur?
nuance: This is a positive programme of ordinary Saiva practice, letters, service, praise, beads and ash, from a poet otherwise read as a renouncer of forms; 825 and 830 keep the same list. It stands far from Sivavakkiyar's dismissal of the same things, though both call the body's end the reason.

reading: Is it the mass of coarse hair, or the stretch of skin the hair grows on, or the wound packed inside the skin, or the blood that wells in the wound, or the bones standing here and there between, or the stinking marrow that drips from the bones, or the slime that oozes within, or the orderly files of crawling worms, or the heap of excrement set in water, or the ropes of tied nerves, or the disease that never leaves the body: which of these is 'I', I do not know; I searched everywhere and found it nowhere. Then, Lord of Marudur who burnt the three cities with one mountain bow, made Kama fine dust with a glance, turned the fire-mouthed poison to nectar so the gods would not die, stood beyond the two who sought you, and scorched Death for the boy's sake, half-woman, lord of Ganga, Lord of the Kaveri-girt grove where nine gems shine without the sun: because your divine grace came into my hand, I tore the veil of maya and gained the pure eye of knowledge; and having gained it I saw your greatness, and seeing it I saw myself, and saw others, and saw myself in all your states; those who do not see you are the kind that do not see themselves.
nuance: The dissection is a search for the self, each part posed as a question (ஓ), and the answer is that the self is not found in the body but given by grace along with the sight of the Lord. The order of seeing matters: the Lord first, then oneself, then others, then oneself in all his states. The variant தெரியாது இன்ன (not discerning, this) for தெரிதரல் இன்ன does not change the sense.

reading: Without thinking the five letters, without offering a green leaf, without pouring water: who are we, that we say we will reach the golden feet of the Lord of Marudur who dwells in the hearts of those who think of him?
nuance: The minimal offerings of 812 (a green leaf) are here the minimum demanded: the venba rebukes those, the poet included, who expect the feet while doing nothing at all. யாராயோ, who are we, is a self-address.

reading: We now know how matters stand between us, and may we say it: the Lord of Marudur, who adorned kings with flowers like the swans of the Marudur grove and made them survive and set a mark on them, should not himself load a burden on those who are already failing.
nuance: The kings saved and marked are taken by tradition as the Pandya Varaguna, whose brahmin-killing left him in this temple (839 names வரகுண தேவர்); the text itself only says he made kings survive and put a dot (பொட்டு) on them. The last line is clearer: it is not fitting to add a burden to one who is sinking, that is, to the poet. இடையுள்ள ஆறு may also pun on இடைமருது.

reading: After a long address, to the king who bent the mountain into a bow so the cities of his enemies burned in fire, white with fine ash, whose strong foot walked Kailasa, with the red-eyed bull of two horns like crescents, husband of the Himalaya's daughter, of Uma whose womb bore the seven worlds, father of the eight-shouldered elephant-eared boy and of Murugan of the cockerel banner and the hill-piercing spear, the poet asks whether the fault is yours: the sinners who do not think of you, do not clear away their crores of troubles, kill angry Death, scorn death and birth and wander like the calf of the gods' cow, the sin is theirs. If a man starves in front of a six-flavoured dish of rice with ghee and three fruits, it is not the food's fault; if he thirsts beside clear water cooled in the sun, it is not the water's fault; if he stands sweating in the open sun beside a grove dripping honey on cool sand, it is not the shade's fault.
nuance: The three comparisons make grace a thing set ready and unused, so the whole burden of failure falls on the one who does not come to it; the verse thereby denies that the Lord withholds. தேவர் ஆவின் கன்று, the calf of the heavenly cow, is the image for the freed one roaming at ease.

reading: Though the six faiths say 'no' and 'yes' and contradict one another, it all comes round to the Lord of Marudur, who dwells in the hearts of those who ever look to the One alone.
nuance: The verse does not refute the six; it lets them argue and says the end of every argument is the one Lord within. ஒருதனையே நோக்குவார் can be those who look to the one God or those who look at one thing with single mind; both suit.

reading: The merit of the Lord of the Kaveri-girt Marudur: his look made Kama's body dust; his toe pressed the rakshasa head downward; his sword-form rolled Daksha's head; and he sent Jalandhara's life away.
nuance: Four of the Lord's punitive deeds hang on one verb each (நோக்கிற்று, தாக்கிற்று, ஓக்கிற்று, போக்கிற்று), and the subject of all four is புண்ணியம், merit, so the deeds are the place's merit rather than the god's violence. The rakshasa is Ravana and the sword-form the discus given to Vishnu, as tradition has it.

reading: The poet addresses the Lord of Marudur who protects from entering the womb those devotees who worship with devotion grown to true love and offer a green leaf, nochi or karanthai. Many people leave children, wife, kin and house, go into forest and mountain, stand in summer in the midst of the five fires with arms raised and one leg bent, in rain and dew lie long in water, wear matted hair or pluck out their hair, go without eating, eat fruits, roots and wind-fallen leaves, air and water, sleep on salt ground and stones, and weaken the weakening body, tormenting themselves greatly for the sake of the Mother's release. We did none of this: in flawless seven-storied mansions, in red-pollen groves, breezy courtyards, painted halls, by lotus tanks and on peacock hills, wherever we wished, on ivory lion-legged cots with five-fold mattresses, white sheets smelling of flowers, cotton in silk, pillows, anklets sounding on the sheet, we embraced soft-spoken women with swan gait, waist-chains, snake-waists, swelling breasts, areca-smooth necks, bangled arms, ears, pearl-studded noses and eyes that carry Death's spear, Kama's arrow and the poison of the sea in moon faces under fresh garlands; we ate six-flavoured rice from gold plates, gave without limit to dancers, singers and the weary, anointed, adorned and garlanded ourselves, filled the five senses and rejoiced with sons and kin. Though we lived like this, because we kept the five letters of the mantra in the mouth unforgotten and sent the mind along your way, we have not lost that release; is this not your greatness? Whether a strong man throws it hard or a weak man throws it idly, the stone does not miss the ground: so those who utter your name do not fall from the good.
nuance: The verse ranks neither life; it makes the ascetic's self-torment and the poet's luxury equally irrelevant and the name and the directed mind the only cause of release. யாங்கள் (we) sets the poet, in tradition a merchant prince before his renunciation, among the pleasure-livers, which fits the legend but is also a rhetorical pose. The closing stone (கல்லே போல் நிலத்தின் வழாஅ) says the result does not depend on the thrower's strength.

reading: Heart, utter the name; can you waste away sinking into women's shoulders and talking lust? Encircle the Lord of the Marudur grove who wears the hide of the elephant he fought.
nuance: நாம நவிற்றாய் picks up the last word of 830 (நாமம் நவின்றோர்) and turns its general claim into an order to the heart. வளைந்து, encircle, is the word for going round the shrine as much as for clinging.

reading: Those who have reached the feet of the devotees of the Lord of Marudur with his golden konrai garland do not suffer hunger, do not grieve in disease, do not waste under Kama's arrow, do not stand yearning at the sight of wealth, and are not bound in this birth to enter the mire of hell: what do they owe to anyone?
nuance: The protection is given to those at the devotees' feet, one step further from the Lord than 820's devotees; 818 and 833 make the same descent, servant of the servants' servants. என் கடவார் (what do they owe) treats hunger, disease, lust and hell as debts the others still carry.

reading: After praising the Lord of Marudur who gives unending joy and undiminishing wealth to those who reach his feet, who has no root, middle or end and is beyond the three times, hidden from the eye of flesh and not from the mind's eye, the unflickering light, the sound that rises from within and does not reach the ear's hole, the divine honey that wells sweetly inside past the tongue, the fragrance of knowledge that comes by no nostril, who is himself all things, in whom all appearing appears while he appears in nothing else, with the white moon on his spread hair and the dark throat, whom Vishnu, Brahma and the Vedas still pursue, the ruby of Marudur with three unwinking eyes, the poet asks him to hear a servant's plea without anger. Dragged by the cruel deeds of long consorting with hard-hearted base men who do not bow to your feet, I lay long in the dark prison-cell called the womb, chained with the chain of the gut, like a caged worm sunk in long filth, suffering, rained on by many diseases, pressed by the punishers, writhing in the belly's fire, beaten by the whip of wind, unable to lie, stand or walk, cramped in the narrow gate; then, placed in the portion of sin, with the five cruel guards set over me, tied in the long rope of desire, I and the body were bound in bonds and let softly out. I too went and roamed in evil, wronged the great, seized others' goods, failed in pity, killed many lives, praised the look of other men's wives, told many lies, kept base company and fed the craving of the five, gathered what I gathered and came back, did not give where giving was due nor fall where falling was due, and now I have met trouble and lie withering for many days and see no road to release. Count me too a slave to the servants of the servants who reached you, with the green leaf I offered make me know, free me from this prison, guard me from entering the prison again, O one with red hair like gathered fire.
nuance: The womb passage inverts 808: the same ten months told from inside as a cell, with the umbilical cord as chain (குடர் என் சங்கிலி), the five senses as the warders appointed at birth (காவல் கொடியோர் ஐவர்), and desire as the rope that binds soul and body together in பாசம். தண்டனாளர், the punishers, and வாத மத்திகை, the whip of wind, are unexplained; the latter may be the womb's wind humour. The variant தத்துவ for தற்பர (833 line 14) would make the Lord the tattva rather than the Supreme.

reading: One woman is settled on his matted hair and another shines on the side of his body; if the bull has gone and this girl gives the Lord of Marudur her conch bangles and her garment, where is she to be?
nuance: An akam fragment: the girl wasting for love of the Lord loses her bangles and her waist's slenderness (the stock signs of மெலிவு), figured as giving them to him, and her companion asks where she can stand when Ganga has the hair and Uma the body. சங்கே கலையே can be conch-bangles and cloth or, in the cipher of love poetry, the slipping bangles and the waist; விடையே போய் is obscure, perhaps 'the bull having gone (as his messenger)'. The variant இடைப்புகு (entering the waist) suggests another reading of the last line.

reading: Within Marudur the gods and the four Vedas crowd and press; going into its long interior in that press they cannot come back out; cutting away crookedness and the harm of the five, he is the bright light that sprouts within the one-pointed gathering of a mind made straight.
nuance: The gods and Vedas that crowd into the shrine do not find their way out, while the light appears in the single-pointed mind: the verse sets the inner finding above the outer press without rejecting the shrine. ஒருக்கும் ஒருக்கத்தின் உள்ளே, within the one-making of the one-pointed, is the yogic word for concentration.

reading: Saying 'you hold the blazing trident', 'you rode the bull', 'you ate the poison none can eat', 'you burnt Kama with your eye', 'you burnt the three cities', 'you wore the elephant's hide', 'you wore the serpent', 'you hold fire in your hand', 'you killed Death', 'you cut Jalandhara's body', 'you trod the boastful rakshasa', 'you broke Daksha's sacrifice', 'you wore the fierce tiger skin', 'you grew till the sky was below you and the boar and the swan could not reach', 'you crushed the fire-eyed dwarf who ate the lives of the earth': praising your countless unimaginable fame is only as far as my trembling mind's words go; your measureless greatness is beyond my measure, but with poor words that do not fit I look to you, so do not fail to clear my troubles and leave me in distress, O rich light seated in Marudur where cloth banners wake the clouds asleep on the seven-storied mansions, wonder-dancer who pours grace: even for the wicked Buddhist who threw a stone at you, because he threw it thinking of you, grace did not fail.
nuance: The list of deeds is framed as inadequate speech (புன்மொழி) offered anyway, and its proof is Sakkiya Nayanar, who in the Periyapuranam worshipped by throwing a stone daily: the act was accepted because of the thought behind it (நின் நினைந்து எறிந்த அதனால்). This makes intention, not form, the condition of grace, as 830 and 848 do.

title: திருவிடைமருதூர் மும்மணிக்கோவை
theme: The close of the Marudur Mummanikkovai: two short verses tell the heart that the dying do not praise the feet and that it must cling day and night to the thousand-formed Lord; the long agaval counts the gods, sages, saints and strange devotees, Sivavakkiyar among them, who gained grace at Marudur and sets the poet last as one who has no devotion at all and will go on thinking of the Lord anyway, since good and evil alike are his doing; a venba says one utterance of the Lord's name scatters all sins, and the final kalitthurai signs the work with the poet's birth name and places the Lord's feet on his head and in his thought.
structure_note: The three-metre rotation and the chaining of last word to first word (அடி / அடியாயிரம், கொண்டே / கொண்டலின், கரந்து / கரத்தினன்) continue from chapter 47; the last word of 841, தாமரையே, chains back to the first word of 812, தெய்வத் தாமரை, closing the garland. Metre labels beside the ids are the previous unit's and not reliable.
source_issues: 839 names சிவவாக்கிய தேவர் among the devotees honoured at Marudur, which bears on the relative dating of the two poets.
839 carries editor's notes [25] and [26] whose anchors are not marked; the variant எண்ணிறந்தோரே அனையோர் நிற்க for எண்ணிறந்தோர்கள் அனைவரும் நிற்க does not change the sense.
841's heading reads கட்டளைக்கலித் துறை with a space in the metre name.

reading: Will mean-headed people, whose business is to be here today and to die tomorrow, praise the red-gold feet of the one with the victorious axe, who owns divine Marudur and owns me, his dog?
nuance: புகழ்வரோ expects the answer no: those whose only occupation is dying do not praise. நாயேனை ஆளுடையான், who owns me the dog, is the poet's usual self-placement; 839 lengthens it.

reading: Heart, learn this and cling day and night to the Lord of southern Marudur: a thousand feet, a thousand works, a thousand thousand names, a thousand heads, three thousand eyes, white ash over all, two thousand shoulders in a thousand bangles.
nuance: The thousands are the Vedic hymn's thousand-headed Person turned Saiva by the ash and the three eyes multiplied; the point is that the Lord to be held is everywhere in every form. படியாய் can be 'recite' or 'bow'.

reading: After praising the three-eyed Lord of Marudur with the dark throat, the snake belt, the crescent in his hair, the Pusam bathing festival and the Kaveri, the poet lists those who bowed to him there and gained great boons that never failed: Uma, the elephant-faced child, Murugan, Vishnu with the conch, four-faced Brahma, the virgin who killed Taruka, Sarasvati and Lakshmi, crores of Rudras, Indra and his four-tusked elephant, the twelve suns, the moon, Agni, Nirruti, Yama, the four Vedas, Varuna, Vayu, Kubera, the eight hells and the eight Vasus, three crores of sages, Vasishtha, Kapila and Agastya, Tumburu and Narada, the three saints of skilled song, the child of Perunthurai of perfected love, and Sivavakkiya devar of the siddha mind who was honoured with such wealth; then the stranger devotees: one who saw white ash on a thief's body and had his hands untied; one who heard a running fox howl and gave it cloths, saying it sang of Hara; one who scattered coins and gold on the frogs croaking in a lily pool, saying they praised the Lord; one who caught a worshipper eating the sesame meant for the bath, asked what this birth was for and ate his leavings; one who saw a lone skull lying in the Marudur precinct, bowed to it and begged again and again that his own head might lie like it; one who took a dog's carcass from the temple courtyard as a thing well come; one who, seeing a fruit fallen from its stalk, built canopies over all the neem trees; and Varaguna devar of great love, who gave his curly-haired queen to the Supreme because what is desired must be given. Let all these countless ones stand aside: I am one man with no stroke of what is called devotion, the last of all, who does not appear even if he is pure; yet though I do not bow to you, praise you, grieve or bless you, I will go on thinking of you, Lord; since all the good and evil in your whole world are your doing, I alone will do for the way that has no good in it.
nuance: The list places சிவவாக்கிய தேவர் among the three Tevaram saints and Manikkavasagar as a devotee honoured by the Lord, which is the earliest naming of Sivavakkiyar in this corpus and tells against the tradition that makes Pattinathar his senior. The anecdotes that follow are told as if known and most are not identifiable from the Periyapuranam; the thief freed for wearing ash and the dog's carcass taken from the courtyard are read here as acts of devotees who honoured anything bearing the Lord's sign, but the syntax lets several be read as the Lord's own acts. The closing நானே அமையும் நலமில் வழிக்கே is taken as 'I alone suffice as the specimen of the good-less way'; it could also mean 'I will make do with the way without good'.

reading: All the sins we have done, straying from the path and acting as we came, sins that escaped blame: if we once say with the mouth 'he of grove-girt Marudur', they do not stay where thought reaches; they vanish and hide.
nuance: வாய்கூப்ப வேண்டா is read as 'one need only say it', with வேண்டா marking sufficiency; read as a plain negative it would say even saying it is unnecessary, which the next line does not support. பழிபிழைத்த பாவங்கள் are sins that went unblamed, so even hidden sins are meant.

reading: Lord of Marudur who gave good boons when Vishnu of the discus hand worshipped your anklets with his own eye: for me who has no sense at all, your feet, the divine lotus, have come to be on my head, within my thought, and in the standing of the one called Venkadan.
nuance: கண்கொண்டு போற்ற is Vishnu's offering of his eye in place of the thousandth lotus, as tradition tells it. வெண்காடன் is the poet's own name: Pattinathar was born Thiruvenkadar, so the kovai closes with a signature, and தாமரையே chains back to the opening word of 812.

title: திருக்கழுமல மும்மணிக்கோவை
theme: Pattinathar's Mummanikkovai on Thirukkazhumalam (Sirkazhi): the Lord who floated on the deluge and fed the child Sambandar the milk of knowledge is praised as the Full One beyond the Vedas and the inner faculties, and the poet makes the ruined room of his mind the Lord's bedchamber, counts every being that has been his parent or his food through endless wombs, and tells how grace turned the whirl of a blind man's road into the sight of the one true thing behind a painted wall. Short verses say the devotees' devotees outrank the gods, that the body is impurity entire, and that when flower, leaf and water fail the heart is offering enough.
structure_note: Twelve units in the three-metre rotation (agaval, venba, kalitthurai) chained by last word to first (ஆங்கே / அருளின், அதற்கு / ஆரண, கருப்பொருளே / கருமுதல்). The metre labels beside the ids are the previous unit's and unreliable. 850 and 852 are akam fragments in a companion's voice. A prose remark printed after 851 is an editor's note on a variant, not verse.
source_issues: 851 ends with a prose line, சடமாகிய வுடம்பெனக்கொண்டு, கல்லா வுடம்பெனவும் பாடாமோதுவர், which is an editor's variant note printed as if it were verse.
The metre labels beside the ids carry over the previous unit's metre (843, 846, 849, 852 are venbas; 844, 847, 850, 853 kalitthurais).
842 line 29 வேதியச்சிறுவன் and line 34 தோஒடுடைய / பீஇடுடைய use the alapedai spelling; 844 and 847 are printed without word spaces so segmentation is editorial.

reading: With the Himalaya's daughter inseparable on one side like an emerald creeper on a coral mountain, with a face like a thousand suns rising from the waves, her young breasts, lotus face, crescent brow, red-lily mouth and lotus hands holding the pot of nectar, and her blue-lily eyes blooming with your splendour, you sat at the Lord's ease in Kazhumalam of the brahmins, which floated above the nagas' land when the upper worlds sank below and stood as the one support of the three worlds in the flood; and when the brahmin child who came with his father, at the toddling age, cried 'Mother' from hunger, she stood before him and gave him the ball of milk kneaded with the food of knowledge; and when the brahmin angrily asked who gave it, the boy pointed with his hand and said he would show him, 'the one with the earring, the one with the bull': there you appeared in grace.
nuance: The second half is the Sambandar legend told in the child's own words, தோடுடைய செவியன் and பீடுடைய பெம்மான் echoing his first Tevaram hymn; ஞான போனகம், the food of knowledge, names the milk as the source of his poetry. The Lord addressed throughout is the one who 'appeared' (வெளிப்பட்டருளினை), so the long praise of Uma leads to his epiphany, not hers.

reading: The sea of grace, the Lord of Pugali who is the mass of substance and the way called the love of me his servant: for those who love and worship with joined hands those who say 'the one with darkness in his throat', who among the heavenly beings is a match?
nuance: The ranking is of the devotees' devotees above the gods (அண்டத்தார்), the same descent as 818 and 833 in the Marudur kovai. அடியேன் அன்பு என்னும் ஆறு, the way called my love, makes the poet's love itself the Lord's path rather than his own act.

reading: Beyond the four Vedas, hard for Narayana and the four-faced one who resolved to know him, the Full One who fills the middle, our father, the Lord of Pugali, the cause of every world, the core thing beyond the inner faculties.
nuance: பூரணன் and கருப்பொருள் are the two names the verse adds to the usual list: the Lord is the Full One and the kernel beyond the antahkarana (mind, intellect, will, ego). Pattinathar uses பூரணம் as a name of the Lord here as throughout his Pooranamalai; the medical Siddhars make it a technical term.

reading: The rubbish of impurity called lust, anger and the great lie had lain without end since the embryo began, through all my long days; with difficulty I scorned and cleared it, untied and drove off the five rutting buffaloes of dark killing anger, swept with love, lit the lamp of grace, left the darkness of sorrow, spread the canopy of truth in front, made the ruined room of my mind, which had lain in flimsy baseness, your bedchamber, and set you on the cushion of the mind's full lotus flower; Lord of Pugali who floated high as the raft on which the gods were saved when the first flood spread over the long earth and the burning sky and the two lights floated like foam and the wind tore up the mountains and Vishnu and Brahma and the gods trembled that this was the end, Pralaya-vidangar whom the Kaveri's dawn pours forth: with your rich anklets sounding softly, bringing the Himalaya's shoot with you in the sight that never cloys, you may deign to come here, my Lord.
nuance: The housework allegory matches the farming one at 821: lust and lies are rubbish, the senses are five buffaloes to be untied and driven out, love is the broom, grace the lamp, truth the canopy, and the Lord is invited to a bed, not a shrine. The invitation includes Uma (இமயக் கொழுந்தையும் உடனே கொண்டு), so the heart is to house the half-woman form of 842.

reading: Bearing the deer and the axe, the darkness that lives in his holy throat and the crescent, he who appeared on the flood for the gods and sat enthroned at Kazhumalam has stood in my heart as light.
nuance: The three stations of the Lord, the flood, the town and the heart, are one sentence, so the shrine's founding legend ends inside the poet. The chain word ஒளி is taken up by 847.

reading: How the light came, so that the darkness in my false mind left; how my inner flood cleared; how it came and grew sweet; how an unthought joy came; how love came; how clarity came at the last hour: that is the sweet grace of the dwellers in Kazhumalam.
nuance: Six exclamations of வந்தவா (how it came) list the stages of grace as received, light, clarity, sweetness, joy, love, clarity again, with no act of the poet's among them. கடைசார் அமையத்து is read as the last hour of life; it could be the final stage of the sequence.

reading: Ripe sweet fruit of grace, unceasing joy, love that does not end, sea of nectar to your devotees, Lord of Kazhumalam whose tall gold tower-tops split the clouds' bellies, supreme yogi who sits with the maiden of young breasts, I will tell you one thing: Father, from the day you first thought that all worlds and endless wombs and all things should appear, through so many wombs of unthinkable difference, there is no one and nothing that has not come as my mother and my father, one by one, and none that have not come as those whose father and mother I was; there is no ground where I was not born before, nor any where I did not die; there are no lives that have not eaten me, nor any that I have not eaten; all that time has gone; I, the dog, cannot weary myself any further. I have not learned the tantra that recites your five letters, light of the sky, nor consorted with those who learned it; even so, in one moment that was possible, taking the flower I placed as the flower and the word I spoke as the mantra, it is your duty to keep me from falling into the sea of the two, troublesome birth and death.
nuance: The kinship argument is complete in both directions, every being has parented him and he every being, and extended to eating and being eaten, so rebirth makes the whole world one family and one food-chain; the poet draws from it only exhaustion. The plea's logic is that the single flower and word, offered without training, must count as the ritual (சொன்னதும் மந்திரமாக), and that keeping him out is the Lord's debt (நின் கடனே).

reading: Those who do not worship with joined hands the Kazhumalam of the three-eyed Lord sink to their feet in the sea called lust and suffer, knowing no means to conquer it: they are those who do not consider that the body is impurity entire.
nuance: உடலாம் முழுமலத்தை ஓர்கிலார் makes the body not merely impure but the whole of impurity, and makes failing to see this the cause of lust and of not worshipping. The venba thus gives the dissection of 824 its doctrine.

reading: This girl worships; this girl loses her bangles; for her distress alone the gossip rises; what is one to do about what is rising? If she has seen with her own hands, so to speak, the unwashed gem that sits in my heart, the Lord of Kazhumalam, the axe-bearer, and come back, there is no blame in it at all.
nuance: An akam fragment in a companion's or mother's voice about the girl love-sick for the Lord: loosened bangles and public talk (அலர்) are the stock signs. கழுவா மணி puns on கழுமலம், the gem that needs no washing, the Lord already in the heart; who speaks the last clause and whether the seeing is a vision or a temple visit is not settled.

reading: After praising the Lord of Pugali whose fame shone in the twelve ages past under different names, the bull-rider, husband of Uma, who bent the mountain and burnt the three cities of the strong-shouldered demons, with young moon on his growing hair and the single eye in his forehead that glared at Kama, the beginning the gods do not know, the poet confesses: in my untaught heart base understanding followed me, and with the empty gaze that looks and forgets, each time I looked, everything everywhere, mine and others', the many that come to be and the many that perish, what goes, comes and passes, more numerous than the sand heaped in the clear-watered world, the non-existent seeming to be and the existent unseen, I lay for many days in darkness; and the way it shook me was like a man who cannot see with his eyes and reels, the pit becoming his road and the road a pit, stumbling without end from one into the other; so it came, until I gained by compassion your look of growing grace, and then everything appeared false to me and you alone, the rare one, appeared true: like the many carved and painted shapes a master painter drew to catch a likeness, which to those who run their hands over them all without stopping show themselves as one wall.
nuance: Two images carry the verse: the blind man for whom pit and road exchange places, which is the unenlightened state, and the painted wall, which is the enlightened one: the painter's many figures differ to the eye but the hand that feels them finds one surface, so the many things are false and the one substrate true. இல்லன உளவாய் உள்ளன காணா is the plain statement of maya in the Vedantic sense. The prose line printed after the verse (சடமாகிய உடம்பு எனக் கொண்டு, கல்லா உடம்பு எனவும் பாடமோதுவர்) is an editor's note that some read கல்லா உடம்பு for கல்லா உளத்தின்.

reading: So she rose; what will she do? Still she says 'show me the angry bull'; the konrai blossom of the Lord of flowery Pugali, on whose matted crown the serpents stretch and rise in swift anger.
nuance: The second akam fragment: the girl rises wanting the Lord's konrai garland, the lover's gift of love poetry. சினவேறு காட்டுதிர் என்னும் may be her plea to be shown the bull, that is the Lord, or the companions' refusal; the venba is elliptical and the subject of பாம்பு கலியா நிமிரும் (the serpents in the hair rising) may be a figure for her agitation as much as the Lord's ornament.

reading: If no flower is to be had, there is the green leaf; if no leaf, there is water everywhere; if nothing at all is to be had, there is the heart, today: so say these, as equal, for reaching the lotus feet, which not even the bee's pollen attains, of the Lord of southern Thonipuram who shares his body with the one of incomparable breasts.
nuance: The descending list, flower, leaf, water, heart, declares them equal offerings (இணையாகச் செப்பும்), so the heart is not a substitute but the same thing. இன்றே, today, refuses deferral. The last word, சார்வதற்கே, chains the kovai's end to its beginning (திரு / திருவளர்) and its claim closes the thought begun at Marudur 812.

title: திருவேகம்பமுடையார் திருவந்தாதி
theme: The opening of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar of Kanchi, a Thirumurai text and not a cipher poem. The first nine verses are a devotee's address: a confession of false service, the Lord's form and feet, the worth of the devotees' company, and a refusal to sing any other god. From 863 the poem turns into kovai-style love poetry set on Ekambar's Kailasa: the hero sees the hill girl in the millet field, comes with the pretext of a lost elephant or a hunt, and the girl and her friend speak of fear, gossip and parting.
structure_note: An antadhi: each verse opens with the sound that closes the one before (854 தொண்டனென்பணிகொள்ளுதியோ கச்சியேகம்பனே, 855 ஏகம்பனே; 878 எய்தியதே, 879 இயங்கும்). Every verse names Ekambar or Kambar of Kachi, and from 863 his Kailasa is the mountain of the love poems. 854 to 862 are bhakti; 863 to 878 follow the kovai sequence of the kurinji field: first sight (863), the hero's pretexts (864, 866, 869), the friend and the girl on fear and gossip (871, 876), and the parrots and the field at the end of the season (877, 878). The speakers are not marked and are supplied from the kovai convention.
source_issues: The work is Pattinathar's Thiruvekambamudaiyar Thiruvandhadhi of the eleventh Thirumurai; its first 25 verses here carry no section headings, and the speakers of the love verses (863 to 878) are not marked.
866 is printed with a terminal full stop and a variant note glossing துரு as ஆராய்ச்சி; the gloss is an editor's and does not settle the line.
872 line 3 has a space inside கும்ப முழ, apparently one word, and the variant மூழ்கும் suggests the word is corrupt.
878 has a variant note தம்மைப் பிறவிக்கடல் கடப்பிப்பவர்தாம் for the first line's நம்மை ... நாம்.

reading: The poet confesses he does not know the path the true servants walk, has never done good service among the hand-servants, speaks a false service and praises the Lord only outwardly, to eat; and asks whether Ekambar of Kachi will take even this servant's service.
nuance: பொய்த்தொண்டு and புறம்புறமே (outwardly, outwardly) are the poet's charge against himself; the verse does not ask forgiveness but whether the Lord will accept the false service as it is. Pattinathar's legend of the renounced merchant is not in the verse.

reading: The poet calls Ekambar the one who rules him, the Lord who pities the gods and gives them enjoyment for many days, who wears the swelling five-mouthed serpent shining like a gold necklace, wears the fine ash, and is like a great golden mountain to the one who cherishes him.
nuance: The verse is an address and not a request. ஐவாய் நாகம், the five-mouthed serpent worn as an ornament, and the ash on a golden body set the Lord's form that 888 to 898 will describe limb by limb.

reading: The poet says he has fixed the Lord's shining name in his mind, has scraped away his hard karma, laughed at the poverty of those who do not serve Ekambar of Kachi with its bee-humming groves, and become clear enough to wear the feet of the Lord's devotees.
nuance: ஏழைமை, wretchedness or poverty, is what the poet sees in those who do not serve; the laugh is scorn and not pity. The feet he wears (அடியார் அடி பூண) are the devotees', not the Lord's, a step down the Saiva hierarchy that the Tirumanthiram also honours.

reading: The poet says his mind has gone and grown clear at the Lord's holy form, that there is no more doubt of the gracious hand that gives, and that he has gained the state of having the dust of the feet of those who rejoice in Ekambar, whose body shines like the red evening sky, set on his head.
nuance: தளிதரு தூளி, the dust the temple gives or the dust of the feet of those at the temple, is loose; the plain sense is that the devotees' foot-dust on his head is the gain. ஐயம் இனி இலை (no more doubt) is the hinge: clarity, not merit, is what the form gives.

reading: The poet says he gained and rejoiced, learned and rejoiced in the Lord's growing fame so as to offer archana always and sweeten his thought, and calls on Ekambar, who delights in the hold of Kachi and comes on the bull with the hooded serpent wound as his belt, naming his twin feet.
nuance: The verse plays கச்சி (Kanchi) against கச்சு (belt): the serpent is the belt the Lord of Kachi wears. அர்ச்சனை marks this as temple devotion, which the later Siddhar poets in this corpus mock; Pattinathar here is a Thirumurai devotee.

reading: The ground where the Lord's feet stood was beyond the reach of Vishnu, and the crown where his head stood became hard for the lotus-born Brahma to see; the poet asks how we are to worship the trident-bearing Ekambar whose bull roars like thunder in dark clouds.
nuance: The myth is the pillar of fire whose foot and crown Vishnu and Brahma could not find. The question யாம் எங்ஙனே வணங்குவதே is not refusal: if the gods could not reach his limits, the human worshipper's bowing is beyond its object, and that is offered as praise.

reading: The poet says that bowing is for the Lord's feet, that we know no fellowship but that of those infatuated enough to bow, and that apart from singing cool Kachi Ekambam of the one who bent the mountain into a bow with the strong serpent as string, the poetic excellence that sings another god does not count.
nuance: கணக்கன்று, 'it is no account', makes the claim about poetry and not about the gods: verse spent on another god is wasted craft. மையல், infatuation, is used of devotion without irony, the word the love verses will use of desire.

reading: The poet tells the good people to listen to one thing for their good: seeing Kachi Ekambam of Haran mixed with love, stand and worship him with the words that he set the fiery discus to cut down Jalandhara and that he made all of Daksha's sacrifice ... permanent.
nuance: நிரந்தரமாகச் செய்தாய் of Daksha's sacrifice is odd, since the myth has the Lord wreck it; it may mean he made it endless by stopping it, or be ironic, or carry a sense of நிரந்தரம் I cannot fix. The frame, a devotee instructing others how to praise, is clear.

reading: Some called his locks lightning, his throat a cloud, his body's colour gold; those who have worn his golden feet, whatever they say of his appearing, do not know parting from him; and the natures by which all the worlds hold their place are said to be those of Kachi Ekambar.
nuance: வெளிப்பாடு, manifestation, is what the comparisons describe; the verse sets the devotees' not-parting (பிரிந்தறியார்) above any description of the form, and then makes the Lord the ground on which the worlds stand.

reading: On the rich Kailasa of walled Kachi Ekambar, whom the gods and the unfailing ascetics worship, the grace of a golden peacock, red-streaked eyes, curled hair and a waist that bends in softness have brought love to birth.
nuance: The love poem begins here without notice: the subject of காதல் விளைத்தன is the hill girl's body, and the speaker is the hero at first sight, by the kovai convention. The peacock and the striped eyes are the stock comparisons of that moment.

reading: The friend tells the girl, their flower-creeper, that a youth like Murugan, asking after an elephant that has not left off its rage, does not leave the millet field while it is day, on the heavenly Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar whose devotees bear the mark of the Lady's embrace.
nuance: Asking after a lost elephant is the hero's pretext for staying near the girl, a fixed motif of the kurinji field (வேழம் வினாதல்). The friend's noticing that he will not leave is itself the sign (குறிப்பு) that she has read him. The first two lines, on devotees who bear the scar of embracing Uma, are the shrine-praise frame and strain the syntax.

reading: On the kongu-crested Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar with its flowering groves, a speaker addresses the golden one who is like a goddess, and says something about seeing and pained feet if she came playing in the spreading stone waterfall.
nuance: கண்டு அடி வருத்தே at the close does not resolve: either the hero fears her feet would be hurt on the rocks, or someone saw her and was wounded by the sight. பாங்கு ஒத்திருந்தனையார் (one fit to be a companion) suggests the hero asking the friend's help; I can't fix the speaker.

reading: The girl or her friend says that the youth has a body that gives pain, a leaf-gift in his hand and questions about a strong beast, and that apart from searching and standing there, the only work for us on the Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar, who grants correction, is guarding the millet field.
nuance: தழை in the hand is the leaf-garment the hero offers as a gift (தழை ஈதல்), and வன்மா வினவும் his pretext of a lost animal; the speaker sets his business against theirs, which is only the field. The editor's note glosses துரு as searching (ஆராய்ச்சி), which gives துருத்து அந்து as 'searching and ending', a reading the line barely supports.

reading: The friend asks whether the youth who left his deer and came into this field, with his elephant, has come to steal our thought and our gaze, and asks the great ones, with the Mother and those flower eyes, to grant grace, on the lovely Kailasa of Kambar who takes us and our service as his.
nuance: கவர்வ என்றோ (is it to steal?) is the friend's guess at the youth's motive. Who the பெரியீர் are who should grant grace, the hero addressed in the plural or the Lady and her flower eyes, is unclear; the request may be the friend's hint that the hero should act.

reading: The girl says that the bowman who went off after the deer with his arrow, urging on the elephant in the darkness of the slope, has by the flicker of his eyelid left her bewildered, and asks whether there is any lord for us in this world, on the golden Kailasa of Kambar who gives grace.
nuance: மருளைத் தரு (that gives bewilderment) and எங்கோ இலை உண்டு (is there a king for us?) are the two clear phrases; the middle, with the deer, the arrow and the elephant in the dark, is a hunt scene whose grammar I can't settle. The 'king' is the hero as the girl's only protector, by convention.

reading: The friend says that in the field on Ingoy hill of Ekambar with the sharp axe, all the hunting of deer, boar and elephant that the youth follows is false, since what is in his mind is our flower-creeper, whose breasts he has not won, and that the serpent-waisted one has come at the scent.
nuance: பொய்யானவை, 'those are false', names the hunt as the hero's pretext outright, the convention stated rather than hinted. ஈங்கோய்மலை is a separate Saiva hill shrine, named here for Ekambar; the last line, with the hooded serpent's waist and the scent (பரிமணம்), is loose.

reading: In the field on the flower Kailasa of Kambar with the three-headed spear, where rutting elephants whose brows shed great pearls and thunder-voiced lions roam, the hero says that because of his desire for the girl whose laugh is like pearls, not approaching the hill has become hard.
nuance: வெற்பு அசார்வு அரிதே reads best as 'staying away from the hill is hard', the hero drawn past the dangers the first lines heap up; it could also be 'reaching the hill is hard', the dangers winning. The pearls from the elephant's brow and the pearls of her teeth are the verse's one image, twice.

reading: The friend or girl tells the mountain lord that this is not the Kailasa ruined by the lion's night, and that what stays hard here for us is that we fear our elders; the frame praises Kambar, who gave an eye's grace to the one who offered his own eye when his thousand flowers fell short.
nuance: The first two lines tell the story of Vishnu offering his lotus eye as the thousandth flower; the third, with அரி (lion, or Vishnu) and கங்குல் (night), is dark to me. The clear close, எம் ஐயர்க்கு அஞ்சுதும், is the kovai moment when the girl's side pleads fear of her kinsmen to the hero.

reading: On the long Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar, who opened his fiery eye so that the five-arrowed Kama fell to ash and who delights to dwell low in loving hearts, the speaker tells of an elephant falling down the slope so that your tusk survives, and asks whether this wide drum is yours or not.
nuance: The last two lines, with குஞ்சரம், கொம்பு, கும்பம், a variant மூழ்கும் and the drum (முரசு), do not yield a reading I trust; it may be the hero's hunting fame or the public noise of the affair. The burning of Kama in the first line, in a verse of love, is the poem's standing irony.

reading: In the dim darkness on the Kailasa of Uma's husband, lord of Thiruvekambam, who gave the son and guards lives as mother and father, the bamboo-shouldered girl is with our swing when a spotted beast leaps at the fragrant vengai and a clash breaks out.
nuance: வேங்கை is both the tree and the tiger, and பகடு is bull, buffalo or elephant; the scene is a fight between animals by the swing in the dark, or a tiger's attack, and either reading leaves the point unclear. The frame, the Lord as mother and father of lives (தாய் தந்தையாய் உயிர் காப்போன்), is the verse's plain claim.

reading: A speaker tells the golden ones that if they come they will gain a marriage, and describes the one who roams the slope of the spotted hill on Ekambar's Kailasa, giving honey, plucking flowers and driving off the parrots that feed on the cool millet.
nuance: The hero at the parrots and the millet is a kovai scene (he helps guard the field to be near the girl); who promises the marriage, and to whom, is not fixed by the verse. வந்தும் மணம் பெறில் can be the friend's reassurance to the girl or the hero's own hope.

reading: On the Kailasa of Ekambar who shot the moving cities, where hill-hunters set out pearls in season, we whose lot it is reached the curling one first; the speaker tells someone to hurry, part, and say there in what way we gained the shining pearl-water.
nuance: முத்தின் நீர் (pearl-water) and சுருள் முதலானும் (the curling one, perhaps the curly-haired girl) are the clues; the verse seems to send a message between the field and the hero, but the lines do not join into one sense I can defend.

reading: The friend says that madmen everywhere ask whether she is a goddess adorned, that the way the bow-armed hill lord parts from her makes gossip spread, and that the shameless noble vengai of the slope is named for you, on the golden Kailasa of Ekambar who smears his beauty with holy ash.
nuance: அலர, gossip rising, is the kovai stage after the secret meetings; the friend turns it on the hero as a reason for marriage. The variant நுமக்கே for நும்மையே changes the close from 'named after you' to 'for you'. Ash as the Lord's adornment (பூசுகையார் திருநீற்று எழில்) is the verse's shrine-frame.

reading: The girl asks the parrots, who have gained the right to stay in the field, to give leave for the hill lord who dwells without pity and for his servant, since her mind, troubled by the sorrow of parting, has run here and gone worshipping after him, on the crescent-touched Kailasa of unshifting Ekambar.
nuance: The field is harvested and the girl must leave it; the parrots that stay are her envy. அடியற்கும் விடை தமின், 'give leave also to his slave', makes her the hero's servant, the devotional word அடி turned to love. The mind that runs and worships (தொழுது சென்ற) is her own.

reading: The speaker asks whether the creeper has reached the cool millet field that gives joy together with the dark-eyed girl, told to make us grieve, on the thick Kailasa of Ekambar with the threefold holy eye, whom we worship as the one who makes us cross the sea of birth.
nuance: வல்லி எய்தியதே can be the creeper reaching the field or the girl (as creeper) arriving; and the one 'told to make us grieve' is either the field or the girl. The variant தம்மைப் பிறவிக்கடல் கடப்பிப்பவர் தாம் turns 'us' to 'themselves'. The first line is the only doctrinal claim in the love verses: the Lord crosses one over the sea of births.

title: திருவேகம்பமுடையார் திருவந்தாதி
theme: The second quarter of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar. The love poems of the millet field close with the harvest and the parting (879 to 881), and the poem turns to the devotee's claims: wealth is for the small, kingship without the ash does not shine, a Brahmin without devotion is a hunter and a hunter with devotion is best of all. The centre is a long description of the Lord's half-woman form from feet to crown, right side Siva and left side Uma (888 to 898), followed by the dance, Tillai and Kalatti, and the begging Lord whose bull and skull frighten the women he came to beg from.
structure_note: 879 to 881 end the kurinji sequence of chapter 50 (the trysting place, the lovers as one life, the harvested field). 882 to 887 are claims about devotion against wealth, kingship, Brahmin birth and low birth, with the Ravana story and the eight forms. 888 to 898 describe the Ardhanari form limb by limb, right side the Lord and left side the Lady: feet and body (888), head (890), hair (891), eyes (892), ears (893), shoulders (894), belly and waist (895), garments (896), feet (897), hands (898). 899 and 900 are the dance and its shrines; 901 the Lord's uniqueness; 902 and 903 open the bhikshatana scenes that continue into chapter 52. The speakers of the love verses are supplied from convention.
source_issues: 886 has a variant note கயிலைகைவாளொடு நாள் for line 3, and the printed line is hard to construe.
899 line 3 reads போர்ப்பச்ச்சடை with a doubled ச், apparently போர்ப்பச் சடை.
The love verses 879 to 881 and the bhikshatana verses 902 and 903 have no speaker marked.

reading: A speaker tells the one of sweet speech to look at the jewel chamber where the lovers embrace, among the shining flower groves, the dancing quail and the waterfall pool on the Kailasa of Ekambar who shot the moving cities, and says the mind is bewildered without ceasing by the haunt the golden one went to and marked out for us.
nuance: மணியறை (the jewel chamber) and சூழல் வகுத்து (marking out a haunt) point to the appointed trysting place of the kovai; whether the hero or the girl is bewildered, and who 'went in gold', I can't fix. The verse is a scene more than a statement.

reading: The friend says that those who arrange this marriage, like these, will heighten the joy of the wedding day, and asks who could split two who are one dear life, while the one with the honey mouth stands softening with flowers on the Kailasa of Kambar whose waterfall scatters gems, in this surrounded field.
nuance: ஆருயிர் ஒன்றாம் இருவரை விள்ள, to split two who are a single life, is the verse's claim about the lovers, and the question who could do it is rhetorical: the match is already made. The marriage arrangers (வகுப்பார்) mark the move from secret love to the open.

reading: The friend or girl says that, trusting the field would not wilt, they plucked the soft millet, and now that the heavy-earringed girl's dancing is to end and parting comes, helplessness falls on us and the eyes that melt the mind arrive; the devotees who sing many melodies worship Ekambar in this Kailasa without faltering.
nuance: The harvested millet ends the girl's duty of guarding the field and so ends the meetings (புனம் விடுத்தல்); கையறவு, helplessness, is the fixed word for that moment. The last line's singing devotees are the shrine frame, placed against the silence of the lovers.

reading: The wealth that reaches small men who are not great of heart belongs only to the small-minded with great deceit; it is not the refuge of the devotees of Ekambar, whose locks hold the Ganga's flood and who fixed the fiery arrow against the forts of the sky.
