nuance: The verse does not say wealth is evil; it says it goes to the small and the devotees do not lean on it (சார்வு அன்றே). தள்ளம்பு எரி கொண்டு அமைத்தார், who set the fiery arrow, is the Tripura myth used as the Lord's title.

reading: Though horses that beat down enemies, rut-streaming hill-like elephants, infantry and chariots gather and shine under the shade of the royal parasol, if the good ash of Kambar is not on their brow, kingship and the royal drum will never shine on the wide earth.
nuance: The fourfold army and the parasol are the Kural's apparatus of kingship, and the verse makes them nothing without the ash. The claim is about the ash as the mark of Siva's devotee on the king, not about the ash as a charm; the Tirumanthiram calls the same ash armour.

reading: Even if born first among the gods on earth, never parting for a moment from the Veda and its limbs, and tending the sacred fire, those who lack the goodness of joining and worshipping at Ekambam in Kachi, of the Lord who shares his body with Uma of the mountain king's line, stand in the midst of the hunters.
nuance: நிலத்து இமையோர், gods on earth, is the honorific for Brahmins, and the verse grants them Veda, limbs and fire before placing them among the வேட்டுவர். It is paired with 885: birth and rite are made to count for nothing in both directions.

reading: Though born at the bottom of a clan that kills living things with weapons and eats them, that walks like cattle, without understanding and with little shame, laughing, those who love the anklets of the Lord who owns us at Ekambam in Kachi are the best of all.
nuance: The description of the clan is harsh and unqualified, and the verse still ranks its devotee உத்தமர், best for all (யாவர்க்கும்), above the Brahmin of 884. The ground is love for the Lord's feet alone, not conduct, learning or reformed habits.

reading: The Lord with the tall elephant's hide made the ten heads and twenty arms of the demon slacken under his toe, and when the demon sang to him with hand and voice, Kachi Ekambar rejoiced and gave him the good sword of the Kailasa people.
nuance: The Ravana story is clear in outline; the middle lines, with கையான, கைவாள் and a variant கயிலைகைவாளொடு நாள், are not. The point is the Lord's turn from crushing to gift when the crusher sings, grace following song.

reading: Space, wind, fire, water, earth, moon, sun and the atom: the one who has these as his form, who wears the elephant's hide, the Supreme who dwells at Ekambam in Kachi without departing, is the fragrant companion of those devotees of the Supreme who know.
nuance: The list is the eight forms (அட்டமூர்த்தம்) of Siva; அணு, the eighth, is taken by tradition as the sacrificer or the soul, and the verse leaves it as 'the atom'. The companion is for அறிவார், those who know, not for all devotees.

reading: The twin lotus feet, thighs like coral columns, broad shoulders and chest, the blue in the throat, matted locks like lightning across the cosmos, three holy eyes and a woman embraced on one side: these are the beauties of our Lord Ekambar.
nuance: This verse gives the whole form once; 890 to 898 then take it part by part, each time right side the Lord and left side the Lady. பெண் ஒர் பக்கத்து அணைத்தார் announces the Ardhanari form that organizes the series.

reading: Those who do not hold to the great who have long matured in knowledge, who know nothing of what is told them of the young Lord's beauty and the victory of Ekambar our father, are struck down by the god of ignorance and lie wasted in the world.
nuance: அறியாமை தெய்வம் கிழகு எறியப்பட்டு, 'struck ... by the god ignorance', is the striking phrase; கிழகு is obscure. The verse makes attaching to the wise (பழகு அறிவில் பெரியோர்) the condition of knowing the Lord, not scripture or rite.

reading: On one side lies the hissing serpent, on one side the moon; the Ganga with tossing waves is held bound and shines; the konrai and the garland of skulls; the fierce war fought with the sword: such is the crown of matted locks of Ekambar on the bull.
nuance: The head carries the standing emblems, serpent, moon, river, konrai, skulls, in a single list; தலைமாலை, the skull garland, keeps the cremation ground in the ornament.

reading: Tufted coral locks with the fragrant konrai garland on the right, the crescent of a moon not yet full, Ekambar with thick hair; on the other side gold and gem shoots and the kazhuneer flower woven in: so the beauty of the crest shines.
nuance: The right half is the Lord's matted hair and konrai, the left the Lady's dressed hair with kazhuneer and gold; முற்றுற்றிலர் மதியின் கொழுந்து is the crescent as 'the moon that has not reached fullness'.

reading: On the right the gracious lotus eye and above it on the brow the flaming eye that shines unsplit, of wealthy Kambar; on the left the dark flower eye of blue, and the musk dot on the brow of the goddess rising to her flower-decked hair.
nuance: The third eye is counted on the Lord's half only; the Lady's half has the brow-dot (நுதற் பொட்டு) in its place. அணங்கு names Uma with the word the love verses use for the hill girl.

reading: Over the spread hood of the five-headed serpent, a gem earring set with red-rayed stones sways on the right ear; on the left, a long diamond, gems laughing in the sunlight and a red-gold makara earring: these are Ekambar's ears.
nuance: The makara earring is the woman's ornament and the serpent-hood with the kundalam the ascetic's; the verse sets them on the two ears of one head.

reading: The right shoulder rises like a coral hill that love shakes, the chest shines with ash like a snow-white golden mountain; on the left a soft shoulder joined by pollen-filled hair, scented with fine sandal, and a breast at which a child might murmur: this is Ekambar's beauty.
nuance: காது அலைக்கும் (that shakes the ear) and காதல் அலைக்கும் (that love shakes) are both possible for the first words; குதலைக்கும் முலை may be the breast at which a child babbles, or a breast with a soft murmur. The ash on the chest is the one Saiva emblem in the series.

reading: The holy belly on the right, firm and strong, of Kambar who with beauty destroyed the three cities of those above and wore down the world that praises him; on the left the ornamented breasts that the body cannot hold, and the young vanji waist that sags: this too is right.
nuance: The first line (தரம் பொற்பு அழியும் உலகு அட்டி எய்த்து) is hard; it seems to praise the Lord's strength through the world's exhaustion. நேர் உடைத்தே, 'has rightness', closes the belly-and-waist pair by calling the uneven halves fitting.

reading: Over the tiger-skin garment a strong belt is tightened and a loincloth on a cord of munji grass shows: that is the right waist; on the other waist a kanchi girdle is fastened over a royal fine thin cloth: so for the lord who dwells at Ekambam with the strong shining bull.
nuance: The ascetic's garb (புலியாடை, கோவணம், முஞ்சி) on the right and the queen's silk and girdle on the left; the Lord's half is dressed as a renouncer, which the Siddhar poets in this corpus take as the garb to be seen through.

reading: The right foot is like a red lotus with roaring anklets, set on the neck of thunder-voiced Death; the left foot is like a young shoot and wears anklets softer than cotton: such is the form of the Lord of Kachi Ekambam.
nuance: The foot on Death's neck is the Markandeya story, told in full at 908; here it is a mark of the right foot only, while the left is the Lady's. The series that began with the feet (888) returns to them.

reading: Shooting down the three cities of the strong and arrogant, pressing Brahma's head, speeding the axe-blade so that ... : the holy bangled hand of Ekambar our father, put on with the holy rope of his serpents.
nuance: நெற்களென்றும் பருக்கவற்றாங் in lines 2 and 3 does not resolve for me; the hand's deeds (the bow, the pressing of Brahma, the axe) are clear and the serpent bangle (கடகம்) is the ornament. The Lady's hand is missing from this verse, unless it is in the corrupt lines.

reading: With the drum's sound in his hand thundering so that the cosmos above splits, his blood-red foot stamping so that the earth is crushed, his locks spread beyond the directions and the cities, Kambar who grants boons dances the great dance even into the evening.
nuance: The dance here breaks the egg and crushes the earth, the destroying dance, and is still வரத்தைத் தரு, boon-giving. எல்லியும் (even at evening) may name the evening dance (சாயரட்சை) of the temple.

reading: The three thousand good Brahmins came together and bowed, saying the Lord delighted in the dance and took us to save us, full of love and knowing nothing but their duty; Tillai's hall and Kalatti are his places, but what is sweet to our Lord is Kachi Ekambam where he dwells.
nuance: The three thousand of Tillai (Chidambaram) are praised here for love and duty, where 884 set Brahmin birth and rite at nothing; the difference is that these are devotees of the dancer. The verse ranks Kachi above Tillai and Kalahasti, as a shrine poem does.

reading: Say that they are sweet, that there are none like them and no others equal: the solitary one who takes form with his lady, the sage who ordained dharma, the three-eyed one who always rejoiced, sweet to Thandi's love, with the hot axe-blade: Kachi Ekambar.
nuance: தண்டி is most likely Thandiyadigal, the blind devotee of Arur whose love the Lord rewarded; it could be another Dandi. The verse's claim is uniqueness (ஒப்பார் பிறர் என்ன ஒண்ணாத் தனியவர்) joined to the pair with the Lady, one who is two.

reading: Thinking of Kachi Ekambar in praise, the infatuation he works arrives in full; the speaker tells of a cruel one, the son of the first ones, who whips the horse so that the night does not dawn, and of taking even the serpent to set the young women dancing in the courtyard.
nuance: The verse does not come together for me: முன்னவர் மகனார் (the son of the first ones) with a horse, a night that does not dawn (விடியா இரவு), the serpent and dancing girls may be the bhikshatana procession or a Kama figure. The one plain claim is the first line, that the Lord himself makes the மையல்.

reading: Seeing the bull that leaps with a crack and the laughing skull on your head, the young women take fright and scatter, you of Ekambam; and before the five-mouthed hooded serpent that hisses they fear still more: how then, beggar, will any alms come to you?
nuance: The begging Lord (பிட்சாடனர்) is addressed by the women he begs from, the Thirumurai convention in which they mock what frightens them. The question is teasing: the emblems that make him the Lord are what keep the alms away. The scene continues in 904 and 905.

title: திருவேகம்பமுடையார் திருவந்தாதி
theme: The third quarter of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar. The begging Lord's scenes end with the women who accuse him of coming for their waists and not for alms, and the mothers who search the street for the bangles that slipped from their daughters (904 to 907). Then a long shrine litany: Ekambar is the Lord of Kadavur, Aiyaru, Kolli, Parvatam, the Kundram hills and some forty Tevaram shrines, and every list ends by sending the hearer to Kachi (908 to 918). The last ten verses are palai love poetry: the girl elopes with the hero across the burning desert, and the foster mother, the mother, the wayfarers and the hero speak of the journey and its end in Kachi country.
structure_note: 904 to 907 continue the bhikshatana scenes of chapter 51: the women address the begging Lord (904, 905), the mothers find the street where the girls grew thin (906), and a mother notes her daughter has no signs of age yet has given her heart (907). 908 to 918 are shrine lists of the Tevaram kind, each verse a run of place names ending at Kachi Ekambam; 912 to 918 are the Kundram hills and the Chola, Nadu and Tondai shrines. 919 to 928 are the palai sequence of elopement (உடன்போக்கு): the mother's lament (919, 921, 923), the hero's company on the desert road (920, 922), the foster mother's report (924), the prayer to the sun (925), and the wayfarers who saw the pair and tell where they now are (926 to 928). Speakers are supplied from convention. From 912 the tool prints the metre field as திருவேகம்பமுடையார் instead of கட்டளைக்கலித்துறை; the metre has not changed.
source_issues: 912 to 928 have the metre field printed as திருவேகம்பமுடையார் (the work's name) instead of கட்டளைக்கலித்துறை; the verses are in the same metre as the rest.
910 line 4 reads ஏகமபர் for ஏகம்பர், and line 3's ஆல்லிந்தம் is garbled.
904 line 4 has a space inside வந் தீரிடைக்குமின்றே, apparently வந்தீர் இடைக்கும் இன்றே.
905 has a variant note நெஞ்சங்கிதுவோ for நஞ்சங்கிதுவோ, and the printed line has a space inside தோத்த நஞ்சங்கிதுவோ.
The shrine names in 911, 912 and 916 are partly unparsed; some words I could not assign to a known shrine.

reading: The women tell the Lord in the handsome tiger skin that his goblins hold the parasol and he came to take alms, that he took a temple in watery Kachi Ekambam where lotuses hold up a flower parasol, and that he has come here to take their waists and their garments; the waist will not break today.
nuance: The verse plays on கொள்ள (take): alms, a temple, a waist, a cloth. The last words இடைக்கும் இன்றே are a pun I can't fix, 'the waist (will not) give way today' or 'there is no room'. The begging Lord as a thief of women's hearts is the Thirumurai convention and is said here with the women's own mockery.

reading: A woman says that even today the elders' harsh words fall on the twin-breasted girl, that Kachi Ekambar whose side-glance is kind came to take alms before his bull, and asks whether this is his heart or his poison, and names it his trickery against these thick-haired women.
nuance: கிறித்துவம், trickery or guile, is the word the women fix on the beggar; the variant நெஞ்சம் (heart) for நஞ்சம் (poison) changes the question from 'is this your heart?' to 'is this your poison?'. தோத்த நில்லே and the middle of the verse are not clear to me.

reading: Speaking many cunning words, walking in the sun with his handsome form and singing many signs to take alms for Kachi Ekambar, he left the women of braided hair wasted in the long street; the mothers search there for the many white bangles that slipped away.
nuance: The slipped bangles (வெள்வளை போயின) are the stock sign of a woman thinned by love, and the mothers who search for them make the whole street the scene. கிறி பல பேசி, speaking cunning, carries over the women's charge from 905 into the narrator's voice.

reading: A mother says that in this girl the sly glance has not appeared, the words are not understood, the hair has not reached the crest, the breasts have not budded and the gem-waist has not widened, that nothing has yet come to her in the land, and yet her heart has gone to the beautiful Ekambar.
nuance: The repeated உற்றில (has not reached) lists the signs of womanhood that are missing, so the love is set before its season; the last line, உள்ளம் நல்கிடத்தே, may be 'in the giving of her heart' or 'as he gives her his heart'. I take it as the mother's wonder at a child's devotion.

reading: The one who, so that the good Brahmin of famed Kadavur might live, crushed the killing Death, himself a fierce Death; the Nectar of Maraikkadu with its cool waves, as the Mountain's daughter calls him and embraces him: the golden mountain who dwells at Kachi Ekambam amid groves.
nuance: The Markandeya story is given with its place, Thirukkadavur, and the Lord is called a Death to Death (கூற்றைக் குமைத்த வெங்கூற்றம்). அமிர்து is the Lord's name at Vedaranyam (Maraikkadu). This verse opens the run of shrine names that continues to 918.

reading: The one whom Agastya worshipped on the Malaya mountain, who sat firm on northern Kailasa for the gods to worship, who made tall Meru his bow, the lord of Thiruvekambam with green-gold walls, is the rare gem of Thiruvaiyaru girdled by the wave-tossed wide Ponni.
nuance: Pothiyil (Malaya) in the south and Kailasa in the north frame the Lord's range, and Aiyaru on the Kaveri is the Chola shrine; the verse makes one Lord of all of them with Ekambam as the name.

reading: Kolli with its gem-filled waterfalls where elephants wander dazed, Siramalai roaring with firm waterfalls, the slopes where parrots take the waterfall's spray: the mountain of Ekambar, which removes the rare karma of those who bow.
nuance: அருவி (waterfall) is repeated in every line, with அருவினை (rare karma) as the pun at the close; the third line's ஆல்லிந்தம் is garbled. பருப்பதம் at the end is both 'mountain' and the name of Srisailam, which 911 then names first.

reading: Parvatam, cloud-crawling Mandara, Indranila, the white-tusked one, Karungundram, Parangundram where he moves, Mahendra fragrant with the bowmen's fire and oblations: among all these, the one who delighted to dwell at Kachi Ekambam is our Lord.
nuance: The names are mythic and real mountains together, Srisailam, Mandara, Mahendra, Parankundram; வெள்ளை மருப்பு அதங்கார் and நெருப்பு அதங்கு ஆகுதி are hard to construe and may hide another name or two. The point is the choice (உகந்தான்) of Kachi among the sacred hills.

reading: Say these are Ekambar's hills: the bowman who shot the cities, who hid something from Himavan's good daughter: Karungundram, Venkundram, Sengundram, the king's hill, Nedungundram, long Kazhukkundram, and Mudhukundram where deeds are cut short.
nuance: The verse is a list of shrines whose names end in குன்றம் (hill), several of them Tevaram shrines (Kazhukkundram, Mudhukundram). மறைத்தார் ... மகட்கும் in line 2 is unclear; it may be the Lord hiding the moon or a lesson from Uma. The imperative கூறுமினே makes it a verse to be recited.

reading: Devotees, say Kutralam, Neyththanam, Thuruththi, Ambar; learn Velvikkudi, Thonipuram, Pazhanam; and of the Lord who set the river in his locks like lightning, Arur and Idaimarudu: so climb up, you people, thinking first of our Lord's Kachi Ekambam.
nuance: Three imperatives, கூறுமின், தேறுமின், ஏறுமின், turn the list into instruction; the shrines are Tevaram shrines of the Chola country, and Kachi is to be thought of first (முன் நினைந்து) before any of them.

reading: The Lord who gives grace to those who think of him, of Chotruthurai and Niyamam, of Pugalur, Purambiyam and Poovanam, of Venkadu with its tall palmyra groves, Pachchil and Adigai: you whose hearts give thought to him, approach Kachi Ekambam.
nuance: நினைவார் opens and closes the verse: the Lord graces those who think of him, and those with thinking hearts are told to come to Kachi. Thought, not pilgrimage to each place, is what the list asks for.

reading: Approaching and praising Avaduthurai and good Nallur, Kadambur shining on earth, Kadambanthurai, enduring Punkur, Parayththurai hard to reckon, and Ethirkolpadi of the one with the crescent garland in his locks, go and see Kachi Ekambam.
nuance: The verse is a plain list with the one instruction காண்மின் சென்றே, go and see; the names are Kaveri-delta shrines.

reading: Annamalai that climbs to reach the sky, shining Vallam, Marperu where flower honey flows, Pasur, lovely Azhundur, the gain the strong charioteer gained at Virperu, walled Otriyur: the places where the Lord of Kachi Ekambam dwells have shone.
nuance: வன்றேரவன் திருவிற் பெறும் பேறு may hide a shrine name (Thiruvirperu?) or refer to Arjuna gaining the bow; I can't tell. The list moves from Annamalai north into Tondai country, toward Kachi.

reading: Oththur of lasting fame, Amaththur, Pulivalam and Vilvalam of the one whose locks swirl with full water, Kochchai, Kondar, praised Panangadu and good Magaral: the temple of Ekambar, who gives grace to the devotees who cry 'alas' when Death comes.
nuance: The list ends with the Lord's act: he graces the devotees at the hour Death comes (கூற்றம் வந்தால்); the shrines are the Tondai-country Tevaram shrines around Kachi.

reading: Karugavur with its temple, Kachchur, Karikarai, Vanmiyur by the rising sea, Ooral, grove-filled Ponthai, Mukkonam, and Alangadu of the one garlanded with konrai: praise Ekambam.
nuance: The last shrine list, closing with the imperative வாழ்த்துமினே; Alangadu is the dance shrine, and Vanmiyur the sea shrine, both near Kachi.

reading: The mother laments that those who do not worship Ekambar of the flower anklets and the thazhai-like locks, who gives sweet grace for us to live, have gone off, if the tender feet that cannot bear the gravel desert, and the breast-burden that bends the waist of our poor flower-haired girl, are made to walk.
nuance: The grammar joins the shrine frame and the lament badly: either those who do not worship are the ones who took the girl into the desert, or the mother says only one who does not worship could make such feet walk. The elopement (உடன்போக்கு) begins here and runs to 928.

reading: A speaker tells the youth who by his generosity gained the creeper-girl who follows behind him, through the great desert where hot flame rises, to make her take it as the short cool water-field where the young of Kachi, ringed by Ekambar's cool soft-flowered groves, pluck blue lilies.
nuance: என்று கொளே at the close is an instruction to the hero to make the desert seem a lily pond to the girl, the palai convention of comforting the eloping woman on the road. ஆலைய பொருள் ஏகம்பனார், the Lord of the temple's wealth, is the frame.

reading: The mother says that to describe my doll going behind the youth through the palai, where under the burning rays the cactus flames and dried bamboos burst, as one who has forgotten even to think of the red feet of Thiruvekambar in clear-watered Kachi, is hard to say.
nuance: உள்ளும் அது மறந்தார் எனப் போவது உரைப்பரிதே can be read two ways: that she cannot call her daughter's going a forgetting of the Lord's feet, or that she cannot bear to tell of a going that is like forgetting them. In both, devotion to the feet is the measure of the girl's act.

reading: The hero tells the golden girl, like Thiruvekambam of the Lord who holds the firm Ganga on his locks, that if the forest men come with their eagle-strong force, his hot boar-like arrows will make them prey for the wing-spreading eagles, and that if he has his firm striped bow he will not hide.
nuance: பருந்து (eagle) is repeated in every line, and வெய்யேனம் may be a hot boar or a fierce arrow; the sense is the hero's reassurance on the robber-infested road. மறைகுவனே at the close is odd as a boast; it may be 'I will not hide' with a lost negative, or 'I will take cover'.

reading: The mother says that the golden goddess came to her as the grace of the king of Ekambam who wears the forest tiger's striped skin, that she gave her dice and her striped ball to the one she called her own, embraced her and left the house, and asks where she now walks on the sweet striped stony path, her faltering poor heart.
nuance: The gift of the toys, கழங்கு and பந்து, is the girl's farewell to childhood and the detail that carries the lament. ஒல்கும் ஏழை நெஞ்சே addresses the mother's own heart, in the Kural's manner of speaking to the heart as another.

reading: The foster mother reports to the friend that the girl like Kachi, of Ekambar whose anklets fill the heart with joy, has set her cotton-soft feet on the road, leaving the thorny company of the one who bore and raised her, going behind while the fearless, crackling, slaying young bull of a man goes ahead, in this world's end.
nuance: வெடுவெடென்ற (crackling, quick-tempered) and வையந்தத்திலே (at the world's end, or in this world) are loose; the picture, the girl behind and the fierce young man ahead, is the standard order of the eloping pair. Who speaks to whom (பாங்கி, the friend, is named) is not settled.

reading: The mother prays to the sun, the hot one of shining light, that there is no refuge but him to worship, Ekambar's own, in the hot silk-cotton forest, and asks him to still his wandering rays and grant grace to the girl, his fit companion, whose tender feet step on cool flowers and whose gravel is cooled as she crosses the desert.
nuance: The sun is addressed as the one to worship (தொழும் சரண்) and tied to Ekambar, so the prayer may treat the sun as the Lord's form, the Saiva reading, or simply ask the sun to be kind as the palai poems do. உன் உறு துணை, the companion fit for you, is the girl, perhaps because she too shines.

reading: Wayfarers say that like a matched pair the lovely young girl and the youth went before them, with matched breasts and matched love, and that they saw the bull-like young man fit to be embraced; and tell the deer-eyed girl to speak with this one.
nuance: ஒத்த (matched) four times is the verse's figure, and the last line may be the wayfarers inviting the pursuing mother to question the girl who was with them, or the pair themselves. The report of those who saw the pair on the road is the next palai stage after the lament.

reading: A wayfarer says that yesterday the lightning-waisted girl and the hero came to this hamlet and were seen in our house, and that those who crossed the hard hills behind them now dwell today in the Kachi country that Kambar's kings choose and worship.
nuance: The pair reach a settled land, and it is Kachi (கச்சி நாடு): the love poem's journey ends where the shrine poem began. The wayfarer's words to the pursuing mother are the palai convention for bringing the elopement to its safe close.

reading: A speaker tells the dark peacock that even when she sees Kachi, with its Siva temple whose coral towers and trident gleam in the sky, its flags tossing as if to catch the heavens, and the shrine of a thousand pillars, of Ekambar who delighted to dance in the forest the hunters call salt-barren, she should look.
nuance: உவரச் சொல் வேடு உடைக் காடு and அவரக்கன் போன விமானம் do not resolve; the first may be the cremation ground as a hunter's forest, the second a shrine of a thousand encircling something. The verse seems to point out the city to the arriving girl (கார் மயிலே), which fits 927's arrival in Kachi.

title: திருவேகம்பமுடையார் திருவந்தாதி
theme: The last quarter of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar of Kanchi: a kovai-like run in which the praise of the god is carried by the land and by love. Kanchi's fields, tanks, groves, bull-embracing greens and seashore are described to a woman, and the lover's departure, the monsoon that is the season of return, the bangles that slip and tighten, and the chariot that arrives are the frame in which Ekambar is named in every stanza. The three closing verses turn to the work itself: service to Ekambar done today and not tomorrow, the hundred verses laid at his feet, and poor words taken as Veda by his true servants.
structure_note: Each verse opens on the last word of the one before (antadhi), and each names Ekambar or Kambar of Kanchi. The sequence moves by landscape: paddy and cane country (929 to 935), the Vishnu shrines within the city (936), the sand-linga legend (938), the monsoon and the lover's chariot (939 to 943), the bull-embracing green (944, 945), the seashore (946 to 950), and the close (951 to 953). The verse keys 929 to 953 are the tool's seq numbers for stanzas 76 to 100 of the work.
source_issues: The VARIANT_NOTES entry under 947 ('[1] நீந்துமயர்வுயிர்ப்பே - எனவும் பாடம்') is a variant of the last line of 942 (நீந்துதும் வெய்துயிர்ப்பே), not of 947; the note is attached to the wrong unit.
947 lines 3 and 4 are corrupt (ரகம்பாகவார்லினளவில்லையென்னின், நகம்பாற்பொழிற்பெற்ற): no reading of வார்லின் or நகம்பாற் is secure.
935 line 1 has a space inside a word (வெண்ணான் கறமும்); read as one word வெண்ணான்கறமும்.
944 lines 1 and 2 (ஏழ்தழுவினும், அண்டர்போதவிட்டார்) are elliptical or corrupt and the sentence does not resolve.
The text is printed without word division throughout (sandhi-joined), which makes several stanzas (930, 936, 939, 940) hard to parse with confidence.

reading: In the Kanchi of Ekambar whose throat is dark as a rain-cloud, the shouts of ploughmen in the rich mud, of those heaping red paddy like golden hills, and the noise of the cane mills together sound like the roar of the great sea, O woman of fine jewels.
nuance: The praise of the god is carried entirely by the plenty of his town: three working noises are heard as one sea. கார்மிக்க கண்டம், the cloud-dark throat, keeps the poison legend in the first line while the rest is harvest.

reading: Because her eyes looked out over the long wilderness of the cruel, strong hunters, they have lost their lids, O golden one; because Kambar wrapped himself in the elephant's hide, Uma could not look at him; and because she joined him in the groves of his Kanchi, the cool of the flowering season now excels.
nuance: The stanza turns on four ...அமையால் clauses whose subjects must be supplied. I take the lidless eyes as the woman's sleepless watch on the road her lover took, set against Uma who could not bear the sight of Siva in the flayed elephant's skin and yet is joined to him in Kanchi: separation and union laid side by side. The grammar allows other pairings.

reading: Lotus tanks where winged bees sing, areca groves whose spathes are full of red-ripe nuts, plantain thickets heavy with sweet fruit: all through the honeyed flower-country of Kanchi of Ekambar of the tawny matted hair it is like this, O woman of fine brow.

The dark eyes and red mouths of the fine-browed women go like this, and the blue lily and the red lily that bloom in the pools of the Kanchi country of Ekambar, the land of women with golden brows and eyes, open as if crying out that nothing can match them.
nuance: The standard comparison of eyes to lilies is turned round: the flowers of the god's tanks are the ones making the claim (வீறிடும்), and it is unclear whether they vaunt themselves or concede. Either way the land, not the god, is what the stanza praises.

reading: Good water, filled deep in close-set moats so that those within are cool, where blade-like vaalai fish and red carp graze; the fair spread of lakes of the Kanchi country where cool blue lilies yield honey, the land of Ekambar, who takes us and gives us no further birth.
nuance: கொள்வார் பிறவி கொடாத ஏகம்பர் is the one doctrinal phrase in a landscape stanza: the god who accepts a person does not hand back birth. எங்களை ஆட்கொள்வார் (who takes us as his own) is the Saiva idiom of being ruled.

reading: In the cool fields where good water lies like a dark cloud settled in the wide sky, thick with moss and spreading taro, a buffalo with flowing udders eats the flowers, and a bull crocodile that crowds in there fights it, O woman of shining brow: this is the flower-Kanchi of wealthy Kambar.
nuance: The fertility is shown as a fight: the field water is deep enough to hold a crocodile. கரா ஒருத்தல் is the male crocodile; பொரப்பார் (will fight) is the verb the stanza ends on.

reading: Where the mountain's daughter with bodice-bound breasts could see, Ekambar in his delight set the four pure dharmas; the shrine tower that the gods and vidyadharas worship so that the Goddess rejoices, the hall of charity whose giving never fails, and the ornamented mansions spread wide and rose high.
nuance: வெண்ணான்கறம் is read as வெண் நான்கு அறம், the four pure dharmas, perhaps the four kinds of giving; the text has a break (வெண்ணான் கறமும்). அச்சாலை is taken as அறச்சாலை, the charity hall, which the preceding தன்மம் அறா (dharma never ceasing) supports. The stanza praises the built city: tower, alms-house, mansions.

reading: Lofty Uragam, Ullagam and the other shrines, and Padagam where Hari dwells in his settled way: the sword-eyed one, the sister-in-law of the other god, stays in that country which the great poets have carried in song, and it is her own house, O woman of ornaments.
nuance: ஊரகம் and பாடகம் are names of Vishnu's shrines inside Kanchi, so the stanza folds the Vaishnava city into Ekambar's. மற்றவர் மைத்துனி, the other's sister-in-law, is read as Lakshmi, wife of Vishnu whose sister is Siva's consort, so that Kanchi is her house too. உம்பருருகிடமாம் and தெவ்விரிய are unclear and the sentence does not resolve; the plain sense is that the city holds both gods' houses.

reading: Think of the shining of the faultless red that came from the brow-eye of Ekambar who wears the serpent as his jewel, the Lady's own colour, and of the rare trident that none may approach: here is a grove of golden cassia thick with leaves, O golden one, and for us there is no weariness.
nuance: The stanza sets the gold of the konrai grove beside the red of the third eye and the Goddess (அருணம் பிராட்டியது). The connections between the lines are loose; I read it as the woman's consolation that in Ekambar's grove, under his signs, there is no tiring, which the next verse carries on with தளரா.

reading: Seeing the great untiring flood, Uma ran and embraced him, and the mark of her bangled hands was pressed in: here he worked that trick, in Thiruvekambam of rich groves; having come and bowed here we have gained being alive in this world, O young woman.
nuance: This is the founding legend of the shrine: Siva sent the Vegavati in flood to test Kamakshi, who clasped the sand linga she had made, and the bangle marks stayed on it. கிறிபடுத்தார் calls the flood his trick, and the pilgrim's gain is put plainly: உளராவது படைத்தோம், we have obtained being.

reading: When the cloud-elephants come in the sky, swinging the lightning as their whip, roaring with thunder from within and streaming with mighty rut, she of the trailing hair, thinking 'who will come after this?', is of the nature of the banner on Ekambar's temple that stood there.
nuance: The rains are the season the absent lover promised to return by; the clouds come as rutting elephants and the woman trembles like a flag in the wind. பின்னர் என்பார் இர் என (who will say 'after'?) is hard; the plain sense is that the monsoon has arrived and she waits.

reading: Though it is only rain, my eyes are dim, see, cloud; heart, do not fear; if anyone asks who, they will say we are kin; within the long walls of Ekambar in Kanchi, which may be set beside Amaravati itself, if one says 'join', the sword-eyed one stays, for her lover's chariot is coming.
nuance: Four என்னிலும் clauses (even if water, even if who, even if equal, even if join) build an address to the heart. The one clear statement is the last: அன்பர் தேர்வரவே, the lover's chariot is coming, which the following stanzas take up. The city is matched with the gods' Amaravati.

reading: You who are like Ekambar's Kanchi, where the gods gain boons and good: before your lover's chariot the dark clouds have come, bearing rain-pearls in their waves, with flowers and gold konrai, holding cool kanthal clusters in their hands and golden powder, to scatter them.
nuance: The monsoon is made a welcoming party for the returning chariot: clouds carry pearls, gold and scented powder as women do at a homecoming. பரங்கொங்கை தூவன்மின் (scatter them from your high breasts?) is awkward and the subject shifts; the welcome is the sense.

reading: Those who worshipped the feet of Kambar who holds the bow in his generous hand and went to conquer their enemies in the face of battle do not think of us; the clouds have darkened and poured like the face of the sea; O woman of fine jewels, with hot sighs we shall swim across the sea of our task face on.
nuance: வினைக்கடல் is literally the sea of deeds; here the hero's task of war that keeps him away, which the woman must swim through. வெய்துயிர்ப்பு, hot breath, is the sigh of separation. The variant note printed under 947 (நீந்துமயர்வுயிர்ப்பே) belongs to this stanza's last line.

reading: Hearing that the lover who is our life is coming by chariot, our many bangles, which had wilted before, have become like crops that gained a rain-cloud: by the grace of Ekambar, bathed in curd, milk and ghee, they have tightened so that they sink in, O dark peacock.
nuance: The slipping bangle, the stock sign of a woman wasting in separation, is reversed: at the news alone the arms fill out and the bangles bite. The god's abhisheka of curd, milk and ghee is the only ritual detail, and it is made the source of the body's recovery.

reading: 'Though the seven embrace him of the colour of the dark bull, today alone, gaining the war-bull, they died facing it': so the gods let them go. In the pastures outside Kanchi of Ekambar with the garlanded bull, the young bulls rush at those who daily win golden ornaments on their chests, to be embraced.
nuance: This and 945 describe ஏறுதழுவல், the bull-embracing of the herding country, which won a bride. The first two lines are corrupt or elliptical (ஏழ்தழுவினும், அண்டர் போதவிட்டார்); the clear part is the young bulls (மழவிடை) and the youths who embrace them for the ornaments and the girls.

reading: Young men whose minds rush to the corner of the spear-like dark eyes of the fine maidens, heedless of the cruelty of the leaping bulls, hold them in Kambar's Kanchi; and in the fields of young jasmine fed by sluices, as fawns and calves bound through every gate, the village green fills and surges like a sea.
nuance: The desire that drives the youths at the bulls is said straight: it is the maidens' eyes, not valour. The sea simile that opened the chapter (929) returns for the crowd on the green.

reading: O slender girl of the fisherfolk on the sand-hill of thick-scented punnai by the wide sea of Kanchi of Ekambar of cool groves of rising flowers: the two things in your face are not the rich-flowered carp, not the sword, not the spear, not the blue lily, but two sharp arrows of full-blown flowers.
nuance: The man's praise of the eyes refuses the four stock comparisons one by one and lands on Kama's flower arrows. The seashore (நெய்தல்) setting continues to 950.

reading: If you weigh the old saying that taught 'the face is half and goods are the other half' against the age, what good is it to me? In the Kanchi of high Ekambar, if there is no measure to what is within, O coral-red mouth, let those who have reached us take up this good infatuation.
nuance: முகம் பாகம் பண்டமும் பாகம், face half and wealth half, is quoted as an old maxim (மூதுரை) on what wins love, and the stanza seems to set inner measure against it. The third and fourth lines are corrupt (ரகம்பாகவார்லின், நகம்பாற்பொழில்) and the sense cannot be recovered with confidence.

reading: They crossed the backwater where sharks that kill in the bewildering dark and striking makara fish ride the tide that sets whirlpools turning, in Kambar's Kanchi by the sea, the Kambar who gives grace to the perplexed; O lord, she cannot bear parting from the embrace of your golden flesh, and she fears the fierceness of the water you come through.
nuance: The woman's companion speaks to the hero: the night sea he crosses to visit is the danger, and the god named in passing is the one who gives grace to the confused (துயக்கத்தவர்க்கு அருளா). ஊன் முயக்கம், the embrace of flesh, is unusually direct.

reading: The heron feeding where it lies takes no notice, the bees that drink honey hum over the punnai, the tide rushes into the wide sea-mouth: on the shore of pure sand by the sea of Kanchi of Kambar, whom the serpent-bedded one worships, who else knows? Our lord of the shore is false.
nuance: The heroine's complaint that the lover has broken faith has only the shore and its creatures for witnesses, and they do not notice. பாயிரை நாகம் கொண்டோன் is read as Vishnu, whose bed is the serpent, worshipping Siva; தூயிரை கானல் as the pure-sanded grove. நந்துறைவர் பொய்யே is the clear line.

reading: Kambar of the great grace that comes as truth, who does not let go even the false-hearted and the deceivers: in his Kanchi of fragrant groves, where tame birds and flocks of conches cry, the firm chariot of our lord of the shore, with its garlands crowding and sounding, is drawing near.
nuance: The answer to 949: the lover called false arrives, and the god's epithet is chosen to fit, grace that will not abandon even deceivers. The chariot's coming (தேர்வரவு) was promised in 940 and 943.

reading: 'We will do it today; how much more good we will do for Thiruvekambar in this; we will do service tomorrow': heart, those who go about in the body thinking so and do not do it, he leaves; those who stand and serve as his slaves without letting a day go, he shows the long path.
nuance: The self-address to the heart (நெஞ்சே) is Pattinathar's usual form; here it carries an argument about deferral. நீள்நெறி, the long path, is the way to the god's feet, shown only to those whose service has no gap. The verse does not threaten death; it says the god lets the postponer go.

reading: They showed themselves so that the flood of love might pour at their holy feet; those who gathered it worship Ekambar; they bound us who had nothing to them; and gaining love for them we have set down ten tens of songs, praised and worshipped their feet.
nuance: The colophon stanza: பதிற்றுப்பத்துப் பாட்டு, a hundred verses, is the antadhi itself, offered at the feet. ஏதுமிலாத எம்மை, us who had nothing, makes the binding the god's act and the poet's love its result, the order Saiva poets keep.

reading: Even if one who praises the feet babbles like a madman, the true servants will take even poor-worded compositions that do not shine with wisdom or substance as the shining meaning of the Veda, so long as they say 'praise Ekambar, whose grace keeps the many services from falling into harm'.
nuance: The last stanza is the poet's apology and its answer: what makes words scripture is the name they praise and the hearers who serve, not their learning. பித்துப் பிதற்றிலும், though one prattles in madness, is the same self-image Sivavakkiyar uses of his own reciting.

title: திருவொற்றியூர்த்தொகை (ஒருபா ஒருபஃது)
theme: Ten asiriyappa poems to the Lord of Otriyur that argue one thing from ten sides: everything is his form, so nothing can be said of him that is not also its opposite. The cosmos is his body limb by limb; he takes the colour each sect gives him like crystal; his heroic deeds are done on his own limbs; all souls rise in him like waves; his marks and weapons are a picture-language for those who cannot read him; his qualities are a list of paradoxes that bewilder each time they are thought. Against this stands the body, drawn as a sea of humours, foam-white hair and shark-like hunger, which his feet alone carry across; and the poet, who lays father, mother, caste, knowledge, the five senses and all else at those feet and ends in a litany of hail.
structure_note: The work is a single ten-part poem (ஒருபா ஒருபஃது), each part ending on the shrine's name. 954 is the cosmic body; 955 to 957 the one form behind sects, deeds and souls; 958 to 960 the paradoxes; 961 the body as sea and the feet as ship; 962 the poet's surrender; 963 the litany. Each poem closes with a question of the same shape, who on the wide earth can know, say or be accepted, except those who have his grace. The verse keys 954 to 963 are the tool's seq numbers for the ten parts.
source_issues: 954 ends with the line 'ஒருபா வொருபதெனவுங் கூறுவர்' (they also call it orupa orupahdu), which is an editor's remark on the work's name and not part of the poem; it is printed inside the unit.
961 has misprints: உருகிய்வார்வப் for உருகிய ஆர்வப், and தூம்ச்சோதிச் for தூய சோதிச் or தூமச்சோதிச்.
959 has ருல for றுல twice (நின்ரும், தெருளநின்ருலகினிற்) and வானேறேறுதல் joined; the sense is recoverable.
957 line 11 reads ஒற்றியுர for ஒற்றியூர.
The VARIANT_NOTES entry on 961 ('[3] ஆலா - ஓர்வகை நீர்ப்பறவை') is a gloss, not a variant.

reading: Lord of great Otriyur, where the earth-maiden wears the warring sea as her girdle: who has gained a form like yours? The lightning is your matted hair, the settled cosmos the shape of your head, fire, sun and cool moon the three lights of your eyes, the stars the garland of your own light, the sky where the gods dwell your body, the eight directions your shoulders, the great sea your garment, the earth-disk your loins, the serpent your feet's custom, the ceaseless wind your breath, all unfailing sound your speech, the flawless knowledge spread through every life your awareness; the standing, shrinking and spreading of the world are your work, making and destroying its effort, and the blinking and opening of your eyes; and in forms of two kinds, three gunas, four births, five senses, six sects, seven worlds and eight shapes, beyond count, in every measure, you join and stand as each thing.
nuance: The cosmos is read as the god's body member by member, the reverse of the Siddhar habit of reading the body as cosmos. The count from two to eight (துப்புரு இருவகை, three gunas, four wombs, five senses, six sects, seven worlds, eight murtis) folds the sects (சமயம்) into his body with everything else. மணிமுடிப் பாந்தள் நின் தாளினை வழக்கே (the jewelled-crowned serpent is the custom of your feet) is obscure; the serpent that bears the earth may be meant.

reading: 'The one with the woman at his side', 'the one who dances in the dead of night', 'wearer of tiger skin and bone', 'practiser of a life that wanders for alms', 'Mal with Lakshmi and the four-faced one', 'formless and formed', 'he exists', 'he does not', 'untiring', 'one who tires', 'the First', 'the lord of the asoka', 'the ancient one shining under the bodhi': looking at the state of people who quarrel, confused in the plurality of their settled books beyond what they themselves can know, you became for each of them what each took you to be, like crystal taking the colour of what it rests on: that is your form, Lord of Otriyur.
nuance: The list runs through Saiva iconography, Vaishnava and Brahma, theism and atheism (உளன், இலன்), and the Jaina and Buddhist teachers (அசோகினன், போதியிற் பொலிந்த புராணன்), and the crystal (பளிங்கு) explains why all are right and none complete. The verse does not rank the sects; it makes their quarrel the colour and him the clear stone.

reading: Great one who are the one for the world that has form: since there is nothing here other than your form, whatever thing is here is a limb of yours; so burning the three cities, circling the old earth to end its sorrow, cutting off the sacrifice-god's head, crushing the shoulders of the ruler of the long sky, removing one face of the high Brahmin, burning the flower-arrowed Kama with a glance, pressing the demon with your toe until his strength failed, crushing Death with a look: all such heroic deeds, since they were done where you stand, are your own doing; those who know the substance, who have seen that those who tell them are no other than you, would they set them in praise, unless it be as things that merely happened?
nuance: The argument is that if all is his body, his victories over Tripura, Daksha, Indra (or Ravana), Brahma, Kama, Ravana and Yama are blows struck on his own limbs, so they cannot be praised as prowess. The last three lines (நிகழ்ச்சியில் நிகழின் அல்லது புகழ்ச்சியிற் படுப்பரோ) are read as 'they would not put them in praise, except as happenings', but the syntax is open.

reading: All the lives that move in bodies with darkness as their companion, from the lotus-born Brahma who rose knowing the substance downward, differ in form, awareness, rank, service, wealth, strength and kind of work, never parting from their deeds; and in their unlike plurality their conduct, like high waves in the settled sea, rose in you and became in you, grew and shrank and shifted and appeared, mingled with you and stood apart from you. First Lord of unaging body, of Otriyur whose ancient fame never ceases: unless those who have gained your grace know it, will others know this bewilderment within you?
nuance: The wave is the figure for the soul's relation to the Lord: the same water, risen and fallen, 'in you and yet apart from you' (நின்னிடையெழுந்து, விரவியும் வேறாய்). இருடுணையாக்கை, bodies whose companion is darkness, is the one phrase that names the souls' bondage. மயக்கு, the bewilderment, is said to be in him, not in the souls.

reading: Though you are the word that does not confuse, the whirl in which the rest cannot know your state; though the heart is your dwelling, the stealth by which you hide there until it is stained; though you do the deeds that are done in the world, the nearness by which the fruit of those deeds does not touch you; the beauty of becoming a sea in the minds of those who bow to you wanting joy in your company; nearness to those who come in love and distance to those who do not, every day; being of a nature that melts the bones: I have understood that for those who have seen this, your body too is passed beyond, Lord of Otriyur, great ascetic of lasting fame, with the pure moon on your dense red hair.
nuance: Each pair sets a quality against its contrary: clear word and confusing whirl, dwelling in the heart and hiding, doing all deeds and untouched by their fruit. The last clause, கண்டவர் தமக்கே உன் உடல் கழிதல் உண்டென உணர்ந்தேன், is read as 'for those who have seen, even your body is left behind', the seer passing beyond the form; it could instead mean that only the seers know your body passes. The verse does not say which.

reading: Wearing the pure moon on your hair is a way of settling 'I am the pure path'; riding the white bull that is dharma's form is a way of performing 'I am the Lord'; for those who do not stand saying 'that, she, he', the thing that taught 'I am the common ground'; being called three-eyed is a shorthand that the three fires of sacrifice are gathered in me; holding the deer of the Veda, a way of declaring 'I am its master'; the trident of three leaves on one stalk, a way of saying 'the three are I'; being called the eight-formed one, a way of teaching 'I am the truth in this world'; being called earth, water, fire, wind and the wide sky, the one of unfailing ancient fame, the one with the army of good spirits, a way of making clear in the world. With these colours and forms your greatness is taught, yet to the self-destroying people who do not understand, who whirl in the richness of word and meaning born among them, led by the men of six duties in Otriyur where recitation never stops, you set them to children's games and sit smiling until they come face to face with you.
nuance: The iconography is read as a sign-language, each emblem a sentence beginning 'I am'; the eight forms and the five elements are included. The Brahmins (அறுதொழிலாளர், men of six duties) and the scholars of word-meaning are those who, having the signs, do not read them, and the god's answer is not anger but a smile and a wait: சிறுவர் தம் செய்கையிற் படுத்து, setting them to children's play. முகப்படும் அளவே, until they face you, is the end of the game.

reading: Though your greatness is beyond measure, you stand shrunk small within my heart and do not leave; though you are body beyond body, the whole earth is called your form; though you are not within reach, you do not fail the distinction those who love you ask for; though by what is said you are no one's companion, you are the master who gathers the good lives; though you are everywhere, you are no refuge to those in whom deceit stays. Beyond that: the birthless birth, the growthless greatness, the renunciationless renunciation, the unlinked link, the unenjoyed enjoyment, the unsubtle subtlety, the undeparting departure, the unapproaching nearness, the undone deed, the unexcelled excellence; hot and cool, exalted and light, red and green, white and black; you make and destroy the many things that are, you remove and gather, you leave and reach: these and the countless other qualities bewilder each time they are thought, Lord of Otriyur girt by the high sea, so that unless those who say this here shrink their standing in words, who on the wide earth knows your nature?
nuance: The paradox pairs (பிறவாப் பிறவி and the rest) are the poem's doctrine: every predicate of the Lord cancels itself. The close draws the consequence for speech, சொல்நிலை சுருங்கின் அல்லது, only by shrinking what one stands on in words can he be known. The one ethical line in the list is that he is no refuge to the deceitful (வஞ்சனை தங்கியவர்), which 963 repeats.

reading: The unfilled body, grown long on craving and a burden on the earth, with its wind and bile joined as one and the five long winds beating together, grey hair as foam whitening daily, wrinkled skin as swelling waves, gathered blood filling it as water, the covered cough roaring as its sound, burning hunger and anger striking as sharks, the entrails crying like a flock of water-birds, the bones within the flesh, the many diseases whirling in it, the sinews of arms and legs as its channels, fat as its salt flats, the sounding holes as its mouths and the slimy nose as its tide: in this great sea of the body, those who fall into the whirlpool called enjoyment and gain the grace that cries 'ah, ah' for them, go first to your feet that are the ship, bow in order, set the mast of thought upright, fill the sail of melting love, bind it with the rope of swelling restraint, cut the bright rope of crowding kin, twist the peg of fixed oneness, and in the harsh open called the weight of desire, holding to the blaze of the pure light and stirring with the oar of unshrinking awareness, you take them as on a voyage and land them on the long shore where none crowd, Lord of Otriyur girt by the high sea.
nuance: The body is the sea and the god's feet the ship, each part of the voyage given a virtue: thought the mast, love the sail, restraint the rope, oneness the peg, awareness the oar. வாதம் and பித்தம் are the medical humours, as the five winds are the pranas, so the anatomy is the physician's. Several items in the sea-list are unsure (மேதகு நிணமே மெய்ச்சாலாக, கால்கையின் நரம்பே கண்டமாக, துப்புரவு as the whirlpool), and the text has two misprints (உருகிய்வார்வப், தூம்ச்சோதிச்).

reading: Lord of Otriyur, since the harsh poor words born in me to praise your unfailing qualities are of a nature not to reach you, I am like a child that cries without stopping for a mother who has gone far and does not hear, bound to her by a nature hard to part from, not knowing its own deeds; confused in countless aeons of births, like the blind gaining sight with the mother come before them, a man of deeds who does not know the gate of bowing at your two feet, unless you who tied the knot made in boundless craving joined with swelling pleasure untie it, I do not know even the least part of this; a man of deeds hiding in the thicket of darkness and longing to see the open ground; father and mother, caste, knowledge, our thought, wealth, the way of the path we go, sorrow and renunciation, purity and wisdom, pleasure and fame and many more, taste, light, touch, sound, smell and appearance: all these that shine I have set together at your feet and stand alone; since there is no refuge but your feet, seeking out the place of meeting that the sight of the weary fails to find, you who are hard to reach, do I know, when I look, what I am now to do?
nuance: The surrender list is complete: parents, caste (சாதி), learning, wealth, the path of the soul's going, grief and renunciation alike, and the five sense-objects are laid down together (ஒருங்குடன் வைத்து), so that renunciation itself is among the things renounced. The crying child whose mother cannot hear is the poem's figure for prayer that does not reach; the verse says the knot of craving was tied by the god and only he can loosen it.

reading: Hail, ankleted one who raged at Death; hail, First, the root of all; hail, Lord of great Otriyur; hail, First who are the whole; hail, nectar sweeter at each approach; hail, Isa without peer; hail, ornament of those who long; hail, honey of unending sweetness; hail, you who forgot the deceitful; hail, you who took poison as nectar; hail, seed of the sea-girt world; hail, you joined with the twisted forest beast; hail, Hara, the ground of the truth seen before and the rightness that dwells in thought; hail, you named woman-and-man for having both heat and coolness as qualities; hail, Siva, the lamp that sets those who reach you in release; hail Mal, hail Vedic one, hail Supreme, hail Brahmin, hail moon, hail fire, hail Indra, hail Lord, hail immortal, hail beautiful one, hail Kumara, hail dancer, hail Substance: unless one says 'hail, hail' to you until the tongue is calloused, who on the wide earth is fit to be accepted?
nuance: The litany names him as every god in turn, Mal, Indra, Kumara, the moon and fire, the conclusion of 954 and 955 turned into worship. Two lines explain an epithet by a reason: he is called woman-and-man because he holds heat and coolness, a naturalistic gloss on Ardhanarisvara. நாத்தழும்பிருக்க, till the tongue is calloused, makes the praise itself the only fitness. புரிவுடை வனமா is obscure (the boar, or the forest beast of the bone?).

title: சிவவாக்கியம்
theme: The opening of the Sivavakkiyam: after an invocation of Namasivaya and of the elephant-faced god, Sivavakkiyar sets the five letters, the breath raised to the skull and the One known within against everything done outside, running to shrines, reciting the Vedas, bathing at the three twilights, building houses and sacrificing. The body is a boat that breaks and a corpse the cremation keeper takes; what holds is the one letter among the five, the name repeated, and the feet of the Lord and the Mother.
structure_note: The editorial section labels (அக்ஷர நிலை, சரியை விலக்கல், யோக நிலை, தேகநிலை, ஞான நிலை, கிரியை நிலை) are a modern editor's and not the poet's; the verses are not grouped by them in the text. Two invocations (964, 965) open the work; 974 to 976 and later 1022 are the ராம verses, unexpected in a Saiva poet and read by tradition as cipher. Several verses close on the same oath line, அம்மைபாதம் உண்மையே (968, 986).
source_issues: The section labels printed beside the ids (அக்ஷர நிலை, சரியை விலக்கல், யோக நிலை and the rest) are a modern editor's headings, not the poet's; they do not group the verses in the text and 970 to 976 under ஞான நிலை include the ராம verses that tradition disputes.
983 line 2 is spaced மங்கிமாளு தேஉலகில் for மங்கிமாளுதே உலகில்.

reading: The poet opens with the rare Namasivaya that is beginning and end, the mantra the gods uttered of old, and says that meditating on the curled letter he will speak the Sivavakkiyam so that fault, sin and maya run far away.
nuance: ஆறிரண்டு நூறு தேவர் is a number of gods (twelve hundred, or six and two hundred); the count is formulaic and recurs at 981. சுரியதோர் எழுத்து, the curled letter, is taken by tradition as Om (whose written form curls) or as the five letters held as one; the verse does not say which.

reading: Worshipping the wish-granting tree with the black face (the elephant-faced god) so that arts, books and knowledge rise in thought, the poet asks all who have learned, great and small, to forgive the errors of one who recites like a madman.
nuance: The invocation follows the convention of beginning with Ganapati, and the apology (பேயனாகி ஓதிடும்) is the poet's own self-description as possessed or mad, a stance he keeps throughout. Grammatically the line can also make the learned themselves the mad reciters; the apology reading fits a preface better.

reading: Within the five letters are the cosmos and what is beyond it, the three primal gods, the letters A and MA; within the five letters everything is contained.
nuance: அகாரமும் மகாரமும் name two of the three letters of Om, so the pranava is placed inside the five letters rather than above them. The claim that the five letters hold the cosmos is the Tirumanthiram's too.

reading: Running and running, seeking and seeking the light that is mingled within, their days passed, they withered and withered and died: people in crores beyond counting.
nuance: The whole verse is four repeated words. உட்கலந்த சோதி (the light mingled within) is the point: what they ran after was inside them. The editor's label reads the verse as a rejection of outward chariyai; the verse itself only shows the futility and the count of the dead.

reading: If by thought you can hold the breath that is contracting in the formed channel and raise it to the skull, the old become children and the body reddens; this is true, by the feet of the Lord of grace and of the Mother.
nuance: The sense turns on உருத்தரித்த நாடி (the channel that has taken form) and கபாலம் ஏற்றல் (raising to the skull); tradition takes the channel as the central one and the raising as the breath carried to the crown. The claim of renewed youth and a reddened body is the classic siddhi of breath, as in Tirumanthiram 805; the closing oath on the two feet recurs at 986 and 1033.

reading: A man who sees another desire the woman he has taken says he will cut him down first; yet when the Arbiter comes and calls, this fine body stinks, and they carry it only as far as the cremation ground and hand it to the keeper.
nuance: நடுவன் (the arbiter) is Yama, and தோட்டி the cremation-ground keeper, of low caste; the body that was fought over is handed to the one its owner would have shunned. The verse pairs jealousy over a body with the body's end.

reading: The One that was in me I did not know; after I came to know the One in me, who else could see it? Staying and staying within myself, I perceived it.
nuance: Line 3 can be read as 'who could see it (but I)?' or as 'who is able to see it?' in general. Either way the knowledge is in-dwelling and not transferable, and the verse gives no method beyond இருந்திருந்து, staying within.

reading: I find nothing to think of; there is nothing but you. Is the maya that stands as remembering and forgetting really maya? You who are everything, boundless, beginningless before the beginningless: how is it that you are within me and I within you?
nuance: நின்றமாயை மாயையோ can be a doubt (is it maya at all?) or a wondering exclamation. The last line is a question, not a statement of union; the mutual indwelling is asked about, not explained.

reading: You are the earth, the sky, the seven rolling seas; you are number and letter and the letters of tuned song; you are the eye, the pupil, the image that dances in the eye; grant that I reach your feet, which stand in the nature of what draws near.
nuance: The catalogue moves from the world to writing and music to the seeing eye itself: the Lord is the seer as well as the seen. Compare 1024 and 1025, which run the same நீ list.

reading: Not Hari, not Brahma, beyond the beyond; the cause that stands past black, red and white; not great, not small; hold to it, hold to it; beyond even turiya, far, far, far.
nuance: கருமை செம்மை வெண்மை (black, red, white) are taken by tradition either as the colours of Vishnu, Brahma and Rudra, matching line 1, or as the three gunas; both leave the cause beyond the triad. துரியமும் கடந்து places it beyond the fourth state. The verse is apophatic until the imperative பற்றுமின்கள், which asks for holding on to what cannot be grasped.

reading: The bathing at dusk, dawn and noon, the twilight oblations, the austerities and the recitations, the knowledge sought in the mind, the mantra recited daily: all of them are the name 'Rama Rama Rama Rama', my father.
nuance: The sense turns on ராம. Read plainly it is the Vaishnava name, surprising in a Saiva Siddhar, and some take 974 to 976 and 1022 as evidence of a different hand. Tradition reads ரா and ம as a cipher for the two breaths or for fire and moon, so that the name is the breath. The verse's own claim is only that this one name does what all the rites do.

reading: The mantra that casts off the five great sins: the poor who go about saying 'this is it, this is it, no, it is not', the good mantra for those who recite without ceasing is this, this: the name 'Rama Rama Rama'.
nuance: பஞ்ச பாதகம் are the five great sins of the dharma texts. இதாம் இதாம் அதல்ல mocks the search from one mantra to another; the answer repeats the same words as a settled 'this is it'.

reading: What is I, what is you, what stands between? What is the king, what is the guru, tell me, slaves! What is it that came to be, what perishes, what is beyond the beyond, what is the low? The name 'Rama Rama Rama'.
nuance: A chain of questions answered by the name; whether the name is the answer to each or dismisses the questions is open. குலாமர் (slaves) is the poet's address to those bound to outward authority, as at 998.

reading: Sattanatha Bhattar who recites the sastras: when sweat and gasping come, will the Veda come to your help? If you can know within yourself for the space of a maatra and hold together, where is the disease of the scripture-bag? Sakti, mukti, siddhi.
nuance: சட்டநாத பட்டர் may be a named Brahmin or a type. மாத்திரைப்போது is a measure of time and also of breath, so line 3 may mean a moment's knowing or a breath held. சாத்திரப்பை நோய், the sastra-bag disease, is the poet's coinage for learning carried as a burden. The closing three words are a list, not a sentence.

reading: You recite the four Vedas but do not know the foot of knowledge; like ghee hidden in milk, sinners, you do not know it; while the one who ate the poison is within your heart you speak of Death, and not even in a dream is that so.
nuance: ஞானபாதம் is the foot of knowledge, the fourth pada of the Agamas and also the Lord's foot. The ghee in milk is the Tirumanthiram's figure for the Lord unseen within. The last line denies Death any reality for one who has the Lord within.

reading: There is no tradition without a seed, above or below; how could a mansion stand without a carpenter? Fools who sell the mother that bore you and buy slaves! Without consciousness there is no life, none at all.
nuance: வித்து (seed) and தச்சன் (carpenter) argue from cause to a first cause. பெற்றதாயை விற்று அடிமை கொள்ளுதல், selling one's own mother to buy a slave, is taken by tradition as abandoning the primal Sakti or the inner source for lesser gods or for outward authority; the verse does not gloss it. சித்து is consciousness, and the last line makes it the condition of life.

reading: The beginningless mantra that is five and three and is not reached: if you think of it in your heart and recite it until you take its form, even a hundred crore of the five great sins fly off like cotton, so the four Vedas declare.
nuance: அஞ்சும் மூணும் எட்டாதாய் puns on எட்டு: five and three make eight, and the mantra is 'unreachable'. Tradition reads the eight as the five letters with the three of Om, or as an eight-syllable mantra. நீருருச் செபிப்பீரேல் may be 'recite till you become it' or 'recite (while) you are water' (that is, at bathing). Compare 1022, which again joins five and three in one letter.

reading: A thousand gates of the cosmos, a thousand fierce gates, a thousand gates that are twelve hundred crore; this gate is the poor one's gate, become a single enjoyment; who can see the gate where our Lord is?
nuance: வாசல் (gate) is Sivavakkiyar's running cipher (1027, 1031, 1032, 1036, 1037): the womb-door, the body's openings, and the one inner door by which the Lord is reached. ஏழைவாசல் may be the gate of the poor, that is the body, or of the poet himself; ஏகபோகம் is single enjoyment or union. The verse asks the question and does not place the gate.

reading: Though you recite the Sama and the four Vedas and all the sastras in safety, you do not know Siva; after you leave the disease of lust and perceive him within your thought, our Lord stays as a mute body.
nuance: ஊமையான காயமாய் இருப்பன் is hard: the Lord stays as a silent body, or the knower becomes a silent body in which the Lord stays. Either way knowing ends in silence, not in recitation.

reading: Because the two conches and the one stream are finely entangled, how many humans in the world dim and die? If you can set aside the two conches and blow the stream, you may live united with the one who shares his body with the breasted woman.
nuance: A cipher verse. Tradition reads சங்கு இரண்டு (two conches) as the two nostrils or the two side channels, ida and pingala, and தாரை ஒன்று (one stream) as the central channel; ஊதல் (blowing) is then driving the breath up the middle. On a plain reading the words are conches and a pipe, and the verse is unreadable, so the coded reading carries it.

reading: Born in the five letters, grown in the five letters, you recite the five letters, sinners made of the five elements; if you can know and say the one letter among the five, the Lord dances in the hall saying 'fear not, fear not'.
nuance: The five letters and the five elements are set side by side, so the reciters are made of what they recite. ஓர் எழுத்து, the one letter, is not named; tradition takes it as சி, or as the five held as one, as in Tirumanthiram 2720.

reading: Five and five and five; the beginningless too is five; is it not unripe, madmen, what you babble? If you can hold the five in your heart and stand joined, there is no five and no six; it appears as the beginningless.
nuance: The fives are not named: tradition supplies the five letters, the five elements and the five senses, or the fives of the tattva lists. பிஞ்சு (unripe) is the poet's word for the others' understanding. The last line empties the numbers once the five are held.

reading: You build long houses and shut tall doors; is it because you want to live, rejoicing people? When the sound of Death comes, all stand with hands wrung; the feet of the one who ate the poison and the feet of the Mother are the truth.
nuance: கைகலந்து நின்றிடும் can be hands joined in helpless appeal or kin standing mingled in grief. The oath line closes as at 968.

reading: While the boat lasts you can run about on the water; while the boat lasts you can make yourself firm; when the boat has broken, in the matchless open there is no play, no pole and no one at all.
nuance: The boat is the body and உறுதி பண்ணுதல் the securing of release while it lasts. ஆடும் இல்லை கோலும் இல்லை is read as no dance or play and no pole or oar; ஒப்பிலாத வெளி (the matchless open) is the void after the body goes, with no one left in it. The verse does not say whether that void is release or mere nothing.

reading: People who build houses, perform sacrifices, mix truth with falsehood and think 'cattle, children, wife, kin': when the summons comes in the hand of the Arbiter who holds the land, this body will not fetch the price of a potsherd.
nuance: ஓலை is the palm-leaf summons, and நடுவர் Yama as at 969. Sacrifice is listed with house-building and family as one more possession.

title: சிவவாக்கியம்
theme: Sivavakkiyar's attack on ritual and caste at full strength. Temples and tanks are in the mind, Siva is not in brick, black stone or copper, the whispered initiation is a trapper's purse, the Vedas chewed in the mouth are spittle like everything else, there is no mark of caste on flesh, skin or bone, and the impurity people flee from is the blood they were born of. Set against this are the Lord who entered the poet's heart and made it his temple, Vishnu and Siva one as gold under many forms, and the place where mind, life, Sakti and mukti are all absent and Sivayam ripens.
structure_note: The verses run in pairs and triads sharing a device: the counted wasted rites (990), the question-and-answer on temples (998 to 1000), the spittle argument (1004, 1005), the catalogue asked and then negated (1008, 1009), caste (1003, 1010) and menstrual impurity (1012, 1013, continuing into 1014). 1013 and 1014 are joined antadi-fashion, the last words of one opening the next, across the tool's chapter split. 994 and 1001 share a closing line.
source_issues: 1012 line 3 reads ப்றையறிந்து with a stray pulli on the first letter; the word is corrupt, probably பறையறிந்து or பிறையறிந்து.
1009 has விலைந்ததே for விளைந்ததே and மூத்தியற்று for முத்தியற்று, both apparently copying slips.
1005 is punctuated with '.,' after each half-line, an editor's marks rather than the text.
1013 and 1014 are joined antadi-fashion (the last words of 1013 open 1014) across the tool's split between chapters 56 and 57.

reading: Lord, beginningless, beginningless before the beginningless: before birth were not woman and man one? On the day the seed of the eyeless man swelled in the womb, how did those of earth and those of heaven come to be?
nuance: கண்ணில் ஆணின் சுக்கிலம் is the semen of the man without eyes, which tradition takes as the father who does not see what he begets, or as seed that has no sight of its own; the phrase could also divide as கண்ணில் (in the eye) and be a cipher. The verse asks how gods and humans arise from the same blind seed, and does not answer.

reading: How many flowers did I pluck and throw in the past, how many mantras did I recite into the void, how much water did I pour wandering about as a brute, how many times did I come circling Siva's temples?
nuance: A first-person confession rather than an address to others: the poet counts his own past flowers, japa, libations and circumambulations and calls them பாழிலே, done into the void. It can be read as mere waste or as a stage he passed through; the verse gives only the count.

reading: Jnanis who have known and perceived where the king of the gods dwells: who can know the way they knew it of old? Having no way to tell it other than the meaning of the opened Veda, they do not raise their hands to the god in a built temple.
nuance: Line 3 is compressed: விண்ட வேதப் பொருளை அன்றி may mean the jnanis speak only the Veda's inner meaning, or that there is no telling their knowing except as the Veda's meaning. கண்ட கோயில் is the temple one sees, built and visible, as against the dwelling they have found.

reading: The lazy say 'far, far, far'; the Supreme is spread everywhere as earth and sky; you mutes who run through town, country and forest searching, know and perceive him straight within yourselves and stand.
nuance: சோம்பர் (the lazy) is pointed: those who say the Lord is far are not the strenuous pilgrims but the idle, since the search outside is a way of not looking within. ஊமைகாள் (mutes) is Sivavakkiyar's regular address for those who recite without knowing.

reading: As gold is one and the forms differ in their nature, so the red-eyed Mal and Isa shine together within us; you shining people who talk quarrels, the name that stands as everything is this name, this name.
nuance: விங்களம் is sectarian wrangling between Vaishnava and Saiva. The gold and its forms is a stock figure for one substance under many shapes; here it is turned on the two gods, and the 'name' at the end is left unnamed, which fits the ராம verses before and 1022 after.

reading: Hear the Vedic saying, you who kindle the fire, pour in the ghee and day after day bathe eagerly in water: if you can think of the fire and the water within you and tell of them, can you not follow and join the unshrinking light?
nuance: வேதவாக்கியம் கேளுமின் turns the Vedic authority against its own rites: the real Vedic word is that fire and water are within. ஆகுமோ with -ஓ is a rhetorical 'will it not?', shared with 1001.

reading: The Supreme who has no song, the lord of the highest world, the lord who has no country, who shares the woman: the mantra muttered about him, drawing the disciple close and covering the mouth, is the trappers' drawstring purse snapping shut without a sound.
nuance: The verse mocks the whispered initiation (the ear-mantra). குசுகுசுப்பை is glossed by the editors as a purse that closes with a string, and வேட்டகாரர் as hunters or trappers, so the secret teaching is a snare that shuts on the disciple. The syntax of the last line is loose and the exact object of the mockery, the guru's greed or the secrecy itself, is open.

reading: As the tender coconut's water is gathered inside the red coconut, the Lord came, entered my heart and made it his temple; and since the Lord entered my heart and took it as his temple, I do not open my mouth before the people of the world.
nuance: The coconut holds its water unseen inside the shell, so the figure is of a presence hidden within. The result is silence toward others, not preaching; compare 982, where knowing ends in a mute body.

reading: Fools who, perversely, ring the bell and carry the bees' leavings to pour over a chiselled stone! Even the gods who stand apart look at me and know; was it to end my being split in parts that the gurus set their feet on me?
nuance: மணி துலக்கி is ringing or polishing a bell; வண்டின் எச்சில் is honey, called the bee's spittle in advance of the spittle argument at 1004; ஊறுபட்ட கல் is the cut stone of the image. The last two lines are hard: கூறுபட்டுத் தீர்க்கவோ may mean the guru's foot on the poet's head ended his dividedness, or that the poet, unlike the fools, was marked out. The placing of the guru's feet is the Saiva initiation.

reading: What is a temple, what are tanks? You slaves who worship temples and tanks! The temple is in the mind and the tanks are in the mind; there is no becoming and no perishing, none at all.
nuance: The last line widens the point: what is in the mind neither comes to be nor passes away, unlike built shrines and dug tanks. Tirumular also makes the heart the temple, but keeps the outer temple as a stage; Sivavakkiyar does not.

reading: Brick, black stone, the red jati lingam, copper and brass: you say Siva dwells in these. After you have known your own doctrine and known yourselves, will not the Lord who fills the hall become dance and song?
nuance: சிவந்த சாதி லிங்கம் is the reddish lingam of a particular stone kind (ஜாதி). உம்மதம் அறிந்து can be 'knowing your own creed' or 'knowing your own self' (உம்மது); the next phrase, உம்மை நீர் அறிந்தபின், makes self-knowledge the hinge. The dance in the hall is the Chidambaram dance made inward.

reading: Fools who do puja crying 'puja, puja': in the self that holds the puja, where was the puja received? Did the one with a beginning receive it, or the beginningless? Which received it? Say exactly.
nuance: ஆதி and அனாதி are the Lord as manifest, with a beginning in form, and as beginningless; the question is who is the receiver of worship if the Lord is without form or place. The verse demands the answer and gives none.

reading: Though you recite the Rig and the four Vedas till the letters wear away, smear on heaps of ash and babble, the Lord is not there; if, melting your heart, you can speak the truth mingled within, can you not follow and join the unshrinking light?
nuance: பிரான் இரான், the Lord is not (there), is blunt: neither recitation nor the ash that Saivas treat as the Lord's own emblem holds him. உருக்கி நெஞ்சை (melting the heart) is the devotional word, placed against the ritual ones.

reading: Water poured and kept in a vessel, when a fierce fire is set under it: did it hide in the vessel, did the fierce fire drink it, did it hide in the earth, did the long sky take it? Removing the maya of the mind, did it hide within the mind?
nuance: The boiled-away water is a figure for what vanishes at death, the life, or for the world when maya is removed; the questions are the ordinary accounts (body, fire, earth, sky) and the last line is the poet's own answer, that it went into the mind. Whether மனத்துள்ளே கரந்ததோ is a question like the others or the answer is a matter of tone.

reading: What is a Paraiyar woman, what is a Brahmin woman? Is there a number marked on flesh, skin or bone? Is the pleasure of the one different, is the pleasure of the other different? Separate the Paraiyar woman and the Brahmin woman within yourselves and see.
nuance: பணத்தி is read by tradition as the Brahmin woman (பார்ப்பனத்தி shortened), though literally it is a woman of money; the argument needs the two ends of the caste order. இலக்கம் இட்டு is a mark or number stamped on the body. The test is bodily, in flesh and in intercourse, not scriptural, and the verse asks for the distinction to be found inside the questioner.
