nuance: ஒன்பதொழிந்து ஒன்றில் (nine ceased, in the one) is usually taken as the nine gates of the body closed and attention held in the one opening above, as in 1452; it could also count nine of something else. அருந்தடந்த பாதமும் is hard to construe. Purity (சுத்தம்) here is defined by this inner standing, which sets up the attacks on ritual purity that follow.

reading: From the time I was mingled in the womb, the cause I saw standing: was it not when form mingled with form that I knew you? Whatever I give up, whatever I hide, in every time I assented to deeds, when we stood mingled in form, were you and I not one?
nuance: A first-person verse of non-duality: the speaker says the Lord and he have been one since conception, through every deed. விரக்கில் என் மறைக்கில் என் is loose; I take it as 'whether I renounce or conceal'. The closing question (ஒன்றலோ) is rhetorical.

reading: Yogis who hunted out the books of knowledge and recited them: you have not sought and known within the light that is knowledge; once the Lord who stands as knowledge is known, there is nothing other than knowledge, and what we have said is true.
nuance: ஞானம் is used four times, moving from a thing in books to the Lord himself: the argument is that knowledge is not about the Lord but is the Lord, so reading about it misses it.

reading: Before conception, where did the body stand? Before it took form, where did the breath of life stand? In the thought wrapped in confusion, where did delusion stand? Jnanis who have come to know what you desired, you must explain this at length.
nuance: Three questions on origins, each ending எவ்விடம் (where), put as a challenge to professed jnanis. The verse does not answer them; whether it means the answers are unknowable or that they are the test of real knowledge is left open.

reading: The seven kinds of birth taken as seed within the womb whirl, born and dying, by the fruit of the two deeds; once the three times of further births by further deeds are apportioned, the jnani who knows says, 'this is the fruit of deed that falls due.'
nuance: ஏழு தோற்றம் is the conventional seven classes of birth; இருவினை the good and bad deeds; மூன்று காலம் the three times. The verse is a compact statement of karma, and the last line may mean that only the jnani can read a present state as the fruit of a deed.

reading: You drink water and spit so that the spittle leaves the mouth; while the mouth remains, where has the spittle gone? Is not the mantra you utter the spittle of that mouth? And when the dog is known, what spittle is there left to seek?
nuance: The attack on எச்சில் (saliva as pollution) turns the rule against the ritualist: the mantra comes from the same wet mouth. The last line is obscure; நாயினை அறிந்தபோது may mean 'once you know the dog', the animal whose saliva is the type of pollution, or may be self-abasing ('this dog, myself').

reading: Dumb ones who start to fall into water saying 'it is pollution': where was the pollution, and where was the purifying? If you could know how pollution arose and make yourselves pure, you could follow and see the light that has no pollution.
nuance: தொடக்கு means both ritual pollution and beginning, so தொடக்கிலாத சோதி is at once the light without pollution and the light without beginning; the pun carries the argument that true purity is knowing the origin of impurity, not washing.

reading: If a buffalo and a cow mated in desire, the form born would show the difference of kind, as is the way; but when a reciter of the Veda goes and joins an outcaste woman, tell me how it is that the child is born with no such difference.
nuance: The argument is from breeding: species differences show in the offspring, caste differences do not, so caste is not in the body. புலைச்சி (woman of the puaiya caste) and வேதம் ஓதுவான் are the two poles of the hierarchy, chosen for the sharpest case.

reading: People who talk of kinds of clans and argue the cases: once you seek and understand the straight truth of all these clans summed up, you find nothing there but a surplus of semen; and daily you seek to burn Manu, to be laughed at.
nuance: சுக்கிலம் (semen) is the whole material basis the verse allows to lineage. The last line is unclear: மனு எரிக்க may be 'to kindle (recite) Manu', the law-book of caste, or 'to burn' it; either way the clan-talkers are made laughable.

reading: The four Vedas recited, the shastras they expounded, the tattvas of the elements, the Agamas that fit them, the 'truth' of caste difference and the wavering books: all of it, born as difference upon difference, has whirled about and stayed.
nuance: The verse lumps scripture and caste together as one product of division (பேதம்). It does not say the texts are false, only that they are born of and breed difference; that is a weaker and more precise charge than outright rejection.

reading: Wearing the linga on your body you perform the puja of the whole universe; you whose chest has settled into wearing the body-linga, you run everywhere, lose your worth and perish: fools who look on brick, copper and stone as the best.
nuance: அங்கலிங்கம் is the linga worn on the body, as Lingayats and some Saivas wear it; அகண்டபூசை may be the claim to worship the undivided whole through it. The materials of line 4 are the materials of built lingas, and the verse's charge is that worship has been fixed on substance.

reading: Fools who bathe every day saying 'pollution, pollution': was it not as pollution that the body gathered and came to be? You ghouls who praise the locked body within you: when the pollution came and took hold, it was then that Sivaayam became clear.
nuance: தீட்டம் is menstrual pollution, and the verse says the body itself was formed from it. The last line is hard: it may say that conception, the moment pollution 'took hold', is where Siva's work shows, or that pollution clears when its nature is understood. பூட்டகாயம் (locked body) is also unclear.

reading: Above the navel, the four and the three are Om Namasivaya; you ghouls who proclaim 'sandhi, sandhi': coming first within us and going through the root channel, know and see the place where dusk and dawn have ceased.
nuance: நாலுமூன்று (four and three) is unexplained; it may count the letters of ஓம் நமசிவாய as seven, or name body-places. சந்தி is the twilight rite; the verse opposes it to the inner place where there is no dusk or dawn, reached through the மூலநாடி. The sense turns on this cipher.

reading: Our Lord who lives in the fire of the three fires: where did he fall in love while the virgin was within? Four heads, two hands, one of the two in the mind: think and think, drive it within yourselves, know and see.
nuance: A cipher verse. கன்னி (the virgin) is read by tradition as the coiled Shakti at the root; the three fires and the four-headed one (Brahma) may name centres in the body. Nothing in the verse fixes these; the plain instruction is only to turn the question inward.

reading: You too, doing service, run about in circles and die; having eaten and whirled about you never look intently within yourselves; our Lord who lives in groves where bees roam stands apart within you, as he did of old, the Lord himself.
nuance: தொண்டு (service) is the servant's path of temple work, and the verse sets it among the things that wear a man out. பகுத்திருப்பன் (he stands distinguished, set apart) may mean the Lord sits within as a distinct presence, or that he has apportioned himself within each.

reading: Supreme One, for you and me there is no other fear, see; to fold my hands to you daily is my duty; Lord of fame who melted the crown and gave nectar; the strength you gave me is truth, truth, truth.
nuance: சிரமுருக்கி அமுதளித்த (melted the head and gave nectar) is, as tradition reads it, the nectar released at the crown in yoga; the verse itself is a plain address of trust. The folded hands of line 2 sit oddly beside the chapter's attacks on ritual, and show that the attack is on empty form, not on worship.

reading: Within myself I ran everywhere seeking myself; within myself I found nothing but myself; as lightning that flashes in the sky subsides into the sky, within me there is nothing other than the Lord and I.
nuance: The lightning image says the self appears and subsides in the same ground, which is the Lord. ஈசனோடு யானும் அல்லது இல்லை keeps two names, Lord and I, while denying anything else; whether that is two or one is left to the reader.

reading: Preparing places, purifying, on the seat you have set up, smearing ash all over, you do rare penances; where does the knowledge of the Lord who withdraws arise? Where does it subside? Know that, and then do puja.
nuance: The verse does not forbid puja; its last words are அறிந்து பூசை செய்யுமே, do puja knowing. ஒடுங்குகின்ற நாதனார் (the Lord who withdraws or contracts) may describe the Lord as he who draws all in, or as hidden.

reading: Carrying books, you babble lies; you do not know how the place of dying and the place of being born are; if you could know and look at all that thought, the light within the Highest would become the enjoyment you know.
nuance: புத்தகங்களைச் சுமந்து (carrying books) pictures learning as a load. The test the verse sets is knowledge of where one dies and is born, which it treats as inner knowledge, not book knowledge.

reading: Born in grace and standing, you take the form of maya and waver in darkness, poor people, listen: if you can wear penance in the Substance and look fittingly, what delusion is there? Sivaayam is hidden in the fire.
nuance: The verse says people are born in grace and only then take maya's form, which is a hopeful ordering. வன்னியின் மறைந்ததே சிவாயமே is the cipher: fire may be the body's fire, the fire of yoga, or the fire of tapas in which the five letters lie hidden.

reading: Dregs whose thought has perished, whirling in the sun of karma-thought for as long as there is dharma-thought, without knowing tapas: the wealthy Lord who cannot be made clear though sought birth after birth, you must see with delight within yourselves, for your good.
nuance: தன்மசிந்தை and கன்மசிந்தை (thought of dharma, thought of karma) are set as a pair and both treated as whirling; the verse seems to say that calculating merit is itself bondage. The first two lines are hard to parse and the reading is tentative.

title: சிவவாக்கியம்
theme: The Lord is within, so every outward search misses him: Sivavakkiyar mocks pilgrimage, bathing, counted japa, darbha-grass puja, spittle rules and the planted stone, and against them sets the light within, the eight and two, the one letter, the nine gates and the gate of knowledge. Several verses end in the refrain சிவாயமே, and a few are plain prayers and confessions of the 'I' destroyed in the ocean of silence.
structure_note: The chapter alternates: attacks on outward practice (1439 to 1444, 1448, 1456 to 1458) and cipher verses on the inner path (1449 to 1454), with prayers and first-person verses between (1445 to 1447, 1455, 1459) and a close on impermanence (1461 to 1463).
source_issues: 1459 line 4 is drum syllables (தானதான தந்தான தாதனான தானனா), not a verse line; it may be a singer's filler that entered the text or a lost line's replacement.
1444 lines 1 and 2 (ஆடுகொண்டு கூறுசெய்து, தேடுகின்ற செம்பினைத் திடப்படப் பரப்பியே) are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
1447 line 4 கானநாடும் may be a corruption of வானநாடும்.

reading: With a thieving heart still in you, you recite transcendent knowledge; when the deceit within is cut away, do you not see that this itself is the way? If you can polish the heart daily and draw near the light, clear knowledge has excelled within you: Sivaayame.
nuance: கள்ளம் (deceit, theft) is the one fault named, and its removal is called the கதி, the way or goal, itself. The verse makes knowledge a result of cleaning the heart, not of reciting.

reading: Wanting to see, you climb seas and mountains; is that not egoism, people without understanding? If you wish it and hold the Lord's feet within the true body, the soul standing as the pillar becomes Siva itself.
nuance: ஆணவம் is the Siddhanta name for the root impurity of self-assertion, and the verse calls pilgrimage itself an act of it. தாணு (pillar, Sthanu) is a name of Siva and here the soul standing firm; the last line says the jiva becomes Siva, stated flatly.

reading: If you mark and look within yourselves, as your own nature, at the immeasurable light that is at once atom and universe, that is release; muttering and counting on your fingers, in a confusion from which there is no return, out of lack of resolve you keep on doing puja.
nuance: அணுவினோடு அகண்டம் (with the atom, the undivided whole) is the Siddhar formula for the light as both smallest and largest. விரலை எண்ணி (counting on the fingers) is counted japa, and துணிவிலாத படியினால் makes repetition a failure of nerve.

reading: Poor ones who shrink saying 'spittle, spittle': was it not from base spittle that the pure body itself came? Is not the honey the bee's spittle, and the flower too? Even the milk drawn with the hand on the cow's teat is spittle.
nuance: Each example is a thing the pollution-keeper eats: honey, milk, and the body itself (from semen, the துச்சில் or base fluid). The verse does not argue that pollution is harmless but that the rule cannot be kept consistently.

reading: Wicked ones who run about seeking 'the holy water, the linga, the image': make clear the soul standing within as the holy-water linga; if you can see the holy-water linga clearly within you, the holy-water linga itself is what has excelled as That: Sivaayame.
nuance: தீர்த்தலிங்கம் repeats as the first word of all four lines, shifting from the thing sought outside to the soul within and then to Siva. The compound may mean a linga bathed in sacred water or a linga at a sacred ford.

reading: Like keeping a goat, dividing it and sitting down; spreading the sought-for copper firmly; while the Lord you seek is within us, what is this puja of throwing darbha grass, what puja, what puja?
nuance: Line 1 may describe animal sacrifice (ஆடு கொண்டு கூறு செய்து, taking a goat and cutting it in portions) and line 2 the copper vessel or image laid out for rites; both are tentative. The thrice-repeated பூசை என்ன is clear enough: the rite is pointless while the Lord is within.

reading: Lord who does not forget me even for a moment, One, God, King of kings of kings: can I stay without you even a moment? Help me, Lord, that your name be on my tongue.
nuance: A plain prayer with no polemic. The one request is for the name on the tongue, which sits beside the chapter's mockery of muttered mantra and shows the difference the poet draws between them: remembering versus counting.

reading: With the limitless light burning as one, the mighty Full Radiance becoming sole enjoyment, pressing good joy into the ocean of silence, I ate the nectar none can seek, and stood on that day with 'I' destroyed.
nuance: நான் அழிந்து (I destroyed) is the verse's end-point, and மோனசாகரம் (ocean of silence) the medium. The verse is in the past tense as testimony, which is rare in the chapter's imperatives and questions.

reading: If you can gladly see within yourselves, showing the flesh, the undivided light that has become as it has: you can rule this fleshly body, rule the burden of the world, rule the forest land too, by the oath of the Lord of colours.
nuance: The three ஆளலாம் promise mastery of body, world and a third realm (கானநாடு, forest land, perhaps for வானநாடு, the sky). ஊனைகாட்டி (showing the flesh) is unclear. The verse is the chapter's only promise of power, and it is conditional on inner seeing.

reading: Daily polishing the bell, going into the long corner to sit, muttering and wailing with eyes closed, what is the use? However many count, are eight and two not ten? Does this suit the Father, people without understanding?
nuance: எட்டிரண்டும் பத்தலோ (are eight and two not ten?) is a cipher: in Tamil numerals ௮ (eight) and ௨ (two) look like the letters அ and உ, so 'eight and two' names the pranava letters, and 'ten' may then be their union. The plain sense is only that counting cannot change what is.

reading: If you can regard within yourselves, in due measure, the god who became the linga when eight and two joined, you can cross the dark sea of hard birth, and you will stay joined with the light you love: see.
nuance: The 'eight and two' of 1448 now form the linga: on the numeral reading, அ and உ (the sun and moon, or the two breaths, in the Siddhars' usage) joined make the inner linga. கருங்கடல் (dark sea) is the sea of births.

reading: The true mantra stays in the light; the cool mantra has taken shape and become form; the white mantra has ripened and become ash; the true mantra is that one alone: Sivaayame.
nuance: Three mantras, true, cool and white, are hard to fix: they may be the mantra as light, as embodied form and as the sacred ash, with the refrain சிவாயமே naming the one that matters. The verse ranks and then collapses them.

reading: At the carpenter's gate, above the crown, as a thousand places; three lights and three-two, the fire-flame that blazed up; where did it grow and stand as the diamond? And how did this flame and the senses become one?
nuance: A cipher verse: the thousand places at the crown are the thousand-petalled centre as tradition reads it, the three lights sun, moon and fire, மூவிரண்டு perhaps the six centres, and வச்சிரம் (diamond, vajra) the hardened state. தச்சுவாயில் (carpenter's gate) is unexplained. The verse asks rather than tells.

reading: The nine strong gates, the gate that is shut and refused, the five gates that speak, and what stood swelling to speak: open the good gate, go through the gate of knowledge, and once the boundary gate is seen there is no more birth.
nuance: The nine gates are the body's openings; the shut tenth gate is, in yogic tradition, the opening at the crown, and the five that speak the senses. The verse sets a sequence of gates ending at the எல்லைவாசல், the boundary gate, beyond which birth ceases.

reading: All the honey that came with the bee and the flower's scents is eaten and subsides within; in that manner, reciting with the root of the linga, if you can see and see and make thought subside at the root, the strong deeds taken on of old fly away: Sivaayame.
nuance: The honey drawn in and settled is the figure for attention drawn to the root (வேர்); லிங்க மூலம் may be the root centre or the base of the inner linga. The verse's claim is that old deeds leave when thought settles there.

reading: In the one letter as the linga, within that letter which you recite, you do not know the truth that one letter moves; the light that sprouted as three from the three letters, the four letters have uttered on the tongue: Sivaayame.
nuance: One, three and four letters: the one is usually Om, the three its parts அ உ ம் as the three gods (மூவராய்), and the four may be சிவாய without the ந-ம. The verse's charge is that reciters do not know what moves inside the letter they recite.

reading: Sinners who grieved saying 'far, far, far, the distance that rose and rose, burden, burden, burden': if you can keep thinking of him time after time, moment by moment, even that far, far, far distance can be joined.
nuance: The verse is built on tripled words (தூர, பார, நேர), and its argument is that distance from the Lord is a matter of attention: continuous remembrance (நினைந்திருக்க) closes it. It answers the pilgrims of 1440, who tried to close the distance by travel.

reading: Wearing earrings you plunge into every tank; like frogs you never scrape the dirt from the mind; if you could keep the bearer of the skull in your mind, you could live bowed to by ancient Mal and Ayan.
nuance: The frog lives in water and stays slimy, which is the whole argument against bathing as purification. மண்டை ஏந்து கையர் (he who bears the skull in hand) is Siva as the beggar; the promise is to be worshipped by Vishnu and Brahma.

reading: As one builds a nest and lays eggs and sits; the goat that bore two kids dances in the hall; you human cattle who keep cows and eat butter: once the house is found, the open space too will be seen.
nuance: A cipher verse. ஆடு (goat) also means 'dance', and the goat with two kids dancing in the hall (அம்பலம்) may encode the Dancer with his two, perhaps the two letters or the two breaths; மானிடப் பசுக்கள் (human cattle) plays on pasu as beast and bound soul. வீடு is both house and release, and வெட்டவெளி the open space of the formless.

reading: Calling a planted stone a god, laying four flowers on it, circling it and muttering, what mantra is this? Will the planted stone speak while the Lord is within? Does the fired pot or the ladle know the taste of the curry?
nuance: The best-known of Sivavakkiyar's verses. The pot and ladle argument is that a vessel is not the thing it holds; the verse's premise, stated in line 3, is that the Lord is within the worshipper, not that there is no Lord.

reading: Not I, not you, not the Lord, I declare; not in the sky, not the light; the light is within us. When I and you have become alike, can it still be sought and seen? Taana taana tantaana taatanaana taananaa.
nuance: The denials remove every term, including the Lord, and leave only a light within; the question of line 3 may mean that once seeker and sought are alike there is no seeking. The last line is drum syllables, a filler or a refusal to say more.

reading: What stands in the middle, neither good nor bad, is one thing; once what is called good has gone and stood as good, if one says 'not good, bad', it becomes bad; therefore stand seeking what is good and say the name.
nuance: The verse says value follows naming: calling a thing bad makes it so. Its conclusion is practical, not sceptical: since names shape things, hold to the good one and say the Lord's name.

reading: In the loveless forest where ghouls gather and eat corpses, where dogs surround him and he dances, what is the life of Namban? If you seek, wishing to be rid of the desire that rises with mothers' milk, look within yourselves at how you whirl, struck by diseases.
nuance: Siva as the cremation-ground dancer is the opening image; the question ஏதடா may be scorn or wonder. தாய்கள் பால் உதிக்கும் இச்சை is desire that begins at the breast, which is the desire for birth itself. How the two halves join is unclear.

reading: A body that rots and becomes a spring of filth if the salt is removed: can you hold desire for it? Tell me, O mind, witless, false, honourless rogue, and listen: the feet of the one with the matchless red matted locks are the truth.
nuance: உப்பை நீக்கில் (if the salt is removed) treats the body as preserved meat; the salt may be the breath or life. The verse is addressed to the poet's own mind, not to others, and ends with the one thing called true.

reading: All that is born dies; foolish people do not understand, and rejoice as if there were no dying, talk in hints of 'our property and yours' and wander about; what is this guise they have put on? When the filled body perishes, will there be love then, Lord?
nuance: கொண்ட கோலம் (the guise taken on) applies the chapter's language of false garb to ordinary householders, whose pretence is that they will not die. The last line asks whether the love bound to property survives the body.

title: சிவவாக்கியம்
theme: The last chapter of the Sivavakkiyam is a catalogue of religious fraud, alchemists, siddhi-showmen, drug-fed kaya-kalpa men, ochre-robed beggars, sacrificers, idol-makers and river-bathers, set against three positive claims: that grace and virtue, not rites, make the beyond; that the householder who feeds the guest and the man who joins a woman are not below the ascetic; and that the world, its lives and true knowledge stand in the five letters, which, chanted with the breath as சிவாயவசி, become a fire with two heads.
structure_note: 1464 to 1467 move from lust to the defence of marriage; 1468 to 1471 concern the siddhar misread as mad, the calm breath and the futility of wandering; 1472 and 1484 bracket the attack on made gods; 1473 to 1481 are the catalogue of frauds; 1482 to 1487 return to idols, rivers and thieves; 1488 closes the work on the mantra.
source_issues: 1469: an editor's gloss line (மன்று - மன்றம்; சபை; விமலன் - மலமற்றவன்) has been printed as a fifth line of the verse text, and the GLOSSES entry attached to 1469 (சருகு) belongs to 1470.
1473 line 3 (நங்கச்சொல்லு நலிமிகுந்து ... மூஞ்சூராய்) is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
1478 line 1 காயகாயம் is probably a corruption of காயகற்பம்.
1480 line 4 ends அலைவரை where the sense wants அலைவரே, probably a copying slip.

reading: Lustful men who gaze longingly at the moon face of a beautiful woman smeared with burnt paste, not knowing how to rise and stand firm: do you not know the trickery of the snake that sleeps in the box? If Brahma unties the knot and looks, what way out is there for you?
nuance: The plain reading is a warning against lust, with the woman as the snake in the box, dangerous when opened. The coded reading takes the sleeping snake as the coiled power at the root, which Brahma, the four-faced one placed there in tantric maps, might loose; the verse fits both. சுட்டெரித்த சாந்து is unclear, perhaps lime or burnt sandal paste.

reading: The labour of reciting the Vedas is wasted on this earth! Running league after league, is a puja of love needed? When the Primal Lord who ate the butter is within us, what worthless puja, what Veda is there? Mark it and look within yourselves.
nuance: வெண்ணெய் உண்ட ஆதிநாதன் (the Primal Lord who ate butter) borrows Krishna's epithet for the Lord within, which is unusual in a Saiva poet and shows the verse's indifference to sect. The verse rejects Veda and puja together as outward labour.

reading: Where is the Supreme absent, and where is it present? For sinners without virtue there is no Supreme, and that is the truth; when there are hands and there is wealth and yet no grace, that is a void without the Supreme, a waste hell.
nuance: The verse answers its own question with ethics, not with a body-place: the Supreme is absent wherever virtue (அறம்) and grace-as-compassion (அருள்) are absent. கரம் இருந்தும் பொருள் இருந்தும் names the able and the rich who do not give. சூனியம் here is plain emptiness, not the yogic void.

reading: There is no god on this earth who has not joined a woman's shoulder! When joined to a woman's shoulder, human life flourishes; because Shakti, who is woman, has become bound up with him, the Lord himself took the blue Ganga, who is woman, with delight.
nuance: A defence of marriage and union from theology: if Siva has Shakti and bears the Ganga, the ascetic's horror of women has no divine warrant. The verse makes the household path a flourishing (சிறக்கும்), not a concession.

reading: Souls who cannot tell the siddhar from the petty man! While siddhars are here you count them mad; and if siddhars were here, would a madman stay in the land? The Father's land and this land are all one to them.
nuance: The siddhar is mistaken for a madman (பித்தர்) because he is indifferent to place: the last line says heaven and earth are one to him. Line 3 is a riddle on the pair சித்தர்/பித்தர் and may mean that a true madman would not endure a land where siddhars live.

reading: When life among men on earth is forgotten, in the sky, if you can set right the life-breath made calm, you can see the feet of the stainless one who dances in the hall as king. Mother of the tresses, not a single crookedness can be found in this; it is truth.
nuance: சாந்தனான ஆவியைச் சரிப்படுத்த (to set right the calmed breath) is a breath instruction, and விண்ணிலே (in the sky) may be the inner space at the crown. The verse is addressed to கூந்தலம்மை, the goddess; the oath that nothing in it is crooked is a seal on the teaching.

reading: Hermits who live on the slopes, chewing dry leaves and drinking water! Eating dry leaves the body wastes and anxiety arises; if instead you eat and dress with the guest who comes and enjoy a growing household, the guest who comes becomes the Lord and grants you life: Sivaayame.
nuance: The verse reverses the ascetic hierarchy: the forest hermit's fast breeds சஞ்சலம் (unrest), and the householder's guest is the Lord himself (விருந்தோன் ஈசனாகி). It is the clearest statement in the Sivavakkiyam that the household is a path.

reading: Will those who leave country and land to wander, clearing forest, mound, hill, hollow and forest river, see the Lord's feet? Because your life, leaving the cage, looks only toward the Dancer's town, there is none among them who has gained release and sat in Hara's state.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard: கூடுவிட்டு அகன்று உன் ஆவி may mean the breath that has left the body at death, so that the pilgrim hopes to reach Siva's town only after dying, or the attention that wanders out of the body. On either reading the verse says the wanderer does not reach release.

reading: Gods made of wood and gods made of stone, gods made of palm-leaf and gods made of turmeric, gods made of cloth and gods made of dung: other than the open space there is no other god.
nuance: Six materials in three lines, from carved stone to the dung image of village rites, all levelled together, and then the one positive claim: வெட்டவெளி, the open expanse, is the only god. The verse does not deny God; it denies him a material.

reading: When your body falls ill, you set pongal at the Pidari shrine and offer goat and cock as sacrifice to it; yet, I tell you plainly, the sickness grows, you waste day by day and shrink to a mouse: it is not your family deity that is deforming you.
nuance: The verse's logic is that the sickness is not the deity's doing, so the sacrifice cannot buy it off. நங்கச் சொல்லு (I say it clearly) and மூஞ்சூராய் (like a shrew or mouse) are read tentatively; the last line could also be ironic, 'your clan god will not harm you', said while the man wastes.

reading: Those who out of greed wander wholly intent on cheating and seizing others' property every day, wicked men who make puja, observances and austerities flourish alongside it: it is truth that the seven hells on this earth wait for them.
nuance: The target is not the thief but the pious thief, whose puja and vows (நேமம், நிட்டை) grow with his thefts. எழுநரகு (seven hells) is placed காசினியில், on this earth, which may mean the hells are here.

reading: Fools who with devotion do puja, smear ash and sandal, wear scent and put the black mark on the brow, and wholly practise deceit, lies and rolled-up fraud: your body is only the white dust where a donkey rolled on the threshing floor.
nuance: The sacred ash on the deceiver is matched to the dust on a rolling donkey: same whiteness, same meaning. The verse does not say ash is empty for everyone, only for those whose conduct is fraud.

reading: 'I will do alchemy: silver, and gold finer than the touchstone's gold'; saying 'give gold and coins enough for the guru's bundle', performing tricks and deceiving, they take the property that was handed over and run a league away; even catching sight of them again is rare.
nuance: A plain account of the alchemist's confidence trick: the fee demanded in advance (குருமுடிச்சு, the guru's bundle) and the flight. The verse treats வாதம் (alchemy) as it is practised, a fraud, and says nothing about whether transmutation is possible.

reading: They show a yoga hall and rise and float upward; they quickly learn the eight siddhis as a trick and stretch up tall; then, seized by lust, caught in the urine-bag of women, they die in this wide world like men possessed by a ghoul.
nuance: அட்டசித்து வித்தை (the eight siddhis as an art) is siddhi as performance. The verse's sequence, display then lust then death, makes the showman's downfall ordinary desire, and the coarse phrase for women is the poet's contempt for the fall, not for women as such (compare 1467).

reading: So that onlookers will esteem them as eaters of kaya-kalpa, they do conjuring tricks everywhere, frauds and cheats; because they smoke ganja at set hours and eat opium straight, they roam the land like dogs, licking and sniffing.
nuance: காயகாயம் is read as காயகற்பம், the body-preserving medicine of Siddha tradition; the verse says its claimants are kept going by hemp and opium instead. It is a witness to the drugs of the wandering ascetic, and treats the kaya-kalpa claim as a cover rather than denying the medicine.

reading: Those who beat the drum through the town that 'the body is as unstable as a bubble on water' and wander as wastrels; saying 'look, I will make jnana-siddhi for you in glory', they go straight on to seize others' property at length.
nuance: The preacher's text is true (the body is a bubble) and the preacher is a thief; the verse separates the saying from the sayer. ஞானசித்தி செய்வேன் is the sale of attainment for money.

reading: Ochre, matted hair, water-pots, a seat, dangling rudraksha and the yoga staff: oxen who carry these, leaving the wife to drift, roam every land and, alas, wander begging a mouthful at every house, the sinners.
nuance: The full kit of the Saiva yogi is listed and its bearers called மாடுகள், cattle. தேவியை அலையவிட்டு (leaving the wife to wander) is the specific charge, and with 1467 and 1470 it makes the renouncer's desertion of his household the fault, not his gear alone.

reading: Those who say 'look, I will first grant siddhi here so you reach release', swear oaths everywhere and put on the swami's garb; to fatten the belly daily they talk of justice and knowledge and, as devotion, snatch money: they fall into the waste hell.
nuance: நித்தியம் வயிறு வளர்க்க (to grow the belly daily) is the motive the verse assigns to the whole trade of religious teaching for money. The promise sold is the double one, siddhi now and mukti after.

reading: In fine red wood you carve the heads of images; from a branch without a knot you make foot-sandals and destroy it; if you could seek and look at the one who shines within you, this mala, the three malas and any mala whatever would be no more.
nuance: The carpenter makes gods and sandals from the same tree, which is the argument against the carved god. The last line's இம்மலமும் மும்மலமும் எம்மலமும் piles up the Siddhanta term for the soul's impurities and says all vanish on seeing within.

reading: Running in every direction and everywhere, plunging the head in countless rivers, will they become pure jnanis? Sinners who do not bow with devotion to Hara's feet will sink without release in the waste hell, grieving and wandering.
nuance: The alternative to river-bathing is not a yogic technique here but பத்தி, bowing to Hara's feet; the chapter's positive note is devotional as often as it is gnostic.

reading: If one fashions the varied forms of mighty gods in stone, silver, copper, iron or dried plates and praises them, does it give the great bliss, the place where troubles end? Say! No, no, no, no, by the Lord's oath, no.
nuance: The four-fold இல்லை and the oath (ஈசன் ஆணை) make this the chapter's flattest denial. தராக்கள் is unclear, perhaps plates or dried clay. The verse answers 1472's list of cheap materials with the costly ones, so that price makes no difference.

reading: This world was born in the Lord's five letters; the moving and the unmoving dwell gloriously in the five letters; the many exalted lives rise in the five letters; certain, true awakening of knowledge stands in the five letters.
nuance: Four lines, four claims, each ending in ஐந்தெழுத்திலே: cosmogony, ontology, life and knowledge all placed in the five letters. After the chapter's destruction of outward forms this is the one form left standing, and 1488 shows how it is to be used.

reading: Because staring and staring at shastras one goes blind, fools praise the sun straight on until their eyes fail; if you can know the fit vessel and practise silent devotion, by that rule all become pure, just so.
nuance: Two kinds of blinding are paired, by books and by sun-worship. பாத்திரம் அறிந்து may mean knowing the fit recipient of devotion, or oneself as the vessel; சூத்திரப்படி may be 'by that rule' or, with the puppet-string sense of சூத்திரம், 'as moved by that string'. மோன பக்தி (silent devotion) is the verse's positive term.

reading: Cattle with no firmness of mind, dull and tethered, who in anger gather up others' property and hoard it, and who day after day roam every town for their food: these are the joyless sinners whom many in their own kind revile.
nuance: The verse joins theft and begging in one figure: the hoarder who still wanders for meals. மனவுறுதி இல்லாத (without steadiness of mind) is the diagnosis, which makes greed a failure of mind rather than a sin of the hand.

reading: Chant 'Sivaayavasi' and this whole world is yours; chant 'Sivaayavasi' and everything is attainment; chant 'Sivaayavasi' and you may rule the sky; 'Sivaayavasi' itself becomes the fire with two heads.
nuance: சிவாயவசி rearranges the five letters சி வா ய ந ம so that they end in வசி, which tradition reads as வாசி, the breath: the mantra is to be chanted on the breath. இருதலைத்தீ (two-headed fire) may be the breath burning at both nostrils, or the fire that burns both good and bad deeds. The closing verse of the work promises what the chapter has mocked when sold: the world, siddhi, the sky.

title: அழுகணிச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The first twenty-five songs of the Azhuganni Siddhar, each ending in a cry to the Mother (என் கண்ணம்மா!). The poet maps the body as a town in cipher, with its root seat, six houses, five ruling men, twelve-legged horse and needle-point gate, and laments that he cannot hold the breath still, cannot find a medicine to change his birth, and has been undone by love, kin, drugs and his own ignorance; the question he keeps asking is whether he will yet see the Mother's play inside this body.
structure_note: Every song is a கலித்தாழிசை of four lines plus the refrain என் கண்ணம்மா! and a closing question. 1489 to 1494 set out the body-town in cipher; 1495 to 1499 are complaints of the body, its boiling, its filth and its death; 1500 to 1503 picture the inner hunt and the ride; 1504 to 1513 turn to attachment, kin, drugs and the poet's own failure.
source_issues: 1505 line 1 and 4 read தங்காயம் / தங்காயந், a word not found in the dictionaries; probably a corrupt plant name.
1503 lines 2 and 3 differ only in வளைபரப்பி / வலைபரப்பி; one is probably a slip for the other.
1504 line 2 reads பாமவலி, probably for பாபவலி.

reading: In the root seat, in the six houses, in the ornamented seat at the middle of the street of quibbles, in the milk seat where a pillar grew up as fire, and in the seat above: will I not see your play, my Mother?
nuance: The four பதி (seats) with the six houses are read by tradition as the body's centres: மூலம் the root, the six houses the adharas, the pillar grown as fire the coiled power rising in the central channel, the seat above the crown. குதர்க்கத் தெரு, the street of quibbling, is unexplained; it may be the mouth or the restless mind. The Mother's play is the goddess at work in the body.

reading: An eight-span body, fourteen gates, five men who hold the council and two towns; you speak without fear, yet fearing punishment you do not stand firm in the heart and wither beyond your state.
nuance: எண்சாண் உடம்பு, the body eight spans long, is a stock Siddhar measure. ஏழிரண்டு வாயில் is fourteen gates where most texts count nine; some read the fourteen as the nine openings plus five senses. The five panchayat men are taken as the five senses or the five elements, and the two towns as the two eyes or the two breaths. Who is addressed, the soul or the Mother, is unclear.

reading: At the pearl gate in the street of three junctions, spreading the ten petals and seating her on the five-fold couch, holding that steady at an hour when no one is near, will I not light the standing lamp and draw the kolam and look, my Mother?
nuance: முச்சந்தி, where three streets meet, is read as the brow-centre where the three channels join; the ten petals are the lotus of the navel or heart, the five-fold couch the five elements or senses. The lamp and the kolam are a householder's puja turned inward: worship done alone, with the mind held still.

reading: Samba rice is cooked and ready; saying 'you must eat', pouring ghee by the measure, serving rice like pearls with three fruits and sugar, sweet honey-nectar: will I not eat and tire of it, my Mother?
nuance: The plain sense is a feast offered to the Mother or by her. In the cipher the rice, ghee, fruits and honey are the nectar (தேனாமிர்தம்) said to drip from the moon-centre when the breath is held, which the yogi feeds on. தின்று களைப் பாரேனோ, 'eat till I tire', suggests the feeding is endless.

reading: Wearing golden anklets, lifting the ornamented foot, dressed in red-gold cloth, with kohl drawn on her carp eyes and fine gold jewels, in the six-cornered street, seated on the pillar: will I not look at her until my eyes are cooled, my Mother?
nuance: The goddess is dressed as a dancing girl. The six-cornered street (அறுகோண வீதி) is read as the six-petalled or six-angled centre, and the pillar (கம்பம், as in 1489) as the central channel on which she stands. கண்குளிர, with cooled eyes, is the devotee's vision rather than a yogic claim.

reading: A horse that cannot be reached, with twelve legs, a burden even when let go: if I stop it in the street, take a rope and bind all four legs tight, could I not rule all the eight-sided land, my Mother?
nuance: The horse is the breath in Siddhar cipher; its twelve legs are the twelve finger-breadths the breath travels, or the twelve kalas. Binding its four legs is holding the breath, and ruling the eight-sided country (அட்டாள தேசம்) is the sovereignty of the eight siddhis, or of the eight directions. The verse is a single image kept in question form.

reading: My belly boils like a smith's forge; when I say 'stop' I cannot make it stand still; and if I could say 'stop' and hold it still, would not Death, who came saying 'kill', flee with his household, my Mother?
nuance: The boiling belly is read as the breath or the digestive fire that will not be held; the claim is the Siddhar one that holding it drives Death away. The repetition of the line with the condition reversed is the song's usual turn.

reading: A body of filth, a pot in which salt has stood: I cannot get the medicine to be born otherwise; if I could get the medicine to be born otherwise, would I not leave this filthy body and reach your feet, my Mother?
nuance: உப்பிருந்த பாண்டம், a pot that salt has eaten through, makes the body a vessel that corrodes from within. The medicine to change birth (மாற்றிப் பிறக்க மருந்து) can be read as the Siddhar's rejuvenating drug or as the knowledge that ends birth; the verse admits having neither.

reading: Told that eating the banana would hurt my mouth, I ate the pandanus fruit and death came to me; if, leaving the pandanus and dying without dying, I ate the banana, would life not come to me, my Mother?
nuance: The two fruits are a code the verse does not open. Tradition takes the banana as the inner nectar or the true teaching, refused because it seems hard, and the pandanus, fragrant but inedible, as worldly pleasure or false doctrine. சாகாமற் சாக, to die without dying, is the Siddhar death of the ego while the body lives.

reading: Living in the town of the bag, born in the town of the waste, I do not know the Vedanta house by which to go to the town of truth; if I knew it, would not the bag-town and the truth-town both end in the waste, my Mother?
nuance: பையூர் is the womb or the body as a bag, பாழூர் the waste or void, மெய்யூர் the town of truth. The closing line is puzzling: once the house is known, even the truth-town ends in பாழ், which tradition reads as the void beyond both, not as ruin. The verse plays on வீடு as house and as release.

reading: Are you my uncle's daughter or my sister-in-law? I do not know; Kama's arrow burns me like fire. If you became uncle's daughter and sister-in-law to me, would not all Kama's arrows burn up as I open my eyes, my Mother?
nuance: The poet asks what kin the goddess is to him, in the idiom of a village marriage; both relationships are those a man may wed. The cure for lust proposed is union with the Mother herself, which turns Kama's fire back on itself.

reading: Making the sky a bow and the five letters an arrow, mounting the chariot of mantra to hunt the deer, in the grove where the moon and sun have gone, will I not come and play and look with a glad mind, my Mother?
nuance: The deer hunt is the chase of the restless mind (மான் as deer and as the mind). Sun and moon are the two breaths in Siddhar cipher; the grove where they have gone is where the two channels end and the central one opens. The five letters are the Siva mantra.

reading: Riding the wild elephant through the market street, will the townsfolk stop us and laugh? Even if the townsfolk stop us and laugh, will I not ride the wild elephant and see with cooled eyes, my Mother?
nuance: The wild elephant is read as the untamed mind or the breath; riding it in public is the yogi's open indifference to the town's mockery. The verse accepts the ridicule in advance.

reading: Below the crown, inside the needle-point gate, climbing above the loft, taking the sky's blood, twisting the cord of the girdle, on the road to Kayalur I set it down and forgot it, and so I was ruined in every way, my Mother.
nuance: ஊசிமுனை வாசல், the needle-point gate, is the Siddhars' name for the opening of the central channel at the crown. வானுதிரம், the blood of the sky, is read as the nectar or the seed drawn upward. காயலூர் is read as a pun on காயம், the body. The lament is of a practice reached and then lost.

reading: Drawing the bud up with the nose and lifting it as six, spreading the net with the tongue and building a four-square house, spreading the net with the tongue inside the four-square house, I do not see the nose and suffer entirely, my Mother.
nuance: Breath drawn by the nose and the tongue turned back are the pranayama and khechari of yoga; the four-square house is read as the root or the brow. The last line admits the practice failed: he cannot find the nose, that is, the breath itself. மூவிரண்டு, two threes, may be the six centres or the breath's measures.

reading: The thought came to me to strew the flowers of desire; to end the strength of sin I did not get the strength of the bond, and if I had, would not the three flowers of desire stand before my eyes, my Mother?
nuance: பாம வலி is read as பாப வலி, the force of sin, and பாச வலி as the strength of the bond, or of love. The three flowers of desire are unexplained; the three desires for land, gold and women is one traditional gloss. The verse may mean that love's bond, rightly placed, is the cure for lust, but the text is too compressed to be sure.

reading: So that the ... would not show, I fenced a span-wide plot, planted onion seedlings and waited many days; without eating the onion I ate only the trouble above, and so, without the ... showing, I die without dying, my Mother.
nuance: தங்காயம் is unknown; it may be a plant name or a corrupt word. The onion planted and never eaten is read as a practice begun and never brought to fruit. சாகிறண்டி சாகாமல் reverses the Siddhar ideal of dying without death into its failure.

reading: Like moss spreading on water that nothing holds, though I look and look your delusion does not lift; if, looking and looking, your delusion lifted, it would be water with nothing clinging, and would the moss be anything else, my Mother?
nuance: பற்றற்ற நீர் puns on பற்று: water with no attachment, and water with no footing for the moss. The moss is the Mother's own மயக்கம், so delusion and the clear water are not two things; once the delusion lifts, the moss is seen to have been water all along.

reading: The learned and the rest, kin and parents, I took as one with the ninety-six; when kin and parents leave the town, how is it that I stand without any kin, having lost all support?
nuance: The ninety-six are the tattvas of the Saiva count. The verse sets family and the body's constituents together: both are the company that leaves. ஊரைவிட்டுப் போகையிலே, leaving the town, is dying or the dissolution of the tattvas at release.

reading: Below the eye is the nose, at the middle beside the ears; climbing above the uvula there is much of your novelty; even for those who have climbed above the uvula and seen your novelty, below the eye is the nose, my Mother, and there are many reasons.
nuance: உண்ணாக்கு மேலேறி, climbing above the uvula, is the khechari of the yogis, the tongue turned back to the cavity above the palate where the nectar is said to be tasted. The repeated 'below the eye is the nose' keeps the body-map in view; the closing காரணங்கள் மெத்தவுண்டே is deliberately unexplained.

reading: Taking dyeing stuffs, adding cinnabar, mixing a magic powder and pouring civet ghee, she put a dot on the brow between the eyebrows, and by the drug she placed there I came to this guise, my Mother.
nuance: The Mother applies the brow-mark as a drug and the poet is changed by it. The plain reading is a woman's cosmetics turned to a charm; the coded one is the brow-centre (புருவ நடு) opened by the goddess. The formula names real materials, சாதிலிங்கம் and வாலுழுவை நெய், but is not a recipe.

reading: A root from the underworld with arsenic added, with the goblin-drug joined and white-thorn ghee poured, a red vermilion ink that terrifies the whole world: by the drug she gave I burn like a coal, my Mother.
nuance: The verse lists alchemical materials, பாடாணம், வேதாளம், செந்தூரம், as the Mother's drug, and its effect is the poet's burning. Whether the burning is the heat of the awakened power or the ruin of a failed preparation is open; both readings are traditional.

reading: Fear of thieves will not let me lift my foot; a child that stands crying is a burden to the mother who bore it; if the child did not cry and the mother's heart did not ache, would I see even a mustard seed of fear of thieves, my Mother?
nuance: The thieves are the five senses that rob the body in Siddhar idiom; the crying child is the poet himself before the Mother. The verse ties his fear to his own clamour: a quiet child has nothing to fear.

reading: The five kings who rule the town, speaking their valour while they do not part, when they part and separate the town itself is lost; how is it that the warrior kings died?
nuance: The five kings of the body-town are the five elements, or the five senses; their parting is death, which takes the town with them. The question at the end treats their mortality as a surprise, since they were kings.

reading: I am an unfit outcast who talks ignorance; I do not know the undying head, I do not know my own knowledge, I do not know the leg that does not cook; I was ruined by fate and, hurting without being hurt, in a moment I turned to wax, my Mother.
nuance: சாகாத் தலை, வேகாத கால் and போகாத புனல் are the Siddhars' triad of the deathless head, the unburnt leg and the unflowing water, read as the crown, the breath and the seed held still; the poet confesses he knows none of them. புலையன் is self-abuse, not caste. Melting to wax is his collapse before the Mother.

title: அழுகணிச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The Azhuganni's songs end in two voices. Seven more cries to the Mother (1514 to 1520) confess that love's play, forgetting her, begging from the base and a lost practice have ruined the poet. Then the refrain changes to ஆத்தாடி (1521 to 1529) and the poet speaks as a woman to her friend, telling how one came as guru, burned the six supports, the fifty-one letters and the tattvas, and left her heart a bare void with the Lord mingled in it like light in a ruby; these stanzas are shared, nearly word for word, with Pattinathar's second Arutpulambal.
structure_note: 1514 to 1520 keep the four-line form with the என் கண்ணம்மா refrain and a closing question. 1521 to 1529 are couplets split by the ஆத்தாடி refrain: the guru's coming (1521, 1522), the burning of the body's parts (1523, 1524), worship given up and the void (1525, 1526), the indwelling Lord (1527), and the poet's fall and the ignorance of others (1528, 1529). The final stanza is a fragment.
source_issues: 1514 and 1516 line 4 read கண்னம்மா for கண்ணம்மா; 1518 line 4 likewise.
1519 line 3 reads காட்டமல் and line 4 போகமல், each missing a vowel sign (காட்டாமல், போகாமல்).

1521 to 1527 are near-doublets of Pattinathar's Arutpulambal 2 (seq 506 to 509, 513, 548 to 550) with the ஆத்தாடி refrain inserted; 1524 splices lines from two of Pattinathar's couplets. Which poet the shared lines belong to is open.
1529 is numbered u1 in the corpus and is a fragment: only the first couplet survives, marked by an ellipsis.

reading: Taking my mother as lasting and my fathers as my equals, I came to the play of delusion and my mind was dazed; if I left the play of delusion and the daze lifted, would my mother be lasting, or my fathers equal, my Mother?
nuance: மாயக் கலவி is the union of maya, read plainly as sexual play and in the cipher as the soul's mixing with the world. The verse makes the family itself a product of the daze: with the daze gone, no mother is permanent and no father is a peer. தந்தையர் in the plural is odd; it may mean elders.

reading: A thief without fear, a sinner without anyone, a cruel one without love who goes and tells the heart's secrets, a ganja-drunkard: before the ruin is done, would it not do to rule him, saying 'do not fear', my Mother?
nuance: The one abused is most likely the poet's own mind, named thief, sinner and drunkard; the plea is that the Mother govern it before it does harm. கஞ்சா வெறியன் is a rare literal reference to the drug among the Siddhars. Some read the thief as the breath that will not stay.

reading: Forgetting you I became a worm-eaten tree; those who forget themselves have no mother or father; if, not forgetting myself, I had a mother, would I not live joined to you without forgetting you, my Mother?
nuance: Forgetting the Mother and forgetting oneself are made one act, and knowing oneself is the condition for having a mother at all. உளுத்த மரம், a tree rotted from within, is the body without that remembrance.

reading: In the seat of the body I bought the root of fragrance, put on the ornaments of maya and took the goods that live; before I had examined them at the testing-ghat, how did the magic scroll fall into my lap, my Mother?
nuance: The verse is a merchant's tale in cipher: buying goods in the body's town, adorning oneself with maya, and the ஆயத்துறை, the toll-house where goods are checked. The சுருளோலை, the rolled palm leaf, is read as the writ of fate or Yama's summons arriving before the examination is done. Nothing in it is certain.

reading: Having pricked the picture and drawn the statue, without showing the beam I became the town's public hall; if I showed the beam and became the hall, would the picture be anything else, and would the statue not fall apart, my Mother?
nuance: சித்திரம், சிலை, உத்திரம் and அம்பலம் are terms of building: the picture and image are the body, the உத்திரம் the roof-beam, read as the central channel or the supporting truth, and the ambalam the open hall, Siva's dancing place. The verse seems to say that once the hidden beam is shown, picture and statue are seen as nothing in themselves.

reading: Going to the base and holding out my hand for goods, I show all my teeth and stare about; will you not give me wealth, my Mother, so that I need not show my teeth, stare about or go to the base?
nuance: பொருள் is both goods and the true substance; the poet asks the Mother for the one so he may stop begging for the other. The grimace of the beggar, teeth bared and eyes wide, is the humiliation the Kural's chapter on begging describes.

reading: Struck by the cut wheel I gave what wealth I had and stood beaten before ten million men; will you not, instead of my standing beaten, cut away my disease before the ten million and, opening your eyes, show me the open space, my Mother?
nuance: வெட்டுண்ட சக்கரம் is unclear: a broken wheel, perhaps the wheel of births, or a cut chakra. கோடி மனு is a crowd of men, or ten million births. வெளி காட்டாயோ, show the open space, asks for the Siddhar's vision of the void.

reading: I became the servant of the five-handed god, friend, asking to receive grace; one came unbearably, friend, and showed me the self's own form.
nuance: The bow to Ganesa opens the sequence as it opens Pattinathar's Arutpulambal 2. தற்சொரூபம், the self's own form, is read either as the guru's own form or as the poet's true self; Pattinathar's text has தன்சொரூபம், his own.

reading: To cut off the plundering birth, friend, he took the guru's form; to cut off the thieving senses, friend, he came as the cause.
nuance: கொள்ளை பிறப்பு and கள்ளப் புலன்: birth is a robber and the senses are thieves, and the guru is the Lord's answer to both. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:2 with the refrain.

reading: The six supports, friend, and the fifty-one letters, the whole fort of deceit, friend, he burned so that no fault remained.
nuance: The six adharas and the fifty-one letters of the alphabet, which the mantra-yoga builds the body from, are here a சூதான கோட்டை, a fort of trickery, and the guru burns the whole structure rather than ascending it.

reading: The five beginning with speech, friend, I saw die and fall; all the tattvas, friend, lost their heads and burned.
nuance: வாகாதி ஐவர் is வாக்காதி ஐவர், the five organs of action beginning with speech. The stanza splices two of Pattinathar's couplets (Arutpulambal 2:4 and 2:8), taking one line from each.

reading: Without bathing her in water, friend, without plucking flowers to strew, my heart became a bare void, friend; I do not see the state in which it stood.
nuance: The rites of image worship are simply dropped, not argued against, and what remains is வெறும் பாழ், an emptiness the speaker cannot locate or describe. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:43.

reading: Having sung and studied, friend, without adorning her with many flowers, without running about, friend, I lost my form.
nuance: ஓடித் திரியாமல் is the pilgrim's running from shrine to shrine, given up; உருக்கெட்டு is plainly 'I was undone' and in the cipher 'I lost form'. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:44.

reading: He stayed mingled in me, friend, like the light within a ruby; he is the greatness, friend, that the devotees who cherish and worship him do not speak of.
nuance: Light in a ruby is indwelling without mixture: the gem is not the light, yet the light is nowhere else. பேசாப் பெருமை is a greatness known and not spoken. The couplet is Arutpulambal 2:45.

reading: My mind confused, friend, I went by the way of the puffed grain; not knowing how to set it, friend, I fell headlong into the pit.
nuance: பொரிவழி, the way of பொரி, is obscure: puffed rice scattered as an offering, or a path that bursts. பாழி may be a pit, a cave or a monastery; the plain sense is a fall through confusion, and it has no doublet in Pattinathar.

reading: The ancient thing that has no arising and no dissolving, friend, they do not know.
nuance: தோற்றம் ஒடுக்கம் இல்லா தொல்பொருள் names the Supreme by negation, as what neither appears nor is withdrawn. The stanza breaks off after its first couplet.

title: இராமதேவர் பூஜாவிதி
theme: Ramadevar's ten-stanza rule of worship (பூஜாவிதி), attributed. It opens as a Shakta instruction: know the primal lamp, see the boundless fullness, hold the root, the maiden and the three letters in the central breath, and recite the three letters a lakh of times for siddhi. It then turns to a rite against an enemy, with offering, cremation ash, a figure, a stake driven under a tree and recitations of a hundred and eight, and closes by naming the auspicious days and promising that the ten verses yield siddhi and release.
structure_note: 1530 to 1533 are doctrine and the mantra: the lamp of the beginning, the fullness, the maiden at the root, the triangle and the three letters. 1534 to 1537 describe the killing rite step by step and its result. 1538 fixes the days and names the powers. 1539 is the colophon, naming Rama and the ten verses.
source_issues: The whole work carries the attribution 'attributed'; 1537 names Rama as the speaker from within the text.
1535 and 1536 have several unparsable phrases (அன்னமின்னா, வன்னமின்னார், சன்னமின்னா, உயிர்புதலாய்); the ritual text is damaged and the readings are approximate.
1532 line 7 தாக்கோண விட்டகுறை and 1537 line 1 அடிதரிசிங் களத்தில் are obscure, possibly corrupt.
1534 to 1537 describe a rite meant to kill; marked here for what the text claims, not restated as a procedure.

reading: One must know the gem-lamp called the beginning, see the boundless fullness; all the paths of the pure space called light, for the sake of bliss, are our Mother Manonmani; the feet of the supreme light called justice, the state in which she stands without qualities, none see; standing within the Vedanta called the Veda, this puja will not go in vain.
nuance: The chapter's goddess is Manonmani, the Mother; the puja is to her as the formless fullness, and the verse says the formless state is unseen even while promising the puja a result. The Vedanta is invoked as the ground of a tantric rite.

reading: You who stand without going: having gained the five kalas of fullness and the creeper of bliss that does not become, in the breath between foot and crown within the six, by the root that bears the maiden, one must utter the three letters by which the way appears; this root dies without dying; the moon-circle, the middle angle, is the triangle.
nuance: அடிமுடி நடுவாசி ஆறுக்குள்ளே is read as the breath held in the central channel through the six centres. The maiden (வாலை) at the root is the young goddess as the body's power; the three letters are taken by tradition as அ உ ம or as the goddess's seed syllables. சசிவட்டம், the moon's circle, and the triangle are the yantra of the next verse. The grammar is loose and the reading is approximate.

reading: The triangle becomes the three whorls and the self-angle, and in the maiden, the first root-gem, the four lines of the square are to be guarded with care; when the Lady, the supreme light, has fixed her gaze, I have told in detail the delusion that stood in the direction of the fire-angle, to be understood; if the lack of the fire-angle has come, the one who sat alone and saw is the siddha.
nuance: The verse describes a drawn chakra, a triangle within a square with a corner of fire (தீக்கோணம், the south-east), while hinting at the body's three channels (மூசுழி). தாக்கோண விட்டகுறை is obscure, perhaps a defect left in the fire-corner; the siddha is the one who has sat alone and seen for himself.

reading: The three letters that became siddhi are the light that acts; they become the fine aim, kilee and sav; to recite them a lakh of times is to complete siddhi even against the ghosts called enemies; this is the seed-knowledge, see where it strikes; hear the three wide face-seeds, and setting their strong seed in the figure, hear in detail the fourfold rule.
nuance: ஐயும் கிலியும் சவ்வும் are the goddess's seed syllables aim, klim and sauh, here as the three letters of 1531, so the earlier reading as அ உ ம is not the only one. The verse turns the mantra toward enemies and introduces the figure (சிலை) into which the seed is set, which the following verses use.

reading: Listen: having given an offering and done the puja, having fixed the form with the gracious recitation, bury it well in the ash of the burning ground at midnight; then, cut at the root, he becomes death, the state of austerity he held is ruined, and, dear one, the sinner will fall; I tell you so the story is understood, see further.
nuance: This is a rite of destruction (மாரணம் in the tantras, though the word is not used): a charged figure buried in cremation ash to bring an enemy's death and the collapse of his tapas. The verse claims it works; the poem offers it as the dark side of the same mantra. It is recorded here as the text's claim, not as anything to be done.

reading: There will be still further tests before the eyes; if you want to be saved, the secret is in this: make a peg of agil wood or devadaru with knowledge, utter the lion-syllable, say the name of the one meant and 'perish', cast the hundred and eight strong forms, and sitting under the tree drive the peg in skilfully with a nail.
nuance: சூட்சம், the secret, is the Siddhars' word for the hidden point of a practice, here applied to a nailing rite. The hundred and eight is the standard count of recitation. Several phrases, அன்னமின்னா, சன்னமின்னா, are filler or corrupt and leave the wood and the place uncertain.

reading: Pull out the peg you drove and set it bound tight; the form of bliss will be broken and perish; from the day begun, on the fourth day, you yourself will see the count finished and the way of this ... come to be; after release the poison rises and the instrument departs; I have told it fully, this is the bolt, it will not go in vain; stop it, strike it in the city and see, the frame is wrecked and life is lost as harm.
nuance: The verse states the rite's effect, death on the fourth day, and calls the teaching a பூட்டு, a bolt or lock, the Siddhars' term for a secret meant to be hard to open. உயிர்புதலாய் is probably corrupt. The reading is a paraphrase of a damaged text.

reading: Yes, if it is at the foot-vision in the arena, see, those who see it will take refuge in wonder; I have spoken opening the space, see, this way is no game; bathe with purity, head and all, and meditate quickly on the Mother's root; I have spoken the truth, see, this is Rama's word, without fail.
nuance: The verse steps back from the rite to its frame: ritual bathing, meditation on the Mother's root mantra, and the author's oath. அடிதரிசிங் களத்தில் is obscure; perhaps the vision at the feet in the ritual ground. ராமனுடை வாக்யம் names Ramadevar as the speaker.

reading: Perform siddhi with the root called 'I'; siddhi lies within the hundred and eight; the eight seats of the gods will dance, all the sixty-four herbs will dance, the trumpeted siddhis will dance in an instant; it is good to do it on the day of Revati, good on the eighth lunar day, and the one who does it in the waxing moon is a yogi.
nuance: தானென்ற மூலம், the root mantra called 'I' or 'that', is left unexplained. The powers promised are the eight siddhis (அண்டர் பதி எட்டு) and command over the sixty-four herbs of the medical siddhas. The timing by star, tithi and fortnight is the astrological frame the Siddhars share with the Tirumanthiram's breath-calendar.

reading: I told you this for becoming a yogi; oho, by the root taught before, as yogis, under the Lady of solitude, since it was written on the leaf all is done; by the grace of the thirsty Mother it becomes austerity, becomes ... , brings good; by the ten rules of root-puja for the infatuated, siddhi ripens for release: the ten are complete.
nuance: The colophon counts the ten verses and claims both siddhi and முத்தி from them. தவமாகும் மவமாகும் is a jingle whose second word is unclear, perhaps 'and un-austerity', that is, good and ill alike. ஏகாந்த வல்லி, the Lady of solitude, is the goddess as the yogi's sole companion.

title: கடுவெளிச் சித்தர் ஆனந்தக் களிப்பு
theme: Kaduveli Siddhar's Anandakkalippu is a song of counsel addressed to the mind (மனமே) in the kalippu metre, held together by the refrain 'do no sin, for tomorrow Yama will come in anger and carry you off'. The stanzas alternate plain moral precept (no curses, no anger, no lies, no lust, no begging, do not push away the good) with the Siddhar themes: the body as a bubble and as a potter's pot, the senses as a forest to be burnt, Kasi and the Ganga useless against karma, bhakti above the eight siddhis, the eight and the two discerned within, and the open space of Vedanta reached in a flood of bliss.
structure_note: 1540 is the pallavi, the refrain; 1541 to 1564 are the first twenty-four charanams. The order is loose: 1541 to 1551 are mostly precepts in the negative (லாமோ, ஆதே); 1552 to 1555 turn to the body, the senses and pilgrimage; 1556 to 1563 move toward the goal, the gold without doubt, bhakti, the goddess, the eight and two, the flood of bliss; 1564 returns to prohibitions and runs on into chapter 80.
source_issues: 1542: நல்லபத்த திவிசு வாசம் and நம்மையாய் நேசம் are garbled; the second half of the stanza is read conjecturally.
1545: ஏடாணை மூன்றும் பொல்லாதே is obscure and may be corrupt.
1563: உள்ளு (line 1) and செத்தேன் (line 3, probably செந்தேன்) look miscopied.

reading: Do no sin, mind; tomorrow Yama will come in anger, seize you and run off with you.
nuance: The pallavi, repeated after every stanza. The whole song is spoken to the mind as a separate hearer, in the manner of Pattinathar's laments to the heart; the only argument it gives for virtue here is death's nearness, not merit or hell.

reading: Can you lay a curse on anyone? Can fate itself be stopped by us? Can you take up anger? Can you hand over your thought to desire's grip? Four questions, each expecting no.
nuance: The second question is odd among the four: cursing, anger and desire are faults, but 'can we block fate' is a statement of limit. The stanza puts them together as things the mind should not attempt, which makes cursing another futile effort against விதி rather than a sin in itself.

reading: Unspeakable fraud, lies and cheating, if done, bring a ruin that wipes out one's whole kin; good faith kept with great trust earns, every day, the affection of people as one's own.
nuance: The second half is garbled in the text: நல்லபத்த திவிசுவாசம் is taken here as நல்ல பத்தி அதி விசுவாசம் (good faith, great trust), and நம்மையாய் நேசம் perhaps as நன்மையாய் or 'as our own'. The first half is clear: deceit's ruin falls on the family, not only on the doer.

reading: This body is a bubble on water; it will not stay but go, and you should know this illusion. Great love for the earth: devise the means to stay without clinging to it even a little.
nuance: உபாயம் (means, stratagem) asks for a method of non-attachment, not merely a resolve; the song later supplies candidates: bhakti (1558), the goddess's feet (1559), the eight and two (1562).

reading: A mendicant in the garden begged the potter for four-six months, brought back one pot, and dancing and dancing he dropped it and broke it.
nuance: A parable with no key given in the text. Tradition reads the garden as the world, the mendicant as the soul, the potter as the Lord, the pot as the body, and நாலாறு மாதம் as four-six, that is twenty-four months or, with 'and' understood, the months of gestation; the dancing is the pleasure-seeking life that breaks the body. On the plain reading it is only a story of a beggar who smashed what he waited for.

reading: Do not speak slander; not a speck of the wealth you seek will stay with you; the three bound by writ and oath are evil; if you set your desire on Siva, Yama's world is powerless.
nuance: ஏடாணை மூன்றும் பொல்லாதே is unclear; ஏடு and ஆணை may be the written bond and the oath, and 'the three' something the song does not name, perhaps the three desires (மண், பெண், பொன்). பொல்லாதே at the end of two lines must carry two senses, 'is evil' and 'cannot hurt', which supports reading the last clause as Yama's world losing its force over one who desires Siva.

reading: Seek the good way; every day seek the Supreme with longing; join the company of the able; praise and celebrate that generous one in your heart.
nuance: வல்லவர் கூட்டம் is the company of the capable or the realised; the stanza makes company a discipline, as 1564 and 1565 make bad company a danger.

reading: Do not push away the good; of the thirty-two dharmas seek at least one and do not let it drop; take nothing from the wicked; do not let evil, lying tales find a place.
nuance: அறம் நாலெட்டு, four eights, is the traditional list of thirty-two charities (feeding, water-sheds, medicine and the rest). The stanza asks for a minimum, one of thirty-two, which is modest beside the song's yogic claims.

reading: Stand by the rule of the Veda; go the way the good walk, seeking it; speak only what fits the state of things; and the vile, outcaste anger, subdue it and kill it.
nuance: சாத நிலைமையே சொல்லு is unclear; சாது (fitting, gentle) is one reading, so 'speak what is fitting'. The stanza calls anger சண்டாளம், using a caste name as abuse, while 1572 asks the hearer to know all castes as one. The approval of the Veda here is qualified by 1564, which warns against the false Veda; the song keeps the Veda and rejects its false teachers.

reading: Do not ask for anything as alms; do not swell and perish in lust for beautiful women; do not let desire rule you; having climbed the way that Siva desires, do not turn back.
nuance: The refusal of begging is notable in a mendicant tradition, and matches Pattinathar's resolve to beg only of Siva. சிவன் இச்சை கொண்ட அவ்வழி sets Siva's desire against the hearer's: the one இச்சை that may rule is Siva's.

reading: Climb the path of true knowledge; be clear in the pure, open space of Vedanta; revile the way of ignorance; and to those who come near you, tell the way that is bliss.
nuance: வெட்டவெளி, the cut-open space, is the Siddhars' name for the goal as formless expanse; here it is called Vedanta's. The last line turns the hearer into a teacher, which the song's own form, counsel to a mind, enacts.

reading: Do not go past the true guru's word; do not hold back from doing good more and more; do not walk by false arts; do not lead a good intellect down a false road.
nuance: பொய்க்கலை, false arts, probably means fraudulent learning or showmanship rather than the sixty-four arts; the Siddhar catalogues of frauds (Sivavakkiyar's last chapter) give the background.

reading: Nothing comes along with you; taking up this bag of worms and toiling here is the trouble; the hard-sought release is the goal, and no one is clear about the way to seek it.
nuance: புழுக்கூடு, a nest or bag of worms, is a standard Siddhar name for the body. The last line is unusually frank: the song admits that the way to release is not clear to anyone, even as it goes on to give counsel.

reading: A forest surrounded by five; a land that the five reach for these five; seek it beforehand, taking trouble; if you know that root, the house of release comes.
nuance: A coded stanza. Tradition takes the forest as the body, the five who surround it as the senses, the second five as their organs or the five elements, and மூலம் as the root centre at the base of the spine; on this reading the land is the inner place the senses are drawn into. The plain sense is only that one must know the root of the body's business before release.

reading: Within is a fourfold fort; if you take it so that the enemy flees, you can rule the land; the forest called the thieving senses, cut it, set fire and burn it, and you can see the house.
nuance: நால்வகைக் கோட்டை is read by tradition as the four inner faculties (மனம், புத்தி, சித்தம், அகங்காரம்), to be captured; the senses are கள்ளப் புலன், thieves. The verse pairs a siege and a forest-burning, two images of the same inward war; who the fleeing enemy is, the senses or desire, is not said.

reading: Will karma leave you if you go to Kasi? Will bathing in the Ganga give you a good end? Will your deeds die as you speak? Though you praise it, will the manifold difference of being born go away?
nuance: Four rhetorical questions against pilgrimage and holy bathing, the Siddhars' common target. பல பேதம் பிறப்பது, being born in many differences, makes rebirth, not sin, the thing the Ganga cannot wash off.

reading: The show that is falsely celebrated, all of it will go; the time of going comes to everyone; if you bring about on earth a time that is truly pure, what a help that is.
nuance: என்ன அனுகூலம் can be an exclamation (what a benefit) or a question (what benefit is there), and the stanza's point turns on it. கோலம் is outward adornment or display, which places this with 1568 and 1573 on false guises.

reading: The gold that is beyond doubt: if one joins it there is a swelling that knows no lowness, an endless height, a fullness filled everywhere with bliss.
nuance: The Supreme is named only as தங்கம், gold, and the stanza is all nouns of plenitude (பொங்கம், துங்கம், புங்கம்). The alchemical register is deliberate in a Siddhar: the true gold is not the alchemist's but the one that fills everything.

reading: Highest on earth is bhakti; for those who hold to it, release comes to them; the renowned eight siddhis come to anyone by Siva's act, through bhakti.
nuance: The eight siddhis are made a by-product of devotion and of Siva's doing (சிவன் செயலினால்), not of technique. This is the song's ranking: bhakti first, release its fruit, powers an aside.

reading: Scattering the good flower called love, reaching the twin feet of the goddess of supreme bliss, with joy, body and life, seek your uplift here every day, rejoicing.
nuance: The only stanza to name the goddess, பரமானந்த தேவி; the flower offered is love, not a plucked flower, which answers the song's rejection of outward rite. இங்கே, here, places the uplift in this life.

reading: Seeing the uplift that works, knowing the way to it and taking it, doing service without wrath to the Primal Siva, that service will join you to him.
nuance: சீற்றமில்லாமல், without wrath, is an odd condition on service and recalls 1541 and 1548: the song treats anger as the fault that spoils even devotion.

reading: The dance is danced by the soul; only when the soul has left the body does the body wilt; set your gaze on the heavenly state, and every day on earth a celebration will come to you.
nuance: The body is a dancer moved by the soul, which picks up the dancing mendicant of 1544. The promise of daily கொண்டாட்டம் on earth is one Kudhambai's refrain (1599) asks the knower to do without.

reading: Weighing the eight and the two, discerning all the Vedas as one within you, reaching the open space, plunging in the flood of bliss, your joy grows great.
nuance: எட்டும் இரண்டும், the eight and the two, is a Siddhar cipher: by tradition the Tamil letters அ (written like the numeral 8) and உ (like 2), so the syllable ஓம், or more broadly the Lord as அ and the soul as உ. The stanza does not explain it; it only says that discerning it makes the Vedas one within.

reading: This world and what is within it, push them away always without setting any desire on them; scoop up that flood of red honey, and take it in until your thought turns sweet and is sated.
nuance: உள்ளு in the first line is unclear (within, or 'think'); செத்தேன் is read as செந்தேன், red honey, the Siddhars' usual figure for the nectar held to flow within in yoga. தெவிட்ட, to the point of surfeit, is a pointed word: the one thing the song permits the mind to take to excess.

reading: Do not look at the false Veda; do not let the words of those preachers enter your understanding; do not go near the dark-eyed women; do not join in gladness the crowds of those on the wrong road.
nuance: பொய்வேதம் is the false Veda, not the Veda called false: 1548 tells the hearer to stand by Vedic rule. The target is the போதகர், the preachers of it, which keeps the song short of Sivavakkiyar's rejection of the four Vedas themselves.

title: கடுவெளிச் சித்தர் ஆனந்தக் களிப்பு
