theme: The last ten charanams of Kaduveli's Anandakkalippu: a run of prohibitions (keep no company with revilers, do not lie though the world lies, do not stone birds, do not play with snakes, do not smoke ganja or drink, do not put on false guises or wash obligations away in Gangas), then the positive close: set up the ladder of bhakti and drive off the sects, discern eight-limbed yoga and rebuke lust, know the many castes as one, and the Lord as the self-luminous one who dwells in lovers' hearts and calls himself the servant of his servants.
structure_note: 1565 to 1569 and 1573 are prohibitions in the ஆதே form; 1570 to 1572 are commands (bhakti as ladder, discernment and ashtanga yoga, all castes one); 1574 ends the song with a description of the Lord rather than counsel to the mind.
source_issues: 1574: துதுக்கிற் is a miscopy for துதிக்கிற் (if one praises).

reading: Do not keep company with those who revile; though this whole world should lie, do not lie; do not do cruel deeds; do not shoot stones at birds for nothing.
nuance: The last line is the song's most concrete: idle stone-throwing at birds, a boy's cruelty, stands for all needless harm. Truth is set against the whole world's falsehood, not against convenience.

reading: Desire nothing but Siva; do not stir up a quarrel harmful to anyone into a blaze; do not leap out of the state of tapas; do not want a book that lacks the good path.
nuance: சன்மார்க்கம் இல்லாத நூல் is a book without the true path, which matches 1564's 'false Veda' and 1569's 'books of ignorance without bhakti': the song judges texts by whether they teach devotion and the path, not by canon.

reading: Do not catch a snake and make it dance; do not disgrace your wives and show it; do not feed the world neem; do not plant your vainglory where it shows.
nuance: On the plain reading the snake is a snake-charmer's show, one of the fraud-tricks the Siddhars list; tradition also hears the serpent of the body, the coiled power, not to be toyed with for display. வேம்பு, neem, is bitterness given to others, perhaps harsh words. பத்தினிமார் in the plural is odd for one man's wives and may mean chaste women generally.

reading: Do not go near the ritual that people praise; do not let yourself be spoken of with praise among the many; do not count up your life as you proclaim it; do not make lowness so that others fall.
nuance: சாற்றும் உன் வாழ்வை எண்ணாதே is unclear: do not reckon your life as something to announce, or do not think of the life you boast of. The first line rejects சடங்கு, ceremony, as such, which goes further than 1555's rejection of pilgrimage.

reading: Do not smoke ganja; do not drink the liquor that shows madness and stupefies; do not kill lives so that they tremble; do not read the books of ignorance that have no bhakti.
nuance: The Siddhars were accused of using hemp and opium, and Sivavakkiyar's catalogue of frauds confirms that some did; Kaduveli's prohibition is from inside the tradition. அஞ்ச உயிர் மடியாதே: do not take lives so that they fear, or do not die in fear; the former fits the list of harms.

reading: Setting up the ladder called bhakti, stretching it to the place seen to be free of the bonds of pairs, gathering what is called truth, daily make it your own, driving the sects away.
nuance: தொந்த பந்தம், the bond of dvandva, the pairs (pleasure and pain, heat and cold), names what the ladder climbs out of. சமயங்கள் ஓட்டி, driving off the sects, sets bhakti itself above sectarian religion, a Siddhar commonplace put here as the last rung.

reading: All the many kinds of lust, past telling: cry fie on them, rebuke them, and take firm discernment; the incomparable eight-limbed yoga, discern it well and know it; the truth of those is enjoyment.
nuance: அவற்று உண்மை சம்போகம், the truth of them is enjoyment, is a striking end: the word for sexual union is used for the fruit of yoga and discernment, after lust has been spat at in the first line. The song does not spell out the eight limbs.

reading: Every kind of good justice, know them all, take them up and teach them; the many castes said not to agree, know every one of them as one, realise it, and declare it as kinship.
nuance: உறவு ஓதி, declaring kinship, makes the oneness of castes something to be taught, not only held. The song's own use of சண்டாளம் as a name for anger in 1548 shows how far the caste vocabulary persists even in the poet who says this.

reading: Do not put on a false guise; do not go wetting your obligations in many Gangas; do not think of plunder; having made a friendship, do not turn to tale-bearing.
nuance: கடன் நனையாதே puts debts or duties into the river: the pilgrim bathes to discharge what he owes. பல கங்கை, many Gangas, mocks the multiplication of holy rivers. The false guise and the bathing stand together as the two public forms of religious pretence.

reading: The self-luminous one is everywhere; he dwells in the joyful heart of lovers; he is the servant of the pure devotees; if one praises him, the Lord grants one's state.
nuance: அடியவர் தாசன், servant of the servants, reverses the order of lord and devotee, a bhakti figure the song saves for its last stanza. சுயபிரகாசன், self-luminous, is the Vedantic name for the Self, placed beside the devotional one without comment.

title: குதம்பைச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: Kudhambai Siddhar's kannis, each a single question to a woman called Kudhambai: for one who has reached a certain state, what need is there of a certain thing? The things dismissed are the instruments of religion and of the Siddhars' own craft: title-deeds, kalpa drugs, mudras, mantras, the hexagon, tantra, diet rules, palanquins, hand-cymbals, and at the top of the list yoga and jnana themselves. The states that make them needless are seeing the open space as truth, sleeplessness with awareness, the crown passed, the deathless walk, bliss welling up. The song is a ladder whose every rung is kicked away once stood on.
structure_note: Every stanza has the same shape: a condition in the first line, the question ஏதுக்கடி with its object in the second, and the refrain குதம்பாய் with the question repeated. The pairs are often rhymed opposites (பட்டயம்/வெட்டவெளி, முக்கோணம்/சட்கோணம், அட்டாங்கம்/முட்டாங்கம், யோகம்/வேகம்). No order is visible beyond a drift from possessions (1575) through ritual instruments (1580 to 1592) to yoga and knowledge (1589, 1595, 1596) and back to festivity (1599).
source_issues: 1585: இச்சிப்பிங்கு runs இச்சிப்பு and இங்கு together; the word division is editorial.
1595: முட்டாங்கம் and 1597: பூத்தானம் are not standard forms and may be corrupt or deliberate puns.

reading: For those who hold the open space to be the truth, what need of a title-deed?
nuance: பட்டயம் is the copper-plate or palm-leaf deed of ownership; the one whose truth is the open expanse owns nothing bounded enough to deed. The whole song's method is set here: a state named, a document made absurd by it.

reading: For the true jnani who has seen the true thing and shines, what need of kalpa drugs?
nuance: கற்பங்கள், the rejuvenating preparations of the medical Siddhars for a long life, are dismissed by one of their own: the knower has no body-span to prolong. The stanza does not deny that they work, only that the jnani needs them.

reading: For those who see without seeing and stay with attention, what need of vain desire?
nuance: காணாமல் கண்டு, seeing unseen or seeing without the eye, is the Siddhars' phrase for inner sight; கருத்தோடு இருப்போர், those who stay with their attention, recurs in 1599 and is the song's name for the settled knower.

reading: For those who have shed deceit and seen the way, what need of agitation?
nuance: The only stanza whose dismissed thing is a feeling rather than an instrument. Deceit and agitation are paired as cause and effect: the one who has nothing to hide has nothing to fear.

reading: For those who have seen the foundation, foot to crown, what need of disputation?
nuance: அடிமுடி recalls the Lord whose foot and crown Vishnu and Brahma could not find; in the yogic reading it is the row of supports (ஆதாரம்) from the base to the crown, seen in the body. வாதாட்டம் is dispute, but in a Siddhar's mouth வாதம் also means alchemy, and 'what need of alchemy's play' is a possible second sense.

reading: For those who have lost sleep and stay in remembrance, what need of a mudra?
nuance: நித்திரை கெட்டு, sleep destroyed, is the yogic wakefulness that Sivavakkiyar calls sleeping without sleeping; the seals of yoga, which aim at that state, are needless once it is held.

reading: For those who stand in the place that is tantra, what need of mantra?
nuance: தந்திரமான தலம், the place that is technique or that technique reaches, is unexplained; tradition takes it as the inner station the practice brings one to, so that the formula that led there is spent. 1588 goes a step further and dismisses tantra too.

reading: For those who stay in true tapas, what need of contrivance?
nuance: உத்தியம் is unclear: உத்தி, a device or stratagem, is the likeliest root, so 'contrivance'; உத்தியோகம், an occupation, is another reading, giving 'what need of a livelihood'. Either way tapas is set against calculation.

reading: For those who hold to the gaze and reach the one in the middle, what need of wasting away?
nuance: நடுவணை, the middle, is read by tradition as the central channel or its opening, reached by fixing the gaze; it may equally be the Lord who stands in the middle of all. வாட்டங்கள், wastings, may be the body's withering in austerity, so the stanza would say the inward path spares what outward tapas costs.

reading: For the true jnani who has learned the three Tamils and embraces, what need of sounds?
nuance: முத்தமிழ் is Tamil in its three branches, prose, music and drama. The stanza does not set learning against silence; it makes silence the end of learning, which is Tirumular's order too.

reading: For those who have gone above the crown and seen the high space, what need of wishing for anything here?
nuance: உச்சிக்கு மேல், above the crown of the head, is the Siddhars' summit of the body-cosmos; the space seen past it makes 'here' (இங்கு) a place with nothing worth wishing for.

reading: For those cooked without being burnt, who have seen the plain open space, what need of the darkness of delusion?
nuance: வேகாமல் வெந்து, cooked without burning, is coded: tradition hears the body ripened by the inner fire of yoga without being consumed, the alchemists' own figure for the perfected body. மோகாந்தம் is read as மோக அந்தம், the blind end of infatuation; the stanza says only that the ripened one is past it.

reading: For those who have leapt across without dying and walk a solitary way, what need of solitude?
nuance: A paradox: the one on the lone road needs no seclusion, because solitude is a state, not a place. சாகாமல் தாண்டி, crossing without dying, is the Siddhars' claim of a deathless passage, stated and not explained.

reading: For the freed ones who sway and dance in the inner sky, what need of tantra?
nuance: அந்தரம் is the sky or the interval within; the dancing freed ones are a figure for the state beyond practice. Where 1581 kept the place that tantra reaches and dismissed mantra, this stanza dismisses the technique itself, the next rung up.

reading: For those who stay with awareness, bliss welling up, what need of jnana itself?
nuance: The sharpest stanza in the song: ஞானம், the liberating knowledge, is dismissed in its turn, with தான் (itself) marking the surprise. The one in bliss and awareness does not need the knowledge that was the way to them, so jnana is treated as a means, like the mudra and the mantra.

reading: For those who see the painted hall day after day, what need of a charm?
nuance: சித்தரக் கூடம், the picture hall, is read by tradition as the body or the inner place where the picture of the Lord is seen; it could also be the assembly of the siddhas. பத்திரம் is a document, a leaf, or a protective charm; the pairing with 1575's title-deed suggests a written thing, perhaps a horoscope or a deed of safety.

reading: For the true jnani who has sprouted in the triangle, what need of the hexagon?
nuance: Both figures are yantra shapes and body-places. Tradition takes the triangle as the root centre or the goddess's triangle in which the power is born, and the six-cornered figure as the drawn chakra of worship or the heart centre; the stanza says that the one born within needs no drawn diagram.

reading: For the Lord who sways and dances in all eight directions, what need of a dance-stage?
nuance: நாதர் may be the Lord or the master, the siddha; நட்டணை is obscure, perhaps a dancing-place or a set dance. The one stanza whose subject is not a kind of person: the all-pervading dancer needs no hall, which reads as a side-glance at Chidambaram.

reading: For the true jnani who has gained release and whose heart embraces it, what need of diet rules?
nuance: பத்தியம், the regimen prescribed with Siddha medicine, is dismissed as 1576's kalpa was: the medical practice of the Siddhars is for the body of one who still needs curing. The near-rhyme of பத்தியம் with பத்தி, devotion, is probably a deliberate tease.

reading: For those who have removed trouble and stay with awareness, what need of a palanquin?
nuance: The palanquin is the honour carried for the great; the song counts it among the things the knower is above, with the title-deed and the celebration, so the list is not only of religious instruments.

reading: For the true jnani who knows eight-limbed yoga, what need of the eight-limbed prostration?
nuance: முட்டாங்கம் is unexplained; read here as the prostration on knees (முட்டு) and limbs, punning on அட்டாங்கம், so that the inner eightfold discipline replaces the outer eightfold bow. Another reading hears முட்டு as obstruction, 'what obstacle is there'. The next stanza dismisses yoga itself.

reading: For the true jnani who has restrained the rush and shines, what need of yoga itself?
nuance: வேகம், speed or rush, is taken by tradition as the breath's or the mind's; stilling it is what yoga is for, so the one who has done it needs no yoga. With 1589 on jnana, this is the song's doctrine: the practices are scaffolding.

reading: For those who have conquered the great elephant and sit on the mountain, what need of a gift of land?
nuance: மாத்தானை may be the great rutting elephant, a usual figure for the mind or the ego, or the great army; the mountain is the ascetic's seat, or in the body-reading the crown. பூத்தானம் is read as பூதானம், the gift of land to a Brahmin or a temple, which pairs with 1575's deed; it could also be பூ + ஸ்தானம், a place of flowers, or flower-offering.

reading: For the true jnani who wanders like the dead, what need of hand-cymbals?
nuance: The hand-cymbals are the bhajan's instrument; the knower who walks as a corpse has no song to keep time for. The dead-while-living jnani is Tirumular's and Sivavakkiyar's figure, used here with a comic edge.

reading: For those who look on whoever they see and stay with attention, what need of celebration?
nuance: கண்டாரை நோக்கி, looking at those seen, is taken as even regard for all who come; it could also mean watching those who have seen, the realised. கொண்டாட்டம், festivity, is the thing dismissed, where Kaduveli (1561) promised daily கொண்டாட்டம் to the one who gazes heavenward.

title: குதம்பைச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The last seven kannis of Kudhambai Siddhar keep the question 'what need of it?' but turn from ritual instruments to the household and the kitchen: adornment for one who has conquered Death, spice for one who has eaten pepper and ginger, coconut milk for one who drinks mango milk on the mountain, a veil for one who walks the town by day, a household shrine for one with no property or house, lingering desire for one who knows himself and has joined the Lord, and permission for the wife who stays with her husband and the Lord.
structure_note: The same three-line kanni as chapter 81. 1601 and 1602 are food riddles that tradition reads in cipher; 1603 and 1604 are the wanderer's homelessness; 1605 and 1606 close the song on union, the last playing on பதி as husband and Lord.
source_issues: 1601: the pun on காயம் (asafoetida and body) means உண்காயம் has no settled sense; the word division is editorial.
1606: பத்தாவுந் தானும் பதியோடு allows several constructions (husband and self with the Lord, or husband and wife at home); the line may be compressed.

reading: For the knowers of the true intent who have conquered Death, what need of adornments?
nuance: கோலங்கள் covers dress, decoration and assumed forms, including the ascetic's costume; the one who has beaten காலன், Death, has no body left to dress for and no role to play.

reading: Onion is eaten, pepper is eaten, dry ginger is eaten: what need of asafoetida to eat?
nuance: The stanza turns on காயம், which is both asafoetida (as in பெருங்காயம்) and the body. On the plain reading it is a kitchen joke: with these three pungent things already eaten, the fourth adds nothing. On the coded reading tradition hears வெண்காயம் as the white or purified body and உண்காயம் as the body that eats, so that the one who has taken the Siddhars' medicines no longer needs a body fed in the common way. The line names medicinal staples; it gives no preparation.

reading: For those who drink mango milk and sit on the mountain, what need of coconut milk?
nuance: Plainly, the hermit on the hill lives on the sap of wild mango rather than the village's coconut milk. Tradition takes the mountain as the crown of the head and மாங்காய்ப்பால் as the nectar that flows there in yoga, against which ordinary food is nothing; the code is not explained in the verse.

reading: For those who roam round the town in broad daylight, what need of a head-cloth to hide under?
nuance: முட்டாக்கு is the cloth pulled over the head to avoid being recognised, or a woman's veil. The knower goes openly by day and has nothing to hide, from shame or from the world's eye.

reading: One has no property and no house of one's own: what need of a household shrine?
nuance: தாவரம் is immovable property; தேவாரம் is both the daily worship kept in a home (the shrine box and its rites) and the hymns of the Saiva saints. The homeless man has nowhere to keep the first; the second reading, a dismissal of the canonical hymns, is possible but harsher than the pairing with 'house' suggests.

reading: For those who have known themselves and joined the Lord, what need of desire that comes after?
nuance: பின்னாசை is desire that lingers or comes afterwards: once the self is known and the Lord reached, there is no further thing to want. The order is the Siddhars' usual one, self-knowledge first and then the Lord.

reading: For those who stay with the husband and themselves with the Lord, what need of a word of permission?
nuance: The stanza plays on பத்தா (husband) and பதி (husband, the Lord, or a dwelling). Addressed to a woman, it says plainly that the wife at home with her husband needs no one's leave; in the devotional reading the soul as bride, united with the Lord, needs no answer or sanction. உத்தாரம் may be permission, command or reply.

title: சட்டைமுனி ஞானம்
theme: Sattaimuni Njanam, six verses attributed to Sattaimuni, teach a Siddhar's puja against the common kinds: not with a book, a lamp, a woman or a drawn chakra but with the Meru of forty-three triangles, through a ladder of goddess-mantras (Balai, Tripurai, Bhuvanai, Yamalai), five initiations, and then vaasi yoga that yields kaya siddhi. The last two verses turn to lament: the world dies and is born like a kavadi carried back and forth, and the poet asks his mind when maya will leave and tells it to look at the root.
structure_note: 1607 and 1608 contrast kinds of puja and warn that teaching the Meru openly loses the siddhis; 1609 and 1610 give the order of mantras, initiations and breath; 1611 and 1612 are complaints to the mind that end by pointing at the root (மூலம்).
source_issues: 1611 line 1 is corrupt (தியங்கினால் கெர்சித்துத் துரத்துச் சண்ணுஞ்); the reading of the line is a guess.
1609 gives Yamalai six letters and 1610 five; either two mantras are meant or one count is a slip.

reading: Listen to the ways of puja: some do it by rote with a palm-leaf book in hand, some set a lamp, some win fame doing puja with a woman set before them, some worship a chakra; our puja is like the Meru, with the forty-three triangles set out, and that is how the Siddhars themselves worship.
nuance: நாற்பத்துமுக்கோணம் (forty-three triangles) is the count of the Sri Chakra, whose raised form is called Meru, so the plain reading is a Sri Vidya diagram. The Siddhars also call the spine Meru, and the verse's 'our puja' may mean worship in the body rather than on a drawn plate; both readings stand. பெண்ணை வைத்தும், puja with a woman, names a left-hand rite without comment.

reading: Those who worship the Meru that is the self: if they curse, the whole cosmos burns like fire; the Meru that is honey needs initiation, and a mere boy cannot touch it; but when one who worshipped the Meru that is the sky opened his mouth and taught it, his disciple plundered the alchemical siddhi and the siddhi of the sky, the one who spoke said.
nuance: Three Merus are named, தான் (self), தேன் (honey) and வான் (sky), probably grades of the same worship, but the verse does not explain them. கவன சித்தி is unclear: ககன (sky-walking) or கவனம் (attention). The last two lines are a cautionary tale about open teaching: the disciple took the powers, so the Meru is to be kept in cipher.

reading: Hear the three letters of Balai I spoke of; know the sign, do her puja, then hear more: hear the eight letters of Tripurai, who changed, and worship her, son; hear the letter of Bhuvanai, who is settled, and worship her with skill; hear the six letters of Yamalai, who is calmed, praise her feet and worship.
nuance: The verse gives the syllable counts of four goddess-mantras and never the syllables: Balai three, Tripurai eight, Bhuvanai (Bhuvaneswari) one, Yamalai six. Tradition supplies them from the Sri Vidya and Yamala traditions, and the sequence is a graded initiation from the girl-goddess to the full form. The participles கூறிய, மாறிய, தேறிய, ஆறிய may be only rhyme-fillers.

reading: After that hear the five letters of Yamalai; when the five initiations are finished in due form, set yourself to the yoga called vaasi, son, and pranayama is completed; knowing all this, there is no obstacle, none, to the siddhi of the body; what is the world the Siddhars spoke of, best of men: it takes up again what was left unfinished, see.
nuance: The order is mantra and initiation first, breath second, and the body-siddhi (காயசித்தி, the deathless body) as the fruit. விட்டகுறை எடுக்கும், taking up what was left off, is usually said of practice resumed from a former birth; here it may mean the Siddhars' world completes what one left undone. Yamalai has six letters in 1609 and five here, which may be two mantras or a slip.

reading: The fierce barbarians who roar and chase ... sink in pleasure; bewildered within the four states, when will the mind become straight, when will it know? Crores in the world hesitated; dying and being born became like a kavadi carried back and forth; drowned in sorrow, knowledge is gone; it is like knowing only in the burning ground: sheer void.
nuance: The first line is corrupt (கெர்சித்துத் துரத்துச் சண்ணுஞ்) and the reading of it is a guess. நாலுபாதம் may be the four states of consciousness or the four feet (stages) of a path. The காவடி image, the pole carried back and forth on pilgrimage, makes rebirth a shuttling; சுத்தப் பாழ், the pure void, is here a verdict on wasted lives, not the yogic void.

reading: When will the ruinous maya go and cease? When will the scattered mind come straight? When will I stand free of the infatuation that joins the woman with sword-like eyes? Mind, alas! When will all the desire for this hard world be cut at the root? Leaving the planet-like instruments you keep thinking on, look upward; and what it is that joins there, look at the root to see.
nuance: Each எப்போ (when) is addressed to the mind, in the manner of the Pattinathar and Pambatti laments. கருவி (instruments) is the Siddhanta word for the tattvas, and கோளான, planet-like, makes them fates that circle one. The answer given is a direction: மேலே நோக்கி, மூலம் பாரே, look up and look at the root, the mooladhara, which the next work (ch 84) takes up at length.

title: திருமூல நாயனார் ஞானம்
theme: Thirumula Nayanar Njanam, nine verses attributed to Tirumular but not found in the Tirumanthiram, is a single meditation on the letter A as the foot (பாதம்) and the root (மூலம்): the A is the Lord who stands as he and she, the root is the mooladhara circle with its triangle and three nadis, and the practice is to look daily at this foot through the sushumna to the brow, seeing the guru as Isa. The light is beyond male, female and neuter, and the Vedas that search for it find only void.
structure_note: 1613 to 1615 define the A as foot, root and all; 1616 and 1617 give the practice of looking; 1618 identifies teacher and Lord; 1619 to 1621 locate the foot in the sushumna where the two lights rise and set and gather all into the one letter. Each verse opens with the last word of the one before (அணுவதாமே / அதுவாகி, நோக்கே / நோக்கமுடன், ஆசானாமே / ஆசானும்), as an antadi.
source_issues: 1616 has six lines where the other stanzas have eight; two lines are missing.
1619 lines 1-2 are repeated as lines 3-4 with minor spelling variants (பரமசிவத்தின் / பரசிவத்தின்), probably a doubled couplet.
1620 line 2 is a fragment (பொருளாகுங் காட்டும் போதே).
1621 line 8 has lost its first syllable (லரிய) and line 6 has a broken form (முடிந்த்).

reading: Becoming the foot and becoming what is beyond the cosmos, the letter called A itself becoming the foot; becoming crown and middle, in the root becoming the three things and the first; becoming the step and, free of the three voids, the supreme light Lord beyond the steps; the root that is the foot becoming A and standing as he and she: that state is the atom.
nuance: அகாரம் (the letter A) is made the Lord's foot, the first of the letters as he is the first of things. முப்பொருள் may be pati, pasu and pasam or the three lights; முப்பாழ், the three voids, is a Tirumanthiram term for the voids of maya, knowledge and their traces. The last word அணு (atom) is unexplained: the Siddhar formula is that the Lord is at once atom and whole.

reading: Becoming That, becoming he and she, becoming all; beginning, middle and end, the undivided whole; common to all, the refuge of every life, the root of every thing; honey, the bee and the taste, the flower and the scent, beyond reckoning: the A that is That becoming the root is the root that holds up all the cosmos.
nuance: The chain of ஆகி (becoming) is the Siddhar way of stating pervasion: honey, bee, taste, flower and scent are one sweetness seen five ways. புகலிடம், refuge, is the one relational word in a verse of identities.

reading: The root is the circle of the adhara: the three lights, the triangle, the three nadis; the water of the Sivalinga's feet called good conduct; it is the holy feet, the holy body and the dance; holding up all the cosmos with its form, the pillar that has sprouted and looks upward; the whole throat that drank the poison standing as itself: know the letter that begins with A, and see.
nuance: The mooladhara is given its usual marks, the triangle and the three channels (ida, pingala, sushumna); முச்சுடர் (three lights) are sun, moon and fire. கம்பம் (pillar) is the spine or the lingam read as the axis of the body. ஆலமுண்ட கண்டம் is Siva's poison-stained throat, so the body's centres are read as the Lord's own body.

reading: What is known is the supreme beyond, which is A; the knowing U is the supreme consciousness; what is born, the whole world, is the sects, and all the kinds of instruments called difference; knowing the foot called A as foot and crown, look at it every day.
nuance: Only six lines survive of an eight-line stanza. A is தற்பரம் and U is சிற்பரம், a Vedanta-coloured pairing of the Om's letters rather than the Tirumanthiram's Siva and Shakti; the born world is lumped with சமயம் (sects) and கருவி (the tattvas) as the realm of difference. அரிந்ததுவும் is probably a slip for அறிந்ததுவும்.

reading: With intent look at the foot called the root within the supreme consciousness, the subtle thing; firmly, crossing past the kinds of adharas, look at the place between the holy eyes, the nose and the brow; those who know the way and can look at this state here are sons of the one with twisted locks; those who daily stand looking at the guru as a flame of grace become teachers.
nuance: The practice is stated plainly for once: gaze fixed at the brow centre (புருவமத்தி) after passing the lower adharas. The verse ends with the guru, and the next takes the word up: looking at the guru is itself the way to become one.

reading: Teacher and Isa are one; he and she are one; it is That itself; the unspoken mantra is this too; it is the form of the great light, and the name; all the arts that are loved are itself; it is the firm seat of Omkara; for those who here see Isa as the teacher, Kailasa may be reached with joy.
nuance: பேசாத மந்திரம், the unspoken mantra, is the ajapa, the breath itself as recitation, as tradition takes it. பூடம் is a form of பீடம் (seat). The verse grants Kailasa 'here' (இங்கு), in the body, to one who sees the Lord as the guru, an inversion of the usual 'see the guru as the Lord'.

reading: In the root of the hard-to-reach Paramasiva, the place where the two lights rise and set; the sushumna, where the body's working ceases, becoming the pillar, stands settled as the light that is the true thing; in this way, worship the foot called the root at the place where the two times are no more, and see.
nuance: இருசுடர், the two lights, are sun and moon, which in the cipher are the right and left breaths; the sushumna is where they rise and sink. இருநேரம் அற்றிடம், the place without the two times, may mean beyond day and night or beyond the two breaths. The first two lines are printed twice with small variants, which looks like a doubled couplet.

reading: What is seen is the vision of the great light, ... when it shows itself as the thing; becoming male, female and neuter, and becoming the foot, the light seated beyond the beyond; all the Vedas practised in vain searched and did not see it and stood settled as mere void; the world-light practised afar, its root: look clearly at it as the foot hard to seek.
nuance: Line 2 is a fragment (பொருளாகுங் காட்டும் போதே), so the sense of the opening is incomplete. வீண்பயிலும் வேதம் calls Vedic study vain, and வெறும்பாழ் (mere void) is what the Vedas end in, a negative use of a word the Siddhars elsewhere use for the goal. ஆண் பெண்ணாய் அலியாகி, male, female and neuter, is the Tirumanthiram's formula for the Lord beyond gender.

reading: The foot hard to make clear becoming the A-letter, becoming itself the supreme consciousness and the supreme beyond, becoming the light hard to destroy, settled as beginning, middle and end; becoming the first hard to speak, becoming the root, becoming the three lights, the completed light; in the whirl becoming the point, becoming ..., the one letter hard to ...: gather it all into that and see.
nuance: சுழியினிலே முனையாகி splits சுழுமுனை into its parts, whirl and point, as a gloss on the name. கோப மாகி is unclear (anger does not fit; perhaps a corrupt கோபுரம், tower). The last line has lost its first syllable (லரிய for சொல்லரிய, hard to speak) and முடிந்த் is a broken form. The sense is clear enough: all the names of the chapter resolve into the one letter.

title: திருவள்ளுவர் ஞானம்
theme: The invocation (காப்பு) of Thiruvalluvar Njanam, a late Siddhar work attributed to Thiruvalluvar and not by the author of the Kural: eight lines of போற்றி to Brahma and Vishnu filling cosmos and body, the fullness, the sun-and-moon light, Agastya of sweet Tamil, the poet's guru, the lotus of the sushumna in the left channel and Guha seated in the kundalini. It places the work in the Agastya lineage of the medical and yogic Siddhars, not in the Kural's world.

reading: Praise to Brahma and Vishnu who fill cosmos and body; praise to the grace of the undivided fullness; praise to the light of sun and moon girt by the mandala; praise to Agastya who speaks sweet Tamil; praise to my guru whom the eight directions praise; praise to the lotus of the sushumna in the left channel; praise to Guha seated within the kundalini; praise forever to the feet of the guru-sage.
nuance: The invocation is wholly a Siddhar's: அண்டம்பிண்டம், பரிபூரணம், சுழுமுனை, குண்டலி, and Agastya and the guru rather than Siva by name. The attribution to Valluvar rests on the title alone; the Kural's own invocation names only the Primal Lord. இடைகலையின் சுழுமுனையின் கமலம், the sushumna's lotus in the left channel, is odd as anatomy and may mean the lotus reached through the left (moon) breath.

title: திருவள்ளுவர் ஞானம்
theme: The body of Thiruvalluvar Njanam, nineteen short verses attributed to Thiruvalluvar but not his: a Siddhar speaks in the first person of his making in the womb, his destruction of the slur of low birth, and the secret no one sees, then preaches impermanence (the cremation ground ends every life), the root whirl and release, the fruit of kaya siddhi, and a run of cipher verses on salt, urine and the moon that read as rejuvenation (karpam) formulas. The Valluvar name is a late attribution; the matter is Siddha medicine and yoga.
structure_note: 1623 to 1625 are autobiographical and claim a secret the world does not see; 1626 to 1631 preach impermanence, each ending in the burning ground or the perishing body; 1632 to 1636 give the way, nectar, the whirl, the Veda's inner sense, karma burned, kaya siddhi; 1637 to 1639 are salt verses in cipher; 1640 and 1641 close on mastering the five elements and gaining siddhi without leaving the body. The metres shift from kattalaikkalitturai through kochchagam to venba, which the tool records under one காப்பு heading.
source_issues: 1632 has three lines; the first line of the venba is missing.
1629 and 1639 have broken syntax and word division (தந்தைவிதி உன்னலழிவ துடலுயிர்; சொற்பாயும் வாசியில் தேகம்); the readings are reconstructions.
1641 போசைவிதி is an unknown form, probably corrupt.
The tool labels every unit of this work காப்பு though only 1622 is an invocation; the metres named (கட்டளைக் கலித்துறை, தரவு கொச்சகம், நேரிசை வெண்பா) are given in the second half of the label.

reading: Having come into the womb called mother and stayed there, I remained well inside for ten months; what wonder: I was formed with all the heights that are set in this world, and they do not see the truth.
nuance: The claim is the Siddhar doctrine that the body formed in the womb holds everything the world holds (உன்னதமெல்லாம் அமைந்தேன்), so the truth is to be found in it. The verse begins a first-person life story that ends in 1625 with the secret no one sees.

reading: Born on the earth, having studied and known the language, caught by the charm of the world's people and parted from it, whirling in the pit, I trusted for some days the golden lotus of the kundalini; they do not see the secret.
nuance: கும்பி is both the hell Kumbhipaka and the belly, so the pit may be the world's suffering or the body; the golden lotus of the kundalini is the root centre. ரகசியம், the secret, is left unsaid and is the refrain of these three verses (காண்கிலரே, they do not see).

reading: The cosmos, the sky and the earth, and the inner meaning of the Agamas, I know clearly and shining within this body; I destroyed the way in which the gadflies called me low-born; they do not see the clear sense of the secret that I opened.
nuance: நீசன் என்ற வாறு, the way they called me low-born, draws on the legend of Valluvar's outcaste birth, and the verse answers it not by argument but by knowledge of the cosmos in the body. வண்டர் (gadflies, or louts) is the only word spent on the accusers.

reading: Men born into the world: your life, which you took to be real, how does its stirring show itself? Living without doubt in the world, wearing the esteem of manliness, this life called a lie goes to the burning ground.
nuance: The question in line 2 is the real content: what makes the body move is not seen, and so what is taken as real (மெய்) is called a lie (பொய்). சுடுகாடு, the burning ground, ends this and the next four verses.

reading: In the house of release, in the house of the sound at the root whirl, the bindu shines, and by it the long sea-girt world flourishes and grows and stands bright; what use to seek a treasure-house that is the thing destroyed by not seeking; they do not see that the land one reaches is the forest of the burning ground.
nuance: மூலச் சுழி, the root whirl, and நாத வீடு, the house of sound, locate release in the body's base where bindu (seed, or the drop of light) shines. The third line is hard: பொக்கிடம் is a treasure-house and தேடாதழித்த பொருள் a thing lost by not seeking; the sense may be that the bindu spent in the world is lost, and only the burning ground remains.

reading: Though one reaches the seven kinds of birth and the four kinds of womb, by the teaching that it is the thing of pouring blood, sound and seed, as it passes and passes the sea of lives wanes like the waning moon, and having seen it, the great earth, however long it stays, is impermanent.
nuance: எழுவகைத் தோற்றம், நால்வகை யோனி are the traditional seven orders of birth and four wombs (egg, womb, sweat, seed). சுரோணிதம் நாதவிந்து is the womb-blood and seed from which bodies come; the verse's claim is that all births are only that substance passing, and so impermanent. The grammar of the middle lines is loose.

reading: However long one lives, this body perishes by itself as it was ordered before, not knowing it; the father's decree makes it so; thinking on how body, life and frame perish and cease, having seen that former order, do they still not know?
nuance: அனுப்படி (as ordered) is repeated and தந்தைவிதி, the father's decree, names the ordering as the Lord's; the verse is a fate verse in a Siddhar text, where fate is usually something to be overcome (see 1635). The line-breaks are garbled and the subject of the last line is unclear.

reading: Desire for the womb does not die; your life is impermanent; is there in that honey-pot a bliss beyond pleasure? In small pleasure, when the flesh is gone and the body is gone and goes, knowing nothing, for the low there is no heaven but the burning ground.
nuance: சுகாதீதம், beyond pleasure, is the word for the bliss of release; the verse asks whether sex gives it and answers with the burning ground. The target is lust alone; the body's other appetites are not mentioned.

reading: This body dies in this world, a life that does not know the way it came; this body, will it come to rule the wish-tree that is the serpent lying in a small pit? See.
nuance: அரவம் அற்பக் குழியில், the serpent in a small pit, is the coiled power at the root centre, and கற்பகம், the wish-granting tree, what it gives when ruled. On this reading the verse asks whether a body that does not know its own origin can master the kundalini. A plain reading (the body's hopes are as vain as a snake in a hole ruling a wish-tree) also stands.

reading: ... drinking that drink out of hunger; if one sees knowledge, body, life and frame grow strong; if one eats, eat the nectar juice.
nuance: The first line of the venba is missing, so what drink (பானம்) is meant is lost. அமிர்தரசம், the nectar juice, in the Siddhars is the fluid held to come from the head in yoga, or a prepared karpam; the verse ties bodily strength to seeing knowledge, which is the Siddhar claim that jnana feeds the body.

reading: What is there for those who do not know the whirl, what for those who do not know the bliss, what for those who do not know the way to reach it; for those who, not knowing the whirl, do not know the root and do not attain release on that path, Yama is Death: for them there is dying. See.
nuance: சுழி (the whirl) and மூலம் (the root) are the technical words, the opening of the central channel and the base centre. The verse states the Siddhar position flatly: death is for those who do not know the whirl, so release is deathlessness in the body.

reading: If the hidden knowledge of the Veda becomes true perception itself, by the Lord's grace one seeks the state; among the four meanings of the Veda's secret, see the good meaning as the ghee churned from milk.
nuance: An unusually friendly verse to the Veda for a Siddhar text, but conditional: only when its hidden sense (மறைஞானம்) becomes மெய்யுணர்வு. நாலு பொருள் may be the four ends (virtue, wealth, pleasure, release) or the four Vedas; the ghee-from-milk image makes the good sense an essence extracted from the whole.

reading: I burned the fate-deed that was there from the first and the triple void, and toiled with an unpanicked mind; born without regard to the good deeds and bad deeds there from the first, I sent my life off out of the strong deeds.
nuance: ஊழ்வினையை ... சுட்டு, burning fate-deed, is a claim to have destroyed karma, and முப்பாழ் (the three voids) is burned with it. The last line is ambiguous: வல்வினையிற் போக்கிவிட்டேன் வாழ்வு may mean 'I freed my life from strong deeds' or 'I wasted my life in strong deeds'; the first fits the boast of the verse.

reading: After the siddhi of the body drove off my karma-deeds, the siddhi of maya and the root whirl will come to me; by the siddhi of the body, by the root tamarind, the first initiation was done; now see it in two years' time.
nuance: காயசித்தி is the deathless or perfected body, and மாயசித்தி here probably the powers over appearance. மூலப் புளி (root tamarind, or root acid) is unexplained; tradition reads புளி in Siddha cipher as a prepared acid or as a body-substance, so the first diksha may be a medicine rather than a rite. The two-year term is the kind of stated period the karpam verses give.

reading: Not knowing the thought behind the rock salt that comes, humans eat and fall into strong deeds and die; though rock salt, white rock salt, comes in many kinds, think that it is in the inner mind.
nuance: கல்லுப்பு (rock salt) is a common Siddhar cipher; tradition takes salt variously as a body-fluid, as the alchemical salt, or as the taste of the world one eats and dies of. The last line, that the salt is 'in the mind' (உள்ளமதில் உண்டு), argues against a literal mineral and for a cipher. The verse makes a claim about where the substance is, not a preparation.

reading: It is always rock salt in this body of eight spans; what is the reason that, seeing it, they do not know it? Always the moon: drawing off that urine, setting it on fire and heating it, I realise the truth as strength.
nuance: அமுரி is the Siddha medical word for urine, used in rejuvenation (amuri karpam), and இந்துப்பு (rock salt) is tied to இந்து, the moon, by sound. The verse claims the body already holds the substance (எண்சாண் உடல், the eight-span body) and that heating it gives strength; a coded reading takes the moon's fluid as the nectar from the head. This is a claim about a substance, recorded as history, not as a remedy.

reading: Because the dross of the salt changed as it oozed, before old age turns it to calx; by the salt this body hardens for crores of aeons, and in the vaasi that leaps at a word, the body.
nuance: சுன்னம் (calx, the calcined ash) is an alchemical end-product and here what old age makes of the body; the salt properly treated is claimed to keep the body for கற்பாந்தம் கோடி, crores of kalpas. The last line brings in வாசி, the breath practice, so the hardened body is kept by breath as well as by salt; the syntax is broken and the reading is a reconstruction.

reading: If one knows the five elements, the five that seem impermanent come under control within the year; those who see and know the five, in the memory of the vision of knowledge, may come to know the opened decree.
nuance: அஞ்சு வசப்படுவது, the five coming under control, is the mastery of the elements (பூதஜயம்) counted among the siddhis. ஆண்டதனில் (in the year) may be a time limit or a slip; விதி, decree, is here something opened and known rather than suffered.

reading: Taking a body of eight spans, what of it, my Lord? Removing the nearness of women, there is great bliss; so that the eye may see, without the body ceasing, the knowledge that gains siddhi, the siddhi of yoga ... decree: think on it.
nuance: தேகம் ஒழியாமல் சித்தி பெறும் ஞானம், the knowledge that gains siddhi without the body ceasing, is the text's statement of its goal: release in the living body. போசைவிதி is an obscure word, perhaps a corruption; the sense of the last foot is lost.

title: அகப்பேய்ச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The first quarter of Agappei Siddhar's songs, each stanza a four-line address to the inner demon (அகப்பேய்), the ego-mind that must be told to keep quiet. After a frame (take in no poison, fear not, say nothing) the poet runs through the Saiva map of manifestation, the Supreme becoming the worlds, nada and bindu, the five elements with their colours, the organs, the ten nadis, the letters அ உ ம, the adhvas and the fifty-one letters, and after each item says that it is not the Lord: all of it is a built thing (சகலம்), the four paths and the thirty-six tattvas included, and only knowing oneself, with the sadguru's feet, is the way.
structure_note: 1642 is the frame; 1643 to 1659 is the catalogue of manifestation (Supreme and worlds 1643, nada and bindu 1644 to 1645, the four paths 1646, the three groups of five 1647 to 1649, the six and the three 1651, the elements and their colours 1652 to 1654, the letters 1655 to 1656, the adhvas and fifty-one letters 1657 to 1658, the tattvas 1659); 1660 to 1666 turn the list into a negation: none of this is the Lord, the religions and the thirty-six do not avail, and the way is to know oneself, not sariyai or kiriyai.
source_issues: 1645: the GLOSSES entry (நாலுபதம் - சரியை, கிரியை, யோகம், ஞானம்) belongs to 1646, which has the phrase நாலு பாதம்.
1649 line 1 வசனாதி ஐந்து does not match any standard group of five and may be corrupt.
1658 line 1 அத்தி வரைவாடி is hard to construe; the gloss itself offers two unrelated senses for அத்தி.

reading: Do not swallow poison, demon within; to gain the Lord's feet, do not let the heart waver, and say nothing at all.
nuance: அகப்பேய் (the demon within) is the addressee of every stanza, traditionally the ego or restless mind; the feminine -அடி endings treat it as a girl spoken to. நஞ்சு may be plain poison, or the poison of the senses and the world as tradition takes it; the stanza also sets the rule the whole work repeats, that the demon is to be silent.

reading: It is the Supreme beyond the supreme, demon; it came as the wide sea, and it alone created the netherworld and the seven worlds.
nuance: பராபரம் is the Siddhars' usual name for the Supreme beyond gods; பரவை (the sea, per the gloss) may be the ocean of manifestation or the formless expanse, and the stanza makes creation its unaided act.

reading: Nada is the Veda, demon; have you seen the good dance? The foot is Shakti, and the para-bindu is nada.
nuance: The stanza stacks equations from the Saiva cosmogony: nada as the first scripture, the dancing foot as Shakti, bindu as the source of nada. The order (பரவிந்து நாதமடி) could also mean that bindu and nada are both named; tradition has nada rise from bindu.

reading: Bindu and nada, demon, came as the real (or as body); the five great elements became their seat.
nuance: மெய் is both 'truth' and 'body'; the elements as the seat (இடம்) of bindu and nada fits the body reading, in which the subtle pair takes gross form in the five elements. The gloss printed under this stanza (நாலுபதம்) belongs to 1646.

reading: You have seen that the four paths are the good way, demon; but unless it is the root, it is not release.
nuance: நாலு பாதம் is glossed as sariyai, kiriyai, yoga and jnana. The stanza grants them as a good way and denies them as release unless they reach the மூலம் (root), which 1656 names as the letter சி and 1706 denies altogether; the poet's view of the paths unfolds in 1666, 1667 and 1676.

reading: The five that begin with speech, demon: hear how they came; they are an aggregate, and they are not the truth.
nuance: வாக்காதி ஐந்து are the five organs of action (speech, hands, feet, excretion, generation), as the gloss says. ஒக்கம் (a gathering, an aggregate) is the stanza's reason for denying them truth: they are a compound, not the one.

reading: The five that begin with sound, demon, became the sastras; they are also falsehood, and I have told you the truth.
nuance: சத்தாதி ஐந்து are the five subtle elements (sound, touch, form, taste, smell). Saying they 'became the sastras' puts learning on the side of the senses, and மித்தை (false) condemns both together.

reading: The five that begin with vasana came in strength, demon; the ten nadis are ten, and see that this is firm.
nuance: வசனாதி ஐந்து is unclear: it may be the five organs of knowledge (completing the groups of five in 1647 and 1648), or a corruption of a word for the five vital airs. தெசநாடி, the ten nadis, is a standard count in the yogic body.

reading: All that is cause, demon, I have told as I saw it; you have seen the destruction too, and all the ways in which they came.
nuance: காரணம் gathers the causes listed so far. மாரணம் is killing or destruction (in tantric lists one of the six rites); here it most likely means that everything that came also perishes.

reading: The Agamas told of the six tattvas, demon; and the unchanging mandalas came as three.
nuance: ஆறு தத்துவம் may be the six adhvas (paths) of the Agamas, the thirty-six tattvas counted as six sixes (as ஆறாறு in 1664), or the six adharas. The three unchanging mandalas are traditionally sun, moon and fire, placed in the body as well as the cosmos.

reading: Earth is golden in colour, demon, and this is no ignorance; water's form, what is within it, is white.
nuance: The colour scheme for the five elements, begun here and finished in 1654, follows the tantric table also found in the Tirumanthiram: earth gold, water white, fire red, air dark, sky smoke. பேதமை அல்ல insists this is knowledge, not fancy.

reading: Fire is red, demon, see that this is firm; air is blue, and I will tell you the matter of the sky.
nuance: நீலம் (blue, or dark) for air matches the 'black' of the Tirumanthiram's table; the colours are the meditator's signs for the elements in the body, as tradition takes them, rather than observations.

reading: The sky is cloud-coloured, demon; hear how it came, let there be no defect, and I have told you what is.
nuance: வான மஞ்சு could be 'the sky is yellow' or 'the sky is cloud (smoke-coloured)'; the Tirumanthiram's table gives the sky தூமம், smoke, so the second reading is likelier. ஊனம் ஆகாதே warns against error in the sequence.

reading: All this arose as the letter அ standing there, demon; the letter உ joined it and it came to have form.
nuance: அகாரம் and உகாரம் are the first two letters of Om; the stanza makes them the stages of manifestation, அ as the first arising and உ as form. அங்கென்று (as 'there') is obscure; it may mean that with அ a 'there', a place, first appeared.

reading: The letter ம is maya, demon, and I have told you it is impurity; the letter சி is the root, so reflect on it.
nuance: The third letter of Om is read as maya and malam, matching the Saiva key in which the ம of நமசிவாய stands for impurity, while சி (of சிவ) is the root. 1684 revisits the letters with அ as anava.

reading: Letters and worlds, demon, mantras and tantras: I will tell you more, and you will listen with a murmur of assent.
nuance: வன்னம் (varna), புவனம் (bhuvana) and மந்திரம் are three of the six adhvas of Saiva Siddhanta; தந்திரம் stands for the Agamic rites. இம்மென்று கேட்பாயே asks the demon to hear without talking back, in keeping with 1642.

reading: From the elephant to the line, demon, and the fifty-one letters: you have seen that they are falsehood, so do not believe them true.
nuance: அத்தி வரை is obscure; the gloss offers elephant or nadi for அத்தி, and the phrase may mean 'up to the elephant' (the whole range of created things) or a drawn line. The fifty-one letters of the Sanskrit alphabet, which the Tirumanthiram treats as the stuff of the mantra-path, are here called மித்தை.

reading: The tattvas, demon, came as the whole of things; I have told you the intellect too: are they not the form of the elements?
nuance: சகலம் is 'everything' and also the Siddhanta name for the soul's state when joined to all the tattvas. Even buddhi, the intellect, is brought under the elements, so that no inner faculty escapes the catalogue.

reading: All these kinds, demon, are not our Lord; that kind is another, so inquire and see.
nuance: The pivot of the chapter: everything listed since 1643 is set aside as not the Lord. அந்த விதம் வேறே leaves what the Lord is unsaid, and ஆராய்ந்து makes inquiry, not instruction, the way to it.

reading: If sin is to end, demon, you must not keep imagining; there is no dying either: it is the sadguru's feet.
nuance: பாவிக்க means to imagine or to meditate on a form; the stanza forbids it, as 1731 does. சாவதும் இல்லை may promise freedom from death through the guru, or state that there is no death to fear; the two clauses are joined only by the refrain.

reading: However much is said, demon, my mind is not consoled; leave both the conscious and the unconscious, and bring them together and see.
nuance: சித்து and அசித்து are spirit and matter; the stanza asks to leave both and then சேர்த்து (join, or gather) and see, perhaps to see them as one from beyond them. The confession that no telling consoles the mind is unusual in the poet's voice.

reading: The six religions, demon, came of their own making; inquire and tell me the place where you stand settled.
nuance: சமய மாறு is the six Saiva or six orthodox religions; தம்மாலே வந்தவை says they are human constructions. The demon is asked where it rests, not which sect it holds.

reading: The thirty-six exist, demon, but I have told you they do not avail; if there is something else, tell it truly.
nuance: ஆறாறு, six sixes, is the thirty-six tattvas. The poet grants that they are (ஆகும்) and denies that they help (ஆகாது), the same move as with the four paths in 1646.

reading: When you know yourself, demon, you will join with nothing; I will tell you what is, the way to know yourself.
nuance: Self-knowledge is offered as the one thing the catalogue did not contain, and its mark is non-attachment (ஒன்றையும் சேராயே). The promise of a method is kept in 1666 to 1668 as a series of denials.

reading: Sariyai will not do, demon: you have seen that it gives salokam; even if you do kiriyai, nothing is gained.
nuance: The stanza accepts the Siddhanta mapping of sariyai to salokam (dwelling in the Lord's world) and values it at nothing: a graded release short of union counts as no gain. 1667 and 1676 do the same for yoga.

title: அகப்பேய்ச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The second quarter of Agappei Siddhar's songs widens the negation from the paths to the practices and the practitioner: yoga does not free, however long it is held; sastras and sutras are mere imagining; wandering to the sky brings rebirth; and the deeds one has done do not leave. Against this the stanzas set one instruction, repeated as a refrain within the refrain, சும்மா இரு, just be still, and a few bare statements: the Lord is bliss, Saivam is what stands by itself, where desire has ended there is right conduct, and the Lord is like fire and like the pillar, neither male nor female. Sun and moon, nectar and poison, and the letters அ and உ as anava and its bent companion show the poet still speaking the Siddhars' cipher while telling the demon to stop.
structure_note: 1667 to 1669 deny yoga and define the Lord as bliss; 1670 to 1674 are a dialogue in which the demon claims to have seen and is told that seeing by another's word is desire, that karma stays, and that sastras are imagining; 1675 to 1678 ask about karma, yoga and shame; 1679 gives the instruction to be still, which 1686 and 1690 repeat; 1680 to 1683 are reproaches and the definition of Saivam; 1684 to 1689 return to the cipher (letters, nothingness, sun and moon, the fire that is neither male nor female); 1690 and 1691 close against study and against forest tapas.
source_issues: 1670: the stanza appears to be spoken by the demon (last line சொன்னாயே, second person), not by the poet; the printed text gives no speaker marks.
1679 and 1686 line 2 and 4 சுட்டது can be from சுட்டு (point out) or சுடு (burn); the spelling does not decide it.

reading: Yoga will not do, demon; when you have seen what is, knowledge is the body itself, and I have told you not to go seeking.
nuance: தேக ஞானம் may mean knowledge of the body, knowledge that the body is (the body as cosmos), or knowledge while embodied. The denial of yoga continues the ladder begun in 1666 and is pressed again in 1676.

reading: It is a five-headed serpent, demon, and the gain from it is small; our Lord, you have seen, is the one who cures this poison.
nuance: The five-headed serpent is read by tradition either as the five senses, whose poison is desire, or as the coiled power with its five faces; ஆதாயம் கொஞ்சம் (little profit) fits the senses better. The Lord as antidote (விடந்தீர்க்கும்) recalls the Siva who drank poison, and 1642's warning against poison.

reading: All that is called 'Lord', demon, of what kind is it? Hear me tell you: it is bliss.
nuance: The poet's one positive definition of the Lord in the work: not a form, a letter or a place, but ஆனந்தம். It answers 1660, which said what the Lord is not.

reading: 'I have found it, I have opened my love, I have taken it in,' says the demon; 'you have told me what is.'
nuance: The stanza reads as the demon's reply, since the refrain address sits inside what sounds like a claim of attainment and the last line is in the second person (சொன்னாயே, you told). 1671 to 1673 are the poet's answer, denying that a told truth is one's own.

reading: Even when what is has been told, demon, you must see it by yourself; the deceit will not end, and for those who merely saw it is desire.
nuance: A rebuke to second-hand knowledge: hearing the truth leaves கள்ளம் (deceit, the hidden self-regard) intact, and even seeing without becoming is a form of காமம், wanting. The point is pressed on the poet's own words too.

reading: Even those who stand knowing, demon, do not fear, I tell you; the strong deeds you have done will not leave you.
nuance: அஞ்சார்கள் can be praise (the knowers are fearless) or blame (they do not fear karma as they should); the second line, that one's done deeds do not depart, suits the warning. The stanza admits what little else in the work does, that karma is not dissolved by knowing.

reading: It is the Lord's bond, demon; all that you have seen in this way is bond practised; you have seen the Supreme.
nuance: ஈசன் பாசம் may mean the bond that the Lord lays (the Siddhanta view that pasam is his instrument) or bondage to the Lord as one more attachment. பாசம் பயின்றது, bond practised or habituated, treats all seeing as bondage, and the last line either exempts the Supreme or ironically includes it.

reading: Sastras and sutras, demon, and all that is imagining: they must not be looked at; you have seen their fruit, the void.
nuance: சங்கற்பம் is the mind's resolve or construction; scripture and aphorism are placed under it. பாழ் பலம் is barren fruit, and 1692 and 1708 give பாழ் a second, positive sense as the emptiness beside the Supreme.

reading: Have you seen the way, demon, for that karma to end? To clear and grow clear, bathe in the holy water too.
nuance: The stanza can be read straight, as a rare endorsement of bathing at a tirtha, or as irony against those who think a bath clears karma, in line with the work's rejection of rites. The inner tirtha of the yogis is a third reading; the stanza does not decide.

reading: However long you hold to yoga, demon, what of it? Will you become one who is freed, and will there be release?
nuance: The two questions expect the answer no; முத்தன் (the freed one) and மோட்சம் are both denied to yoga held for any length of time. This is the sharpest of the stanzas against yoga, and sits oddly with the breath lore in 1688 and 1702.

reading: Do not seek your own destruction, demon, I tell you; even when the bond has gone, the souls do not go.
nuance: பசுக்கள் (souls, in the Siddhanta sense of pasu) remain even when paasam is removed: the stanza may be stating the doctrine that the soul is eternal and is not destroyed in release, or warning that the self (the demon) persists after its bonds loosen. நாசம் ஆவதற்கே நாடாதே forbids seeking annihilation.

reading: What is shame for, demon, once good deeds have ended? If you want to see it, it cannot be seen.
nuance: நல்வினை தீர்ந்தக்கால் may mean the exhaustion of good karma along with bad, after which shame has no object; or that when one has stopped doing even good works there is nothing to be ashamed of. The last line denies that the real can be an object of seeing.

reading: Just be still, demon; I have told you the formula. The place where you stayed still is what was pointed to.
nuance: சும்மா இரு (simply be, do nothing) is the work's one positive instruction, called a சூத்திரம் in mockery of the sutras rejected in 1674. சுட்டது is from சுட்டு (to point out) or சுடு (to burn); the stillness is either the thing indicated or the thing that burns away the rest. 1686 and 1690 repeat it.

reading: Without seeing yourself, demon, you entered into flesh; without seeing me, you came to this place.
nuance: Who speaks as 'me' is unclear: the self addressing the mind, the guru, or the Lord. On any reading, embodiment is traced to a failure of seeing, and the mind's arrival in the body is a mistake it can undo by seeing.

reading: Even if you run to the sky, demon, you will come back and be born; without eating the honey you have roamed the streets.
nuance: The sky-run is the yogi's ascent (to the crown, or to the heavens); the stanza says even that returns to birth. தேன் (honey) is the nectar within, which the Siddhars say is nearer than any journey; the street-roaming is the seeker's wandering, condemned again in 1698.

reading: Saivam, demon, is what stands as itself; if there is no Saivam, trouble comes, you have seen.
nuance: தானாய் நின்றது, standing as itself, defines Saivam as a state rather than a sect; 1695 and 1696 define it as the place where self has gone and as self-knowledge. சலம் is agitation or the flux that comes without it.

reading: Where desire has ended, demon, you have seen right conduct; wherever you go, there is the Lord's bond.
nuance: ஆசாரம், the rules of conduct that the poet otherwise disdains, is redefined as desirelessness itself. The second line repeats 1673 and can be read as a consolation (the Lord's hold is everywhere) or a warning (bondage follows wherever one goes).

reading: Anava is the root, demon, and it came as the letter அ; the crooked letter உ was born along with it.
nuance: A second reading of Om's letters after 1655 and 1656: there அ was the first arising and ம was maya; here அ is ஆணவம், the root impurity of self-regard, and கோணும் உகாரம் (the bent உ) its companion. The two schemes are not reconciled; tradition reads them as keys to different levels.

reading: There is nothing at all, demon; it has come to be just as it is; there is no good, no evil, and no shame.
nuance: ஒன்றும் இல்லை and உள்ளபடி ஆச்சு sit side by side: nothing is, and what is is as it is. The denial of good and evil is the stance of the one beyond the pairs, as 1709 and 1711 extend it to caste, self and Lord.

reading: The place where you stayed still, demon, is what was pointed to, I have told you; I do not know what maya this is, and I do not see even myself.
nuance: The repetition of 1679's second half is followed by a confession: the poet does not know what the appearance is and cannot see himself. Not seeing oneself (என்னையும் காணேன்) may be failure or the goal, since 1711 denies the self altogether.

reading: What are the arts for, demon? Will not those who see laugh? What are the stages for? Who are you? Tell me.
nuance: கலைகள் are the sastras or arts and நிலைகள் the graded states of practice; both are mocked. நீயார் (who are you) is the one question the work keeps asking the demon, and 1665 promised the way to answer it.

reading: The moon is nectar, demon, and the sun is poison; the moon is white and the sun is red.
nuance: In the Siddhars' cipher the moon and sun are the left and right breaths, or the crown and the lower fire; the moon's nectar and the sun's poison (that dries the nectar) are Tirumanthiram doctrine. The colours match the two mandalas. The stanza states the cipher without applying it, and 1702 then says that even riding the breath does not bring the Lord.

reading: Not male and not female, demon: you have seen the fire; the pillar is likewise, and so is the sadguru, you have seen.
nuance: அக்கினி (fire) and தாணு (the pillar, Siva as sthanu, the fixed one) are given as images of what has no sex; the guru is placed with them. Fire as the Lord's likeness recalls the linga of flame; the stanza says nothing of Siva's male and female halves.

reading: Whatever you study, demon, it will not be our word; you have heard what was said: just be still.
nuance: எம்முரை (our word) sets the guru's spoken teaching against books. The instruction of 1679 returns as the conclusion of all the saying: the demon has heard, and the rest is stillness.

reading: Forest and hill, demon: what if one does hard tapas there? Will release be laid open? Is it not the truth that is needed?
nuance: The stanza puts the standard Siddhar case against ascetic retreat: place and severity do not open வீடு; மெய் (truth, or the real) does. 1697 and 1720 continue it against renunciants and beggars.

title: அகப்பேய்ச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The third quarter of Agappei Siddhar's songs is the work's most radical stretch. Beside the Supreme stands the void; Saivam is the place where self has ceased, and belongs only to those who know themselves; the four Vedas end at the guru's feet and do not see the Lord; there is no root, no three categories, no caste for one who stands as himself, and at the end no self, no Lord and no sadguru either, no mantra, no tantra, and religion itself destroyed. Puja is a ghost and even the Lord is maya; what remains cannot be spoken, and the stanzas say so by saying 'no, no' and naming solitude and the realm beyond speech.
structure_note: 1692 to 1696 set the void beside the Supreme and define Saivam through the guru's raised foot and self-knowledge; 1697 to 1699 counsel the renunciant's stillness and non-seeking; 1700 to 1704 test what is real (silver and copper, awareness as bond, the breath that does not deliver, the far that is no distance, the unmade); 1705 to 1709 deny the Vedas, the root, the eighty-one words and caste; 1710 to 1716 are the great negation, from the hollowed fruit through 'no self, no Lord, no guru' to the realm beyond speech.
source_issues: 1704 line 4 கற்வனை is a misprint for கற்பனை.
1700 line 3 உண்டோ டி and 1731 line 2 மெய்கண்டோ ம் have a space inserted inside a word.
1715: the GLOSSES entry (வாசாம கோசரம் - வாக்குக்கு எட்டாதது) belongs to 1716, which has the word.
1696 onward: the refrain is printed அகப்பேய்! with an exclamation mark, where 1642 to 1695 print it without; the change is editorial, not textual.
1712 line 2 வாதனை is probably வாசனை (impression); the printed form is ambiguous.

reading: Even if you go to the Supreme, demon, you will return to the earth; the place next to the Supreme, you have seen, is the void.
nuance: பரம் (the Supreme, or the highest heaven) is not the end: one comes back from it, as from the sky in 1681. பாழ், the void beside the Supreme, is here the Siddhars' positive emptiness, the place past all forms, while in 1674 it was barren fruit.

reading: What are the five faces, demon, when the five are laid down like cotton? The raised foot of the dance is the guru's foot, you have seen.
nuance: பஞ்ச முகம் is Sadasiva's five faces; பஞ்சு படுத்தாலே puns on பஞ்சு (cotton) and பஞ்ச (five): when the five (elements, senses, faces) are flattened or made soft as cotton, the five faces are nothing. குஞ்சித பாதம் is the dancer's lifted foot at Chidambaram, which the stanza equates with the guru's foot.

reading: There is no stain, demon, in the place where the foot stood; see all that came in the Ganga and become clear.
nuance: கங்கையில் வந்ததெல்லாம் may refer to what the Ganga carries (everything washed down, which the Lord's foot is beyond), or to the Ganga in Siva's hair, so that the foot's place is beyond even his own attributes. The stanza follows 1693's raised foot.

reading: The place where self has ceased, demon, is Saivam, you have seen; for those who stand with flesh ceased there is no defect.
nuance: தான் அற (self gone) defines Saivam as a state of selflessness; ஊன் அற may mean the body-sense gone, or flesh renounced as food. The parallel of தான் and ஊன் suggests the first: self and body both set aside.

reading: Whose is Saivam, demon? It is for those who know themselves; the place where Saivam comes to be is the sadguru's feet.
nuance: The third definition of Saivam (after 1682 and 1695): self-knowledge, located at the guru's feet. The question ஆருக்கு denies that Saivam belongs to a sect or birth, which 1709 makes explicit.

reading: If birth is to end, demon, make no distinctions; those who have renounced stay still.
nuance: பேதகம் பண்ணாதே forbids making differences, of sect, caste or doctrine; the true renunciant is marked not by garb or austerity but by சும்மா இருப்பார்கள், the stillness of 1679.

reading: Whoever wanders, demon, do not you wander; even if the town wanders, seek nothing.
nuance: அலைதல் (wandering, restlessness) is the demon's native motion; the stanza sets the mind's stillness against the crowd's. ஒன்றையும் நாடாதே, seek nothing, is repeated in 1699 and matches 1665's 'join with nothing'.

reading: A river of honey flows, demon, for those who have seen the holy feet; there is no river of flesh; seek nothing.
nuance: தேனாறு is the nectar-stream of the yogis, here given to those who see the feet rather than to those who work the breath. ஊனாறு (river of flesh) may be the body's fluids or the stream of births in flesh; either way the feet replace it.

reading: Can white become black, demon? Can silver become copper? Is there what is? On your oath, you have seen.
nuance: The questions may deny alchemy's reverse (the real does not change into the base) or deny change in general: what is, is, and does not become its opposite. உள்ளது உண்டோ (is there what is) may ask whether anything at all exists, in the spirit of 1685. உன் ஆணை, 'on your oath', becomes a seal in 1722 and 1725.

reading: Awareness abides within, demon, and there is no support; awareness is bond, and grace is what you have seen.
nuance: ஆதாரம் இல்லை denies either any support for awareness (it rests on nothing) or the six adharas of the yogic body. அறிவு பாசம், awareness is bond, sets even knowing on the side of bondage, with அருள் (grace) as the only thing that is not; the stanza compresses more than it explains.

reading: You have mounted the breath, demon; will you not seek the thing of the sky? Even mounting the breath, I tell you, it will not come.
nuance: வாசியில் ஏறுதல், riding the breath (or the horse, in the cipher), is the Siddhars' breath practice. The stanza grants that the demon has done it and denies that it brings வான்பொருள், the thing of the sky; the breath lore of 1688 is thereby set aside as a means.

reading: It is farther than far, demon, and there is no distance at all; look without looking, if the barren karma is to end.
nuance: The paradox of distance (தூராதி தூரம் and தூரமும் இல்லை) is the standard way of saying the Lord is both beyond and within. பாராமற் பார் (look without looking) is the seeing of 1678, which cannot be done by wanting to see.

reading: It is not something made, demon; I have told you what is; will those who saw it tell? Imagination has ceased.
nuance: உண்டாக்கிக் கொண்டதல்ல declares the real uncreated, the Siddhars' அனாதி. Those who have seen do not speak of it, and கற்பனை (printed கற்வனை), the constructing mind, has stopped; 1714 and 1716 say the same of speech.

reading: The four Vedas do not see him, demon; who then will see the Lord? At the end of the four Vedas is the good guru's foot.
nuance: The Vedas are not denied but ended: their முடிவு is the guru's foot, the Vedanta made personal. The question 'who will see' expects that no one does by scripture, as 1725 says no one has seen at all.

reading: There is no root, demon, and no three categories; if there were a root, there would be release too.
nuance: முப்பொருள் are the three categories of Siddhanta, Pati, pasu and pasam; the stanza denies them together with the மூலம் that 1646 and 1656 had posited. The conditional cuts both ways: release is denied along with its ground, as in 1723.

reading: It is Indra's net, demon, the eighty-one words; the mantra is just the same; do not open your mouth.
nuance: இந்திரசாலம் is the conjuror's illusion. எண்பத்தொரு பதம், the eighty-one words, is the pada-adhva of the Agamic scheme, which the Tirumanthiram counts among the paths; here it and mantra alike are sleight of hand, and the answer is silence.

reading: If you would become the void, demon, do not believe what you have seen; I have told you without your asking, and there is no hearing either.
nuance: பாழாக வேணும், to become the void, is here a goal, confirming 1692's positive sense of பாழ். The stanza denies seeing and then hearing as means, and admits that the teaching itself was unasked (கேளாமற் சொன்னேன்).

reading: There is no caste distinction, demon, for those who stand as themselves; even for one who has recited and understood, there is nothing at all.
nuance: Caste is denied to the one who stands தானாகி, as oneself, not argued away on social grounds as Sivavakkiyar does. The second line removes learning and understanding (ஓதி உணர்ந்தாலும்) from the same person: nothing is gained or held.

reading: The sky all around, demon, and all around in the grove of trees; the fruit the elephant ate is the truth, you have seen.
nuance: வேழம் உண்ட கனி is the proverbial wood-apple hollowed by the வேழம் (the gloss reads it as a disease of the fruit, tradition as the elephant): whole outside, empty within. The stanza may say that the world ringed by sky is such a fruit, or that the truth itself is the hollow, the emptiness inside appearances; both readings suit the chapter.

reading: There is no self, demon, and there is no Lord; there is no self, and there is no sadguru.
nuance: The guru, who in 1696 and 1705 was the end of Saivam and of the Vedas, is denied along with self and Lord. The repetition of தானும் இல்லை in lines 1 and 3 makes the denial of self the ground for the others.

reading: There is no mantra, demon, and no impression; there is no tantra, and religion has been destroyed.
nuance: வாதனை is most likely வாசனை (the latent impression, karmic residue), or else torment; some read it as வாதம், alchemy. சமயம் அழிந்தது destroys the religions of 1663 outright, where 1663 only asked where the demon stands.

reading: Puja is a ghost, demon, and knowledge is crookedness; the Lord is maya, and everything is like this.
nuance: பசாசம் (ghost) for puja is deliberate blasphemy; போதம் (knowledge, awareness) as கோட்டம் (bend, crookedness) and ஈசன் as maya extend the negation to the Lord himself. On the chapter's logic this is not atheism but the clearing of every object, the Lord-as-object included.

reading: It must not be said, demon; even if said, it is a fault; no, no: you have seen solitude.
nuance: தோடம் is தோஷம், a fault; speaking of the real is one. இல்லை இல்லை, 'no, no', is the stanza's only content, and ஏகாந்தம் (solitude, aloneness) names the state left when speech stops.

reading: The god of the tattvas, demon, is Sadasiva; all the other gods are forms of maya.
nuance: A momentary return to doctrine: Sadasiva is the deity at the head of the tattvas in Siddhanta, and lesser gods are maya's forms. After 1713 made even the Lord maya, this ranks the gods rather than denying them, so the two stanzas sit in some tension. The gloss printed here (வாசாமகோசரம்) belongs to 1716.

reading: It is not a word, demon; it is in the realm beyond speech; it is not something that fits, and it did not come with me.
nuance: வாசாமகோசரம் is the Sanskrit phrase for what speech cannot reach, as the gloss says. என்னுடன் வந்ததல்ல, 'it did not come with me', denies that the real is the poet's possession or his teaching; it is not carried by anyone.

title: அகப்பேய்ச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The last fifteen stanzas of Agappei Siddhar close the work on the inner demon with a string of prohibitions: no sastra, no study or doing, no begging, no adornment, no sophistry, no agitation, no wanting even of moksha or initiation, no eating of the five, no joining in samadhi, no seeking in nadanta, no reciting the Veda, no claiming to have seen the truth, no trusting even the feet. Between them stand the few affirmations the poet allows: one must know oneself and join without joining, and everything else known is a ghoul's knowledge; where desire has ended, there is the Lord; the real is like salt in water; what appears is void, appearing without appearing in the pure space; and the world is mere coming and going, which, called true, yields release.
structure_note: 1717 to 1719 move from sastra and study to the one requirement, self-knowledge; 1720 to 1722 deal with the renunciant's outward signs (begging, adornment, show) and give the salt-in-water figure; 1723 to 1725 describe those who want nothing and deny that anyone has seen; 1726 to 1729 dismiss the yogic goals (samadhi, nadanta, union) and name the void and the pure space; 1730 and 1731 close with the coming and going of the world and a last set of prohibitions.
source_issues: 1726 line 1 அஞ்சயும் is a misprint for அஞ்சையும்.
1731 line 2 மெய்கண்டோ ம் has a space inserted inside the word.
1727 line 3 சூதானம் is obscure; the gloss (சாக்கிரதை, alertness) is a guess at a word that may be corrupt.

reading: There is no sastra, demon; it has gone beyond motion; it must not be looked at, and it does not reach imagination.
nuance: சலனம் கடந்தது, past all movement, is a description of the real; the sastras, which are movement of thought, do not touch it. பாவனை (imagining, visualising) is denied as a means here and in 1731.

reading: What if you study, demon, and what if you do anything? All the ways that were told, you have seen, are what was pointed to (or, were burnt).
nuance: The stanza dismisses study and action together. சுட்டது, as in 1679, is either 'pointed out' (the told ways are only pointers) or 'burnt' (they are consumed); the first reading makes the ways signs, the second makes them refuse.

reading: You must know yourself, demon; you must join without joining; everything known after that is a ghoul's knowledge.
nuance: The work's positive teaching in one stanza: self-knowledge, and union that is not attachment (சாராமற் சார). பேயறிவு (a ghoul's knowledge, with a pun on the demon addressed) is the Tirumanthiram's phrase for knowing that leaves out the self.

reading: Even if you take to begging, demon, birth will not end; where desire has ceased, you have seen our Lord.
