nuance: பிச்சை, the mendicant's bowl, is set aside as 1691 set aside forest tapas: outward renunciation does not end birth. இச்சை அற்றவிடம் repeats 1683's desireless place, now with the Lord in it.

reading: No adornment, demon, and no sophistry; no trickery, and no agitation.
nuance: கோலம் (adornment, the ascetic's painted guise), குதர்க்கம் (perverse argument), சாலம் (deceit) and சஞ்சலம் (restlessness) are four faults in two lines, the outer show and the inner unrest of the false renunciant.

reading: It is no pretence, demon, on your oath I have told you; like salt with water, inquire and remain.
nuance: அப்புடன் உப்பு, salt in water, is a classic image of the real pervading the world without being seen apart from it; the stanza asks the demon to inquire and then stay (இருப்பாயே) in that dissolved state, the stillness of 1679 given a figure.

reading: They want no moksha, demon, and want no release; they want no initiation, those who have become pure consciousness.
nuance: சின்மயம் is the state of being knowledge itself, as the gloss says. The stanza denies to such people even the wish for release and for தீட்சை (the guru's initiation), completing 1665's 'join with nothing' and 1706's denial of release's ground.

reading: The child is a ghost, demon; if you look, he is a madman; he is not the three times, and he is not an effect.
nuance: பாலன் may be the Lord as the child (Murugan, or the infant Siva of the Siddhars' cipher), who seems a ghost or madman to ordinary sight, or the jnani whom the world calls mad, as Sivavakkiyar says of the siddhar. காலம் மூன்றுமல்ல and காரியம் அல்ல deny time and causation to him, so the Lord reading fits the second half.

reading: What was seen is not, demon; if there were any who had seen, would they want what they had taken in? On your oath I have told you.
nuance: The syntax is compressed: either no one has seen, since what is seen is not the real, or those who truly saw would no longer want (உண்டது வேண்டடியோ, would they want what was eaten?). Both readings deny that seeing and wanting can go together, as 1671 did.

reading: Do not eat the five, demon, and do not want desire; let go of the heart too, and do not join in samadhi.
nuance: அஞ்சு (the five) is the five senses' objects, or perhaps the five grains; 'eating' them is indulgence. நிட்டை, the yogic absorption the gloss calls Siva-yoga, is forbidden along with desire: even the yogi's goal is a joining, and the poet has said to join with nothing.

reading: Do not seek in the truth of nadanta either, demon, I tell you; the alertness above it, do not believe to be true.
nuance: நாதாந்தம், the end of nada, is one of the six ends (ஆறந்தம்) where the Tirumanthiram places high attainment; the stanza says not to seek even there. சூதானம் (glossed as alertness or caution) is obscure; the watchfulness of the yogi above nadanta seems meant, and it too is denied.

reading: If one joins with another, demon, the one will perish, see; even the Parasiva that stands will not stand.
nuance: ஒன்றோடு ஒன்று கூடில் may describe union with the Lord as the loss of the one who joins, so that even the standing Parasiva 'does not stand' as a separate object; or it may warn that any joining, any dualism of two things, destroys. On the first reading the stanza describes sayujya from the far side.

reading: All the deeds that appear, demon, you have seen to be void; they appear without appearing, in the pure space.
nuance: சூனியம், the void, is used of the appearing deeds (or appearances, தோன்றும் வினைகள்); சுத்த வெளி, the pure space, is where they appear without appearing. The stanza gives the work's ontology in one breath: what shows is empty, and the ground is open space, the Siddhars' பாழ்.

reading: Do not say it is false, demon; it is only coming and going; when you call it true, release may be had.
nuance: A correction to 1729: the world is not to be dismissed as பொய் but seen as போக்குவரத்து, traffic, mere passage. Calling that true, that is, seeing impermanence as the truth of appearances, is itself release; the stanza refuses both the realist and the illusionist poles.

reading: Do not recite the Veda, demon; do not say 'we have seen the truth'; do not trust the feet; do not look by imagining.
nuance: The last stanza turns the prohibitions on the poet's own supports: the guru's feet, named as the end in 1661, 1696 and 1705, are not to be trusted either, and the claim to have seen the truth (மெய்கண்டோம், the name of the Siddhanta's founding teacher) is forbidden. The work ends in the silence it began by asking for.

title: இடைக்காட்டுச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The opening of Idaikkadar's songs, cast as the talk of two cowherds. Thandavaraya Konar tells his fellow herdsman that worlds come from Siva's word, that the Brahman shining like the sky must be known as the void, that release needs worship, tapas and love held night and day; Narayana Konar answers that taming the mind, killing anger and killing desire are only steps, that attachment must be cut while a little desire for Brahman is kept, that the unheard Veda is heard when the guru speaks, and that cattle, gold and kin do not stay.
structure_note: 1732 is the invocation (காப்பு). 1733 to 1742 are Thandavaraya Konar's kannis, each closing on the refrain கோனாரே (herdsman) and most framed as a condition, 'unless you do this, that will not come'. 1743 and 1744 are two kochchakam verses in which Narayana Konar speaks in the first person; 1745 to 1754 are his couplets to தாண்டவக்கோனே, which is at once the other cowherd's name and 'the dancer-king', so each line is also addressed to Siva; 1755 and 1756 are a kattalaikkalithurai and a venba that close the section. The herding setting shows in the images: driving sheep at the hour of thought (1741), the mind as a bull, anger as a snake, desire as a cow (1745 to 1747).
source_issues: 1740 line 3 prints நாறி where the sense and the gloss require நாரி (woman): நாரி இடப்பாகன், the Lord with the woman on his left.
1756 line 4 prints ஓதுபிர மரத்துஉற்றக் கால்; the sense requires பிரமத்து (Brahman), and the extra letter looks like a print error or a word broken for the metre.

reading: Let us hold with love in the mind the Primal One, who has neither beginning nor end, so that evil-bringing birth is struck down like cotton touched by fire, with the three faculties brought into one accord.
nuance: முப்பொறி, the three faculties, are named in 1781 as mind, speech and body. The syntax of lines 2 and 3 is compressed: birth is what burns like cotton, and the three faculties are what must agree for the thought to be made; the verse is a vow, not a petition.

reading: All worlds, all lives and all things come to be by the word of the mighty one beyond count, the primal supreme Siva.
nuance: Creation is by சொல், the word, not by act or by maya; the verse makes Siva's utterance the sole cause, as 1800 makes his thought (எண்ணப்படி) the plan.

reading: Unless you know and praise the Brahman that shines like the sky as the void, there is no way for the soul housed in flesh; consider this, herdsman.
nuance: சூனியம் here is not nothingness but the name under which Brahman is to be known: what has no form or mark, like the sky it is compared to. The verse makes this knowing a condition of the soul's passage (கதி), so the void is a positive object of praise, not a denial.

reading: Unless you worship the Form that is the seed of release and do the firm acts that lead to release, siddhi, bhakti, sakti and mukti will not come together.
nuance: The four rhyming attainments are listed as one bundle that arrives together or not at all; siddhi (power) and bhakti are not ranked against release. முத்திக்கு உறுதிகள், the firm acts for release, are left unspecified; the surrounding verses supply tapas, thought and love.

reading: Unless, with the bond of the old round of births cut away, you shake off sloth and do tapas, reckon that you have no strength to reach the limitless God.
nuance: The order is notable: the bond (தொந்தம்) of birth is to be cut 'entirely' (அறவே) before tapas, and tapas then gives the strength (பலம்) to reach God; sloth, சோம்பல், is named as the one obstacle.

reading: Think fully, with love and with good nature, on the root of the Vedas, the form of supreme bliss, and rest in the awakening of true knowledge.
nuance: ஆரண மூலம், the root of the Vedas, is the Lord as the source of scripture rather than scripture itself; the verse pairs love (அன்பு) and character (பண்பு) as the manner of thinking, and knowledge (மெய்ஞ்ஞானப் போதம்) as its end.

reading: To see in the inner gaze the light that passes beyond time and all its ages, the wonder beyond imagining, the subtle thing the great ones of the books have spoken: that is the task, herdsman.
nuance: The verse does not reject books: the subtle thing is what the learned great ones said, but it is to be caught in the gaze (நோக்கம்), not in their words. காலாகாலம் may be 'time and the timeless' or 'time and death-time'; either way the light stands past it.

reading: If, without putting into words the ineffable one who is both with form and without form, you keep him within night and day, will Death come near you?
nuance: சகளம் and நிட்களம் are the Agamic pair, the Lord with form and the Lord formless; the verse names him as both at once (ஆனதை). The instruction is to hold him 'without saying by saying' (சொல்லினாற் சொல்லாமல்), an inward holding past speech, and the reward is that Antaka, Death, cannot approach.

reading: As pure dew dies when struck by the sun's blade, fierce deeds are ground to dust when one praises in the heart the feet of the Lord who has the woman on his left side, and one reaches the good abode.
nuance: நாரி இடப்பாகன் is Ardhanarisvara, the Lord whose left half is the goddess; the printed text has நாறி. The verse makes praise of the feet, not knowledge or yoga, the solvent of karma.

reading: To remove the three impurities, keep in thought, even at the hour when you drive the sheep, the triple void that lies beyond the reach of the three faculties.
nuance: The sense turns on முப்பாழ். An editor's gloss takes it as the three mayas (bindu, mohini and maan, the pure, mixed and impure maya); in Tirumular the three voids are the states past speech where the soul comes to rest, and 1734 has just named Brahman as the void. On either reading the verse asks the herdsman to hold a nothing in mind while at work, so that the three malas fall away. செம்மறி ஓட்டிய வேலை, the time of driving the sheep, is the cowherd's working day.

reading: So that agitation in its five kinds flies away, hold with love in the heart that which stands free of all attachment, and cherish it night and day.
nuance: The fivefold agitation (பஞ்ச விதமாய்ச் சஞ்சலம்) is most naturally the unrest that comes through the five senses. The remedy is a reversal of attachment: hold (பற்றி) the one who is without holding (பற்றற்று), a turn the Kural also makes.

reading: Narayana Konar vows to live keeping always and straight in his heart the glorious tender shoot of Siva, the clear nectar and red honey, the heavenly thing that is earth and the other elements, the one that became the five forms, the great light of the sky, the ocean of great bliss.
nuance: The epithets move from the tasted (nectar, honey) to the cosmic (the elements, the five forms) to the inner (light, bliss); the Lord is both the sweetness in things and the things themselves. 'Straight' (நேராக) and 'every day' (எந்நாளும்) make the holding a constant practice.

reading: Narayana Konar says he will attain likeness to the Lord (சாரூபம்) by holding within the pupil of the eye, the wish-tree, the gold, the one whose half is a woman's form, the three things hard to speak of, the sky's nectar, the lamp's light, the hot sun and the cool grace.
nuance: சாரூபம், taking the Lord's own form, is the third of the four graded states of release, so the claim is high but not the highest. முப்பொருள், the three things, is unexplained; tradition would supply pati, pasu and pasam, or the three gods. The list sets the hot sun beside the cool grace as one object, the Lord as both.

reading: Thandavakkona, do not think release has been won merely because the bull called the mind has been brought under.
nuance: The first of three couplets that name a herdsman's victory and deny it is the goal: the tamed bull, the dead snake, the slain cow. The address தாண்டவக்கோனே is the fellow cowherd and also the dancer-king, so the warning is spoken as if before Siva.

reading: Thandavakkona, do not think that everything is accomplished because the snake called anger has died.
nuance: சித்தி here is accomplishment rather than the eight powers; the end of anger is a real death of a real snake, but not the whole.

reading: Thandavakkona, if the cow called desire is slain, you will see and know this whole cosmos.
nuance: Unlike the two before it, this couplet promises rather than warns: desire's death is the decisive one, and its fruit is sight of the whole egg of the world. For a herdsman to kill the cow is the strongest image available; and பசு is also the bound soul, so the line can be heard as the end of the soul's bound state.

reading: Thandavakkona, before it is absorbed into sound, see and know the root Omkara.
nuance: What is to be absorbed (அடங்கும்) is not named: the life-breath at death, the mind in meditation, or the senses in the inner sound are all possible, and the root Om is to be known before that absorption, so that it is known rather than merely undergone. The order, Om before sound, is the reverse of the usual descent from Om into nada.

reading: Thandavakkona, so that the root portion is cut away, pull up the root that has sprouted in the heart.
nuance: மூலப் பகுதி is most likely mula prakriti, the root matter of the tattva scheme from which the inner faculties grow; the verse then asks that the growth in the heart be pulled out by the root so that the root itself is gone. A plainer reading is that the root is desire or the ego, planted in the mind.

reading: Thandavakkona, discern and know that the nature of this pot of a body is in truth that of a jar of filth.
nuance: கடம் is the pot and சால் the jar: the body is a vessel and what it holds is மலம், excrement, here in its plain sense rather than the three impurities. The line is a standard renouncer's image put in the herdsman's mouth.

reading: Thandavakkona, attachment is what belongs to all who have taken birth; do not hold to it but cut it off.
nuance: The first half can be read as 'attachment is the lot of the born' or as 'attachment is the cause of those who are born'; either way it ties பற்று to பிறப்பு, and the remedy is to cut rather than to loosen. The next couplet makes the one exception.

reading: Thandavakkona, a little desire for Brahman you must keep within you, without wavering.
nuance: After the order to cut attachment comes the one desire that is kept, and kept small (சற்றே) and steady (சலியாமல்): the pair reproduces the Kural's turn of clinging to the unclinging one in order to let go of clinging.

reading: Thandavakkona, a roasted seed will not sprout; those without devotion will not reach the goal.
nuance: The roasted seed is usually the image of karma made barren by knowledge, so that it cannot sprout into rebirth; here it is turned on the devotionless, who are the seed that will not grow. The verse makes bhakti the condition of attainment, where 1736 made it tapas.

reading: Thandavakkona, the Veda that the ear has never heard becomes plain when the guru speaks it, does it not?
nuance: The unheard Veda (செவிதனிற் கேளாத மறை) is not the recited text but the secret it stands for; it is revealed in the guru's speech (செப்பில்), an oral transmission set above hearing the books.

reading: Cattle, houses, children and kin, high goods, home, gems, silver, gold and bronze, forests and river banks, stone ornaments, elephants and horses, the many wares one seeks: none stays; join the way of Siva.
nuance: The list begins with cattle (மாடு), the cowherd's own wealth, and ends in the shopkeeper's பண்டம், wares; the one verb is நில்லா, they do not stand. சிவகதி, the Siva-way or Siva-state, is the only thing offered in their place.

reading: Enjoyment goes, experience goes, eating goes, meanness goes, infatuation goes, fierceness goes, ruin goes and thirst goes, when one reaches the Brahman which the Vedas and then the Agamas repeatedly declare the highest.
nuance: The eight things that go (போம்) are mixed: pleasures and even eating stand beside meanness and delusion, so what ends is not vice alone but the whole life of experience. The printed பிரமரத்து is read as பிரமத்து, Brahman; the gloss on போக்கியம் as experience is followed.

title: இடைக்காட்டுச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: Idaikkadar's cowherds continue. Thandavaraya Konar, to a drum refrain, claims the work done: the goat of the inner faculty and the forest of ignorance cut with the sword of tapas, the five sense-goats driven into the space of yoga, both attachments cut, the nectar drunk at the palate, the six centres passed to the Lord above them. Narayana Konar then speaks to his cow, the bound soul, promising release, the flight of karma and the gods' service to one who bows with love at the Lord's feet and clings to the void past pointing; the section to many begins, praising the light in the eye and the sun beyond mind, speech and body.
structure_note: 1757 is the drum refrain (தாந் திமித்திமி) printed once and marked (தாந்) after each of 1758 to 1765, Thandavaraya Konar's first-person stanzas of attainment and one of command (1765). 1766 to 1779 are Narayana Konar's quatrains, each with the call பசுவே (cow), which in Siddhanta also names the bound soul. 1780 and 1781 open the couplets to many (பலரோடு கிளத்தல், kural venchendurai), each ending போற்றீரே, praise, which run on into chapter 93. The herding images (goats for the senses and the inner faculty, the forest as pasture, the cow as soul) carry the teaching.
source_issues: 1757 (idaikkadar:u2) is the refrain of 1758 to 1765 printed as its own unnumbered unit; the stanzas carry only the cue (தாந்).
1760: வீறு heads the list of sense objects where smell would be expected; possibly corrupt.
1769: printed அரிவாயே, read as அறிவாயே.
1765: the gloss on கோசம் (womb) does not fit கோசமைந்தும், which reads more naturally as the five sheaths.

reading: The refrain of the dance: drum-syllables (thaan thimithimi) addressed to the herdsman, who is hailed as the herdsman of bliss, of grace and bliss.
nuance: The unit is the refrain sung after each of 1758 to 1765 (marked (தாந்) there). கோனார், herdsman, is both Thandavaraya Konar and, through தாண்டவம், the dancing Lord; the drum-syllables put the cowherd's song in the rhythm of Siva's dance.

reading: I have seen the thousand and eight circles and what stood within that circle; I have looked at the hundred and eight of the great wide world, and the doubt that clings to a dull mind is gone.
nuance: The numbers carry the sense and are not explained. The thousand and eight circles are most often taken as the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown, and what stands within it as the Lord there; the hundred and eight of the world may be shrines, scriptures or a sacred count. On a plain reading the boast is that inner sight has settled what outward search left in doubt.

reading: With the sword of tapas in its measured rhythm I cut down the goat called the inner faculty and the dense forest called ignorance, and I built a fort to live without dying.
nuance: அந்தக்கரணம், the inner instrument (mind, intellect, will and ego), is made the goat, the cowherd's own beast and the usual animal of sacrifice; the sacrifice is turned inward. The fort for not dying (சாவாது இருந்திட) is the claim of the body made deathless, as tradition takes the Siddhars' kaya siddhi; it can also be read as the soul made safe. சந்தம் may be rhythm or beauty.

reading: The five goats called body, mouth, eye, nose and ear, and the forest of their objects, taste, light, touch and sound, I drove without shooting an arrow, wore them down and set them dancing, within the one space, the space of yoga.
nuance: The senses are the herd and their objects the pasture; the herdsman masters them by driving, not by killing (எய்யாமல், without shooting). வீறு at the head of the objects is odd where smell is wanted and may be corrupt. ஏக வெளி and யோக வெளி, the one space and the yoga space, name where the herd is penned: the inner sky of the Siddhars.

reading: With both attachments cut I came to good nature and friendship; I took in the milk and saw the eye above; I put away petty pleasure and looked to the other pleasure; I joined the supreme of consciousness and reached the supreme of the self.
nuance: பற்றிரண்டு, the two attachments, are traditionally 'I' and 'mine'. The milk (பாலை) and the eye above (மேலையாம் கண்) are coded: tradition takes them as the nectar from the crown and the inner eye of the brow; in plain terms they are the sweetness and sight that come after detachment. சிற்பரம் and தற்பரம் are paired names of the Supreme, as consciousness and as the self's own highest.

reading: Closing the palate within, I drink the nectar; I think then on the station in the sky; holding the word that rules the heavens I do worship; I go to nothing but true knowledge.
nuance: அண்ணாக்கை அடைத்து, closing at the palate, is the yogic seal in which the tongue is turned back to block the passage and the nectar from the crown is drunk, as tradition reads it (Tirumular's khechari). The verbs in -ணேன் are ambiguous: the last line must mean 'I will not approach anything but knowledge', and some take the first three as refusals too, 'I will not drink, think, worship'; the run of claims in 1758 to 1763 favours the affirmative.

reading: I have seen the five elements from earth up; I have broken from all the changes of maya; I have taken into my body the word of the ruler of the sky; I do not want life on earth as the higher thing.
nuance: விண்டேனே may be 'I split off from' or 'I laid bare'; on either sense maya's transformations no longer hold the speaker. The word of the sky's ruler taken into the body (மெய்யினுள்) is the mantra or teaching made inward; மெய் also means truth, so it is held 'in truth' as well.

reading: I have known well the five that begin with speech; I have parted from the five bonds of maya; I have practised the five yogas that are hard to see; I have cherished the vision of the fivefold yoga that is beyond telling.
nuance: வாக்காதி ஐந்து are the five organs of action (speech, hands, feet, excretion, generation) among the tattvas. The five bonds of maya and the five yogas are not named; the fivefolds may answer the Lord's five acts or the five kalas, as tradition sometimes counts them. The stanza is a ledger of fives, more claim than teaching.

reading: Seek the gods of the six supports; search for the Primal One above them; join the bliss of the circle that is his portion; see all five sheaths and climb the hill and dance.
nuance: ஆறாதாரம் are the six centres of the yogic body, each with its presiding god; the Lord is placed above all six. கோசம் ஐந்து is most naturally the five sheaths of the self; an editor glosses கோசம் as the womb instead. The hill (குன்று) is the crown, as tradition takes it, and the dance answers the refrain's drum.

reading: If you think with love on the Primal Lord, cow, will the supreme way of light not become your own?
nuance: Narayana Konar's songs (1766 to 1779) each address பசுவே, 'cow'. In Saiva Siddhanta பசு is also the bound soul, so the herdsman talking to his cow is the teacher talking to the soul; the pun runs through the section. ஆதிபகவன் is the Kural's opening name for God.

reading: If you think on the thing that fills everywhere and bow, cow, you will always reach the supreme way that abides.
If you seek the primal feet day and night, cow, you will see the fullness, the state of release that embraces.
nuance: புல்லும் may be 'that embraces' (புல்லுதல்) or, less likely, 'grass', the cow's fodder; the first fits the sense and the second the herding frame. அல்லும் பகலும் makes the seeking constant.

reading: Truth comes into the power of those who hold to the One alone, cow; in the state where you stand, know what is straight.
nuance: ஒன்றைப் பிடித்தோர், those who have seized one thing, makes single-mindedness the condition of truth. The printed அரிவாயே would mean 'you will cut'; the sense wants அறிவாயே, 'you will know'.

reading: Though you have everything, cow, if the Lord's grace is not there, reckon it as nothing and bow.
nuance: இல்லாத் தன்மை, the nature of what is not, turns possessions into absence when grace is missing; the verse does not reject wealth, it makes grace its only value.

reading: If you look closely, cow, without God's help there is nothing else; the father's holy feet are the life of life.
nuance: ஆவிக்கும் ஆவி, the life of life, puts the Lord's feet inside the soul as its own animating breath; அத்தன் is father.

reading: Is not he who is within Shakti more loving than a mother, cow? He will never leave those who love him.
nuance: The mother image recurs at 1809. சத்திக்குள் ஆனவன் puts the Lord within his power, so the tenderness of the mother is Shakti's and the Lord is inside it.

reading: Praise him, cow, who is the seed of release, who became the root substance, who is kin to Shakti.
If you bow with love at the Lord's holy feet, cow, you will see all your cruel deeds run away.
nuance: The same claim as 1740, that worship of the feet, not knowledge or yoga, scatters karma; the verb விட்டோடும், they leave and run, makes the deeds flee like a frightened herd.

reading: If you bow low at the feet of the moon-crested one, cow, Indra, Mal and the others will do your bidding.
nuance: The reward is a Siddhar boast: the gods become servants of the devotee. Bowing low (தாழ்ந்து) is set against the gods' service, so humility before Siva is what makes one master of the rest.

reading: Praising with the inner sense the twin feet of the Maker that the outer eye cannot see, cow, you will reach the height.
nuance: கட்புலன் and உட்புலன், outer sense and inner sense, are paired again at 1801; worship is moved from the image the eye sees to a sense within.

reading: If you cling close to that which became the void, which cannot be seen even when pointed at, cow, who will equal you?
nuance: சூனியமானவத்தை is read as சூனியமான அத்தை, that which became the void. As at 1734, the void is the object to be clung to (ஒட்டிப் பிடி), not a denial; சுட்டியும் காண ஒண்ணா says it is past all pointing.

reading: Those who do not reach the Lord by their own mind, cow, live in the world like hard trees.
nuance: தானு is Sthanu, a name of Siva, 'the fixed one'; the irony is that those who fail to reach the fixed one become fixed themselves, like trees. தன் மனம் தன்னாலே stresses one's own mind as the means.

reading: If you do not praise the light that is the good meaning called the word, cow, everything will tell you there is no state of release.
nuance: சொல்லெனும் நற்பொருள் may be 'the good meaning that the word carries' or 'the good thing that is the Word itself', the Lord as utterance (1733). The last line is compressed: perhaps every thing declares release absent for such a person, perhaps every scripture says so.

reading: Praise the great light held to be the pupil within the eye, the jewel of the sky, the light of the lamp.
nuance: The section to many (பலரோடு கிளத்தல், 1780 to 1789) changes the address from the cow to everyone, in couplets ending போற்றீரே. The three images go from the body (the eye's pupil) to the cosmos (the sun, the sky's jewel) to the household lamp.

reading: Worship and praise in the heart the sun that the fit faculties of mind, speech and body cannot reach.
nuance: These are the three faculties (முப்பொறி) named in the invocation at 1732. The Lord is past all three, yet is served in the heart (நெஞ்சமதில்), which is not counted among them.

title: இடைக்காட்டுச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: Idaikkadar ends the praise to many with images of what is in things and inseparable from them (taste in milk, honey in fruit, meaning in a book, oil in sesame), then turns on his own stony mind: desire to rule the earth, for women and for gold closes the way, true learning is the learning that ends in silence, and the mind that draws things to itself like a magnet holds nothing that lasts. In the address to petty knowledge he asks his understanding to know the one who made all by thought, who stands everywhere as the inner sense, and to set its own lamp in grace.
structure_note: 1782 to 1789 complete the couplets to many (பலரோடு கிளத்தல்), each ending போற்றீரே. 1790 to 1799 address the heart (நெஞ்சொடு கிளத்தல்), each ending கல்மனமே, stony mind: three desires (land, women, gold) in 1790 to 1793, then learning, restlessness and impermanence, and the questions of kalpa, yoga and silence in 1797 to 1799. 1800 to 1806 open the address to knowledge (அறிவோடு கிளத்தல்), each ending புல்லறிவே, which continues into chapter 94.
source_issues: 1786: printed பலமறவே; the gloss explains பவம் (birth), so the intended reading is probably பவமறவே, 'so that birth ends'.
1777: சூனியமானவத்தை is run together; read as சூனியமான அத்தை.
1792: the first line's syntax (பொறிகடமை மேலிடவொட் டார்க்கு) is loose and may be corrupt.

reading: Praise without wearying, holding it in the heart without deceit, the radiant light that has passed beyond the three times.
nuance: காலம் மூன்று are past, present and future; சாலமின்றி, without trickery, asks for a holding that is not show, and சலிப்பற, without weariness, one that does not flag.

reading: Praise the subtle thing that is like the taste in milk, the honey in fruit and the meaning in a book.
nuance: All three similes are of something inside a thing and not separable from it; the third, meaning in a book, makes the Lord the sense of scripture rather than its letter.

reading: Praise the First of the Three, the three fruits, the sugar, the treasure of the gods, the clear nectar.
nuance: மூவர் முதல் is the head of the three gods (Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra). The sweet things, the three fruits (mango, jack and plantain), sugar and nectar, give the Lord as a taste.

reading: Praise the pure meaning of the Veda, the sea of joy, the good nectar, with love, so as to gain the state that lasts every day.
nuance: நேயமுடன் நாளும் நிலை may be 'the state that endures daily, with love' or 'the state of ruling with love'; the first fits the run of the couplets.

reading: Praise the Supreme called the lone root of the sky, who gave the moving and the unmoving, so that you grasp him and your birth is cut off.
nuance: பராபரம் is the Supreme beyond the supreme. The printed பலமற would be 'so that strength goes', which makes little sense; an editor's gloss explains பவம் (birth), so the intended reading is பவமற, 'so that birth ends'.

reading: Praise with your mind in accord the great thing of the sky that set out the elements beginning with earth, so that you may see it to the full of your eyes.
nuance: கண்ணாரக் காண, to see with eyes full, is the promise of sight in a section that elsewhere says the outer eye cannot see him (1776, 1801); the seeing is a fruit of praise, not of looking.

reading: Leaving the false things, praise daily with longing the true thing that the senses cannot know.
nuance: பொய்ப்பொருள் and மெய்ப்பொருள், false thing and true thing, is the Kural's pair (chapter 36); the desire (விருப்பு) that is forbidden for the false is commanded for the true.

reading: Praise within, coming to awareness, the thing that fills everything as oil fills sesame.
nuance: Oil in sesame is the standard image of pervasion: present in every grain and drawn out only by pressing. உணர்வடைந்து, having reached awareness, makes the praise follow the realising, not precede it.

reading: Stony mind, if you set your desire on ruling all the earth under one umbrella, is there any way for you?
nuance: The address to the heart (நெஞ்சொடு கிளத்தல், 1790 to 1799) calls it கல்மனமே, stony mind, in every line. One umbrella over all the earth is the emperor's mark; the desire itself, not the ruling, is what closes the way (கதி).

reading: If you go about cherishing desire for women, there is no way left to set your desire on heaven, stony mind.
nuance: The second of three desires named in 1790 to 1793: land (rule), women and gold, the stock triad of the Siddhars. விண்ணாசை, desire for the sky, is the one desire that is allowed.

reading: Tell yourself on the good way, stony mind, that for those who do not let the grazing senses get the upper hand, karma wears away.
nuance: மேயும் பொறி, the grazing senses, keeps the herding image of 1760. The syntax of the first line is loose: பொறிகள் தமை மேலிட ஒட்டார்க்கு, 'to those who do not allow the senses to rise above them', is the likely sense.

reading: If you wander the whole earth with a desire for gold, will the vision of desire for the lasting one come to you, stony mind?
nuance: மன்னிச்சை may be 'desire for the permanent' (மன்னுதல், to endure) or 'desire for the King', the Lord; on both readings the one desire is set against the other.

reading: Without learning false learning and falling into confusion about things, desire the true learning of knowledge, stony mind.
nuance: The verse does not reject learning but splits it into பொய்யான கல்வி and மெய்யான ஞானக்கல்வி; பொருள் மயக்கம் may be confusion about meanings or about wealth, and the false learning may be learning pursued for gain.

reading: Setting desire on the great world like a possessed monkey and wandering like dogs and jackals, is there any good in it, stony mind?
nuance: பேய்க்குரங்கு, a monkey with a ghost in it, is the doubled restlessness of the mind; the dogs and jackals add the scavenger's roaming.

reading: You desired many things as a magnet by its nature draws iron; tell me, stony mind, do they last?
nuance: The mind is the magnet and the world's goods the iron; the pull is real and natural (இயற்கை), but what it draws in does not stay. Elsewhere in the corpus the magnet is the Lord drawing the soul.

reading: Is it not by the kalpa state that one crosses the ages of kalpas? See the subtle thing, stony mind, the slight state and the other state.
nuance: கற்பநிலை may be the state reached by the kalpa preparations of the medical Siddhars, said to give a body that outlasts the ages (கற்பகாலம்), or a state of mind as lasting as a kalpa. சொற்ப நிலை, the slight state, and மற்ற நிலை, the other state, are not explained; one reading sets the passing life against the lasting one, and makes the subtle (சூட்சம்) the thing to see in either.

reading: Did I do japa and tapas only to lose the body? And what if one does yoga alone? Consider it, stony mind.
nuance: The verse is two questions and the stance is unclear. On one reading japa and tapas wear the body away while yoga keeps it, so yoga is preferred (the kaya siddhi view); on another, even yoga alone is not enough, and the mind must weigh what each yields.

reading: Is not the fit true learning the learning learned in order to be silent? Work it out, stony mind.
nuance: Learning has silence as its end, not speech or debate; வாகான, fitting or well-formed, marks this as the true kind among the learnings of 1794.

reading: Discern, petty knowledge, the mighty one who created all things by his thought.
nuance: The address to knowledge (அறிவோடு கிளத்தல், 1800 to 1809) calls the poet's own understanding புல்லறிவு, petty knowledge. எண்ணப்படி, according to his thought, pairs with 1733, where worlds come by his word.

reading: Bring to knowledge, petty knowledge, the One that is not seen by the eye even as much as a sesame seed, and stands everywhere as the inner sense.
nuance: உட்புலனாய் நின்ற, standing as the inner sense, makes the Lord not the object of an inner faculty but the faculty itself, as in 1776.

reading: In the hour of waking, sleep comes on quickly; examine and know the soul that shines and flourishes, petty knowledge.
nuance: The first line may be the yogi's waking sleep, the state of rest within waking that tradition counts above the ordinary states, or a plain warning that death, like sleep, falls suddenly on the waking life; on the second reading the verse urges knowing the soul before it is too late.

reading: Know the field that becomes a truth within truth, rises above, becomes the wind, and is a falsehood within falsehood, petty knowledge.
nuance: மெய் is both truth and body, so the first phrase may be 'a body within the body'. கால் is wind, the breath, as a gloss confirms. The verse seems to say that the one reality takes the character of what it dwells in, true in the true and false in the false; the reading is tentative.

reading: Know the scheme of the limb-ghost, a portion of the self, that dances along with you, petty knowledge.
nuance: அவயவப் பேய், the ghost of the limbs, is most likely the body, or the bodily faculties, which move with the self like a possessing spirit. ஆத்துமத்தின் கூறு makes it part of the self, not a stranger; கோள் may be its plotting or its grip.

reading: Your power, which is a good lamp for a dark room, set it in the ford of grace and become a lamp yourself, petty knowledge.
nuance: Knowledge is already a lamp in the dark room of the body; the change asked for is to stand it in grace (அருள்துறை) so that it shines of itself, not to replace it. 1807 continues the lamp image.

reading: Why go by the killing way and shrink, petty knowledge, instead of going on the good way and reaching our station?
nuance: கொல்வழி, the way that kills, may be the way of harm to others or the way that leads to one's own death; நம் பதவி, our station, includes the poet with the knowledge he addresses.

title: இடைக்காட்டுச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: Idaikkadar, the cowherd Siddhar, turns the pillaitamil's addresses to creatures into a yoga teaching: he scolds his own petty knowledge for drowning with the true lamp inside it, tells the dragonfly, the cuckoo and the peacock to proclaim the attainments already won (ignorance gone, egoity shed, the five senses subdued, the void seen), gives the simple swan six similes for how knowledge clears the mind and the soul is made to shine, and begins the flute songs in which release is the end of birth and silence its state. The claims are of a finished man, and the practice behind them is inward: the mind held still, the senses penned, devotion and renunciation set above household life.
structure_note: 1807 to 1809 end the address to knowledge (அறிவோடு கிளத்தல்); 1810 to 1815 are kannis to the dragonfly (தும்பீபற), each line a claim of attainment; 1816 to 1819 address the cuckoo, 1820 to 1822 the peacock, 1823 to 1828 the swan (each a simile with the lesson in the second line); 1829 to 1831 open the flute songs (புல்லாங்குழலூதல்), which continue into chapter 95. The sections follow the stock forms of the pillaitamil and the kummi, with the refrain carrying the form and the stanza carrying the sense.
source_issues: 1810 to 1815 and 1817 print a space inside words ending in -ோம் and -ோர் (கண்டோ ம், விட்டோ ம், அகன்றிட்டோ ம், விட்டோ ர்), a transcription artefact of the ோ sign; the words are read whole.
1822 lines 1 and 3: காற்றூனைப் போல் and பாற்றூடு உருவவே are hard to construe and may be corrupt; the readings follow tradition's guess (wind-body, milk-way).
1823 line 2: மறுவாயைத் தான்கலக்கின் is obscure; no variant is given.

reading: Like a man who carries a hand-lamp and jumps into the sea, why do you sink, petty knowledge, when the true lamp is inside you?
nuance: The hand-lamp is outward learning or ritual light, useless in the sea it is carried into; மெய்விளக்கு, the true lamp, is the inner light. The poet addresses his own understanding as புல்லறிவு throughout this section, so the scolding is self-directed.

reading: When the shining way that is higher than the breath is within you, is the higher goal, if you only think, so hard for you, petty knowledge?
nuance: வாசி is the Siddhars' word for the breath as practice (and for the horse); வாசிக்கு மேலான வாள்கதி, the bright state above the breath, sets the goal beyond even breath-yoga, as tradition takes it. வாள் may be brightness or a sword, and கதி the way or the goal; the plain sense is that what is sought is already inside.

reading: See the Primal One who guards every life with love as a mother does, petty knowledge, and gain release.
nuance: முன்னவன், the one before all, is the poet's name for the Lord here; the mother image makes his care impartial (எவ்வுயிரும், every life), and release follows from seeing him, not from any rite.

reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that ignorance has gone, that we have seen supreme bliss, that true knowledge has come to hand and that we have climbed up above.
nuance: The dragonfly kannis (1810 to 1815) are a list of attainments in the perfect tense, each in the first person plural; the form is boast as teaching. பர மேலேறிக் கொண்டோம் (we have mounted above) can be the ascent of the breath to the crown or simply rising above the world.

reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that the net of affliction is no more, that we have shed the full load of egoity, that old karma has left and that we have seen the supreme light.
nuance: ஆணவங்கள் is the Siddhanta term for the first of the three malas, the soul's self-darkness, though the plural and the plain sense allow 'prides'. The verse pairs the loss of egoity and karma with the sight of the light, as cause and effect.

reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that the five senses have been subdued, that full knowledge alone is the real, that the true things have come to us and that we have seen a divinity.
nuance: அறிவே பொருள் makes knowledge itself the substance that is sought, a Siddhar commonplace; செம்பொருள்கள், the true things, is plural and unexplained, perhaps the truths of the tradition, perhaps the goods gained.

reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that we have left the three desires, that the state of supreme release is itself the attainment, that we have set our desire on God and that we have done away with this world.
nuance: The three desires are the stock triad of land, gold and women. முத்தி நிலை சித்தி turns the Siddhar word for powers toward release: the only siddhi worth the name is mukti. தேவாசை keeps one desire, for God, after the three are gone.

reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that we have looked to the void expanse and lost our hold on maya, that we have reached our dwelling place and joined the state of the full and bounteous one.
nuance: பாழ்வெளி, the void expanse, is Tirumular's பாழ் and the Siddhars' open space, seen as the goal rather than feared as nothing. வள்ளல்நிலை, the state of the giver, is the Lord's state; நிறை (fullness) qualifies it, so the void and the fullness are the same place.

reading: Fly, dragonfly, and say that every thing is a dream, that all the world will perish, that the body is a letter written on water and that only the First is without end.
nuance: அப்பில் எழுத்து, writing on water, is the verse's own image for the body's impermanence; the gloss confirms அப்பு as water. The stanza sets three perishables against one imperishable, ஆதி, and that contrast is the whole argument.

reading: Call out in full joy, cuckoo, that the four inner instruments have been subdued, that the evil six beginning with lust have been contained, and that we have seen the four feet.
nuance: கரணங்கள் நான்கு are mind, intellect, will and ego in Siddhanta reckoning; காமமுதல் ஓராறு the six enemies (lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy). சரணங்கள் ஒருநான்கு is unclear: the Lord's feet, the four paths (சரியை to ஞானம்) or four refuges have all been proposed, and I cannot fix it.

reading: Say, cuckoo, that the world is a thing to retch at, that our Noble One is hard to see, that the many religions are falsehood and that we have gone past the seven births.
nuance: ஒக்காளம் is vomit, the poet's physical word for disgust with the world, repeated at 1843. பலமதம் பொய்மை rejects the sects wholesale, as Tirumular's அறுசமயப் பிணக்கம் does; எழு பவம், the seven births, is the stock count of the cycle.

reading: Say, cuckoo, that those who perform the practices will die and those who have mastered all the tattvas will burn, that a fruit like that of great austerities will not come, and that only the root mantras bring greatness.
nuance: A hard verse: சாதனங்கள், the practices, and தத்துவங்கள், the tattvas, are dismissed in favour of மூல மந்திரங்கள், the root mantras, which tradition takes as the seed syllables and the five letters. வேவார் may be 'will be scorched' or 'will suffer'; மாதவங்கள் போலும் பலன் வாயா (the gloss gives வாயா as 'will not accrue') is read as the fruit of great tapas not coming either. 1855 tells the herdsman to hold fast to the practices, so the dismissal here is of practice without the mantra, on one reading.

reading: Say, cuckoo, that those who know the eight and the two have no trouble, that if the mind stands without straying one reaches the goal; know it by coming close to the play, and sing with the Primal Lord in your thought.
nuance: எட்டிரண்டு is Siddhar cipher: tradition reads the Tamil numerals for eight (௮) and two (௨) as the letters அ and உ, the first two sounds of Om and the sun and moon breaths; the plain sum is ten, or eight twos, sixteen. நட்டணை is glossed as acting or performance, perhaps the Lord's dance, perhaps the world's show; the line is obscure.

reading: Dance, peacock, dance, having seen our Primal One adorned with the serpent; before the cage goes, take the way, and take the path of silence without ever failing.
nuance: ஆதியணி சேடன் is read as the Primal One who wears the serpent (Siva), though அணிசேடன் could be Adisesha himself. கூடு, the cage or nest, is the body; the urgency is that the way must be taken before death, and the way named is மோனநெறி, silence.

reading: Dance, peacock, saying that household life is affliction and that for those without devotion there is neither release nor attainment; see that the good dharma is the dharma of renunciation, and seek the pure open space at the end of sound.
nuance: The verse ranks the two dharmas flatly, இல்லறம் as sorrow and துறவறம் as the good, and adds a second condition, பத்தி, without which no attainment comes. நாதாந்த வெட்டவெளி, the open space beyond nada, is one of Tirumular's six ends (ஆறந்தம்), the place where sound itself ceases.

reading: Show the mind to be like a body of wind, peacock; drive Death far off when he comes; leap so as to pass through the milk-way; and make the mind without the least inward clinging.
nuance: காற்றூனை and பாற்றூடு are both obscure and may be corrupt. Tradition reads காற்று ஊன் as the mind made as light as breath, and பால் ஊடு as passing through the milk, the nectar of the head that the milking songs (1840 to 1845) are about; plainly the lines are a peacock's flight and a leap through a stream. The clear part is the last line, no inner attachment.

reading: If a small frog stirs the water, the reflection of a picture is lost; so, simple swan, if one stirs the other mouth, the understanding is confused.
nuance: The swan verses are each one simile. Still water showing an image is the still mind; the frog is the small disturbance that ruins it. மறுவாய் is unclear: the second opening, the mouth of blemish, or speech itself; மதி is both intellect and the moon, which the tradition places in the head, so the stirred moon is also the lost nectar.

reading: As a tree is broken in the wind, simple swan, so if good knowledge blows, ignorance goes far away.
nuance: தூற்றிவிடில் is to winnow or to scatter, so knowledge acts as the wind, not the tree; the simile makes ignorance something brittle that cannot stand once knowledge moves.

reading: As a bale of cotton is destroyed by fire, simple swan, so by ripe good knowledge sin departs.
nuance: பக்குவ நல் அறிவு, ripened knowledge, is the condition; the fire-and-cotton image makes the destruction total and instant. பாவம் here is the deed's stain rather than karma as a principle.

reading: As a wasp brings a grub to its nest and shapes it into form, simple swan, so bring the rich, hard mind under control.
nuance: The simile rests on the old belief (the பிரமரகீடம் figure) that the wasp turns the grub into a wasp by brooding over it; so the mind is remade by steady attention rather than broken. வளமுடைய வன்மனம் grants the mind both strength and richness before asking that it be mastered.

reading: As salt put into water becomes one with it, in the same measure, simple swan, so stand fittingly united with Brahman.
nuance: அளவு சரியானது, becoming equal in measure, is the point of the simile: the salt does not vanish but is everywhere in the water. The union named is with பிரமம், the Vedantic word, where the rest of the work says சிவம் or பரம்.

reading: As heated iron shows its colour, simple swan, so make the soul shine to its full and grow rich.
nuance: The iron glows by the fire in it, and the soul by the practice (the heat of tapas, on the usual reading) that is applied to it; the glow is the soul's own light made visible, not something added.

reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that for those who have done away with the old round of birth there is no further thing called release.
nuance: The flute songs (1829 to 1839) are addressed to கோன், the herdsman or king, that is the poet himself. முத்திதான் இல்லை can mean that release is nothing other than the ending of birth, so nothing remains to be gained, or, less likely, that such people do not need release; the first reading fits 1831, which places release in silence.

reading: Blow the flute to the end, herdsman, saying that even if one gains the pleasures of Indra, they are trouble.
nuance: இந்திர போகம் is the summit of worldly and heavenly enjoyment, and it is placed under தொல்லை, trouble, the word used of the round of birth in 1829. அந்தமாய் is either 'beautifully' or 'as the final word'.

reading: Blow the flute as a song, herdsman, saying that in the state of silence release comes to be.
nuance: The verse answers 1829: release is not a further thing but a state, மோன நிலை. That silence is to be proclaimed on a flute is the poem's joke and its method, for the flute is the one instrument that sounds without words.

title: இடைக்காட்டுச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The herdsman's work made into yoga. The flute songs end by penning the senses: dogs let loose cannot guard, the demon-mind must subside like a snake before the charmer's pipe, and 'I' and 'mine' must go. The milking songs then draw the nectar that tradition places in the head, above the palate, in the skull's egg, so that the body does not die, burn or stink and Yama is turned back. The herding songs pen the cattle of Saiva Siddhanta one by one, the two deeds, the three egoities, the souls of one, two and three malas, the three bodies, the three karmas, and leave the herdsman to see the great light in the crown and sit in silent nishta.
structure_note: 1832 to 1839 close the flute songs (புல்லாங்குழலூதல்), each stanza a two-line lesson with the refrain ஊதுகுழல் கோனே; 1840 to 1845 are the milking songs (பால் கறத்தல்), four claims per stanza about the milk; 1846 to 1856 open the herding songs (கிடை கட்டுதல்), in which each stanza names a herd of cattle to be penned, usually a numbered set from Siddhanta, and the section runs on into chapter 96. The refrains carry the form; the readings are what each stanza adds.
source_issues: 1832 prints விட்டோ ர் with a space inside the word, the same ோ transcription artefact as in chapter 94.

1841 line 1 and 1842 line 1 lack the dash and the extra syllable (வெறு, மிக) that the other milking stanzas carry before the second refrain, so the metre of these two stanzas is short; no words seem lost.
1851 line 2: என்றும் இல்லை என்றே மரணக்குழல் எடுத்து ஊது is loosely constructed and may have lost a word.

reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that those who have let the senses loose in every direction like dogs are demons.
nuance: பேயர், demons or madmen, is strong: the unrestrained are not merely unwise but not human. The dogs return in 1835 and 1836, where the sense is worked out: an unleashed dog cannot guard.

reading: Blow the flute with a rebuke, herdsman, so that those who run and roam about come to awareness.
nuance: ஓடித் திரிவோர் may be the pilgrims and wanderers the Siddhars mock, or the straying mind of the next stanzas; சாடியே makes the flute's call a scolding. உணர்வு, awareness, is the recovery of attention, not new doctrine.

reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, driving off the tigers that close in on the flocks of goats.
nuance: The plainest herding line in the sequence, and the one most open. Tradition reads the flocks as the souls or the senses and the tigers as desire, disease or death; the verse itself gives only the shepherd's scene, and the Saiva pun on பசு (cow and bound soul) lies behind the whole section rather than in this word.

reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, having tied up the Maricha dogs of dull nature.
nuance: மாரீசம் is the name of the demon who deceived as a golden deer, so the dogs are the senses as deceivers, dull (மட்டி) in nature yet able to mislead; they are to be tied, not killed.

reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that dogs that are never tied are never fit for guarding.
nuance: The argument of 1832 completed: restraint is what makes the senses useful. The claim is not that the senses are evil but that unleashed they cannot do the one thing a dog is for.

reading: Blow the flute close, herdsman, so that the demon-mind subsides like a snake in its box.
nuance: Here the flute is the snake-charmer's pipe, which makes the snake sway and settle back into the basket, so the image is literal for once: the mind is charmed down, not forced. The snake in the box is also the coiled power of Siddhar cipher, and the verse admits that reading too, as the Sivavakkiyam does at 1464.

reading: Blow the flute as the Lord's own, herdsman, so that there is neither 'mine' nor 'I'.
nuance: தனதாக, 'as his own', is read as the flute played as the Lord's and not the player's; the two words that go, எனது and யான், are the Kural's pair at 346. The sense of ownership is dissolved by handing the act itself over.

reading: Blow the flute, herdsman, saying that what is learned is only this: the one place where all has fallen away, and the joining of what has fallen away with what is reached there.
nuance: அற்ற இடம் ஒன்றே, the one place where things have ceased, is read as the void or the stilled mind; அற்றதோடு உற்றதைக் கற்றது is a play on three rhyming participles that I can only paraphrase. The verse sets a learning that is the end of learning against ordinary study.

reading: Milk so as to remain without dying, the milk that is in the head; milk so as to remain without burning; milk within the bare open space.
nuance: The milking songs (1840 to 1845) are cipher: பால், milk, is the nectar that tradition says the yogi draws from the moon in the head (சிரம்) once the breath is raised, and the deathless, unburning body is its fruit. Plainly they are a cowherd's work-song, and the poet keeps that surface throughout. வெட்டவெளி, the open space, is the place of the milking in both readings.

reading: Milk the milk that stays untainted; milk so that old karma ends; milk the milk that is spat from the mouth; milk so as to eat it with an empty belly filled.
nuance: வாயால் உமிழ்ந்திடும் பால், the milk the mouth spits out, is the stanza's riddle; tradition reads it as the nectar that drips from the palate when the tongue is turned back (கேசரி), swallowed rather than spat. வயிறார உண்டிட is the yogi who no longer needs food, and the plain sense is simply a full meal.

reading: Milk the milk that does not go bad; milk so as to live on day after day; milk the milk that flows without ceasing; milk the milk that grows in the skull.
nuance: தலை மண்டை, the skull, names the source directly; the three qualities (not stinking, unceasing, giving long life) are the tradition's claims for the inner nectar against the body's milk, which sours.

reading: Milk the milk by which the world is loathed, the milk that is sheer retching; milk so that it falls into the pot; milk so that the full milk falls within the throat.
nuance: ஒக்காளம், vomit, repeats 1817's disgust; here it is either the milk that makes the world nauseous to the drinker, or a milk that is itself a retching, which would make the stanza about the nectar rising rather than falling. கலசம், the pot, and கண்டம், the throat, place the milk in the body.

reading: Milk without belching; milk so as to turn away Yama when he comes; milk so that the spark of fire goes to rest; milk so as to join supreme Siva.
nuance: ஏப்பம், belching, is the sign of ordinary digestion that the nectar is said to be free of. தீப்பொறி ஓய்ந்திட is unclear: the body's heat, the fire of desire or the kindled fire of the breath, which the tradition says is cooled by the nectar; all three fit a stanza that ends in union with Siva.

reading: Milk the milk that comes above the palate; milk the milk that oozes in the great egg; milk the milk that is not found in heaven; milk so that old torment ends.
nuance: அண்ணாவின் மேல், above the palate, is exactly where khechari places the nectar, and பேரண்டம், the great egg, is the skull as cosmos in the Siddhars' body-as-egg doctrine; the two words make this the stanza where the cipher is nearest to plain. விண்ணாட்டில் இல்லாத sets this nectar above the gods' amrita.

reading: Let the cattle that are the two deeds go, herdsman; pen the one cow that must be subdued, the mind.
nuance: The herding songs (1846 to 1863) make each herd a numbered set of Saiva Siddhanta and the penning its mastery. Here the two deeds, good and bad, are released and only the mind is tied, which inverts the usual order: let karma run out, hold the mind.

reading: The celibate ascetics beyond description reach the Supreme; those who spend every day as austerity come into the subtle presence.
nuance: நைட்டிகர் are the lifelong celibates (naishthika), and தற்பரம், glossed as the Supreme, is the Vedantic word for the goal. சன்னம் is unclear: the subtle, or சந்நிதி, the presence; the stanza drops the herding image for a plain statement of who arrives.

reading: Drive away the three cattle of egoity, herdsman; and daily subdue the cow called the states.
nuance: Siddhanta counts three ahankaras (தைசதம், வைகாரிகம், பூதாதி) by the gunas, and the states (அவத்தை) are waking, dream and the rest; the verse treats both as herds that stray unless worked on daily (நாளும்).

reading: Set apart and tie the cow called the one-mala being, herdsman; and drive off and tie the two malas that dwell in you.
nuance: ஒருமலத்தன் is the soul with one mala, the விஞ்ஞானகலர் of Siddhanta who have only ஆணவம் left; the two malas of the herdsman himself are read as the other two, maya and karma. The pun on பசு (cow, bound soul) carries the stanza: the classes of souls are literally herds.

reading: Twist and tie the cow called the three-mala being, herdsman; then you will know in advance all the truth of the three times.
nuance: மும்மலத்தன் is the சகலர், the soul with all three malas, which is the human state; முக்கால நேர்மை, the truth of past, present and future, is a siddhi claimed as the fruit of penning it. முறுக்கி, twisting, suggests a harder beast than the one-mala cow of 1849.

reading: Bind tight the three groups of senses, herdsman; and take up the flute of death and blow it, saying 'never'.
nuance: இந்திரியத் திரயம் may be the senses of knowing, the organs of action and the inner instruments, or body, speech and mind. மரணக்குழல், the death-flute, blown to say என்றும் இல்லை, is either the flute that announces that death is no more or the flute that drives death off, as in 1844; the construction is loose.

reading: Drive off the three goats called upadhi, herdsman; then all the deceit that is within you will run away.
nuance: The three upadhis are the limiting adjuncts; tradition names the three bodies or the three kinds of affliction (தாபத்திரயம்). கள்ளம், deceit, is the inner falseness that depends on them; it goes by itself once they go.

reading: Tie the cattle of the three bodies first, herdsman; after that there is no deceit, no ruin, and release is there.
nuance: முக்காயம் are the gross, subtle and causal bodies of Vedanta and Siddhanta; முன்னம், first, gives the order of work. The stanza claims release as the direct fruit of penning the three.

reading: Tie the cattle of the karma-mala at the end of the yard, herdsman; and tie the cow of the other karma-triad there too.
nuance: கன்மமலம் is the second mala; the karma-triad is accumulated, ripening and fresh karma (சஞ்சிதம், பிராரத்தம், ஆகாமியம்). கடை is the end or edge of the pen, and perhaps 'last' in order, so karma is penned after the body and the ego.

reading: Hobble the legs of the three causal cows, herdsman; and keep the practices firmly in hand.
nuance: காரணக்கோ மூன்று may be the three causal bodies, the three causes of bondage (anava, karma, maya) or the three gunas as causes; the herding verb is hobbling, which fits a beast kept but not killed. சாதனங்கள், the practices, are endorsed here where 1818 dismissed them.

reading: See the great light in the brahmarandhra, our herdsman; stay without speaking of release and reach great nishta.
nuance: பிரம்மாந்திரம், the brahmarandhra, is the aperture at the crown, the top of the body-egg in Siddhar teaching, and the great light is seen there. முத்தி பேசாதிருந்து, not speaking of release, makes nishta a matter of silence, continuing 1831.

title: இடைக்காட்டுச் சித்தர் பாடல்கள்
theme: The last seven herding songs leave the cattle behind and tell the herdsman what to see: the lotus in the head, the Real sought in the sky with true knowledge, the mirror that only the eye of knowledge can see, the void that only the subtle intellect can point to, the eternal that stands forever, Shakti and the Supreme blended within oneself in nishta, and, like an owl, silence, by which the kindled round of birth is cut.
structure_note: 1857 to 1863 complete the கிடை கட்டுதல் of chapter 95 and the whole work. The herding image survives only in the address கோனே; each stanza is a two-line instruction on seeing (தெரிந்து, காண், கண்டு), ending in silence and the cutting of birth.
source_issues: Chapter 96 holds only seven verses because the work ends at seq 1863; the chapter break falls inside the கிடை கட்டுதல் section, which runs from 1846.
1859 line 2 prints கண்ணடி for கண்ணாடி, a shortening or slip; the sense is unaffected.

reading: Know the sight of the lotus in the head, our herdsman; and know in your mind the technique by which the mouth attains its power.
nuance: சிரமதில் கமலம் is the lotus at the crown, the highest of the supports in the yogic body; சேவை is service or, as here, the sight of a deity. வாய் சித்திக்கும் தந்திரம் is unclear: the method by which speech gains power (வாக்குசித்தி), or the mouth's part in drawing the nectar of the milking songs; tradition takes it as the former.

reading: Seeking the sky, see the Real in true knowledge, herdsman; always holding truth in truth, go on in true knowledge.
nuance: வத்து is வஸ்து, the Real; மெய்யே மெய்யில் கொண்டு piles the word for truth three times in a line. விண் நாடி is 'seeking the sky', though a coded ear hears விண்நாடி, the sky-channel, that is the central channel; the plain reading stands on its own.

reading: Look and see inside the mirror, herdsman; without the eye of knowledge the mirror cannot be seen, our herdsman.
nuance: The mirror is the mind or the inner faculty in which the Real is reflected, as in Tirumular's magic mirror of the mind; the twist is that the mirror itself is invisible to the ordinary eye, so ஞானக்கண், the eye of knowledge, is needed before any reflection can be sought. கண்ணடி is a shortened கண்ணாடி.

reading: Where are those who can point to the void, herdsman? Hold the thought that only the subtle intellect can point it out.
nuance: சூனியம், the void, is the Siddhars' word for the nothing that is the goal; சுட்டுவார், those who can point, denies that it can be shown from outside, and புத்தி சூக்குமம், the subtle intellect, is the one faculty allowed to reach it. The claim is that the void is known, not that it is unknowable.

reading: If the eternal comes straight to you, that is the state, herdsman; see that it stands forever and see it with certainty, our herdsman.
nuance: நித்தியம் is the eternal, set against the perishing world of 1815; நேர்படில், if it comes straight or meets one, suggests a meeting rather than an effort. நிச்சயம் காண், see with certainty, makes settled conviction part of the seeing. The syntax of line 1 is compressed.

reading: Shakti and the Supreme are blended within you, herdsman; if you achieve nishta, both can be seen within you.
nuance: The gloss gives நிட்டை as Sivayoga, the fixed absorption; the verse makes the union of Shakti and Param an inner fact first and a thing seen second, so nishta reveals rather than produces it. The body as the place of the divine pair is the Siddhars' body-as-cosmos claim in its devotional form.

reading: Stay like an owl and achieve silence, our herdsman; see the supreme root-state and cut off the kindled round of birth.
nuance: The owl is still and silent by day and awake in the dark, so it is the figure for the sage's silence here, where in Pattinathar it is the figure for blindness to the light; the same bird carries opposite senses. பர மூலநிலை, the supreme root-state, is the source itself; மூட்டுப் பிறப்பு, birth kindled like a fire, is the round that silence puts out. The work ends on this cutting of birth.

title: வாலைக் கும்மி
theme: The opening of Konganar's Valaik Kummi, a women's clapping-dance song addressed to the Maiden (வாலை), the young goddess who is at once Shakti, the power at the root of the body and the flame in the lamp. After seven invocations the song claims that she, without mother or father, made earth and sky, and that the five letters (அஞ்செழுத்து) made the world, the soul and the ages; the mute letter is the body and Om is the life, and the unseen can be seen by meditating on the five rather than by reading sastra and Veda. The chapter ends by turning from the open word to cipher and from the filthy body to the lamp that burns above the crown.
structure_note: 1864 to 1870 are invocations (a venba to Vinayaka, then kummi stanzas to Vinayaka, Saraswati, Siva, Murugan, Vishnu and Nandi), each naming the Maiden under a different epithet; 1871 to 1874 announce the song and its subject, how world, Veda, gods and the Maiden arose; 1875 to 1883 are on the five letters, Om and the mute letter; 1884 and 1885 on the Chidambara chakra and the firm mind; 1886 to 1888 turn to cipher, the body and the lamp above the crown. The refrain வாலைப்பெண்ணே begins at 1871 and is not present in every stanza.
source_issues: 1864 is a venba, not a kummi stanza, and its second half is run together without word division (வேதனஞ்சு போதன்மிஞ்சி மானகஞ்ச பாதம்வஞ்ச); the sense is partly lost.
1879: பார்த்த்தாலுந் has a doubled த.
1882: நிலையா மலந்த is corrupt, probably for நிலையான அந்த.
1883: the first line ஏய்க்கு தேய்க்கு ஐந்செழுத் துவதை is metrically short and ஐந்செழுத்து is a misspelling of ஐந்தெழுத்து or அஞ்செழுத்து.
1886: the second line தீமட்டு திந்தவரி விழிக்கே is corrupt.
The refrain வாலைப்பெண்ணே appears in 1871, 1873, 1874, 1882 and 1883 only; the other stanzas end on their own fourth line.

reading: To tell this kummi on the Lady whom the learned call the Maiden full of learning, their beloved, we set in the heart the lotus feet of the one who excels the wise and whose word is sweet to the gods.
nuance: A venba invocation, not a kummi stanza. The second half (நல்விசய நாதனின்சொல் வேதனஞ்சு போதன்மிஞ்சி மானகஞ்ச பாதம்வஞ்ச நெஞ்சினில்) is run together and partly garbled; the god addressed is Vinayaka by the section heading, and வஞ்ச நெஞ்சு (deceitful heart) seems to be the poet's own.

reading: Shakti, who bears the matted locks, is the Maiden; to tell the kummi on that excellent one, the one-tusked Siddhi Vinayaka who helped in the art is our protection.
nuance: சடாதரி (bearer of matted hair) gives the Maiden an ascetic Siva-like form; வித்தைக்கு உதவிய (who helped the art) makes Vinayaka the patron of the song's craft.

reading: The Maiden whom the Siddhars praise is that Shakti; to tell the kummi on her, the golden feet of Saraswati, the wife who dances to the drum's beat, are our protection.
nuance: சித்தர்கள் போற்றிய names the Maiden as the Siddhars' own goddess, which is the song's claim throughout. தத்தமித்தோம் is a drum-syllable string, placing Saraswati in the dance.

reading: The Maiden is she who fills everything, Vishnu's younger sister; to sing the kummi on her, the lotus feet of Siva Sambhu who wears the Ganga, the true guru, are our protection.
nuance: எங்கும் நிறைந்தவள் gives the goddess the pervasion usually predicated of Siva. Siva is invoked as சற்குரு, the true guru, which is how the Siddhars take him.

reading: She is the woman of knowledge, the woman of the light of grace, the primal Maiden; to sing the kummi on her, Murugan, who made the deer a woman and who suits Valli, is our protection.
nuance: மானைப் பெண்ணாக்கிய refers to Valli, born of a deer in her legend; the epithets ஞானப்பெண், அருள்சோதிப்பெண் make the Maiden knowledge and light before she is a person.

reading: She is the beggar-woman and the royal Pandya woman, the Maiden Ambika; to sing the kummi on her, the golden feet of the lord of Vaikuntha, who took up the service of the Gandiva-bearer, are our protection.
nuance: ஆண்டிப்பெண் is the wife of the beggar Siva and ராசபாண்டிப்பெண் the Pandya princess, Meenakshi of Madurai; the two epithets give the goddess both poverty and royalty. காண்டீபனாம் பணி பூண்டவன் is read as Krishna who served Arjuna as charioteer, so the god is Vishnu.

reading: Antari and Sundari are the Maiden; to sing the kummi on that Ambika, the golden feet of Nandi, who comes first into the thought as a fine wonder, are our protection.
nuance: Nandi here is the guru of the Siddhar lineage, as in the Tirumanthiram, rather than the bull. அந்தரி (she of the inner space) carries the yogic sense beside the name.

reading: On the Maiden, the able one who danced within bounds at Thillai and at Mullai, to sing the sporting kummi in Tamil removes old karma.
nuance: The dancer at Thillai is Siva in the Saiva tradition; the song gives the dance to the Maiden. சல்லாபக் கும்மி, the sporting kummi, names the genre as play, and the claim that singing it removes karma is the song's warrant for itself.

reading: Without mother or father, in the open space, to make earth and sky, the innocent girl, the first Maiden, entered as its ruler; this world is contained in her.
nuance: மாதா பிதா கூட இல்லாமல் makes her unborn and so beginningless, which the Siddhars elsewhere ask of the letter and the soul. பேதைப்பெண் (innocent girl) and the ruler of the world are the same person: the Maiden is young and supreme at once.

reading: How the Veda and the elements arose, how space became science and sastra, how nada and song arose: listen, I will tell the way.
nuance: The stanza is a table of contents: Veda, elements, sciences and sound are all to be derived. வெளி (space) as the source of the sciences is the Siddhar cosmology in which all comes from the void.

reading: How the three worlds arose, how the first god and the gods arose, and how, wondrously, the Maiden arose: see this exposition of knowledge.
nuance: The Maiden too has an arising (வாலை உண்டானது), though 1872 made her unparented; the song does not reconcile the two. ஞான விளக்கம் is both exposition and lamp of knowledge, the image taken up at 1888.

reading: What preceded Hari is the letter A; what stood within Hari is the five letters; what preceded holding is the five letters; and what stood within the breath-horse is the five letters.
nuance: The stanza turns on அரி, which is Hari, Vishnu, but in cipher can be the sun or the letter; வாசிப்பரி is the horse that is the breath. Tradition takes the stanza to place the five letters in the breath, so that the mantra is breathed rather than said. தரிக்கும் (holding, or bearing) is unclear.

reading: In the beginning the Maiden became the five letters and took the name five letters; she is not the mute letter of the nadi; she became the way of knowledge itself.
nuance: நாதியின் ஊமை எழுத்து is unclear: நாதி may be a corrupt நாடி (channel) or an echo of நாதம் (sound). The stanza distinguishes the Maiden from the mute letter that 1877 then makes the body, so she is the sounded five, not the silent one.

reading: The mute letter became the body, and the letter Om became the life; know this letter and dance the kummi in play.
nuance: ஊமை எழுத்து, the mute letter, is in tradition the unsounded letter beyond the fifty-one, sometimes the half-letter of Om; here it is assigned to the body and the sounded Om to the life. Sangili Siddhar reverses the assignment (2111).

reading: What created the world is the five letters; what created the soul is the five letters; what ended the age is the five letters; and what made it arise again is the five letters.
nuance: Creation, destruction and re-creation of the age (உகம்) are all given to the mantra, which stands here for Siva's acts, as in Tirumular's chapter on the five letters.

reading: What if you have looked at the sastras, what if you have looked at the Veda too? It is the formula you must see and master; it is by knowing the five words that you must see.
nuance: சூத்திரம் (sutra, formula, also the puppet-string) is set against the books: knowing the five letters is the thread that works the rest. The dismissal of scripture is mild beside Sivavakkiyar's; the Veda is useless only without the five.

reading: If you think the five are not seen, not gained, not reached, and nothing comes of them, know that by the five letters the unseen can be seen, and there is effect in them if you meditate.
nuance: The stanza answers a doubter in his own words (காணாது கிட்டாதே எட்டாதே) and makes meditation, not recitation, the condition of the letters' effect.

reading: The cowherd is within the fifth letter; the knowing one is within the fifth letter; the speaking one is within the fifth letter; and this Maiden is within the fifth letter.
nuance: ஐந்தாம் எழுத்து may be the fifth letter (in சிவாயநம, ம or ய) or the five letters together. ஆயன் is Krishna, the cowherd; அறிவாயன் and வாயன் are read as the knower and the speaker, but may be further names of gods. The stanza places god, knower and Maiden in one letter.

reading: The five letters became eight letters, and then the fifty-one syllables; will you know the truth that stands by the letter of the heart, Maiden?
nuance: Five, eight and fifty-one are the Siva pancakshara, the eight-letter mantra (ஓம் நமசிவாய with its seeds, or the Vishnu ashtakshara) and the full alphabet; Pattinathar names the same three (659). நெஞ்செழுத்து (heart-letter) is unclear: the letter held in the heart, or a letter that is the heart. நிலையாமல் is corrupt for நிலையான or நிலையாம்.

reading: The five letters deceive and wear away; reach out and grasp the two letters; watch the breath and, above, see the state of the breath, Maiden.
nuance: ஏய்க்குது தேய்க்குது (it deceives, it wears) is a strange thing to say of the five letters; the stanza may mean the spoken five fail and the two (tradition says சி and வ, or the in and out breath, or அ and உ) are to be held. வாசியை மேலாக (the breath above) points to the raised breath at the crown. The first line's metre is broken.

reading: The great ones in this land know the Chidambara chakra; but if it is the Chidambara chakra, you must know the deity within it.
nuance: The plain reading is of the drawn yantra of Chidambaram, known to the learned; the coded reading, following Tirumular's claim that the body is Chidambaram, makes the chakra the body and the deity the Maiden within it. The stanza rebukes those who know the diagram but not what it holds.

reading: If there is no mind and intellect, what can she do, though she tells of changing the way? One must keep firmness of mind, and then the Maiden's grace must come.
nuance: Grace is set after effort: the goddess cannot help a mind that will not hold. வழி மாறுதல் (changing the way) is read as the turning of the breath or the way of life; the stanza does not say which.

reading: I will not say it in the open any more; you with lined eyes, sweet-voiced women, come here, and I will tell you a little of the core; listen.
nuance: வெளியினில் சொல்லாதே announces the turn from plain speech to cipher, and கரு (the core, the embryo) is what follows. The second line, தீமட்டு திந்தவரி விழிக்கே, is corrupt; it seems to address the women by their painted eyes.

reading: Do not think this a filthy corpse; do not think it a salted pot; for those who have seen there is no filth in it; look at it within your own body.
nuance: The stanza turns against the Siddhars' own stock images of the body (ஊத்தைச் சடலம், உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம், the salted pot that will not last): the body is foul only to those who have not seen what it holds. It is the premise of the body-map that follows in the next chapter.

reading: Straight above the crown, above the uvula, a lamp set there burns daily; the lamp with an axis is the Maiden, and it burns without going out, Maiden.
nuance: உச்சிக்கு நேராய் உண்ணாக்குக்கு மேல் places the lamp at the crown above the palate, where tradition puts the thousand-petalled centre and the Maiden as the flame in the wick. அச்சுள்ள விளக்கு (the lamp with an axis or pivot) is unclear; a hanging or turning lamp, or the lamp that is the axis of the body.

title: வாலைக் கும்மி
theme: The second part of the Valaik Kummi maps the body as a cosmos in which the Maiden lives: the lamp that burns in the six houses without oil, the breath (வாசி) to be practised through the nostril, Sadasiva at the brow, Maheswara at the throat, Rudra in the heart, Vishnu at the navel and Brahma at the root, the body as a chariot of five hundred nails and a fort of nine gates. The letters of the mantra are placed in the body too (நகார, வகார, உகார, மகார, சிகார), Om is said to hold the mute letter, and the stanzas on the untied bull and the dying body make the point of the map: the deity is in the body and men die without seeing her. The chapter closes in cipher, riddles of flower, fruit and sons, and a place-name map from Melur to Kaalur.
structure_note: 1889 to 1894 follow the lamp of 1888 into the breath practice and the upper house; 1895 to 1899 place the five gods in the body from brow to root; 1900 to 1902 figure the body as chariot and fort and ask why men die with the deity inside; 1903 to 1905 place the letters and Om; 1906 and 1907 are on taming the breath before the body dies; 1908 to 1911 are riddles of conception; 1912 and 1913 read the body as a map of towns and a burning fort.
source_issues: 1899: முலத்திலே for மூலத்திலே.
1904: lines 2 and 3 both end மாய்கையாச்சே; one is probably a copyist's repetition and the value given to SI is lost.
1907: மார்க்க்கமாய் has a doubled க.
1908, 1909 and 1911 to 1913 vary the refrain or lack it; 1909 is a blessing formula of the kummi genre rather than a stanza of the argument.

reading: It burns in the house of six, and there is no oil in it and no nectar-water; the way to go is seen, yet there is no path; the path is tangled, tangled, Maiden.
nuance: ஆறு வீடு is read as the six adharas, the centres of the yogic body, in which the Maiden's lamp of 1888 burns without fuel, which is the point: her light is not fed. பாதை சிக்குது, the tangled path, is the central channel the breath must find. அமிழ்தண்ணீர் may be the nectar of the head or plain water for a lamp.
