reading: It is heard like the ring of anklets; the tangled path is very steep; the right-whorled conch sounds; above, look at the breath, Maiden.
nuance: Anklet-sound and conch are the inner sounds (நாதம்) heard as the breath rises; tradition lists them among the ten sounds of yoga. துடுக்கம் (steepness, or roughness) is the difficulty of the channel. The stanza joins sound and breath without explaining how one leads to the other.

reading: One must know the practice of the breath, and build the houses of the mandala; taking the way of the nostril, see the aim of yoga and of the breath, Maiden.
nuance: நாசி வழி, the nostril's way, is the plainest statement in the song that the practice is breath control. மண்டல வீடுகள் கட்ட (building the mandala-houses) is unclear: the centres as houses to be built up, or the period of a mandala (forty-eight days) of practice.

reading: Within the three-flamed lamp, in the practice of the breath in the root mandala, whatever flame it becomes, that flame is the Maiden; there is none other than her, Maiden.
nuance: முச்சுடர் is the three lights, sun, moon and fire, taken in yoga as the three channels or the three eyes; the Maiden is the flame they become in the root centre. The stanza identifies goddess, flame and breath-result in one line.

reading: Because the Maiden stays unheated and is within the Siva perfected by the horse, let us look at the practice of the breath without leaving it; we can see the upper house, Maiden.
nuance: The stanza is cipher: சூடாமல் (without heating, or without crowning) may mean the kundalini not yet roused; பரி சித்த சிவன் is the Siva accomplished through the horse, the breath. மேல்வீடு, the upper house, is the head centre and also release; both senses stand.

reading: He who saw the upper house is the skilled one; he who stood in the lamp in the sky is the one of speech; he who saw the mother's house is the knower; he who leapt the horse is the soldier.
nuance: Four names are given for four attainments; பாணி, வாணி and பட்டாணி may be puns on hand, speech and the Pathan soldier, rhymed with ஞானி. The one who leaps the horse (பரி தாண்டிக் கொண்டான்) is the one who has passed beyond the breath. The sense of each title is tradition's guess.

reading: The hand in the fig, the mind in devotion, in the intellect in the very middle; the forehead is Sadasiva, I have said; look at your own state, Maiden.
nuance: The first line is a rhyming cipher (அத்தி, பத்தி, புத்தி, மத்தி) whose terms are unclear; அத்தி may be fig, elephant or bone (அஸ்தி). The one clear claim begins the body-map: Sadasiva, the highest of the five, at the forehead.

reading: In the press I told the five letters; I praised them in the fruit of knowledge; at the throat there is Maheswara too; see with the eye and look, Maiden.
nuance: The map continues: Maheswara at the throat, below Sadasiva at the brow. அழுத்தில் and பழத்தில் are rhymes for கழுத்தில் and are read as the pressing (of the breath) and the fruit (of knowledge); they may be filler.

reading: In the five, in the tender one, you creeper-women who daily play fondly: in the heart Rudra stays all round; he is straight with you, Maiden.
nuance: Rudra at the heart is the third station of the map. அஞ்சிலே பிஞ்சிலே is cipher, perhaps the five (elements or senses) and the young fruit (the embryo) of 1908; the address to the dancing women is the kummi's frame.

reading: In the belly, in the middle row, in firm thought, before you: in the navel Vishnu too stays; see this truly, Maiden.
nuance: Vishnu at the navel, the fourth station. உந்தி is the navel and, in older Tamil, the breath's base; the stanza asks that the placement be seen as true (உண்மையாய்), not taken on faith.

reading: In the banyan, in this world, in the time to come, in what is favourable: at the root Brahma stays, finishing the breath and holding the body, Maiden.
nuance: Brahma at the root completes the five gods from brow to base, which is the Saiva order of the five faces turned into a body-map. வாசி முடிக்கிறான் பிண்டம் பிடிக்கிறான் makes Brahma the one who ends the breath and seizes the body, a creator who is also the maker of death; the first line is rhyming filler.

reading: There is a chariot with five hundred nails; in it there are gods and there is music; see who is there: the Maiden deity is contained in it, Maiden.
nuance: The chariot is the body; ஐஞ்சூறு ஆணி (five hundred nails) is probably a count of bones or joints, though tradition gives several numbers. The gods and music are the five of the preceding stanzas and the inner sounds of 1890.

reading: There is a fort with nine gates; inside it the keepers of the post are five; with love, the attendants are six; it is contained there, Maiden.
nuance: The nine gates are the body's openings, a stock figure; the five keepers are the senses or the elements, and the six attendants (பரிகாரர்) the six adharas or the six faculties, as tradition takes them. The stanza's point is that the fort is guarded from within.

reading: While the deity stays in the body in this way, through what the intellect does not know, men die without seeing the joyful Maiden; what is this, Maiden?
nuance: The map's conclusion is a complaint: the goddess is in the body and men die anyway. புத்திக்கு அறிக்கையினால் is read as 'because of the intellect's knowing', that is, its wrong knowing; the word is strained.

reading: Because the letter NA became the fixed one, the house became the letter VA of the sky, with grace; the letter U became the head at the crown; look at this closely, Maiden.
nuance: The letters of the mantra are now placed in the body, as Tirumular places them (NA at the feet, MA at the navel). திட்டிப்பு is unclear (fixing, or dizziness); வான வகாரம் makes VA the sky-element, and உகாரம், the U of Om, the crown. The exact placements are the stanza's cipher.

reading: The letter VA became sound; that letter MA became maya; the letter SI became maya too; make this clear and see, Maiden.
nuance: Two letters are given the same value, மாய்கை, which is probably a copyist's repetition; the third line should give SI a different term, perhaps சிவம். Tirumular gives MA to impurity and VA to form (975), so the correspondences are not fixed across the tradition.

reading: There is the syllable Om, and within it there is the mute letter too; now that we have known this letter, seek out the deed and see, Maiden.
nuance: The mute letter is placed inside Om, the half-letter or the silence after the sound, as tradition takes it. வினை நாடிப் பாரடி, seek the deed, is unexpected: knowing the letter is to be tested on karma, or the deed is the practice to be sought.

reading: The untied bull must be tied; desire must be cut; the breath must be joined; the branch out of reach must be bent; how long will the body last, Maiden?
nuance: The bull is the mind, or the breath itself, in tradition's reading; the branch out of reach is the crown the breath must be bent to. The last line gives the reason for haste: the body does not wait.

reading: Staying in the way one was, the breath must be held in without taking more; wandering, running, roaming and burning, the body has died, Maiden.
nuance: வாசி ஏற்காமலே அடக்க (to restrain the breath without receiving it) is read as holding the breath rather than drawing it in; the stanza contrasts the still body with the one worn out by motion. The first line, இருந்த மார்க்கமாய்த் தானிருந்து, is read as staying in one's own state.

reading: From the flower that bloomed there is the young fruit, and there are many young fruits without a flower; by the eldest son there is life, and by the other three there is ruin.
nuance: Cipher. The plain reading is of conception: flower as the woman's period and fruit as the embryo, with fruits without flowers as conceptions that defy the rule. Tradition takes the eldest son as the seed kept (or the breath, or Om) which gives life, and the other three as the three malas or the other three states that waste it. The stanza has no refrain.

reading: Long live the line of chaste women; long live those who gave the chastity they stand by; praising the supreme consciousness, dance the kummi; praising the supreme self, dance the kummi.
nuance: A kummi commonplace, blessing the dancers' chastity, is joined to the praise of சிற்பரன் and தற்பரன், the Supreme as consciousness and as self. கற்பை அளித்தவர் (those who gave chastity) is read as the women's husbands or parents, or the goddess herself.

reading: In the five, two did not perish; in the six, four were not removed; it sleeps in the young fruit and in the flower; it can be tended and set, Maiden.
nuance: Number cipher continuing 1908: five and six may be the elements and the adharas, or the counts of the letters; what sleeps in fruit and flower is the seed or the breath. The arithmetic is not recoverable from the stanza, and the reading keeps to its surface.

reading: The handless dwarf embraced; the legless tall one butted; he dropped it like honey without a bee, and it is no longer sweet, Maiden.
nuance: A riddle in the Siddhars' cipher. The plain reading is of the sexual act and the spending of seed, which the song then calls tasteless; a coded reading takes the dwarf and the tall one as the breath and the mind, and the honey without a bee as the nectar that comes without effort. The stanza fits both and favours neither.

reading: In support of the fort of Melur, the lamp shines well on the Kannanur road; because the hall of Kaalur was left, it is a hard walk, Maiden.
nuance: The towns are body-parts punned into place names: Melur the upper town (the head), Kannanur the eye, Kaalur the foot. Leaving the hall of the feet for the lamp of the head is the ascent of the breath, called a hard walk. The puns are the stanza's whole method.

reading: In the triangular fort within the throat, on the flag-mast fixed and planted there, she fought and came and ran away; the fort burned and became embers, Maiden.
nuance: The triangle at the throat is the vishuddhi centre of the yogic map; the she who fights and flees is the Maiden, or the life, leaving the body, which then burns on the pyre. The stanza is the song's picture of death, the counterpart of the fort of 1901.

title: வாலைக் கும்மி
theme: The third part of the Valaik Kummi runs from the nets of desire and attachment through a string of animal riddles in the Siddhars' cipher (swan, tiger and parrots in the hall, cuckoo and owl, fish and honey, crow and eagle, crocodiles, bears and blind men, egg-laying birds, two moons on a chariot) to the Maiden seated in the triangle at the root. It then praises her as the one who kicked Death, drank the poison, burned the cities and killed Kamsa, who comes as mother, wife and sister, and asks whether Shakti or Siva is greater, answering with figures of mutual need: food and water, flesh and bone, earth and sky, woman and man. It closes on the worship that made the Siddhars, and on the claim that there is no deity above the Maiden and no song above this one.
structure_note: 1914 opens with the nets of desire and the burning house; 1915 to 1923 are animal and number riddles for the senses, the soul and death; 1924 to 1927 seat the Maiden in the root chakra and credit her with Siva's deeds; 1928 to 1930 give her kinship roles and the paradox of the barren mother; 1931 to 1935 pose and answer the question of Shakti against Siva; 1936 to 1938 end on worship, past merit and the song's self-praise.
source_issues: 1915 is overlong: its fourth line carries two refrains' worth of matter (எட்டிப் பிடிக்குமே மூன்று கிளியடி வாலைப்பெண்ணே) and the stanza may conflate two.
1917: தூரணி and கலசாவல் are obscure and may be corrupt.
1920, 1925 to 1930 and 1932 to 1933 lack the refrain வாலைப்பெண்ணே; 1929 and 1930 run on as one sentence.

reading: That one is caught in the net of desire, that the house burned and perished at once, that the net of attachment came and covered it: for all this, praise the feet of the Lord, Maiden.
nuance: The house that burns is the body of 1913; the two nets, ஆசை and பாசம், are the ordinary cause of its ruin. The remedy offered is devotion, not breath, which the song elsewhere prefers.

reading: The swan is in the hall; a male tiger wanders there at play; five parrots still remain there, and three parrots reach out and catch them, Maiden.
nuance: Cipher. Tradition reads the swan as the soul or the breath (hamsa), the tiger as the mind or death, the five parrots as the senses and the three that seize them as the three gunas or malas. The stanza is overlong by a foot and its line division is doubtful.

reading: In the grove the cuckoo of the mango calls, and the new bridegroom comes to eat; the five-six owl sits deceiving in this way and stares; look at it, Maiden.
nuance: Cipher. The bridegroom who comes to feed may be the soul entering the body, or the lover of the plain reading; அஞ்சாறு ஆந்தை (the five-six owl) is unexplained, perhaps the mind with its five senses and six faculties, which watches and deceives. The reading keeps to the surface.

reading: There is a fish in the pool, and the kalasaval bird grazes on it and roams; there is honey in the field to eat, and it never cloys, Maiden.
nuance: The honey that never cloys is the nectar of the head in the yogic reading; the fish and the bird that feeds on it are less clear, perhaps the breath and the mind, or the eye and its object. தூரணி and கலசாவல் are obscure words, the second perhaps a bird's name.

reading: The crow sits on the branch, and the story lies in the strength; it is not far to see; this is knowledge, and if you look it shows, Maiden.
nuance: The stanza says the secret is near and visible, which is the Siddhars' recurring claim; the crow on the branch is its figure, perhaps the mind on the body, the branch of 1906. கதை and தெம்பு rhyme with the first line and may be filler.

reading: In the pond of the belly there is a hall; in Karuvur of that pond there is much mud; come with strength by the forest paths within, join them and examine, Maiden.
nuance: Place-cipher as in 1912: கும்பி is the belly or the stomach, and Karuvur, a real town, is punned on கரு, the womb or embryo, so the muddy pond is the place of conception. The forest paths within are the channels.

reading: Long ago, in the deep well two carp lay and showed off; the crow that stood watching them took fright, and the eagle killed it; look, Maiden.
nuance: Cipher. Two carp in a well are the two eyes, or the sun and moon breaths; the crow is the mind that watches them and the eagle the breath or death that kills it. The parable is not explained and the reading is tradition's.

reading: In the river there are five crocodiles; in the anthill two bears; Death is three blind men, and he takes with the noose, Maiden.
nuance: The five crocodiles are the senses in the river of the body, the two bears perhaps the two deeds or desire and anger in the anthill (the body, or the root where the serpent sleeps), and the three blind men who are Death the three malas. பாசம் is both Yama's noose and the Saiva bond.

reading: One bird lays an egg, and one bird spoils the egg; in the snare of circling Arur two deer struggle, Maiden.
nuance: Cipher. The bird that lays and the bird that spoils may be the two breaths or the two deeds, the egg being the body (அண்டம்); ஆரூர் is a town-pun of uncertain target, and the two deer the soul and the mind in the snare of birth.

reading: In the open ground of the eight great sky-circles, two moons stand on the chariot; they do not come and strike exactly, and the body has become red embers, Maiden.
nuance: The two moons are the two eyes or the sun and moon breaths, on the chariot of the body (1900); அட்டமா விண்வட்டம் may be the eight directions of the sky or the eight centres. Their failure to strike together ends in the burning body of 1913.

reading: Within the triangular round well, in the practice of the breath in the root mandala, in that cornered round chakra the Maiden sits, Maiden.
nuance: The clearest doctrinal stanza of the chapter: the Maiden is seated in the triangle of the root centre, where tradition places the sleeping kundalini, and is reached by breath practice there. The riddles that precede it are, on the coded reading, about the same place.

reading: On two legs there stands a tower; staying a long time, it will sink; when one sees it, the tower stands; the Maiden lets it neither be seen nor stand, Maiden.
nuance: The tower on two legs is the body; the Maiden who neither lets it be seen truly nor lets it stand is the goddess as maya, the same power that seats herself at the root. The stanza gives her both the veil and the tower's fall.

reading: Creating the five elements and joining them, creating the adharas, creating fond desire for women, the Maiden brings them together and fastens on Death, Maiden.
nuance: Creation is hers, and so are desire and death: the goddess who makes the body also sets the trap that ends it. The stanza does not soften this; 1927 answers it by making her Death's conqueror too.

reading: The Maiden is she who kicked Death with her foot, she who ate the halahala poison, she who created the undying world, she who demolished this human's fort.
nuance: The kicking of Yama and the drinking of poison are Siva's deeds in the Saiva stories; the song gives them to the Maiden, as 1929 gives her Murugan's and Krishna's. மானுடன் கோட்டை இடித்தவள் recalls the burning fort of 1913: she builds and breaks the body-fort.

reading: She came as mother and gave milk; she came as wife and gave pleasure; she became the supporting younger sister; for us she became the sister-in-law of desire and the mother-in-law.
nuance: Every woman in a man's house is the goddess, which the kummi, sung by women, can say lightly. அமுதம் is milk here and also nectar; கொழுந்தி (wife's younger sister) is paired with ஆசை, which the stanza does not disown.

reading: Smiling, she gently burned the cities; the Maiden kicked the Chetti of Senkadu; alone she conquered the Suras; single-handed she killed Kamsa.
nuance: The burning of the three cities is Siva's, the conquest of the Suras Murugan's and the killing of Kamsa Krishna's; the goddess is made the agent of all. செங்காட்டுச் செட்டி is unclear: Yama kicked at Thirukkadaiyur is the likely story, but the name does not fit, and a merchant of Senkadu may be meant.

reading: Such, you see, is her work; she is the barren one who never bore, the cruel one who is pregnant; you kohl-eyed women, listen: that young Maiden is the trident-bearer.
nuance: ஈனா மலடி (the barren one who has not borne) and கொடுஞ்சூலி (the fierce pregnant one) are held together: she bears nothing and is always with child, the paradox of a creator without birth, as 1872 made her without parents.

reading: Is the knife greater or the sheath? Is her eye greater or her face? Is Shakti greater or Siva? You tell me a little, Maiden.
nuance: The question is posed with two homely pairs that cannot be ranked, knife and sheath, eye and face, and so is already answered: neither is greater. The song nevertheless returns to it (1967) and there decides for Siva.

reading: It is not that food is greater and water not, and so with the Maiden being greater; it is not that gold is greater and silver not; I say it without lie, listen, you women.
nuance: The syntax is loose; the sense taken is that the Maiden's greatness is like that of food beside water, each needed and neither above the other. A different reading makes food greater than water and so the Maiden greater than Siva; the gold and silver pair tells against it.

reading: If it is flesh there is bone; take away the flesh and the shell of bone falls apart; the substance is Shakti in this way; play and dance the kummi.
nuance: Flesh and bone answer the question of 1931 by a body: Shakti is the flesh that holds the bones, Siva the frame that falls without her. ஆமிசம் (substance, or flesh) is the pun that carries the claim.

reading: Though what sprouted of old is the rice, if the husk is gone it will not grow: Avvai saw this and said it long ago; is it so or not, Maiden?
nuance: The husk is the body, or maya, or Shakti: the soul-grain grows only inside it. The appeal to Avvai is to the proverb-poet, not to a known verse. The claim cuts against the ascetic use of the same image, in which the husk is the impurity to be removed.

reading: Without earth there is no sky; without a little fragrance there is no flower; without woman there is no man; cherish this and see, Maiden.
nuance: Three dependencies close the argument of 1931 to 1934: the goddess is the condition of the god, as earth of sky and scent of flower. The stanza reads as doctrine and as a women's song's plain boast.

reading: In the pleasure garden there is light; for those who have ploughed the land there is paddy; to worship the Maiden wondrously, one needs what was left unfinished in a former life, Maiden.
nuance: விட்ட குறை, the unfinished remainder, is the practice carried over from a past birth without which this worship cannot begin; the paddy for those who ploughed makes the same point. The Maiden's cult is a reward, not a starting point.

reading: By worshipping the Maiden they became Siddhars; by firm desire for the Maiden they became the doers of Siva's work; they set the wage after looking at the work; will you know this manner, Maiden?
nuance: சித்தர் ஆனார் is the song's account of what makes a Siddhar: worship of the Maiden, not alchemy or breath alone. கூலி, the wage set by the work, makes attainment proportional to practice, with no shortcut.

reading: There is no deity above the Maiden; nothing guards honour better than the sari; there is no fortune above milk; and there is no song above the Maiden's kummi.
nuance: A closing boast in four parallel lines; the sari and milk keep the stanza in the women's world of the kummi. The claim that no deity is above the Maiden is later qualified by the song itself (1967), which sets Siva higher.

title: வாலைக் கும்மி
theme: The fourth part of Konganar's Vaalai Kummi turns from the goddess to the household: wife, children and parents are false and follow the dead only to the field and the burning-ground, so give while you can and finish your temple work before Death takes you off the mattress. A run of plain prohibitions follows (do not strike the poor, lie, steal, abuse devotees or covet chaste women), then caste is refuted by the one milk that becomes ghee, curd and buttermilk, and the part closes in riddles that only the one who has seen the mouthless horse can read.
structure_note: 1939 to 1942 are the gate, the seed and the false hut; 1943 to 1949 the falseness of kin and the duty of giving before death; 1950 to 1957 a list of do-nots in the manner of a conduct text, each stanza four prohibitions; 1958 and 1959 caste and offering; 1960 to 1963 riddles and the scholar who dies like anyone else.
source_issues: 1946 line 1 மகள் போக்கியம் is probably a slip for மகா போக்கியம்.
1951 line 4 கிளப்பம் is not a word; read as இளப்பம்.
1957 line 3 யூகம் is a spelling of ஊகம்.
1960 line 2 கூனிக் மூன்றுகால் has broken sandhi (for கூனிக்கு மூன்று கால்); the riddle text of 1960 to 1962 is worn throughout.
1961 line 2 பானைக்குப் பானைக்குநிற்கு மேல்சூல் is corrupt, with a doubled word and no clear construction.
1955 line 4 புளிப் பழம்போ லுதிர்த்து விழுந்தானே is loosely attached to the stanza and may be a half-remembered proverb.

reading: If you see the inner gaze you can know; you can cross the four-and-six gates and open the locked door; this is not false but true, Vaalai girl.
nuance: நாலாறு வாசல் is four-and-six, ten gates, or four-times-six, twenty-four; the body is usually given nine gates, and the tenth, closed, is the opening at the crown through which the yogi leaves, as tradition takes it. The locked door (பூட்டைக் கதவு) is then that tenth gate, and நாட்டம் the fixed inner gaze that opens it. A plain reading, that attention itself is the key, also stands.

reading: You say a child came of man and woman joining; is it not that from man and woman joining there came one seed in which difference is gone?
nuance: பேதம் அற்ற ஒரு வித்து, one seed without difference, carries the stanza: the plain sense is that every birth comes from the same undifferentiated seed, which prepares the caste argument of 1958; a coded sense takes the seed as bindu, the drop from which the body forms. The stanza does not choose.

reading: What stands today is not false, nor is the house; that this is my life is not false; but it ends on that day as the writing says; so praise mother Vaalai.
nuance: The stanza grants that the present and the house are real, against 1942 and 1943 which call them false; the two are reconciled by எழுத்தின்படி முடியும், the end written on the head. Konganar's point is not that life is illusion but that it is dated.

reading: Do not wander in vain desire; this is not true, it is a false life and a false hut; if you find the unseen Vaalai you can see the vision and rule the sky.
nuance: பொய்க்கூடு, the false hut, is the body, a usage shared with Punnakku Siddhar (2265, 2266). ஆகாயம் ஆளலாம் can be the siddhi of moving through space or the mastery of the inner space; the stanza allows both.

reading: Is not becoming a wife false, and the children one bore false? The father who made much of you is false; is even the mother who gave the breast real?
nuance: The question form (நிசமாமோ) leaves the mother last and hardest; the answer comes in 1944 and 1945, where she is matched with the wife and both are left at the boundary.

reading: Mother and wife are alike, for both gave of their own body; but are the unripe and the ripe fruit the same? Look to your own intent, Vaalai girl.
nuance: தன்யம் is unclear; read as தனம், the breast or one's substance, both women gave it. காயும் பழமும், green fruit and ripe, may distinguish the two gifts or the two women; the last line puts the difference in the looker's கருத்து, which recalls Pattinathar's resolve to see woman as mother.

reading: The wife comes only as far as the common ground, the children one bore only as far as the burning-ground's edge; the dharma of service comes in between, joins you, and gives the highest state.
nuance: மந்தை is the village common or cattle-ground at the edge of the settlement, the first boundary the funeral passes; the children go one boundary further. தொண்டாட்டுத் தர்மம் is dharma done as service, and it alone goes on.

reading: If fortune, the enjoyment of offspring and royal enjoyment have come to you of themselves, do charity quickly and finish some temple work.
nuance: மகள் போக்கியம் is odd; it may be a slip for மகா போக்கியம், great enjoyment, or mean the joy of daughters. The three goods are listed only to be spent: the stanza's verb is சீக்கிரம், quickly.

reading: Those who have finished temple work are counted among those who, though they die, do not die: so Vaalai, who knows it, said in the grace-shining Veda.
nuance: செத்தும் சாகாத பேர், those who die and do not die, is the Siddhar phrase for the undying; here it is promised to the temple-builder rather than the yogi, and the authority is Vaalai's own word called Veda.

reading: While we lie on the mattress laughing with soft women, if warlike Death comes and seizes us, we too are only a dead corpse, Vaalai girl.
If a poor wretch has nothing and you have, you must give him food; you must not say 'tomorrow': so the four Vedas thunder.
Do not strike the poor and destitute, for that sin cannot be worn away; do not ruin those who said 'you are my refuge'; do not think of deceiving anyone.
Do not repeat what you saw and heard; do not give an answer about what your eye has not seen; do not tell your wife what has befallen you; do not belittle the children you bore.
nuance: உற்றது in line 3 is what has happened to you, your troubles or secrets; கிளப்பம் in line 4 is read as இளப்பம், slight or disgrace. Both are guesses at a worn text; the first two lines, on hearsay and on speaking of the unseen, are clear.

reading: Do not abuse Siva's devotees, Brahmins or the great ones of clear knowledge even in silence; do not do anything to pain their minds.
nuance: மவுனமாகவும் வையாதே extends the prohibition from spoken abuse to the silent kind, the inner contempt; a Siddhar who elsewhere mocks Brahmins here lists them with devotees and gnanis among those not to be hurt.

reading: Do not speak words that bring ruin in disputes; do not set your mind on chaste women; watch the breath you have practised, and praise Vaalai's feet.
nuance: பழக்க வாசி, the vaasi of practice, is the one yogic term in the list of do-nots; tradition takes it as the regulated breath, and the stanza slips it between a rule of speech and a rule of praise as if it were a rule of conduct like the others.

reading: Do not tell concerted lies; do not commit wicked robbery and theft; do not strike the dancing snake: this is wisdom, Vaalai girl.
nuance: ஆடிய பாம்பை அடியாதே is plain advice (do not provoke a snake that has risen) and, in the Siddhar cipher, the coiled power that has begun to move, which is not to be forced. The stanza's own word for its content is அறிவு, practical wisdom, which favours the plain sense.

reading: Even a man of deeds is not seen to speak boastfully, said Avvai; do not make mischief in the world: he who did fell shed like a ripe tamarind.
nuance: The Avvai saying is not quoted exactly and the last line is loose; புளிப்பழம் போல் உதிர்ந்து, dropping like ripe tamarind, is the image of the braggart's fall. The first line could also be read as a question, 'has anyone seen a doer boast?'.

reading: Do not make enemies of men of money; do not stand before a tiger in the deep forest; do not travel to foreign lands; do not take up the ways of an illusory courtesan.
nuance: The four prohibitions are prudential, not spiritual; the one on foreign lands matches 1957, where wandering is folly because the goal is in one's own house.

reading: Do not go to the neighbour's house while your own house stands; do not abuse mother and father; while the means is right inside your own house, you run about, Vaalai girl.
nuance: ஊகம் (printed யூகம்), the thing to be reasoned out, is what lies in one's own house; read as cipher the house is the body and the thing within is the goddess or the breath, and the stanza becomes the usual Siddhar rebuke of pilgrimage. The plain reading, stay home and respect your parents, also stands, and the stanza pairs them deliberately.

reading: You talk of caste differences; is there any difference in bodies that marks one as god? From the one milk that is spoken of came ghee, curd and buttermilk.
nuance: The milk image makes castes products of one substance, as 1940 made every birth one seed. தெய்வம் தான் என்று ஒரு உடல் பேதம் உண்டோ asks whether any body is marked as divine, which is the ground on which caste rank is claimed.

reading: The cat too has eaten the milk that was eaten; nothing higher is seen above it; cast off that desire for what is above and do your puja with longing in the heart.
nuance: The first two lines are obscure. One reading: the milk offered to the god is drunk by the cat, and no higher taker is seen, so the outward offering is futile and worship belongs within. The stanza's advice in lines 3 and 4 is clear whatever the image.

reading: I said the hen has six legs; I said the hunchback of the east has three legs; I said the hunchback has two letters; I said the whole pot has no mouth.
nuance: A chain of riddles whose keys are withheld, in the manner of the Siddhar cipher; 1961 and 1962 show that the hearer is being tested, and 1962 names the mouthless horse, the breath, as the key to the beasts. The pot with no mouth is in other Siddhar verses the closed body or the sealed crown; the hen and the hunchback are not explained here, and no tradition is cited for them.

reading: I said the goat has two legs; our pot stands on a pot, with a womb above; I said the cow has no legs: tell me the kinds in the tale, Vaalai girl.
nuance: Line 2 is corrupt (பானைக்குப் பானைக்கு) and மேல்சூல் is unclear, perhaps the belly or womb set above the pot. The stanza's demand, கதை வகையைச் சொல்லடி, makes the riddles a test of the hearer's initiation rather than a teaching.

reading: The one who robbed the temple and the cow, the one who has learned the noise of shouting, and the one who has seen the mouthless horse: does he know the kinds of cattle, Vaalai girl?
nuance: வாயில்லாக் குதிரை, the horse without a mouth, is the breath in the Siddhar cipher (the horse that is reined but not fed), as tradition takes it; the stanza asks whether even such a one can read the riddle-beasts of 1960 and 1961. The syntax is loose and the three men may be one or three.

reading: If people who have studied all these sastras die, the world will laugh; even in dying he must mingle, he must join the gods.
nuance: The scholar is mocked not for learning but for dying like anyone else; the Siddhar standard is that true knowledge shows in the manner of death, joining rather than ending. The 'he' of line 3 is the knower, in contrast to the learned who die.

title: வாலைக் கும்மி
theme: The close of Konganar's Vaalai Kummi: Avvai's saying defines the guru as the one whose fit word makes what is lacking fit, against the instrumental guru who knows no fullness and grabs goods, and the self-styled full gnanis who wander to feed their bellies. Vaalai is then praised as the one who gives life, drives off disease, sorcery and Death and stands in all things like oil in sesame, yet Siva is declared greater than she; a colophon names Konganar's guru and patron and wishes all siddhas long life. Five appended stanzas, with a different refrain, tell the hearer that the lamp of Annamalai, the god of Kadaiyur, the dance of Chidambaram and the lord of Tirupati are all inside her, so there is no need to travel.
structure_note: 1964 to 1966 the true and false guru; 1967 to 1970 the praise of Vaalai and her rank below Siva; 1971 to 1974 the colophon, guru, patron and benediction, which is where the Vaalai Kummi proper ends; 1975 to 1979 are a separate kummi with the refrain கும்மியடி, five stanzas on pilgrimage places found within.
source_issues: 1975 to 1979 carry unit ids of a different form (valaik-kummi:0701-111 to 0701-115), a heading சரஸ்வதி துதி, and the refrain கும்மியடி in place of வாலைப்பெண்ணே; they are a separate kummi appended after the benediction of 1974, and their second heading, பெண்டாட்டி யாவதும் பொய்யல்ல வேறு, is the first line of 1943 with a trailing word, apparently an editor's cross-reference taken as a title.
1976 line 4 காணம் is a slip for காணும்.
1978 line 2 வருத்தண்ட தாண்டவம் is not a known name of a dance; possibly ஊர்த்துவ தாண்டவம்.
1972 line 1 ஆறு படைப்புகள் வீடுகடை சூத்ர has no clear construction.
1964 line 1 and 1965 line 2 are metrically long for a kummi line and may have intruded words.

reading: If one says the fitting thing, what was lacking falls into place: is there such a one in the world, Avvai asked; he who says the fitting thing so that the lack fits is the guru, Vaalai girl.
nuance: உற்றது சொன்னால் அற்றது பொருந்தும் is a proverb credited to Avvai: the right word supplies what is missing. Konganar makes it a definition of the guru by the effect of his word rather than by lineage or learning, which sets up the two false gurus of 1965 and 1966.

reading: He who does not know the state in which fullness stands tells many lies and recites crores of mantras; he is not the causal guru; this one is an instrumental guru who grabs your goods.
nuance: காரணகுரு and காரியகுரு, the guru who is cause and the guru who is only means or occasion, are a traditional pair; Konganar's mark of the first is knowing பூரணம் நிற்கும் நிலை, the standing of fullness, and his mark of the second is the quantity of mantras and the taking of fees.

reading: Calling themselves all-knowing, proclaiming themselves full gnanis on this earth, they run about at their ease to feed their bellies, Vaalai girl.
Though the primal Vaalai is great, is her elder sister great, or Siva? Though the Vaalai of the nadi is great, it is not her lord: Siva is great.
nuance: The stanza ranks the goddess below Siva after a hundred stanzas in her praise, and its terms are unclear: அக்காள், the elder sister, may be a form of the goddess (Vaalai as the youngest of three), and நாதிவாலை may pair with ஆதிவாலை as a sound-play or name the goddess in the channel (நாடி). Line 4, அவள் நாயகன் அல்ல சிவம் பெரிது, may mean that it is not her consort but Siva as such who is great, or simply that her lord Siva is the greater.

reading: She gives long life; diabetes and every other disease will not come near; ghosts fly off and sorcery is undone in a moment, if one says the name of the chaste Vaalai girl.
nuance: நீரிழிவு, diabetes, is named first among diseases; பில்லி is sorcery by charm. The power is in saying the name, a devotional rather than yogic claim, and பத்தினி gives the goddess a wife's virtue.

reading: Even in sleep she sits enthroned; at every hour Vaalai stands before you; if an enemy comes she thrusts him aside, and Vaalai kicks away even Death when he has come.
nuance: காலனையும் உதைப்பாள் gives the goddess Siva's own act, the kick that felled Death for Markandeya at Kadaiyur, a shrine named in 1976.

reading: She who created as herself everything, from the many thousand crores of cosmic eggs and the fourteen worlds to the gods with form: Vaalai stands in it all like oil within sesame.
nuance: எள்ளுக்குள் எண்ணெய் போல, like oil in sesame, is the stock image of a pervasion that is hidden until pressed out; தானாய்ப் படைத்தவள் makes her both creator and material.

reading: She taught me to make this Vaalai Kummi in Tamil that the country praises; celebrate and praise the long feet of the loving, heroic Veerapperumal, my guru.
nuance: The colophon credits the composition to the goddess's instruction and names a human guru, வீரப் பெருமாள் குருசாமி, who is otherwise unknown; the song is thus signed twice.

reading: Knowing the kinds of the six creations, the house and its end, the sutra and the five letters, the high Valaventhiran, generous lord and king, declares them: celebrate that he may live.
nuance: A praise of a patron or chief, வல வேந்திரன் துரை வள்ளல் கொற்றவன், whose name is not otherwise known. Line 1, ஆறு படைப்புகள் வீடு கடை சூத்ர, is a list without clear syntax: six creations, house, end or shop, sutra. The stanza is a dedication, not teaching.

reading: Dance, all you women, the Tamil that loving Konganar spoke; sing, all you siddhas; celebrate praising Vaalai's feet.
nuance: The kummi is a women's circle dance, and the stanza addresses two audiences at once, the women who dance it and the siddhas who are to sing it, which is how Konganar frames the whole work.

reading: Long live the siddhas, long live Siva, long live the sages, the gods and the rishis; long live the devotees, long live the feet, long live the guru; long live Bharati, the Vaalai girl!
nuance: பாரதி, a name of Saraswati, is given to Vaalai, which may explain why the following stanzas carry the heading சரஸ்வதி துதி.

reading: People go, each in their turn, saying they must see the lamp of Annamalai; the lamp of Annamalai is inside you: see it whole, and dance the kummi.
nuance: The Karthigai lamp on the hill at Tiruvannamalai is the first of five pilgrimages relocated within the body; அகண்டம், the undivided, is how the inner lamp is to be seen.

reading: They say they must go to have sight of the lord of the lingam at Thirukkadaiyur; Thirukkadaiyur and the lord of the lingam, see them within and have sight of them: dance the kummi.
nuance: காணம் in line 4 should be காணும். Kadaiyur is where Siva kicked Death to save Markandeya, the act given to Vaalai in 1969.

reading: They say they must see the dance at Chidambaram and all must hurry there; the dance of Chidambaram is inside you: serve it there, and dance the kummi.
Lifting one foot, inside you he dances the tandava; if you see and serve that holy foot, why go to Chidambaram? Dance the kummi.
nuance: வருத்தண்ட தாண்டவம் is unclear; it may be a corruption of ஊர்த்துவ தாண்டவம், the dance with one foot raised, which the first line describes. The stanza's question, சிதம்பரம் போவானேன், is the sharpest of the five.

reading: Saying 'the northern hill', the people of the earth all go; but for Venkatesa who lives on the northern hill, he stands grown tall here: dance the kummi.
nuance: வடமலை is Tirupati, and the stanza treats the Vaishnava shrine exactly like the Saiva ones before it, which is characteristic of the kummi's indifference to sect. Line 4 lacks the 'inside you' of the other stanzas; வளர்ந்து நிற்குறான், he stands grown, presumably within, as the pattern requires.

title: பாம்பாட்டிச் சித்தர் பாடல்
theme: The opening of Pambatti Siddhar's song, a snake-charmer's kummi whose every stanza ends by telling the snake to dance (ஆடு பாம்பே). The first nine stanzas worship the Lord as the fullness in all lives, the void that cannot be pointed at, and the flood of bliss that becomes the worlds it made; the next ten praise the true guru who takes the disciple's body, goods and life, shows the Real like a fruit in the palm, corrects false gurus, and has powers such as leaving one body for another and circling the sky with a pill. Then the serpent itself is praised, ornament of Siva, Vishnu and Parvati, and the Siddhar begins to boast of his power over the eight nagas.
structure_note: Four sections by the printed headings: கடவுள் வணக்கம் (1980 to 1988), குரு வணக்கம் (1989 to 1998), பாம்பினது சிறப்பு (1999 to 2003) and the start of சித்தர் வல்லபங் கூறல் (2004, continued in chapter 103). The refrain shifts from ஆடு பாம்பே to the imperative ஆடாய் பாம்பே at 1989. The snake addressed is on a plain reading the charmer's cobra and on the traditional reading the mind or the coiled power in the body; the readings below give the stanza's own content, not the refrain.
source_issues: 1985 line 2 தொழுதழு தலற்றிற் தொந்தோந்தோ மெனவே: தலற்றிற் is unmetrical and probably a slip for அலற்றி; தொந்தோந்தோம் is left unexplained by the text.
1986 line 1 அந்தியாயும் may be a corruption of a word paired with அந்தமாயும் in the next line.
The refrain changes form from ஆடு பாம்பே (1980 to 1988) to ஆடாய் பாம்பே (1989 to 1998) and back to ஆடு பாம்பே (1999 to 2004); the section headings are the editor's.

reading: The opening stanza is almost all refrain: be clear, be clear, snake, having seen Siva's fine feet, and dance saying that we have seen the Lord's feet.
nuance: தெளிந்து (becoming clear) is repeated five times; the song's first instruction is clarity, and its first claim is the sight of the feet. Tradition takes the snake as the mind or the kundalini; the stanza itself only addresses a dancing snake.

reading: Thinking on the First One's feet even while toiling, and saying that the lasting state is for ever our own, eternal, and the great release, praise him again and again and dance.
nuance: நீடுபதம் (the lasting state) and பெரிய முத்தி are claimed as நமக்கு சொந்தம், our own property, a confidence that marks the whole song.

reading: Bow to the feet of the Giver who is everywhere as fullness like the light in gold, who abides with beauty like scent in a flower, and who dwells fitted within the many living beings, and dance.
nuance: The three similes make pervasion inseparable rather than spatial: light is not apart from the gold nor scent from the flower. பூரணம் is the Siddhars' name for God as the whole.

reading: Thinking again and again of the fragrant flower-feet of the Lord who fills every life as oil fills the sesame seed, so that love and devotion rise as they truly are, shrink, be contained, be clear and dance.
nuance: எள்ளில் எண்ணெய் is a stock Siddhar image for a presence that pervades without being visible (Sivavakkiyar uses it for the Vedanta). ஒடுங்கி அடங்கி, shrink and be contained, is addressed to the snake and reads naturally as a yogic withdrawal of the senses.

reading: Think without ceasing on our First God who gave the cosmos and the body, bow with love, praise him so that the eight directions resound, and seek him with a single mind, and dance.
nuance: அண்டபிண்டம் தந்த names the Lord as giver of both macrocosm and body in one word. ஏகமனம், a single mind, is the stanza's practice.

reading: Worship the pure Substance made of light, weep and cry out தொந்தோந்தோம், stand firm on the path that does not swerve from right, think and think and melt, and dance.
nuance: வஸ்து (the Substance, the Real) is the song's favoured name for God, used again in 1986 and 1993. தொந்தோந்தோ(ம்) is read here as a cry of joy or a drum sound, like the Naladiyar's டொண்; a reading that hears தொந்தத்தசி (that thou art) in it is possible but not secure.

reading: Praise the dense Substance that is formless and formed, that is the twilight and the end, the light and the Agama, the Lady and the guru and the living soul, and dance.
nuance: அருவாயும் உருவாயும் is the Saiva pair of formless and formed. அந்தி may be twilight (the junction, as the yogis' time) or a corruption of அந்தம் doubled with the next word. திரு here could be Lakshmi, Shakti or simply the holy; the stanza's point is that one Substance is all these.

reading: Knowing by subtle intellect the void and emptiness that cannot be pointed at or shown, so that fault is gone, and saying that we have reached and caught it, spread your hood in bliss and dance.
nuance: சுட்டிக்காட்டி ஒண்ணாத, what cannot be pointed at, is the stanza's definition of the void, and பாழ் and சூனியம் are set side by side as its names. சூட்சமதி, subtle intellect, is the faculty that knows it. The claim to have caught (எட்டிப் பிடித்தோம்) the uncatchable is the Siddhar's deliberate paradox.

reading: See the flood of bliss that gave birth to every life and every world, stood outside them and enjoyed its holy play, and afterwards stood as those very lives and worlds, and dance.
nuance: The stanza holds transcendence and immanence in sequence: first புறம்பாய் (outside), then ஆகியும் நின்ற (standing as them). திருவிளையாட்டு, holy play, is creation as the Lord's sport.

tamil: தானம் வாங்கி நின்ற வெங்கள் சற்கு ருவினைப்
reading: Praise our true guru who stood and received as gift the body, the goods and the life that were declared his, so that mind, speech and body all three are in accord, and dance.
nuance: உடல் பொருள் ஆவி, body, wealth and life, is the formula of total surrender to the guru; தத்தம் ஆக ... தானம் வாங்கி says the guru accepted them as a gift. மனம் வாக்கு காயம், the three instruments, must agree in the praise.

reading: Praise the feet of the true guru who talks sense to the false gurus who preach false religions and sends them off on the good path, and who declares which religion is true and makes one join it, and dance.
nuance: பொய்ம்மதம் and மெய்ம்மதம், false and true religion, frame the stanza; the true guru is defined by his effect on false gurus, correcting rather than destroying them.

reading: Dance having seen the feet of the full true guru who, having seen the true Thing that is beyond the Vedas, sets his mind on it and declares what the meaning of the Veda is, and teaches what the meaning of knowledge is.
nuance: The guru knows the Veda's meaning because he has seen what lies beyond it (வேதம் கடந்த மெய்ப்பொருள்); the ordering is deliberate, experience first and scripture explained from it.

reading: Having thrown off the thieving mind, find with love the true guru who is able to show the Thing that is as it is, truly, like a fruit in the palm of the hand, and smile and rejoice and dance.
nuance: உள்ளங்கையில் கனி போல, like a fruit in the palm, is the stanza's measure of the guru's teaching: direct and graspable. கள்ள மனம், the thieving or deceitful mind, is what must be set aside first.

reading: Bow constantly without doubt to the guru who is our life and who makes the First Substance known like a mirror in the palm, and raise your golden hood and dance.
nuance: The mirror in the palm pairs with the fruit in the palm of 1992: the guru does not describe the Real, he reflects it. எங்கள் உயிரான குரு makes the guru the disciple's very life. தமனியப் படம், the golden hood, is the one place the snake's body enters the praise.

reading: Worship the feet of the pure guru who saw the body's state perish, then took the state of firmness within and found the pure state that lives for all time, and dance.
nuance: கற்புநிலை is read as a state of steadfastness (கற்பு as firmness, not wifely chastity); a reading that hears கற்பம், the rejuvenating kalpa of the medical Siddhars, in it would make the guru one who outlives the body by medicine. எக்காலமும் வாழும் is the Siddhar claim of deathlessness.

reading: Who can tell the power of the guru whose practice is to leave one body and leap into another? Bow to the true guru who shows the way to win release more and more, and dance.
nuance: கூடுவிட்டுக் கூடுபாய்தல், leaving the cage for a cage, is the Tamil phrase for entering another body, one of the eight siddhis; the stanza joins that power to showing the way to release, so the siddhi is not set against liberation.

reading: Say that your refuge is the flower-feet of the able guru who, with a pill that contains the eight directions and the open space of the cosmos, goes round swiftly in a circle, and dance.
nuance: குளிகை is the pill of the alchemists and sorcerers, traditionally a mercury pill held in the mouth that lets the siddha fly or vanish; the stanza has the guru circle the sky with it. அடக்கிய may mean the pill holds the directions within it or that the guru has subdued them. Read as a claim of power, not a method.

reading: Praise as refuge the golden feet of the causal guru who lives without his vessel perishing, alongside the First Maker who is beyond the kalpa-ages, and dance with a mind full.
nuance: கடம் (the pot, the body) that does not perish continues 1994's claim that the guru's body outlasts time; காரணக்குரு, the causal guru, sets him beside the ஆதி கர்த்தா as cause rather than creature.

reading: Even if a flaw can come to the diamond, no defect will come to the strong body of our Veda-guru who has a vessel to be admired; praise his soft feet and dance.
nuance: The body harder than diamond is the Siddhar ideal of the perfected body (வல்லுடம்பு). வேதகுரு may mean the guru who knows the Veda or, hearing வேதை, the alchemist guru who has transmuted his body; the stanza does not decide.

reading: Naga snake who sits on the Lord's crown, good snake who keeps the poison-sac, hooded snake who makes your home in the underworld, sing and sing and play, and dance.
nuance: The section on the snake's glory begins with three of its homes: Siva's head, its own venom and the nether world (பாதலம்). The poison is called நல்ல, good, kept and not used.

reading: Snake that draws in its head as it enters the hole, coloured snake that coils its body in a circle, true snake that stands without fearing bonds, lift your head and play, and dance.
nuance: The three traits, withdrawing the head to enter the hole, coiling in a mandala and standing unafraid of fetters, are plain snake lore and also the traditional marks of the yogic breath or power entering the channel and coiling at the base; சத்தியப் பாம்பே (true snake) leans the stanza toward the coded sense.

reading: You became the earring of the faultless Siva, the umbrella of the praised Vishnu, and the bracelet of thick-haired Parvati; rejoice at heart without hiding, and dance.
nuance: Three gods, three ornaments: the snake is honoured by the whole pantheon, which gives the charmer's animal its dignity. Vishnu's umbrella is the hood of Adishesha.

reading: You took the great strength that holds up the earth, you became the coloured mat for Vishnu's bed, you gained a sight that makes the armies that see you tremble, and you took the eye for an ear; dance.
nuance: கண்ணே செவியாகக் கொண்டாய் records the belief that snakes hear through their eyes, hence their Sanskrit name chakshushravas; the stanza is natural history and myth together.

reading: You leapt and touched the moon and the sun, you became an ornament for Shankara, you were brought under control by mantra and you coiled in a circle; bend and bend and dance.
nuance: Touching the moon and sun is Rahu the eclipse-serpent on the plain reading; in the Siddhars' cipher sun and moon are the right and left breaths or the fire at the base and the nectar at the crown, so the line can also say the coiled power reaches both. மந்திரத்திற்கு அடங்கினாய் keeps the charmer's craft in view.

reading: We will take the eight nagas in our hands and make them dance, we will show Indra's world right here, we will bind and release the snake that no binding holds; spit out your fierce poison and dance.
nuance: The Siddhar's boast begins. The eight nagas (Ananta, Vasuki, Takshaka, Karkotaka, Padma, Mahapadma, Shankhapala, Kulika) are named in 2014 and 2015; the uncontrollable snake made to spit its poison is on the coded reading the mind or the kundalini emptied of its venom. The stanza presents a power, not a procedure.

title: பாம்பாட்டிச் சித்தர் பாடல்
theme: Pambatti's boast of the Siddhars' powers, then his first sermon on detachment. The boasts (2005 to 2013) are hyperbole in the first person plural: making Adishesha dance, turning a pillar to a straw, drinking the seven seas, bending the sky as a bow, turning three worlds to gold, creating like Brahma and living as the Lord's equal, with the sixty-four arts and the one beyond them. A short dialogue section (2014 to 2018), without the refrain, sets the eight nagas in a chakra of eight directions with letters, mantra and ash. The sermon (2019 to 2029) turns to the hearer: land, armies, jewels, mansions, gold, feasts, finery, kin and the beauty of women all stay behind when Yama comes, and only the one who has set his heart on the Lord does not perish.
structure_note: Three printed sections: சித்தர் வல்லபங் கூறல் continued (2005 to 2013), சித்தர் சம்வாதம் (2014 to 2018, each stanza ending சித்தனாரே, a Siddhar addressing Siddhars), பொருளாசை விலக்கல் (2019 to 2028) and the first stanza of பெண்ணாசை விலக்கல் (2029, continued in chapter 104). The boasts in 2007, 2009, 2012 are addressed to a king (மகாராஜன், தார்வேந்தன், மன்னன்), which suggests performance before a court; the sermon stanzas each name one class of possession and end with the same verdict.
source_issues: 2014 names பதுமன் twice (மகத்தான பதுமன் and செய்ய பதுமன்); the eight nagas need மகாபதுமன் for one of them, so one name is probably corrupt or abbreviated.
2017 lines 1 and 2 are near-identical (அட்டதிக்குஞ் சக்கரங்க ளமைத்து விட்டோம் / அவ்வவற்றிற் சக்கரங்க ளமைத்து விட்டோம்), possibly a copyist's doubling.
2014 to 2018 drop the ஆடு பாம்பே refrain for சித்தனாரே; the section is in a different voice (address to Siddhars) and may be a separate piece interpolated into the kummi.
2021 line 3 ஆணிப் பொன்முத் தாரமம் பொன் அந்தகடகம் is overlong and garbled; read as ஆணிப்பொன் முத்தாரம் அம்பொன் அந்தக் கடகம்.

reading: Even if it be Adishesha himself, we will make him dance with our hand within our command, and make him stand there joined to right, without falling from the state in which he stands; dance.
nuance: ஆக்கினை (ஆஞ்ஞை), command, is the key word: the Siddhar claims authority over the cosmic serpent that bears the earth. On the coded reading Adishesha is the kundalini held steady (நின்ற நிலை தவறாமல்) once raised.

reading: We will make a pillar appear as a small straw and a straw appear as a great pillar, we will make a man a woman and a woman a man; stand before them with a roar and dance.
nuance: தோன்றிடச் செய்வோம், make it appear, admits that these are shows of appearance; the stanza's own verb puts the power on the side of illusion rather than substance. Pillar and straw correspond to the siddhis of greatness and minuteness.

reading: We will pick up the eight mountains and throw them like balls, drink the seven seas and belch, and count the uncountable sand; stand before the great king and dance.
nuance: The eight mountains are the guardians of the eight directions and the seven seas the puranic oceans; the boast is of cosmic scale. மகாராஜன் முன்பு places the performance before a king.

reading: We will hide the whole earth with our hand, bend the sky itself as a bow, and show the void to our followers by telling of it; stand before the prince and dance.
nuance: சூனியம் சொல்லிக் காட்டுவோம் can mean teaching the followers the void of 1987 by speech, or showing them a conjuring (சூனியம் as sorcery in common Tamil); in a stanza of stage-feats both readings stand, and the ambiguity may be the poet's.

reading: We will plunge into blazing fire and come out, hold our breath though we sit in the three waters, and strike down the strong tiger that leaps at us; stand before the garlanded king and dance.
nuance: மூச்சு அடக்குவோம், holding the breath under water, is the one feat in the list that is also a practice: breath control is the Siddhars' method, and here it is displayed as a power.

reading: We will turn the three worlds that cannot be described into red gold, make the hot sun's rays cool, and make this great world not exist; see our power and dance.
nuance: Turning the worlds to gold extends the alchemist's transmutation to the cosmos; making the world not exist is read traditionally as the jnani's dissolving of the world in the void, as well as a feat of illusion.

reading: We will make creations other than those Brahma made, we will make Brahma himself stand beneath us, and we will live equal with the Lord; this is what we do, dance.
nuance: நாதனுடன் சமமாக வாழ்வோம், living as the Lord's equal, is the peak of the boasts, and it sits oddly with the song's worship of the Lord's feet (1980 to 1988); the Siddhar claim of becoming Siva and the charmer's bravado are hard to separate here.

reading: We have known all the sixty-four arts, and we have known the one art above them; we have a mind without the least attachment to anything else; king, we are the teacher, dance.
nuance: அதற்கு மேல் ஒரு கலை, the one art above the sixty-four, is not named; tradition takes it as the knowledge of the self or of the breath. மன்னனே யாசான் is read as the Siddhar telling the king that he, the Siddhar, is the master (ஆசான்), the inversion that closes the court boasts.

reading: We will order the small tiger, the elephant, the yali and the lion to do menial service for our small feet, and we will make the great mighty God play along with us; dance.
nuance: The boast ends not with mastery of God but with making him a playmate (எங்களுடனே விளையாடச் செய்குவோம்), answering 1988 where the Lord's creation was his own play.

reading: Set Vasuki on one side, king, and the great Padman on the other, join the shining Takshan in his direction, and take the red Padman, Siddhars.
nuance: The dialogue stanzas lay out the eight nagas in the directions as a snake-charmer's or sorcerer's diagram. Padman is named twice (பதுமன் and செய்ய பதுமன்), and one of them should be Mahapadman to complete the eight; the stanza does not say what the arrangement is for.

reading: Set Anantan on one side, join Gulikan beside him near the egg, and show the heavy Karkotakan so that he sees, and the fierce Sankhapalan, Siddhars.
nuance: With 2014 this completes the eight nagas. அண்டச் சேர்த்து, joined near, may hide அண்டம், the egg or cosmos, in which case the diagram is the cosmos itself; the syntax of காணக் காட்டும் (show so as to see) is loose.

reading: Scoring the eight directions as chakras, setting the letters in the places of the angles, recite the mantra with resolve and stand; do not let your mind waver, Siddhars.
nuance: This is the yantra procedure of the Tirumanthiram's chakra tantra in miniature: draw, place letters at the corners, recite. சித்தம் தடுமாறாதீர், do not waver, is the only instruction about the practitioner's inner state in the whole section.

reading: We have set up chakras in the eight directions, we have set up chakras in each of them, and we have placed them where the eight nagas are; tell us what to do now, Siddhars.
nuance: The second speaker reports the work done and asks for the next step, so the section is a real dialogue between a teacher and practitioners. The doubled line (chakras in each) suggests chakras within chakras, or is a copyist's repetition.

reading: Plant Adishesha himself in the middle, scatter mantra-charged ash to the four directions, and take the hooded ones in your hands and dance so that they spit out their fierce poison, Siddhars.
nuance: The rite closes with the serpent at the centre, consecrated ash (மந்திரித்த நீறு) and the handling of cobras until they discharge venom, which is 2004's boast performed. On the traditional reading the centre is the suzhumunai and the poison the mind's passions; the stanza's own words are a charmer's.

reading: Will country and town, house and cattle and all your fine goods seek you out and come when the arbiter arrives? Once the cage is gone, what profit do you get from them? Fix your aim on the Dancer's feet and dance.
nuance: நடுவன், the impartial one, is Yama, and கூடு (the cage) is the body. The sermon's first stanza sets its pattern: a list of possessions, the question whether they come along at death, and the turn to the feet of the Dancer (கூத்தன்).

reading: Elephants, armies, chariots and horses, every one of them: understand that they will be no help when Yama comes; dance so that sense comes to the dogs who have not the least knowledge.
nuance: The hearers are நாய்கள், dogs without knowledge; the abuse is part of the Siddhars' sermon style, and the snake's dance is meant to teach them.

reading: Ruby, great gem crowns and armlets, pendants hanging on the chest and other jewels, pure gold, pearl strings, gold anklets and bracelets: stand knowing them as goods that perish, and dance.
nuance: A catalogue stanza; the verdict is only the last line, அழிவான பொருள். The jewels are a king's, continuing the court setting of 2007 to 2012.

reading: Upper storeys, halls and mansions, painted pavilions, palaces girt with walls and all such things will not come along; those who know this truth do not take pride in them but turn from them in distaste; dance.
nuance: வெறுப்பார், they will feel distaste, is stronger than detachment: the knower of the கொள்கை (the principle that nothing accompanies) comes to dislike what others prize.

reading: Those who have kept heaps of red gold like mountains, will they sweep them up and go when Death comes? Those who without wavering set their heart on the Father will not perish; be sure of it and dance.
nuance: The stanza pairs its two halves: the hoarders cannot carry gold away, the devotees do not perish (அழியார்). The claim is not that devotees avoid death but that something in them does not end.

reading: Will cotton beds, flower beds and mats be of any use in that bare burning ground? Know clearly that the scent of turmeric will go and the stench of burning will come, and dance.
nuance: The contrast is of smells: மஞ்சள் மணம், the turmeric of the bath and the bed, against சுடு நாறும் மணம், the smell of the pyre. The body is seen from its end.

reading: The mouth that first ate the three fruits, sugar, sweetmeats and ripe-tasting dainties: once the great life has gone it swallows earth; we have seen this to be true, so dance.
nuance: மண்ணை விழுங்க, swallowing earth, is the buried or burnt mouth; the stanza reverses the eating. மெய்யாகக் கண்டோம், we saw it truly, is the Siddhar's appeal to his own observation rather than scripture.

reading: Coloured silks and perfumes and the well-made adornment, the fine umbrella, the round fan and the other insignia will certainly not be able to come along at the time of going to Yama's city; dance.
nuance: கவிகை (umbrella), ஆலவட்டம் (circular fan) and சின்னம் (insignia) are royal emblems; the sermon is still addressed to the king of the boasts.

reading: Children, wife, kin, sons-in-law and the rest do not die together with one when one dies; so leap and leap and praise the Maker who gave this whole fitting world, and dance.
nuance: The kin fail not by faithlessness but by the plain fact that they do not die with you (கூட மாள்வதில்லை). The only relation that holds is to the one who gave the world.

reading: Like a deer that takes a mirage for water and goes after it, fools see the life of this earth and rejoice; those who have seen the higher state do not talk empty bluster, but seek the feet of the True One; dance.
nuance: The mirage-deer (கானல்மான்) closes the section on possessions by naming the error: not that wealth is bad but that it is not what it seems. மேனிலை கண்டார், those who have seen the higher state, are set against the வீம்பு (vaunting) of the world, which sits uneasily with the Siddhar's own boasts in 2005 to 2013.

reading: Men who desire women's beauty, which is like turmeric that has seen the sun, and fall upon it and join it, will run off when the body goes, like the parrot that guarded the silk-cotton tree and flew away on seeing its pod; dance.
nuance: Two similes: turmeric paste that fades in sunlight for beauty, and the proverb of the parrot that waited on the silk-cotton fruit, found it empty cotton and fled, for the lover's disappointment. The section on desire for women opens with the lover's own flight, not yet with the body's filth.

title: பாம்பாட்டிச் சித்தர் பாடல்
theme: Pambatti's sermon continues through three sections. Against desire for women (2030 to 2038) he lists the lover's similes, breasts as Meru, eyes as swords, hair as cloud, saliva as nectar, bird-names and sweet-names, and sets against each the body's filth, saying we have scolded, renounced and thrown it off. On the body's nature (2039 to 2048) he reads it as a potter's vessel of filth and blood not worth a dry stick, a ten-month kiln not worth half a coin, a pot that breaks for dogs and vultures, a water bubble, a stinking fish that washing cannot clean, a nine-holed bellows, a wooden puppet on the string of life, and a ship of ten nadis, ten airs and seven dhatus. Against inner attachment (2049 to 2054) he gives the images of the lotus leaf, the tamarind in its shell, oil and water, and the insect leaving the mud, and tells the hearer to open the eye of knowledge and see the open space and the form of consciousness.
structure_note: Three printed sections: பெண்ணாசை விலக்கல் (2030 to 2038), சரீரத்தின் குணம் (2039 to 2048) and அகப்பற்று நீக்கல் (2049 to 2054, continued in chapter 105). The stanzas against women fall into two kinds: 2031 to 2034 and 2038 answer a flattering simile with the body's reality; 2035 to 2037 are bare lists of endearments followed by the refusal to utter them. The body stanzas each carry one image. The refrain is ஆடாய் பாம்பே throughout.
source_issues: 2035 line 4 ஓதாமற் கடிந்துவிட் றாடாய் is defective; a syllable (டோ or டே) is missing before the refrain (compare 2036 கடிந்தோமென் றாடாய்).
2045 line 4 வத்துத்திரு வடிதொழு தாடாய் is garbled; வத்து is read as வஸ்து (the Real) but may be a corruption of another word.
2030 line 2 சித்தப்பால் விழுங்கியே is obscure and may be corrupt.
2052 line 1 திரிபிள்ளைப்பூச்சி is an unidentified insect name; the simile is read from the context of leaving the mud.

reading: The peacock-woman with globed breasts and bee-like eyes we spat on and scolded, swallowing her with the mind as if she were milk; and we killed and ate the Death-kite that rides the thick-bodied buffalo; dance.
nuance: சித்தப்பால் விழுங்கி is obscure; it may say the woman was consumed by the mind (as a figure of seeing through her), or that the Siddhar drank the milk of the mind, or read சித்தப் பால், the side of the mind. The buffalo-rider is Yama, and the kite (பருந்து) his bird; the stanza boasts of conquering both desire and death, in the Siddhar's first person plural.

reading: They call a skin that will shrivel away a round breast and liken it to great Meru; be sure that those who have fallen into the stinking well of the womb will be ruined, and dance.
nuance: The stanza sets the poets' simile (மகமேரு) against the physician's fact (வற்றும் தோல், skin that will shrivel). யோனிக் கேணி, the well of the womb, is the Siddhars' usual image for the pit of desire and birth.

reading: Those without strength of mind describe an eye that oozes filth as the equal of a sharp sword; the owl-men who talk of its fine quality become food for the belly of the pit; dance.
nuance: குருநலம் is read as குரு (the eye's beauty or lustre) rather than the guru; கும்பி, the pit, is a hell in Siddhar and Saiva usage, so the owl-men (கூகை, blind by day) feed hell. The reading of கும்பிக்கே இரை as hell's food rather than the belly's is traditional and not certain.

reading: They call tangled stinking hair a rich cloud and say the breasts are like golden cups; melting and melting, they think of the woman in their heart and do not think of the Stainless One; dance.
nuance: நெக்கு நெக்கு உருகி, melting and melting, is the devotee's vocabulary of bhakti, here given to the lover; the stanza's charge is a misdirected melting, for the woman instead of the நிமலன்.

reading: The owl-men without sense call reeking spittle good nectar and a nose full of mucus a fine bud; they do not know the state of the King; dance.
nuance: எச்சில், saliva, is ritually polluting in Tamil usage, and the stanza turns the lover's kiss into a breach of purity. கோனிலை, the King's state, is the state of the Lord that the lovers miss.

reading: Peacock, cuckoo, ruby, deer, honey, heavenly nectar, the one who matches the graceful swan and peacock: we have stopped saying these and driven them off; dance.
nuance: The first of three stanzas that are only lists of endearments; the content is the refusal to speak them (ஓதாமற் கடிந்து). The Siddhar's renunciation is of a vocabulary.

reading: Lightning-creeper, bright lamp, slender one, vine, Menaka, cane-sugar lump, sugar-candy: we have scolded these away without uttering them; dance.
nuance: Menaka is the celestial courtesan who seduced Vishvamitra; the list moves from light to sweetness and ends with the Siddhar's refusal, as in 2035.

reading: Lady, doll, gold, flower-Lakshmi, my treasure, koel-fruit, garlanded one, cuckoo: we have renounced them without saying them; dance.
nuance: என்றன் பொக்கிஷம், my treasure, is the one word of possession in the three lists; the stanza's துறந்தோம் (we renounced) treats the words themselves as the possession given up.

reading: Knowing it for ourselves as turmeric smeared on a pot of filth, as a coloured skin over a swarming nest of worms, as stinking mud in a pit of water, we threw it away; dance.
nuance: The three images answer the three kinds of flattery: the painted surface, the skin, the wet hollow. தான் அறிந்து, knowing it oneself, is the ground of the renunciation; the Siddhar does not cite a text.

reading: Taking clay from a pit of filth and mixing the lump in a stream of blood, the vessel the clever potter makes is not worth even a dry stick; dance.
nuance: The potter is the Lord or the father, the clay and blood the seed and the womb's blood; வறகோட்டுக்கும் ஆகாது, not worth a dry twig, is the body's price. The image is the Siddhars' and Tirumular's pot, with the making added.

reading: Two people gathered the clay and one shaped it; the kiln set for ten months, however precious it is, that kiln is not worth half a coin; dance.
nuance: The riddle continues 2039: the two are the parents, the one who shapes is the Lord or the embryo's own karma, the ten-month kiln the womb. சூளை (kiln) is also read as the body baked in it; either way the valuation is the point.

reading: The snake that bit as if in jest: it swelled greatly for many to see, and when a woman physician looked at it, it came away together with the bag; dance.
nuance: The stanza is a riddle and the sense turns on the cipher. One reading: desire bit like a joke, the body swelled in pregnancy or pride before all, and when the woman (death, or Shakti, or the vaalai) looked, life left with the bag of the body. Another: a plain anecdote of a snakebite misdiagnosed, ending in death. பரியாரம் is read as பரிகாரி, physician. The reading above keeps the stanza's images and does not fix the cipher.

reading: If the pot that holds the foul stench of pus and excrement, thick blood and fat should break, dog and jackal, the great ghoul and the vulture will eat it saying it is theirs; dance.
nuance: நமதென்றே தின்னும், eat it as their own, is the stanza's edge: the body that was 'mine' becomes theirs. The list of eaters is the burning-ground company of the Naladiyar and Pattinathar.

reading: Like a bubble that rises on water and loses its standing, the body will not stay but will surely depart; so seize and keep following the one who created the many lives on earth, and dance.
nuance: நிச்சயம் என்றே, as a certainty, is the stanza's weight; the bubble is the common image, and the instruction is to hold the Creator instead of the body.

reading: If you wash a stinking fish many times in good water every day, will its stench go? So the body you speak of, by bathing in many rivers, will not lose the impurity it holds; dance.
nuance: The stanza is an argument against holy bathing: the fish's stench is in the fish, and the body's மலம் is in the body. மலம் is both the bodily filth of the section and the Saiva impurity that binds the soul, and the stanza lets the two senses meet.

reading: The fruiting tree takes many blows from stones; the body that carries the fruit of its deeds takes its rebukes; say that those who have gained a fitting austerity are the ones who live, and worship the holy feet, and dance.
nuance: The tree stoned for its fruit and the body struck for its karma make a proverb-like pair; கண்டனை is read as rebuke or chastisement, and வத்து (for வஸ்து, the Real) in the last line is a guess at a garbled word. The stanza's claim is that tapas, not the body, is what lives.

reading: A torn bellows with nine mouths that cannot be described: because a great wind entered it, speech arose; for those who do not know the Lord's state, this bellows is food for the burning earth; dance.
nuance: நவவாயில், nine gates, is the standard count of the body's openings; துருத்தி, the smith's bellows, is the Siddhars' image for a body that lives only by the wind in it. Speech itself (பேச்சு) is reduced to the wind's effect.

reading: Making a figure of earth like a wooden puppet and fitting to it the string called the fat living soul, the moment the one who moved it from behind the screen has finished, the body falls; know this clearly and dance.
nuance: The puppet has three parts: the earthen figure, the string that is the jivan, and the hidden mover behind the curtain (திரைக்குள் இருந்து அசைப்போன்). The body falls not when the string breaks but when the mover stops, which places the cause of death in the Lord's will.

reading: The wooden ship joined of ten nadis, ten airs and seven dhatus will lurch and fall; resolve to sail the fitting ship on the one flood for ever, and dance.
nuance: The body is counted as the ten channels, ten vital airs and seven bodily constituents of the medical texts, and called a ship that will capsize. இசைவான கப்பல், the agreeable ship, that sails on the ஏக வெள்ளம் (one flood) is not identified; tradition takes it as the breath or the soul carried on the flood of grace or of the Supreme.

reading: As water does not stay on the lotus leaf, push away desire for the world everywhere, and worship and worship and worship the feet of the Light that shines as a pure gem; dance.
nuance: The lotus leaf is the Gita's and Sivavakkiyar's image for living in the world untouched by it; the stanza pairs it with a triple தொழுது, so detachment and worship are the same act.

reading: Cutting the bonds of everything that has been forbidden, deceit, killing, lust and the rest, open the eye of knowledge, examine and see the clear open space and the form of consciousness, and with a clarified mind dance.
nuance: The stanza puts ethics first (கள்ளம் கொலை காமம், the forbidden deeds) and vision second: ஞானக் கண், the eye of knowledge, sees the வெட்டவெளி, the open space, and the சிற்சொரூபம், the form of pure consciousness. The two names for what is seen, space and consciousness, are given as one.

reading: Like the tamarind fruit with its shell, stay among kin without ties to them; stand, mind, in the supreme stainless one, and dance knowing that your companion there is the bare void.
nuance: The ripe tamarind lies loose inside its shell: present but unattached. நின் துணைதான் வெறும் பாழ், your only companion is the empty void, can be read as consolation (the void is the companion) or as warning (you will have no companion but emptiness); the Siddhar sense of பாழ் as the Real favours the first.

reading: Like the insect that moves in the mud and then leaves the mud, after seeing the doings of those who live in step with the country, one must take and walk the path that reaches the supreme space that is spoken of; dance.
nuance: திரிபிள்ளைப்பூச்சி is read as the mud-wasp or larva that lives in mud and flies free of it; the identification is not sure. தேசத்தோடு ஒத்து வாழ்வார், those who live conformed to the land, are the worldly, and the stanza asks the hearer to watch them and then leave as the insect leaves the mud.

reading: As oil and water have no bond between them, so one must always be on this earth; see the light that is the eye of the eye, cut your bonds and live, and dance.
nuance: கண்ணுக்குக் கண்ணான ஒளி, the light that is eye to the eye, is the Upanishadic figure of the awareness behind seeing; the oil-and-water simile makes detachment a difference of nature, not of effort.

reading: As vomited rice and curry and roots are a clean sight to the eyes, scold the world you are caught in with a 'faugh', and be clear so as to see the fine feet, and dance.
nuance: The simile is strained: கக்கிவிட்ட சோறு, vomited food, a clean sight, is read ironically (what was eaten returns as what no one wants) or as the way the vomiter sees it, with disgust and finality; the stanza wants the world seen with the same finished disgust (சீயென்று ஒறுத்து).

title: பாம்பாட்டிச் சித்தர் பாடல்
theme: Pambatti's kummi to the snake continues the section on removing inner attachment (அகப்பற்று நீக்கல்): the passions are named one by one as beasts and tools to be mastered (anger the rutting elephant, the mind the horse, desire the sandal, Death the enemy cut down with the kalpa-sword), and against pilgrimage, temple-building, puja, the Vedas and caste the poet sets love, self-knowledge, the guru's foot, the breath at the whirl-point and the light that pervades all like taste in milk.
structure_note: The chapter opens with first-person boasts of conquest over the passions in allegory (2055 to 2061), turns to snake-cipher stanzas on the body and breath (2062 to 2066), then runs a series of attacks on outward religion each paired with an inner alternative (2067 to 2079): pilgrimage, lovelessness, idols and fools, false teachers, temples, scripture, caste and puja. Every stanza ends in the refrain ஆடாய் பாம்பே (dance, snake); the readings give what each stanza adds.
source_issues: 2057: சினமென்னுஞ் சீனிமேற் (the saddle called anger) reads oddly and may be corrupt.
2058: காசையெனுந் துர்குணம் has no clear sense; காசை may be a corrupt word.
2065: வருடிக்கு in line 2 is obscure and probably corrupt.
2075: பற்றுப்பொன் பற்றவைத்த பான்மை in line 2 does not parse cleanly and looks damaged.

reading: We killed the rut of the mad elephant called anger with the goad of sharp reasoning, and joined in kinship with the red Thing, the form of pure awareness that is called the lamp.
